# The Vigil's End

_Dame Lyra M-101, Knight of Ocipheus, pursues thieves who stole her House's founding Relic across the entire Cauld — around the Sinter quarantine Wall, through Vierna and Atrament, by pirate airship to Pallor's northern coast — and comes home to find a corrupt Liturgy Canon waiting to confiscate it. Along the way she assembles a found party: a Myrmidon conscript from Sphere 31 who is slowly assembling the words to say what the Liturgy has been doing to his world; an Atrament battle-rig pilot who cannot be removed from her machine; and a Lacerta pirate with his own code. The book's core question: what are you loyal to when you find out what the thing you loved actually is?_

[Beat 1]
THE THEFT AT OCIPHEUS

The membrane parted for her the way it always did - not like a door, like a wound reopening. The cold lasted less than a breath, and then she was standing in the inner archive, three metres from where she'd been, and the room's warmth took a moment to find her.

The younger one came through four seconds later. He arrived sideways - not badly wrong, but wrong enough that he caught the shelving unit with his shoulder, and a codex slid two inches before he steadied it with one hand. He looked at her. She looked at the codex, then at him. He straightened.

She had forty-one folds on her record by this time last year. She'd stopped counting at thirty. The residual feeling was the same every time: as if the membrane leaves something in you each crossing, too small to measure, compound interest on a ledger nobody had found yet.

The inner archive smelled of seven hundred years of Catalyst seepage and oiled iron and old stone that had never been properly dry. The Liturgy had built Ocipheus Station at the membrane's edge - the Oculus Memoriae required proximity to what it remembered through - and the closeness made the room feel slightly wrong at the periphery, the way rooms feel wrong when you've had too little sleep, or when something very old has been watching from the corner for seven centuries.

The case was on the display table. Leather and iron, purpose-built, unremarkable. If you didn't know what was inside it, you'd look past it.

She crossed the room in four steps and put her hands on the case.

The Keeper opened its eyes.

---

She had read the founding deposition before the mission. The Liturgy's first Scriveners had documented the Keeper's construction with the thoroughness of people who knew they were building something they could not undo. Six arms, each articulated at three points. Iron and canonical stone - the grey-green stone quarried from the Ocipheus headland and carved with the founding compact's seals. Not smooth. Every surface carved. Every surface had always been carved. The founding Canon had spent three years on the iconography before a single strut was assembled, and the result was something that looked like it had been made to worship what it guarded rather than simply stop you from taking it.

Seven hundred and forty-one years in this room. Facing the Oculus. Doing nothing.

Its first movement was its head - the slow rotation of a thing that has been still so long that motion itself is a commitment. Then the first pair of arms, unfolding from a position they had held since Year 397, the canonical stone at the joints cracking with seven centuries of compressed stillness.

"Fold," she said.

The younger one folded - vanished and reappeared at the far side of the chamber, the case between him and the Keeper now. She kept her hands on the case. She had three folds left in the preparation. She needed to get out with the case before she used them.

The Keeper came across the chamber with the slowness of a tide.

The signal came from the side passage - one short, two long. On schedule. The outer guards were handled. The others were at the main door, holding the corridor.

The Keeper's second arm swept the display table as it came. The table hit the far wall with enough force to open the stone. She was not at the table - she'd moved left, the case against her chest, between the shelving units. The Keeper tracked her. It did not hurry. Inside this room, it did not need to hurry.

The younger one was trying to hold its attention. To his credit, he was doing it effectively - fold to its left, sword drawn (optimistic; she had never seen a blade do anything useful to canonical stone), fold again when it turned. Each fold cost him. She could see it in the way he landed.

One more, she thought, watching him. You have one more in the preparation.

The Keeper turned from him because he was not the problem. She was the problem. She had the case.

She heard the door open. Someone coming in from the door - she had told him to stay in the corridor, she had been precise about this - and then the Keeper's rightmost arm, the lowest one, swung in a flat arc that she had read about in the deposition and had, until now, only understood intellectually.

It was fast. Not the rest of the Keeper. Just that arm.

Fifteen years of Pallor training. Two infusions. Good instincts. He had come through the door because she was in trouble and there was a door. He had the instincts for the situation. He did not have the clearance.

The arc took four seconds and cost everything he had.

She did not look away. Looking away would have been kinder to herself and wrong about him. He had come through the door. She owed him the honest accounting.

Then she folded.

---

She came out in the outer corridor, the case in both arms, the fixer already moving toward her from the gate end. The younger one emerged a moment later - wrong angle, but controlled, and he stayed on his feet. She counted his breathing.

"The third?" she said.

"Staying," the fixer said.

The answer she'd expected and not hoped for.

The Heloth couriers were at the stableyard. The fixer had the leads already. They loaded the case into the carry-pack, sealed it, confirmed the straps. Her hands were steady. She had been training them to be steady since she was twenty-three.

The case was warm against the carry-pack's lining. Warmer than leather and iron had any reason to be. She noted it and did not discuss it. The Relic had been in that room for seven hundred and forty-one years, watching whatever it watched through the membrane boundary. It had been watching without rest, without interruption, since Year 397.

She mounted the Heloth without looking back.

"Move," she said.

[Beat 2]
THREE BODIES AND AN EMPTY CASE

The note was still on the scribing table.

Back in three days. Don't eat the station bread.

Lyra had been back in two. The Sinter-line emergence had resolved cleanly — three kin-variants and a harrower juvenile, standard extraction, she'd filed the report at the transit post and ridden the Heloth hard through the night. Whatever instinct had pulled her back early, she had learned not to argue with it.

Orim was in the corner of the inner archive. He had been there since the fourth hour — his pre-dawn membrane observation, the same schedule he had kept for the eleven years he'd worked the Ocipheus installation. He was sitting against the wall with his Rod across his knees, looking at the space where the display table had been.

"When," she said.

"Before the fourth hour. My scry read the aftermath." He didn't look up. "Three bodies. I have identified the two guards."

She looked at the third body. Someone had placed the arm at a less wrong angle, which meant Orim had done it. She looked at the display table's absence — the impact point in the far wall, stone cracked outward, the shaped impression of iron and mass. She looked at the Keeper in the far corner, still and forward-facing, eyes closed. As it had been since Year 397.

"They used folds," she said.

"Yes. The membrane trace is consistent. Two practitioners, possibly three." He paused. "The younger one's exit angles were suboptimal."

---

She heard Vega before she saw her. The sound of someone trying to be quiet in an old stone corridor and not quite managing it — a small scrape, a caught breath. She turned.

Her sister was standing in the doorway in the clothes she'd slept in, holding a candle that was losing to the dawn light coming through the passage window behind her. She was looking at the third body.

"Lyra," Vega said.

"Yes."

"Is it—" She stopped. She was twenty-six years old. She had been copying canonical authorizations for three years and she had never been in a room with a dead person before. "Whatever they were doing — is it finished?"

"They took the Oculus." There was no other way to say it. "The case is gone."

Vega was quiet for a moment. She looked at the Keeper in the corner, motionless. Then at the impact in the wall. Then at her sister.

"You've been awake for two days," she said.

"Don't."

"You have a cut on your face that you haven't addressed. From the Sinter line."

"Vega."

"I'm not saying anything about the rest of it." She said it the way she said everything — with the particular care of a woman who has been writing other people's words for three years and is now choosing her own. "I'm saying you have a cut on your face."

Lyra touched her cheek. Found it. Yes.

"There's a kit in my pack," she said.

"I know where your kit is," Vega said, and went to get it.

---

They sat in the corridor outside the archive while the station came to life around them, and Vega cleaned the cut with the precision of someone who had done this before — not because she'd trained for it but because she was Lyra's sister and had been addressing things on Lyra's face since she was old enough to reach. The candle was unnecessary now. The morning was handling it.

"Do you know who took it?" Vega asked.

"Not yet."

"But you have a direction."

She did. The membrane trace, the fold angles, the exit vector from the archive. Orim was already refining the Scrying. The direction was Pallor. It had the weight of confirmed knowledge before she had confirmed knowledge of it.

"Yes," she said.

Vega tied off the bandage. Did not move back. She was looking at Lyra in the particular way she'd been looking at her since she was old enough to assess anything — three years younger, shorter, with their mother's coloring where Lyra had their father's, and the same habit of waiting for the full sentence before responding.

"Three days," Vega said.

"The note was optimistic."

"The note was wrong." Just the fact, without weight. Then: "Come back with it."

"That's the assignment."

"I didn't say come back for the Liturgy." She picked up the candle and stood. "Come back with it. Then come back here. The Liturgy can file the appropriate recovery instruments."

Lyra looked at her.

Vega was already walking back toward the archive, toward her scribing table and the certification instruments she'd been hired to finish. At the door she paused.

"The bread is fine," she said. "I don't know where you get these ideas."

---

The canonical property recovery mandate arrived at the sixth hour — counter-signed by the Canon Immaculate himself, which meant the authorization chain had been moving since before dawn, which meant the Liturgy had known before she woke up, which meant someone had been watching for exactly this.

She read it once. T-044, Templar, Ocipheus Station. Authorized pursuit, full inter-House transit authority across the Compact. Recover the Oculus Memoriae. Return it to Liturgy custody.

It did not name who had taken it.

She folded the mandate, put it in her kit, and went to find Orim.

"The Scrying?" she said.

He was already standing. His coat was on. The Rod was in his hand.

"Pallor exit vectors," he said. "Fast Heloth. Four riders out. Three riders back." A pause at the door. "The moor-hounds will lose the thermal trace in two days if we don't move."

She had her kit and her plate and her blade. She had the mandate. She had two days.

"Then we move," she said.

[Beat 3]
THE WALL FROM OUTSIDE — REFUSED

The Sinter Wall was not what she had expected the first time she'd seen it, twelve years back. She'd expected something martial — a fortification that announced its defensive purpose through stone and intent. What she'd found was something more geological than that. Eleven hundred years of building and rebuilding by coalition forces with different materials, different philosophies, the particular fatalism of people fortifying a border that cannot be held, only maintained. The Wall remembered every House that had built it. The stone changed texture every hundred meters.

This morning it looked like something that was deciding whether to stay standing.

The Heloth supply construct on the repair scaffolding was a freight variant — three meters at the shoulder, steam-chemical engine running at low operational heat, the exhaust port venting white puffs into the cold alpine air. It was hauling dressed limestone in the carry-cradle at its chest, each block the size of a large chest, moving in the alternating rhythm that the research literature described as "locomotion optimized for load stability in irregular terrain." The literature was correct. The reality of watching it was something the literature did not capture, which was the wrongness of something that large moving without effort.

Below the construct, on the scaffolding, eight people were cutting stone. Not soldiers — they had no House insignia, no standard gear, no equipment she could place in any House's catalog. Their work was competent in the specific way that comes from training rather than improvisation. She watched them for a moment longer than she needed to and then kept riding.

The soldiers at the checkpoint were three Houses — Vierna, Ocipheus, Atrament — on six-month rotation, none of them looking glad about it. Wall duty produced its own solidarity, she had observed before: distinct from House loyalty, grown from the shared experience of being rained on from the same direction long enough that the rain became a commonality.

Four of the Atrament soldiers were standing apart from the checkpoint structure in a cluster, not talking — listening. The Gate commander stood before them.

She was a woman of approximately forty, three infusions, the compact physical authority of someone who had been making decisions under pressure long enough that uncertainty had stopped being a primary state. She was delivering a briefing. She had not looked up when Lyra arrived.

"What you're looking at," the commander said, without raising her voice, "is a mountain basin eighty kilometers across, sealed on all sides by the alpine range. The floor of that basin is flat. Unnaturally flat." She let that sit for a moment. "Something struck it approximately a thousand years ago — a bolide, falling from above the sky. It struck Sinter and it flattened everything that was there. Then it seeded the basin with what it brought from wherever it came from."

None of the four soldiers moved.

"Nothing that has gone into the basin since has come back out. What has come out are the things that grew in what the bolide left behind. A thousand years of growing. They've mated with the wildlife that was enclosed in the basin at impact, and with whatever has wandered in since. What crawls out of the Sinter approaches is the offspring of that. It is alien to this world. It has been here long enough to look like it belongs. Some of it looks exactly like you."

She looked at the four of them.

"If something comes out of the approaches, you kill it. You do not ask what it is. You do not respond to anything it says or does. If it is weeping, you kill it. If it looks like a child, you kill it. If it looks like Wylla —" she held the pause exactly as long as it needed to be "— if it is walking toward you bare to the waist with its arms open, with everything about it designed to make you want to let it close — you kill it before it reaches twenty meters. Then you burn what you killed. Then you burn the ground where it fell."

She waited.

"Wylla walked out of the approaches in Year 1104. Fourteen soldiers did not maintain the protocol. None of them lasted the winter. It took a full company and fire to put her down. The soldiers who survived called her Mother Unto All Men. She never spoke. She only walked toward them with her arms open."

Silence. The four soldiers. The tone, low in the chest — Lyra could feel it from here.

"Any questions."

It was not phrased as a question.

No one had questions.

"Good." The commander turned and registered Lyra for the first time. She took the sealed authority. She looked at it for an interval that was longer than it needed to be.

Then she produced a second document.

"Field authority suspension," she said. "Filed three days ago. Canon Immaculate, Ocipheus Station." She held it out.

Lyra took it and read it and held it and stood there in the alpine cold with the document in her hand and the Sinter Wall in front of her and the zone beginning somewhere behind the stone that she could feel in the low center of her chest.

The suspension covered her field authority — the operational authority required to invoke the Meridian Compact. Without it, the Keeper's sealed letter was correctly executed and legally meaningless. It was a correct document. It had been correctly filed. The Canon Immaculate had the authority to suspend a Knight's operational standing pending review. This was in the codebook. She had read this section of the codebook. She had not read it in the context of considering whether it might apply to her.

"The review it cites," she said.

"Canonical property certification dispute." The Gate commander's voice was flat and precise — the voice of a professional delivering bad news without inflection because inflection complicates things. "Your Relic. The Keeper's authority doesn't override a field suspension in a certification dispute. I've already sent the confirmation inquiry. My legal advisor on Wall compact matters confirms it. I'm sorry."

"When was the inquiry sent?"

"Yesterday."

Yesterday. The suspension had been filed three days ago. The thieves had four days on her. Someone had filed the suspension before the theft's pursuit had begun — filed it the same day as the theft, possibly, or close enough that the distinction did not matter. She calculated. The suspension had been filed. The emergency that had drawn her to the Wall's eastern sector and kept her three days from the archive had been manufactured. Both operations — the one that removed her from the archive and the one that prevented her from crossing the Wall — had been executed by the same person.

She handed the suspension back.

"I need to see the Gyldir Shore Accord authorization for the western bypass roads," she said. "Specifically the Lacerta coastal passage and the route to Vierna's river system through the western border entry points."

The commander looked at her. "You're going around."

"Through the western approaches. Do you have the current bypass road status?"

The commander's expression shifted very slightly — not sympathy exactly. Something adjacent. She went to the checkpoint's document cabinet and returned with a route notation sheet. "The Lacerta coastal approach is open. The Vierna western entry — Bressant is two days by Heloth from the junction, if the passes are clear." She looked at the route. "You'll lose four days on the approaches versus direct crossing."

Four days added to the four days already lost was an interval she could calculate without assistance. She did not calculate it aloud. "Thank you," she said.

Ardea had arrived beside her during the exchange and had said nothing, which was Ardea's contribution to situations where speaking would only confirm what was already obvious. She took the route sheet. She looked at the bypass road. She looked at the Wall.

The suspension had been filed three days ago. The inquiry had been sent yesterday. Someone had wanted her to reach the Wall and have the door closed in her face.

She handed the route sheet to Ardea and turned her Heloth west.

—

The tone.

She had read the practitioner literature — papers from Ocipheus and Pallor researchers documenting the subjective sensory qualities of proximity to the Sinter zone. The terminology was cautious. "Membrane-adjacent phenomenology" was the institutional category for things practitioners noticed near active or disturbed membrane sites that atmospheric conditions alone couldn't explain. The literature was careful about making stronger claims. The literature was generally careful about stronger claims that touched on what the membrane might be doing on its own initiative.

She felt it now.

Low in the chest. Below the sternum, in the space where the lungs had room to expand. A pressure that was not pressure — it did not feel like the air weighing more than it had before. It was directional. From the south, from the west, from below. The Sinter zone's interior lay in those directions. The aperture sites within the zone — the original tears in the membrane from the Year 1079 event, which the Descent Corps documented on every return expedition as "ongoing structural adjustment" — lay in those directions.

The Wall soldiers called it *the tone*. She had heard the word before, on previous checkpoint visits. Not a sound. The thing you feel at the center of your chest when you are near something very large that is vibrating at a frequency below what ears can register.

Orim rode beside her for a moment without speaking. Then: "I was here for a winter in Year 1228. Verification contract on a coalition construction dispute. Four months. By the fourth month I could feel the tone in my sleep." He paused. "It's stronger than it was. By a measurable amount."

"The Descent Corps reports seasonal variation."

"Yes. Seasonal variation." The way he said it was not disagreement exactly. More like: *this is what they say, and it is one of the things they say.*

She did not ask what he meant. She was thinking about the bypass route and the four days and the suspension document and what it meant about who had filed it. The person who had filed the theft also controlled whether she could cross the Wall. These were not two separate operations. They were the same operation, and she had been in it without knowing it for at minimum four days.

She kept riding.



—

The western approach road ran along the Wall's outer face — the face that did not look into the zone — for approximately three kilometers before diverging north toward the Lacerta coastal passage. She rode it at the pace the Heloth courier's gait allowed: fast, consistent, the construct's chemical reserves sufficient for two days without resupply if she managed the intervals correctly.

The Wall's outer face was not what she had expected either, the first time. The defensive structures faced inward. The outer face was maintenance surface: drainage channels, inspection ladders, the scaffolding that the repair crews worked from. The people she had seen cutting stone at the repair site had been working on the maintenance face. Doing careful, competent work.

She thought about what they were wearing. No House insignia. No standard gear. The Atrament soldiers who were working above them on the scaffolding inspection level, who wore Atrament unit markings, and the eight people below them who wore nothing that marked them as belonging to any House or any compact.

She had categorized this and moved on. She was a researcher — she categorized and moved on. She thought about what she had categorized.

The Wall, as the institutional description had it, was maintained by a coalition labor force — volunteers, contracted workers, soldiers on rotation. She had read this in the coalition maintenance documentation. She had not, in her reading of that documentation, thought about the word *volunteers* in the context of what she now knew about how the Liturgy acquired labor from other Spheres.

She did not stop. There was a pursuit ahead and a bypass route and a four-day deficit and no time to stop.

She noted the thing and rode on.

—

At the junction where the western approach road split north, she stopped and looked back once.

The Wall was visible behind her — the full height of it, the different sections with their different stone, the repair scaffolding at the eastern end of the visible section still active, the supply Heloth still moving with its regular mechanical patience. The Sinter zone was behind the Wall. She could not see the zone. She had never been inside the zone. She had never asked whether a researcher might be authorized to enter the zone.

The zone's founding aperture sites were in there somewhere. The Year 1079 event was in there. The Long Seat, whose territory included the northern Pallor approaches, had said something once in a research context that she had read and filed: *what the membrane holds at Sinter is not what the Houses have described it as holding.* She had read this and filed it. The Long Seat was Pallor's principal institutional voice, and Pallor and Ocipheus maintained a formal diplomatic distance that made cross-institutional research exchanges complicated, and she had not followed the comment up.

She thought about following it up, briefly. The thought dissolved. The bypass road was north.

She turned north.

Orim, riding beside her, did not comment on the direction change or the interval before it. He had been doing this long enough, she thought, to know which moments were for commenting and which were not.

"Bressant," she said.

"Two days, possibly three," he said. "Depending on the pass conditions."

"And the thieves are four days ahead, plus the Wall bypass time."

"Yes." He paused. "Though they're not running directly. The Vierna approach roads are checkpointed — Pallor Knights with Descent Corps transit authority cross clean, but they leave a trace. The checkpoints log everything. I've worked in enough border crossings to know that people who are running are either very careful or not careful at all, and careful people are slower than they plan to be."

She considered this. A trace was not a catch. But a trace meant she would know she was on the right road.

"What do you need for the pass conditions?" she said.

"A good omen." He did not say this ironically. He said it the way a man says things that are true about his relationship with the world after sixty years of working in it. "I'll take a look when we get to the junction. Minor range, but sometimes it's enough to tell me whether the road ahead is passable or whether someone has recently passed."

He would see what he could see. She would ride.

[Beat 4]
THE MILL — SPHERE 31

He walked the same route every morning.

Down the back stairs of the boarding house — third stair from the bottom had a loose tread that he stepped over without thinking, out of habit older than the particular floor of the stair — through the side passage past the coal shed, left at the corner where the ironmonger kept a terrier that had never, in three years, barked at Rowe, which he had come to think of as a small arrangement between them. Then the canal path.

The canal was the best part of the walk. Twenty minutes from the boarding house to the mill, and twelve of those minutes ran along the water. In autumn the canal surface held the morning in a particular way — the light coming in low and lateral from the east, the water giving it back at an angle that made everything along the far bank look like an engraving of itself. Specific and clear and slightly unreal. He had grown up with the canal and he noticed it the way you notice things you grew up with: intermittently, in flashes, when the light was doing something he hadn't seen before.

The city smelled like coal smoke and wet stone and, on days when the wind came from the east, the particular chemical sweetness of the dye works three streets from the mill. He had stopped smelling these things years ago except on days when the wind shifted and brought something different, which made the usual smells briefly visible before they returned to background. This morning the wind was from the west. The canal smelled like canal — waterlogged wood, sediment, cold.

His breath made small clouds. High autumn, the kind of morning that committed to cold. He wore his good coat — the wool one, not the canvas work coat he kept on the hook inside the mill entrance. The canvas coat was for inside, where the heat from the machines and the bodies working them kept the floor warm enough that you shed your outer layer by the second hour of the shift. The wool coat was for the walk.

At the canal path's midpoint there was a bench. Rowe did not sit on it in the mornings — he was never early enough for sitting — but he knew it by its position relative to the elm tree that grew at an angle over the water, its roots having found the wall and worked along it. In winter you could see the roots clearly, the way they had bent and adapted to find what they needed. In autumn the elm kept its leaves until the last possible moment, and then shed them all at once over the course of a single week, and the canal path was orange for that week before the maintenance crew cleared it.

He was a week ahead of the shedding.

—

The mill ran six days a week, three shifts, the second and third shifts broken by a paid half-hour and the first shift broken by nothing because the first shift ran from four in the morning until noon and the management's position was that half the shift was the break. Rowe had been on the first shift for seven years, which had given him seven years of four-in-the-morning starts and had reorganized his body around that fact so thoroughly that he woke without an alarm at quarter to four regardless of what day it was, which he had come to find useful on his rest day.

The walk to the mill took twenty minutes. He arrived at three forty, which gave him fifteen minutes before the shift clock, which gave him enough time to change into the canvas coat, check his station for anything the previous shift had left that would require address before he could begin, and exchange approximately twenty words with his neighbor at the adjacent machine — a man called Hartner who had been on loom work for twenty-two years and had the particular calm of someone who has mastered a thing so completely that it no longer requires attention, which freed his attention for whatever he wanted to think about while his hands worked. Hartner thought about his garden.

The loom floor, when the first shift started, made a noise that Rowe had come to understand as a kind of weather. At full run — all sixty-two machines, which was the complement when there was a supply contract active and the management pushed production — the floor sounded like standing inside something that was alive in the mechanical sense, not the biological one. The rhythm was not quite regular. Each machine had its own character, small variations in timing and tension that the operators learned to read as diagnostic information. His machine — he thought of it as his because he had worked it for three years and knew its variations the way he knew the loose tread — ran with a very slight hesitation in the left-side shuttle return that the floor supervisor had twice marked for maintenance and the maintenance team had twice addressed without resolving.

He had learned to work around it. Two years of learning a hesitation's specific timing until the compensation was automatic.

The floor supervisor was Greiss. Foreman-grade, responsible for the first shift's production numbers and the quality of the work, answerable to the mill manager upstairs and ultimately to the contract holders whose names Rowe had never had occasion to learn. Greiss was a compact man who moved through the loom floor with the specific economy of someone who had grown up on a loom floor and had internalized its geometry — when to duck, when to step sideways, how to pass between machines without breaking either his pace or anyone's concentration. 

Rowe had read Greiss's hands for seven years. He could read them from across the floor in conditions where the lamplight was poor. He had never spoken more than thirty words to Greiss outside of the shift evaluation twice yearly, and he had come to think of Greiss as someone he knew very well in exactly one dimension.

—



 He had mastered his machine to the degree that the work did not consume him, which was the most comfortable relationship with labor he could imagine having.

He ate the same breakfast most mornings: bread and the strong tea that the boarding house put out in the common room between three and four in the morning for the mill shift, and sometimes a hard-boiled egg if the boarding house cook had bothered. The cook's relationship to the egg question was variable. Rowe had no opinion about this. He ate what was available and was grateful for the tea, which was always hot and always strong enough to do its job, which was to move his body from the state it was in at three forty — a state he had learned to recognize as operational-but-not-awake — into the state required for six hours of concentration on machinery.



—

Thursday morning in autumn: the light coming in from the east at four in the morning was no light at all, which was familiar. The lamps along the canal path were gas, maintained by the district authority, and the particular color of gas-lamp light on autumn canal water was a color Rowe could have reproduced exactly from memory, which he never had occasion to do. He walked.

The mill was lit before he arrived. The night shift was still running — he could hear it from the street, the loom floor's particular weather, the slight hesitation in his machine audible even from outside if he listened for it. He listened. The hesitation was consistent. No surprises.

He changed into the canvas coat. He checked his station. The previous shift had left it clean, which was Hartner's third-shift equivalent doing his job, which Rowe appreciated in the specific way that workers appreciate the people adjacent to them doing their work correctly. He had left Hartner's station clean for seven years. Hartner's third-shift equivalent had left his station clean for approximately four years, since the original person had moved to the dye quarter for reasons Rowe had been told at the time and had since forgotten.

"Good run last night," Hartner said, when the shift clock brought them both to their stations. This was within Hartner's twenty-word budget for the morning; he distributed his words with the same economy he applied to everything else.

"Tension's still high on mine," Rowe said.

"It settles by the second hour." He had noticed this too, evidently.

They did not speak again until the half-hour break that wasn't a half-hour break, which was a fiction they all maintained with Greiss because Greiss maintained it with the manager. In practice the first shift paused for approximately twelve minutes at the midpoint for water and, in winter, for the additional warmth of the tea that the day crew brought in from the outside. In autumn the twelve minutes was about water and standing still.

Rowe stood at the east window that ran along the top third of the mill's outer wall, high enough that it showed sky rather than building. The light by mid-morning had moved from the low easterly angle to something closer to overhead. The sky was clear and cold and specifically blue in the way of autumn mornings that commit to cold without committing to cloud. Below the window, invisible to him from this height, the canal would be catching the same light. The waterfowl from Tuesday might be on the water, conducting other negotiations or continuing the same one; he had no way to know.

He drank his water.

He thought about nothing in particular. He had learned to do this — to let the twelve minutes be the twelve minutes, without planning the afternoon or the rest day or the week's schedule. Hartner thought about his garden. Rowe thought about nothing. He had found this useful in the same way that sleep was useful: the body continued its functions, the mind moved into a different register, and he returned to the machine afterward with something that felt like a reset.

He returned to the machine.

—

At the midpoint of the shift, the morning sun came through the east windows at an angle that crossed the loom floor laterally, and for approximately forty minutes in high autumn this angle was low enough to catch the thread-dust that the machines raised into the air, the fine particulate that was part of the loom floor's weather and that the workers breathed and that accumulated in the margins of the floor and was swept out at the end of each shift by the cleanup crew. In that forty minutes the dust was briefly visible — a golden haze at midfloor height, moving in the slow currents of the machinery's exhalation, lit by the sideways sun.

He had first noticed this years ago, the first autumn after he started on the loom floor. He had stopped his machine to watch it, which had earned him a gesture from Greiss — flat hand, redirect — and he had returned to work and had not stopped for it again. But he noticed it every year, in the specific way he noticed the canal's autumn light: intermittently, in a flash of recognition, the familiar thing made briefly visible by the right conditions.

The morning was half done. The tension in his machine's left shuttle return had settled, as Hartner had predicted, into its usual range, and he was working at the pace he worked when the machine was running correctly, which was a pace that did not require conscious management — his hands knew the job, the job was his hands, and his attention was on the material and the thread count and the specific indicators that something was about to go wrong before it went wrong, which was the core skill of the work.

Nothing was about to go wrong.

The sun was at its lateral angle. The thread-dust moved in the light.

The shift was on its regular course. The floor was loud in the way it was loud when everything was working correctly. His machine ran. Beside him, Hartner's machine ran. Down the row, sixty other machines ran. The canvas coat was warm from the floor's heat and from his own. His shoulders had the specific tiredness of sustained motion, the comfortable tiredness that had a different quality from the end-of-day kind.

Thursday morning in autumn, the shift half done.

Nothing remarkable in the air.

[Beat 5]
THE AUTHORIZATION

The canonical property recovery instrument arrived on her desk on a Tuesday, filed by Canon Immaculate Tomasz Prelacze under the standard dispute-resolution authorization number, routed through the Scribe's office for copy and notarization in the ordinary course of business. It was the eleventh authorization she processed that morning. It was not the kind of document that required unusual attention.

Vega read it twice anyway.

Not because there was something wrong with it — she had been copying canonical property recovery instruments for three years, and this one was standard in every technical aspect, the language correct, the authorization code valid, the Canon's seal properly affixed. She read it twice because of the thing she had been noticing for the past eight months, which was that the sum of several ordinary documents could add up to something she did not have a category for yet.

She set it down and picked up the next instrument in the stack.

—

The Scribe's office was on the second floor of the Station's administrative building, a room with a south-facing window that looked out over the main courtyard and, beyond it, the archive building's roof with its membrane-apparatus housing visible on the east end. She had a desk, a copying stand, a reference shelf of canonical code, and a lamp that she replaced herself every four days because the maintenance rotation used a smaller wick than she preferred and the smaller wick produced a light that made her eyes hurt by midafternoon.

The desk was organized in the way that three years of the same work organizes a desk: everything in the position that minimized unnecessary motion. Blank instrument forms on the left, incoming stack in the center, outgoing — completed and sealed — on the right. The canonical codebook open to the section she was working in, weighted at the relevant page by a smooth stone she had carried since her posting began.

She had been copying canonical instruments for three years and she was good at it. This was not modesty or immodesty; it was the assessment of someone who understood the skill involved and had reached the point where the work was accurate and fast and required the minimum possible conscious management. She could copy an instrument of standard length in approximately twelve minutes. The notarization added three minutes. A complex instrument — multi-clause, multiple signatories, extended geographic scope — took longer. She had never been slow.

What she had developed, in the three years of becoming good at this, was the thing that accompanied any sufficiently practiced skill: the capacity to do it without thinking, which freed her attention for the thing adjacent to it, which was the text itself.

This was, she had come to understand, not part of the Scribe's official function. The official function was accurate copying and notarization. The text was not her concern.

She had stopped believing this approximately eight months ago.

—

The canonical property recovery instrument for the Oculus Memoriae read as follows:

*By authority of the Canon Immaculate, exercising plenary jurisdiction in matters of Relic provenance and custodial accountability under the Liturgy's founding compact with the House of Ocipheus:*

*Whereas the Oculus Memoriae (Registered Relic, Ocipheus Station, Year 397, Inventory Reference O-001) has been held under a vigil custodian arrangement requiring renewal of custodial certification every fifty years, and*

*Whereas the founding compact of Year 397, Article Seven, provides as follows: the Liturgy assumes perpetual stewardship of all Relics registered at vigil stations under its authority, with right of canonical review, custodial reassignment, and transfer as the law provides, the registering House retaining nominal title in the interim only; and*

*Whereas the most recent custodial certification (Year 1226, Keeper Halvard Nystrom, countersigned Canon Adrienne Lecourt) has not been renewed in the current canonical period, and*

*Whereas this failure of renewal creates a custodial gap in the Ocipheus Station archive's formal record, generating grounds for canonical property review:*

*Therefore, let this instrument authorize the Canon Immaculate to initiate review of the Oculus Memoriae's current custodial status and, if review finds the custodial certification gap material, to take such steps as canonical law provides for the resolution of custodial disputes in Relic provenance.*

*Seal of the Canon Immaculate, Ocipheus Station, 14th day, Month of the High Autumn, Year 1267.*

Vega read it twice.

The custodial certification argument was technically correct. The Year 1226 renewal had been countersigned by Adrienne Lecourt, who had died in Year 1243. The current Canon Immaculate had been posted four years ago. The fifty-year renewal window had opened in Year 1276 — nine years hence. The gap that the authorization identified did not exist yet.

She did not note this on the instrument. Her function was accurate copying, not legal review. She copied the instrument correctly, affixed her notary seal, and added it to the outgoing stack.

She picked up the next instrument.

—

The transit suspension for T-044 — a Templar field designation, the Liturgy's registry code for active Templar personnel — arrived in the afternoon, as part of a batch authorization covering a series of operational adjustments to the Station's field personnel deployment. She almost missed it — the batch was eleven pages, the suspension was on page eight, one clause among six under a heading that read *Authorized Field Authority Modifications, High Autumn Period.*

T-044. Templar designation. Three infusions. Field authority suspended pending canonical review of relevant certification.

The review this referenced was the same review. The property recovery instrument and the transit suspension were the same operation, filed separately to prevent the operational connection from being visible to anyone reading either document in isolation.

She had been doing this for three years. She had copied approximately six thousand instruments. She understood what documents looked like when they were designed to be read separately.

She copied the transit suspension accurately. She affixed her notary seal.

She did not know, at this point, whose designation T-044 was. The Scribe's notary function did not require her to cross-reference field designations against personal records. She would have needed to request access to the Knight deployment registry to match the designation to a name, and she had not done so, and would not, because her function did not require it.

She filed the batch authorization in the outgoing stack and went to look out the window.

—

In the courtyard below, the Descent Corps had set up an apparatus.

This was not unusual. The courtyard was used for practice operations, for certification exercises, for the periodic activation of the Station's emergency Scrying apparatus when maintenance required a live test. She had looked down at apparatus setup in the courtyard perhaps a hundred times in three years.

This setup was different in scale. The primary frame — a full-size Scrying apparatus, not the portable certification unit — had been positioned against the east wall, which was the wall that faced the archive building's membrane-adjacent housing. Two apparatus crews, not one. A Descent Corps evaluator she did not recognize, standing to one side with a clipboard and a notation kit. Three Descent Corps soldiers in field gear, not the station's regular complement.

She watched from the window.

The apparatus activated in the way that full-size apparatus activates: a visible shift in the air at the frame's center, the membrane's surface becoming briefly translucent, the quality of the light at the aperture different from the light surrounding it in a way that was difficult to describe except to people who had seen it. She had seen it perhaps forty times. She watched.

Something came through.

She could not see it clearly from the second-floor window. The aperture was at ground level, and the thing that came through was not at her line of sight. She saw the evaluator write something on the clipboard. She saw the soldiers step back. She saw the thing — the construct, she thought, whatever it was — being moved toward the south end of the courtyard under Corps direction.

She went back to her desk and waited for the assessment summary.

It arrived an hour later. Standard Corps evaluation document, routed through the Scribe's office for copy and canonical registration as an official Station activity record.

The heading read: *War Construct Evaluation — Sphere 42 Origin — Designation: WC-Eirene (provisional).*

She copied it accurately. The summary described a construct of substantial size — specific measurements that she copied without particular attention — evaluated for load capacity, command response, and field deployment suitability under the standard Descent Corps assessment rubric. The evaluator's recommendation: *suitable for forward staging, pending secondary structural assessment.*

One entry among many.

She filed it in the outgoing stack.

—

Her sister had left three days before.

This was not unusual. Lyra went on field deployments, on research trips, on the vigil-related work that required travel to other installations for comparative methodology. The Descent emergency at the Sinter Wall's eastern sector had drawn her overnight. Three days was within normal range.

The note had been on the scribing table when Vega arrived at the office the morning of the emergency: a folded square of paper, Lyra's handwriting, which was the handwriting of a researcher — dense, lateral, with the specific compaction of someone who had been taking notes in small spaces for thirty years.

*Back in three days. Don't eat the station bread.*

The bread in question was the Station common room's standard provision loaf, which had been underproofed in Vega's experience approximately two-thirds of the time for the past three years. Lyra's opinion of it was well established and had been communicated to the Station kitchen twice, diplomatically. Vega ate it anyway because the alternative was not eating, and she was not the kind of person who skipped breakfast over principle.

She had eaten the bread that morning and had thought of Lyra and had gone to work.

Three days was within normal range. Four days was within normal range. She was not, at this point, concerned.

—

In the afternoon, she took the outgoing stack to the distribution window — the narrow pass-through in the administrative corridor where the morning's canonical output was collected by the Canon's staff for routing and filing. She had done this every working day for three years. The distribution clerk was a man she had spoken to perhaps three hundred times and whose name she had learned in the first week and had since come to use without thinking.

"Busy morning," he said, taking the stack.

"Eight authorizations, one batch, one assessment registration." She handed over the stack in the organized way she always did — outgoing separated from reference copies, notary seals facing the same direction. Habit older than thinking about it. "The batch has a transit suspension buried on page eight. Flag it for the deployment record."

He noted this. He was good at his job in the same way she was good at hers: accurately, without excess.

She went back upstairs.

—

The property recovery instrument was in the outgoing stack. The transit suspension was in the outgoing stack. The war construct evaluation was in the outgoing stack.

She sat at her desk and looked at the empty incoming tray — the afternoon had been lighter, three short authorizations that she had processed quickly — and thought about the morning's work in the way she had been thinking about things for the past eight months, which was not as an evaluator or a reviewer but as someone noticing pattern.

The custodial certification gap for the Oculus Memoriae did not exist yet. The transit suspension for T-044 covered the same operational period. The war construct designation was provisional — *Eirene*, which was the name of the last Sinter champion, which was also the name of the Wall checkpoint — and had been marked for forward staging.

None of this was her function.

She picked up her pen and held it and looked at the south-facing window. The courtyard below was empty now. The apparatus crews had disassembled the frame, removed the construct, left the courtyard looking the way it always looked: stone, lamppost, the well that nobody used because the plumbing had been updated forty years ago but the well remained as structural support for the east retaining wall.

The day was ending. The light through the window was the specific amber of late autumn afternoon, the sun low enough to come in at an angle that lit the papers on her desk from the side. She could see the texture of the vellum on the notarized copies — the small variations in the surface that you could feel with your fingers and see in the right light. She had looked at that texture for three years.

She thought about T-044. She thought about why someone who needed to review a Relic's custodial certification would also need to prevent the Knight responsible for that Relic's vigil from being in the field.

She thought about the Wall's eastern sector, and the Descent emergency that had been dispatched three nights ago, and the fact that the T-044 transit suspension had been authorized two days before the Descent emergency.

She picked up her pen and opened the reference codebook to the section on canonical property review, and she read it carefully, for the first time, rather than copying from it.

The review process, as the codebook described it, included a provision for temporary custodian reassignment pending resolution of disputed certification. The Relic could be moved. The movement required canonical authorization. The authorization for movement was the document that had been on her desk that morning.

The authorization for movement had been filed before the certification dispute was raised. The dispute citation referenced a gap that did not yet exist.

She closed the codebook.

It was her function to copy accurately and notarize. It was not her function to identify legal irregularities in the instruments she processed. If she identified an irregularity, the correct procedure was to flag it to her supervising Scribe, who would escalate to the Canon's legal review office, which was staffed by Canon Immaculate Tomasz Prelacze's administrative staff.

She understood this to mean something specific.

She set her pen down and did not pick it up again until the next instrument arrived.

—

She ate supper in the Station's lower common room, at the table she usually sat at, with the people she usually sat with. She did not describe the morning's work in any detail. The people she sat with did not ask her to — they talked about what they usually talked about, which was the Station's routine, the coming winter weather, the question of whether the maintenance rotation for the west wall heating element had been scheduled correctly.

She listened. She added observations where she had them. She ate the bread.

The note was still on her scribing table. She had not moved it.

*Back in three days. Don't eat the station bread.*

It was the fourth day.

She went back to her quarters. She lay on her bed with her hands on her chest and looked at the ceiling in the dark, which was what she did when she was processing something that did not fit any of her existing categories. The categories were not the problem — she had good categories, developed over three years of careful work. The problem was that what she was processing was not something that belonged in any of the categories that existed.

It belonged in a different kind of record.

She did not know yet what kind.

She thought about T-044 for a long time before she went to sleep, and then she slept, and in the morning she got up and went to work.

[Beat 6]
MYRMIDON INTAKE RECORD — STATION VIERNA NORTH — HIGH AUTUMN, YEAR 1137

Origin: Sphere 31. Batch 12 of the High Autumn rotation.
Designation: Rowe, E. [Transcription approximate; original name not fully parseable.]
Physical assessment: Adult male, factory worker, suitable for conscript service. Language: non-Cauld, unidentified. No membrane history. No prior catalogue entry.
Oath of compact administered at time of processing by station intake officer. Designee's comprehension of oath contents: not assessed.
Status: Received. Transferred to conscript regiment, eastern barracks. No follow-up required.

—

THE TAKING

The thread-dust catches the sideways light off the high windows the way it always does at this hour — the morning half-done, the machines at full weight. Edvard Rowe does not look at the dust. He has been looking at it for nine years and it no longer registers as something to see. His hands know the shuttle. His hands know when the warp tightens on the left side, when to ease, when the shuttle pace needs backing off before the thread can have an opinion about it.

The machine under his hands is running right. This is all the information that matters.

It is Thursday. He ate breakfast at Marte's counter — the same stool, the same bowl, the same sour black coffee — and walked the canal road in the dark with his wool coat buttoned to the throat and his breath visible in front of him and the ironmonger's terrier barking at nothing from behind its gate, same as it did yesterday and same as it would do tomorrow. By the time he reached the mill his face was cold and his hands were not yet ready. They had to warm on the machine before they were his again.

Now they are warm. He is two hours into the shift. The loom floor is running at full volume — the sound of it is not noise when you have known it this long, it is weather, it is atmosphere, it is a kind of air in which you go about your work. The thread-dust moves in the columns of light off the high windows. The floor under his boots is a thing he has not thought about since he walked through the door.

Then the floor stops being a floor.

This is the only way he will have to describe it later, in words that do not fit: *the floor stops being a floor.* There is no warning. There is no sound that does not belong to the mill. One moment his hands know the shuttle. The next moment the machine is gone and his hands do not know where they are and the floor is —

Not down.

Down is wrong. Down has moved. Down is somewhere to his left and also behind him and also in a direction that does not have a name and his stomach knows this the way it knows falling, except he is not falling, except the rightness of his body's relation to the ground has simply — stopped — and his legs are trying to compensate for a direction they cannot find and —

The cold hits him. A cold that has no business being inside his chest, inside his mouth, inside the air his lungs are trying to process. Not the cold of the canal road, not the cold of high autumn. A cold that does not know what the temperature is supposed to be. He is not breathing correctly. His body knows this before he does. His body is running a fast and frightened calculation about how much air to take in and getting a wrong answer every time because the air is wrong and his lungs cannot tell him why because his lungs have never had to figure out why before.

The pressure is wrong.

He has a word for this. He has stood at the edge of the quarry on the north side of the city, where the cut goes down thirty meters, and felt the particular quality of that air — the pressure-absence of a very large empty space. This is that, except it is everywhere and he is inside it and his lungs cannot find the floor of it.

Then stone. His knees hit stone. His palms hit stone. He can feel it: cold, grained, the roughness of dressed stone that has been walked on for a long time and is neither smooth nor sharp. He is on his hands and his knees on a stone floor and he is not in the mill.

His body has no larger understanding available to offer.

---

He is sick. Not immediately — there is an interval between the stone floor and the sickness, an interval in which he is aware of lamplight and of the air being different and of voices that are not shouting. People are speaking. Calmly. Near him, not to him.

Then he is sick, and the stone floor in front of him is wet, and he is shaking.

Someone to his right says something. He looks up.

Robed figures. Dark robes, light wool or something close to wool, practical cut, nothing ceremonial about them. There are several. They are spread across the room — a large stone room, lower ceiling than the mill, lit by lamps mounted at intervals on the walls. The lamps burn something that smells faintly oily but not unpleasant. It is not the smell of machine oil. Nothing here is the smell of anything he knows.

The figures are not looking at him. One is, briefly — a quick assessment, the kind you give something that has arrived in the expected place and needs filing. Then that one's attention moves elsewhere, to a long surface of some kind. A table with things on it that he cannot make out from the floor.

He gets to his feet. His legs do not help much. He gets to his feet anyway.

Through a door at the far end of the room — open, no one standing in it — he can see the edge of a hallway and the partial outline of another room beyond. Through that doorway: other people. People not wearing the dark robes. People sitting against walls or standing in the particular posture of people who do not know what to do with their bodies. One man's hands are pressed flat against his thighs, pushing down. One woman has her back very straight and her eyes fixed on the middle of a wall. The man with his hands on his thighs meets Rowe's eyes for a moment and looks away.

Rowe does not know what he sees in his own face. He does not want to.

Someone approaches him. A woman, he thinks, though the robe makes it hard to be certain. She is not hurrying. She is holding something in one hand — a flat surface with paper on it, or something like paper, and a long instrument for writing. She stops at a distance that is not quite close and says something.

Rowe says nothing. He does not have a response for what she has said.

She says it again, slower. As if the slowness might help. He watches her mouth with more attention than he has given anything in the past two hours. He can see every movement her mouth makes. Not one of them produces anything he can match to anything he knows.

She tries a different phrase. Behind her, one of the other robed figures watches the exchange and makes a brief gesture with one hand — flat, dismissive, something that means *proceed* — and goes back to the table.

The woman with the board says something short. She makes a brief motion with her free hand: open, close, the shape of reaching toward something and withdrawing. Then she tilts the board slightly in his direction. He looks at it. He sees marks — writing, or what he understands to be writing — and reads nothing.

She speaks again. The same phrase, same pattern of sound, same measured tone. Not unkind. Not impatient. The tone of someone who has a task requiring completion and is completing it.

He does not respond. He cannot locate his voice.

He watches her make a mark on the board. It takes a moment — the writing instrument moves twice, a short stroke and a longer one. She files him in whatever record she is keeping and she moves on.

He is still standing in the same place when she reaches the next person across the room. That person — a young man, younger than Rowe, still damp-faced with shock — also says nothing. She makes a mark for that one too.

The mark is the same mark she made for Rowe.

There is a mark for this. He does not understand what this means yet. He will.

---

He is moved.

Two of the robed figures come to him and make gestures indicating he should follow. He follows. His legs are working better now.

They take him into an adjacent room — smaller, a low table, a lamp. Two different robed figures are waiting. These ones are interested in his body.

He wants to say, later, that it was not unpleasant. He will try to say it and find it is not quite right, but it is not quite wrong either. These people are doing a job. The job requires his body and they are using it precisely and nothing about what they do carries cruelty in it, which is not the same as care. It is the absence of deliberate harm. He notes the distinction because the distinction is all he has.

They look at his teeth. They look at his hands — the backs, the wrists, the skin of his forearms. He rolls up his sleeve without being asked because they have made the gesture and rolling one's sleeve to show the skin of one's arm is apparently the same gesture in any language. They feel along his collarbone. One of them looks into his eyes with a small lamp held close, and the light is very bright, and he does not flinch because what would be the point of flinching now. One of them writes things down on a board similar to the first woman's board but smaller.

They speak to each other throughout. Not to him. They have stopped addressing him — whether they've concluded he cannot respond or whether the response was never the point, he cannot determine.

He has not tried his voice yet. He does not know what it sounds like at the moment. He is not certain what would come out.

A younger robed figure brings in a bundle of cloth and sets it on the table and steps back. One of the examiners unfolds it and holds it out: dark cloth, a loose shirt, trousers, something to wrap around the waist. Then the examiner reaches toward his coat.

Rowe steps back.

No one moves for a moment. The examiner's hand does not lower. The younger one by the door does not step forward. One of the examiners says something. The tone is not threatening. It is explanatory — the specific patience of a person explaining something to someone without the words, who might still understand tone.

He lets them take the coat.

His canvas work coat. The heavy one, the one he wears because canvas doesn't catch the way wool does, the one that has nine years of machine oil and thread-dust worked into the weave. It goes. His wool coat follows — the one he walked in, buttoned to the throat, against the canal road dark. He watches both of them fold and be carried somewhere he cannot see.

They leave his boots. They look at his boots and say something to each other and leave them on his feet. He is grateful for this in a way that is not rational given the rest of it. His feet are cold and the boots are his and he has not been able to keep much else.

The new clothes are not his size perfectly but they fit. The cloth is rough but not punishing. He gets dressed and the younger figure by the door watches him do it with the focused inattention of someone whose job is to confirm a task is completed rather than to observe a person.

---

They put him in a room with other people.

The room has a low ceiling and several lamps and bare stone walls and not enough warmth. Fifteen people in it, maybe twenty — he counts and loses the count because people are moving. All of them are wearing the same dark cloth he is now wearing.

A heavyset older man sitting against the far wall watches Rowe come in with an expression he recognizes: the expression of someone who has been waiting for the next arrival and has felt something particular about each one. Not malice. Something that has moved past malice into a larger territory.

The man says something. Not the robed figures' language. Different sounds entirely. Rowe has no more footing in them.

He says nothing back.

The man says something else and holds his hand flat, palm down, and moves it slowly: settle, maybe, or easy, or *sit, it does not help to stand.* Rowe does not sit down. Not yet.

A woman nearby holds up one hand and points to herself. Makes a sound — short, two syllables, the shape of a name. Then she points at him.

He knows what she is asking. He has a name. He opens his mouth and his throat produces a sound that is not a word and he closes his mouth. She nods once. She has seen this. She has been here long enough to have a category for it too.

He sits against the wall with his knees up. The stone is cold through the cloth. The lamps smoke faintly. His eye keeps trying to reconcile the quality of this light with something familiar and failing.

Through the door — no guard he can see, but not open to him; he understands this without testing it — he can hear other rooms. Movement. Someone crying in the controlled way of someone who has done the large crying already and is left with the small ongoing kind. Someone saying something low and repetitive. A prayer or a self-address or both.

The older man who gestured at him has gone back to sitting with his forearms on his knees, staring at the floor. He has the look of a man who has done his accounting several times and gotten the same number each time and is deciding whether to do it again.

Rowe does not pray and does not talk to himself. He sits against the wall and breathes and does his own accounting.

The mill. His hands on the shuttle. The thread-dust in the sideways light. The weight of the wool coat on his shoulders when he walked in. Marte's counter and the sour coffee and the canal road in the dark.

Then — the floor.

The floor stops being a floor.

He cannot get past it. He keeps arriving at it in memory and finding nothing in his experience that can receive it. He approaches it and turns back and approaches again and turns back again. His experience has no vessel for what the floor did.

His hands are in his lap. He looks at them.

---

Food comes. A robed figure he has not seen before. A tray with several items and a cup of water.

He does not recognize most of the items. There is a smell coming off the main dish — hot, something cooked in oil, something his stomach understands to be food in the abstract and refuses in the specific. He pushes the dish aside.

There is bread.

He eats the bread.

It is flatter than he is used to and the grain is different but it is bread, and bread is bread in a way that almost nothing else is, and he eats all of it and he does not have a larger thought about it than that.

He drinks the water. He does not drink all of it at once because he does not know when more water comes.

The older man across the room is watching him. Not unkindly. Watching the way a person watches when he has seen new arrivals come in and not eat the dish and eat the bread and hold the water back and he knows the shape of all of it and is simply confirming that this one is the same.

Rowe does not look back at him.

Later something warm comes. Not water — something warm to drink, something that smells of plant matter he does not know but which his throat does not reject. He drinks half. His stomach accepts it.

His hands are still shaking. They shake through the bread and they are shaking now, finely, the small sustained tremor of a body running a process it did not agree to run. He presses them flat against his thighs and holds them there.

The nearest lamp burns low. Someone comes and does something to it and it burns higher. The light shifts and the shadows of the room rearrange themselves. The room is the same room.

He sleeps.

He does not mean to sleep. He means to stay alert, to keep watching, to understand if he can what comes next. What he actually does is fall asleep against the cold stone wall with his knees drawn up and his head tipped back and his hands finally still in his lap. He sleeps the way bodies sleep when they have received more than they can process and have decided, without being consulted, that processing can wait.

He wakes up.

The same room. The lamp burning low again. The other people sleeping or sitting with their eyes open in the middle distance. The older man asleep at an angle against the wall. The woman who pointed at herself has her face turned away.

Rowe sits in the dark for a while. He is trying to find the thread-dust in his memory. The high windows. The sideways morning light and the thread-dust catching it, specific and his, a thing he has known for nine years and therefore a thing that ought to be stable — and it is there, but it is going. The way things go when the mind is making room for what has replaced them. The way the details of a place dissolve when you have left it long enough that the mind sees no point in keeping them sharp.

He has not left the mill long enough for that.

He presses his palms flat against his thighs and holds them there.

Present. Alive. Still here.

The particular cold of the stone floor — dressed stone, grained, walked on for a long time — is the thing his body is most certain of right now. The cold and the grain of it, coming through cloth and boot-sole and palm. Real. Solid. The floor is still a floor.

He closes his eyes. Across the room the woman who pointed at herself breathes with the evenness of someone finally asleep. The older man shifts once and is still. Somewhere beyond the door someone is still doing the low repetitive speaking, quieter now, working down toward silence.

Behind Rowe's eyes the thread-dust dissolves, and the sideways light dissolves, and the sound of the mill at full weight dissolves, and what is left in their place is cold stone and lamplight and twenty people doing the same accounting in the dark.

The lamp burns.

The morning — if morning is what comes — has not yet come.

He is still here.

[Beat 7]
VIERNA ENTRY — THE LAW DOESN'T APPLY HERE

She crossed at the goat path.

A day and a half on the coastal bypass road — the Wall behind her, the Lacerta-adjacent approaches before her, the Sinter zone somewhere to her right behind eleven hundred years of stone — had given her time to study the Vierna western border the way a researcher studies a problem: systematically, without preference for the answer. The formal western entry was at a place called Pontecôte, two hundred meters of checkpoint wall and a flag tower and a garrison of fifteen Vierna border soldiers whose job was to process commercial cattle traffic from the Lacerta hill-farms and to turn back anyone without the right papers. She didn't have the right papers. She didn't have the right authority. She didn't have anything except a sealed letter from the Ocipheus Keeper that the Canon Immaculate had already neutralized and a dissolution blade she hadn't drawn and a Heloth courier that had been running for thirty-six hours on its chemical reserves and was starting to show it in the way its left-side gait had gone marginally uneven.

Pontecôte was not where she crossed.

The goat path was three kilometers north of Pontecôte, through a section of border scrubland that Vierna hadn't bothered to checkpoint because nothing valuable had ever come through it except goats. Goats didn't need transit papers. Neither, for the next forty seconds, would she.

The path was narrow and the ground was damp from two days of rain and the Heloth courier was not designed for this kind of terrain — not bad terrain, just irregular in a way that the courier's load-stability programming kept compensating for, a slight hesitation in the gait that she had learned to read as the machine recalculating. She did not push it. At the path's highest point the Vierna border was a low stone wall, waist-high, the kind of marking that said *this is where the jurisdiction changes* and not the kind that said *we will stop you.* She took the wall at a step-through and the courier followed with the particular patience of a machine that did not have an opinion about property lines.

On the far side of the wall, she was in Vierna without authorization.

Her body knew this the way it knew other practical facts — the weight of armor in the third hour of wearing it, the specific taste of the air before rain. No guilt. Just the information that the protections she operated under at home — the Meridian Compact authority, the House compact that made another House's soldiers hesitate before engaging a Knight, the institutional weight of the Liturgy's sanction that she had spent thirty years assuming made her harder to stop — were not operative here. She was a large woman with a dissolution blade on a tired Heloth courier in Vierna without papers, and the only thing between her and a formal response from Vierna's border cavalry was whatever speed she could make before the observation post network noticed her.

She had, by her estimate, until the first post sighted her.

That was now.

—

The signal mirror caught the morning light — a flash, directional, toward the valley below — at exactly the moment she saw the post. Eleven meters up on the fourth terrace above the road, a box of cut stone with a slit-window and a mirror housing on the south face. The flash was instantaneous with her recognition of it. The watcher had been waiting for her. Not for her specifically — for anyone who crossed at the goat path, which apparently people did, because otherwise Vierna wouldn't have a relay post covering it.

She put the courier to the climb protocol.

The wine-country terraces were old — three centuries of cut hillside, each terrace stepped back from the one below by a retaining wall of fitted limestone that the deepvine's root system had grown through and around until the stone and the root were mutually supporting. The vines themselves ran in rows along each terrace, the autumn foliage that particular Sphere-origin purple-black, alternating with bands of native yellow where the vine hadn't taken hold. Stripes, running the length of every hillside, readable as a record of how far the imported variety had spread in each generation.

The next observation post triggered as she passed it. The one after that. She watched the signal mirrors without slowing — each flash, each relay in sequence, the alert moving faster than she was. The cavalry was faster than she had estimated.

They came around the upper switchback three terraces above her — not mounted in the conventional sense. Heloth freight models, three meters at the shoulder, riders sitting high on the shoulder housings with a clear sightline over the terrace walls in both directions. Practical adaptation for irregular terrain: the freight models could manage the terrace approaches that horse cavalry couldn't, and the shoulder-riders were high enough to fire over obstacles that would have blocked a ground-level engagement. She had read about this in Vierna's military deployment literature. There was a gap, it turned out, between reading about something and watching three freight Heloths come around a switchback at a pace that said the relay notification had reached the depot forty minutes ago and they had been moving since.

"Pontis," she said. Not to anyone. To herself, as a decision. The Pontis barge landing was half a kilometer below. River barge was faster than anything Vierna could put on the bank roads at this season — she knew this from the Gyldir Shore Accord documentation, which included river-speed tables in the commercial freight section. If she made the barge, the cavalry would have to coordinate a riverbank intercept at Bressant, which meant the Bressant landing would be alerted before she arrived, which meant she would arrive to Vierna border authority with a stamped entry log and no transit documentation. Which was the situation she was in anyway.

She put the courier to the descent.

The switchback path was not designed for courier speed. The courier was using its own gait protocols rather than following instructions, doing what it was designed to do — getting a difficult load down difficult terrain without losing it — and what it was designed to do was not comfortable for the load. She held the grip bar across her chest with both hands and kept her weight low and watched the valley come up.

The formal challenge came from behind her. One of the cavalry riders, Vierna border protocol, one challenge required before pursuit engaged. She did not respond to it. She was not required to stop for a challenge she had the right to ignore. Whether the cavalry commander had been properly briefed on the Compact's provisions was something she would not know until she was either on the barge or not.

She was on the barge.

—

The Pontis barge operator had a manifested look — the face of a person who has spent a career watching commercial river traffic and has learned to distinguish routine cargo from everything else, and who was currently revising his assessment of the morning's routine. He looked at the sealed authority with the care of someone encountering it for the first time. He stamped it. He did not ask about the cavalry on the upper switchback, which was professional.

The courier went into the cargo space — folded into rest-state, steam pressure managed, chemical reserves on standby. She paid the crossing fee. The barge pushed off.
