Behind her, on the Pontis bank, the cavalry reached the landing. One of the shoulder-riders had a signal mirror. The relay went north toward the Bressant landing, which would have a full description of her party before the barge arrived.

She went into the cargo space and sat beside the courier's rest-state housing, which was warm.

—

Vierna river-country in autumn had a particular quality she had not anticipated, which was density. Not natural density — the density of a landscape under continuous documentation. Every village on the Veil River had an archival post. Every archival post had a flag. The flag indicated what was currently logged in the village's river records: green for commercial cargo, yellow for passenger crossings, red for any passage under special authority. As they moved north the red flags went up at each post they passed. She watched them from the cargo hatch — the flag-change taking approximately thirty seconds from when the barge was spotted to when the notation was entered and the flag was raised.

She was being logged in real time by an administrative infrastructure that had no authority to stop her and no intention of letting her passage go unrecorded.

Orim came to sit beside her at the cargo hatch in the third hour. He had been on the forward deck since departure, doing the thing he did when he was thinking, which was look at nothing in particular with the specific attention of someone who had forty years of practice at looking at nothing in particular and finding something there.

"You're counting the flags," he said.

"Fourteen since Pontis."

"There's a cluster at Archival Gate — that's the border town, historically significant, they have three posts and they all flag independently." He looked at the passing bank. "The Gate's named for Arnault d'Archival, who established Vierna's river-rights claim by crossing this river in Year 312 in pursuit of a Calyx raiding party. Vierna has been charging for river use ever since. The Accord your Compact references is simply the current version of a principle they invented here."

She had known the Accord. She had not known d'Archival. "You've been on this river before."

"Four times. Three verification contracts and once in my own interest." He paused. "The Treachery Quarter in Bressant — the old merchant district — is called that because of the Year 634 occupation. Vierna merchants sold supply routes to Ocipheus forces during the occupation and then sold the same merchants' names to the Vierna resistance when the occupation failed. The district has been called Treachery Quarter for six hundred years. They are proud of it." He looked at her. "This is a country that takes its record-keeping seriously."

"I know."

"What they are watching for," he said, "is whether we are who the documents say we are. The documents say we are a Meridian Compact pursuit under Ocipheus authority. The documents are correct. What is not in the documents is that the authority has been suspended by the same institution that issued it."

She said nothing.

He nodded and went back to looking at nothing. She remained at the cargo hatch and watched Vierna document her passage through its territory without her permission, which she had entered without Vierna's permission, which seemed fair.

—

Bressant arrived in the early afternoon.

It was a dense city, the kind that had accumulated around a function — in Bressant's case, the grain warehouse district that handled Vierna's upriver agricultural output. The buildings were pressed together against the hillside behind, leaving the landing frontage wide and practical. The Veil River here was sixty meters across, running swift and dark with autumn rain-depth.

The Bressant landing's flag was red.

Two Vierna border soldiers were waiting at the landing approach. Young, formal, going to handle this correctly because they knew it was going to be examined later. She showed the sealed authority. They logged her in with the precision of people who were going to do this correctly if it took all day.

The senior of the two said: "You have approximately forty minutes before the interior command can coordinate a formal review response." He said it in the way people say things when they are telling you something useful within the constraints of what they are authorized to tell you.

"Thank you," she said.

The courier came off the barge and went to active protocol. She had forty minutes.

—

The grain warehouse district's southern approach was a narrow passage between two large storage buildings, stone-floored, sheltered from wind. She walked it slowly.

Three different sets of boot-prints in the settled grit along the wall. She could date them roughly by layer depth — the deepest were three or four days old, overlaid by two days of weather. All three had been here three days ago. The most recent layer showed two sets. The third was gone.

The third had been a lighter print than the other two. Different construction: narrower heel, longer toe-box. Not Cauld-standard equipment.

Someone had separated from the party between the Sinter Wall crossing and Bressant. Two had continued north. The third was somewhere south — or east — or not continuing on this particular route.

She checked the direction of the remaining two prints. North. The river barges north from Bressant served the Atrament rail junction at the border. She already knew where they were going.

One of the three who had taken the Relic was no longer where she needed them to be. She filed this and kept moving, because the more important question was whether the third had continued south or had stayed.

The lighter prints in the passage oriented toward the entrance. Not departure-posture — the weight was forward, toward the passage opening, the angle of someone watching for arrivals rather than preparing to leave. Someone had waited here for hours, and the most recent trace showed they had not yet walked away.

She checked the time she had left. Twenty minutes.

The main warehouse access was along the district's north side — the loading bays, the freight doors, the formal commercial entrance. She didn't use it. She went around to the service entrance at the east face, which the loading crews used and which the supervisors did not usually watch in the middle of the day because the middle of the day was when the loading crews were outside working the barge transfers.

Inside: the smell of grain, warm and dusty, the specific smell of large quantities of dry material in an enclosed space. The warehouse was built in sections — the main storage floor with the large sealed grain bins running in rows, the smaller bin room at the back for the premium contract lots. She moved through the main floor without hurrying, reading the bins as she passed. Standard rope seals, the kind required by the Bressant archive record system, all intact.

She reached the fourth row.

On the third bin from the left wall, the rope seal was broken. Not cut — the rope had been worked loose from the peg, carefully, the kind of careful that took time and left the rope itself intact enough to be pushed back into approximate position. It looked sealed if you weren't examining it. She had been examining every seal in the room.

She stood in front of the bin for a moment. She had forty minutes when she'd entered the district. She had perhaps fifteen now.

She put her hand on the bin latch.

[Beat 8]
NO ACTION INDICATED

The copy desk faced north, which in winter meant it faced a column of pale light that came off the courtyard stones and produced no warmth and did nothing useful. She had spent three years angling her lamp to compensate. By now she did it automatically, the way a person learns to walk with one bad leg: efficiently, without grace, without complaint.

The instruments arrived in the morning, as they always did. The runner — a junior canon, fourteen years old and still wearing the expression of someone who had not yet learned what the documents he was carrying said — set the stack on the corner of her desk and left without speaking. She noted this. He had worked for six weeks delivering things to her desk, and in the first weeks he had always asked, out of some sociable reflex, whether she required anything else. He had stopped asking. She had not asked him why. She suspected she knew why.

Six weeks was enough time to learn what a stack of instruments contained by looking at it. The weight. The binding method. Whether the lead sheet was written in the Canon's hand or a secretary's. She had become accurate in this the way she had become accurate in everything: by repetition, by the slow compression of judgment into reflex, by allowing the work to teach her what the work required. In the first weeks of the posting she had read every instrument before she began copying; now she read them in order, one at a time, completing each before she touched the next. Accumulation was the danger. You read everything and you began to understand the shape of it before you had language for the shape, and then you were working at a register that made the act of copying feel like something other than what it was supposed to be.

The instruments from the previous afternoon's session were still drying. She moved them to the side shelf and uncovered the new stack. The notation sheet on top listed three instruments for copying and notarization, plus one summary assessment pending the Canon's counter-brief, which would arrive separately. She noted the instrument types without reading them yet: two she recognized as new from the notation codes; one was a maintenance authorization, the fourth that week. She set the maintenance authorization to the bottom of the stack and started with the second.

---

The Lacerta document was formal, carefully constructed, and written by someone who understood that they were arguing upward through an institution that did not share their institutional interests. She recognized the structure: the diplomatic preamble, the supporting observations arranged in descending order of provability, the specific and careful language around what was being requested. The delegate had chosen the word *deterioration* in preference to *encroachment* — she could see the calculation in it. Encroachment implied an active threat; deterioration implied a condition that might be addressed through maintenance rather than mobilization. The delegate was trying to make it easier to be agreed with.

The request was modest. The Lacerta delegate asked only for Liturgy acknowledgment of the sector conditions and response planning — not action, not troops, not resources. Acknowledgment. A record that someone in the Liturgy had read the report and noted that the Wall's western boundary showed evidence of boundary drift over an indeterminate but non-negligible period. The delegate's closing paragraph was almost apologetic in its narrowness, as though he had written a larger version and then removed everything that might be refused.

She had seen this before in inter-House correspondence — the gradual reduction of a request to its irreducible minimum, the careful trimming of everything that gave the Liturgy grounds to refuse. What remained after enough trimming was sometimes not worth refusing. The Liturgy refused it anyway.

She copied the document accurately.

She had been copying things accurately for three years. Her master had noted it as her primary virtue in the certification assessment: *exact hand, no interpretive drift, consistent performance across instrument type.* The Scribe's office had one virtue, and she had it. The instrument said what the instrument said. She said it again, in the canonical hand, under the Liturgy seal. It became official in the saying of it. That was the arrangement.

She finished the Lacerta copy and set it to dry.

The Carnyx document was different in register. If the Lacerta delegate had been persuading, the Carnyx border commander had been reporting. There was no diplomatic preamble. There was a statement of conditions, a methodology section describing how the measurements had been made and over what period, and a set of survey maps folded into the back cover — she had to unfold them carefully, the paper was good-quality and resisted the crease, they spread across her desk and onto the narrow auxiliary shelf she kept for reference volumes. The notations on the maps were in the Carnyx field system, which she was not familiar with, and she had to read the legend twice.

The numbers resolved clearly enough.

Fifteen years. The boundary had moved outward by a measurable distance in the eastern sector. The commander had included the margin of error in the annotation, at each of three survey points along the observed line. She added the margins against the measurements. The margins did not account for the difference. The Wall had moved.

She looked at the maps for some time before she began copying.

She had located, in the archive's methodological standards register, the document the counter-brief had cited as its authority: *Assessment Protocol for Membrane Boundary Variation, Revision Four, Article Twelve, Year 1199 revision: A boundary variation falling within one standard deviation of the fifty-year mean, as calculated by the Liturgy's approved archive methodology, constitutes acceptable variation. Observation is required. Response is at the Canon's discretion.*

The Carnyx commander had measured fifteen years. The Protocol required a fifty-year mean. The standard deviation of the fifty-year mean, calculated by the Liturgy's methodology, absorbed fifteen years of change without triggering the threshold. This was not an error in the Protocol. It was what the Protocol was designed to do.

There was a detail she had not expected: the commander had included a rate projection in the final data block. If the observed rate held, the boundary would reach the first civilian settlement outside the exclusion zone in approximately forty years. The projection was annotated *high-uncertainty, extrapolated from 15-year sample.* It was there. He had put it there. He had added it knowing that it would be read by a Scribe before it reached anyone with the standing to act on it.

She copied it accurately.

The runner returned with the Canon's counter-brief while she was finishing. She had not heard him come in. He set the document on her desk and was already leaving when she looked up.

"Did you wait for this?" she said.

"It was ready," he said. He did not look at her.

She was aware that the Liturgy employed many people who did not look at the things they carried. She had been one of them, at the beginning. She was less certain what she was now.

The counter-brief was brief. Three paragraphs. The Canon's characteristic cadence — institutional and polished, nothing that could be cited against him in a subsequent review, every sentence defensible in isolation. The western boundary conditions fell within acceptable variation; sector commanders were reminded that local observational data should be interpreted against the long-term baseline record, which was the Liturgy's to maintain. The eastern sector report's survey methodology was noted as non-standard, and the findings would require reconciliation with the Liturgy's established baseline before action thresholds could be assessed.

The Canon had not mentioned what the action thresholds were. She had not seen them specified in any instrument she had copied.

The final line: *No action indicated at this time.*

She applied the notation to both the Lacerta and Carnyx instruments in the disposition column. She folded the counter-brief and added it to the Lacerta file. She folded the Carnyx maps carefully — along the existing creases, not new ones, the paper was too good for new creases — and she held them for a moment before she put them in the review sleeve. The boundary line at Year 1685. The boundary line at Year 1700. A distance she could measure with her thumb. She had measured it with her thumb. She put the maps in the sleeve and sealed it.

The file would go to the archive room at the end of the day. It would be catalogued under *Review Deferred: Sector Correspondence.* The catalogue was organized by date and then by subject. This file would sit between a supply reassessment from three months ago and a quarterly water usage report from the eastern garrison. Nobody would look at it until someone needed to prove they had read the reports. That was what it would be for.

She set the sealed sleeve on the transfer stack.

---

The WC-Eirene units came through the courtyard in the middle of the afternoon.

She had been stretching her hand — she had a habit of pressing her fingers back at the knuckle when the joint stiffened, which happened every day around this hour — and she had moved to the window to do it. The window gave a partial view of the courtyard's northern corner, which was usually empty: a food service cart, sometimes a courier's Heloth idling in the shade. Nothing of interest.

She counted them while she stretched. Twelve. They moved in file, at the deliberate pace of machines being led at maintenance speed — not operational, but not inert. The handlers walked alongside, not in front. That was the position for units with active tracking systems; a handler in front of active tracking was a handler in the unit's registration field, which created a compliance conflict the unit was designed to resolve by following rather than being followed. You walked alongside. She had filed enough evaluation summaries in six weeks to know the procedural specifics. The handlers were following correct procedure.

The designation in the first evaluation summary she had filed had been WC-Eirene-provisional, origin notation sphere-42. By the third summary the provisional flag had been removed. She had filed seven summaries since then. The volume had been increasing at a rate she had not been tracking against anything, because tracking accumulations against each other was not within her assignment.

Twelve units was more than she had seen cross the courtyard at any one time.

They moved toward the south utility wing and turned the corner at the loading dock approach, the handlers maintaining their sidewalk positions through the turn. She watched until the last unit was around the corner and the courtyard was empty again.

She knew the south utility wing. She had been fourteen years old when the lock authorization for the staging hall landed on the copy desk where she was doing her junior apprentice hours. A senior Scribe had given it to her because it was a straightforward maintenance lock: the kind of instrument that required documentation but not judgment. She had copied it and filed it and not thought about it again. Her master had told her she had done it correctly. The authorization had specified no end date, which was unusual, but she had not known then that it was unusual.

The staging hall had not appeared in any instrument she had copied in six weeks. It was not locked now.

She returned to her desk. She wrote nothing in the margin of the instrument she had been working on before the window. The courtyard observation was not an instrument category she had been given to work from. She completed the maintenance authorization for the south utility wing — the fourth that week, specifying expanded storage calibration in the lower west section — and added it to the stack.

---

She went to the registry room in the late afternoon, when the light in the main office had gone gray enough that she would need to angle the lamp again and she was tired of angling the lamp.

She told herself, going in, that she was cross-referencing. She had a legitimate purpose. The designation T-044 appeared in thirty-one instruments she had processed in six weeks, and while each of those instruments was individually within the scope of her assignment, together they mapped to an operational structure she had not been given context for. Understanding the structure was not intervention. Understanding what she was recording was what allowed her to record it accurately. She was a Scribe. Accuracy was the virtue.

She signed the access log with her name, the time, and *cross-reference, canonical processing* in the purpose field. She went to the M-shelf.

The Knight deployment registry was a bound volume, thick-spined, the pages dense with the specific notation of active service records: designation, posting date, current station, active assignment, any suspended authorities. She had worked in documents like this in her apprentice years and she knew how to move through them. She found T-044 in the first third of the volume.

She had half-known, she thought afterward, in the way you know things before the knowledge has arranged itself into words — the way you know a room has changed before you've identified which thing changed. She had been copying T-044 for six weeks. She had filed the transit suspension. She had filed thirty additional instruments in the authorization chain around it. She had understood, at a level below language, that T-044 was the center of a structure. The structure had a shape she could feel in the accumulation the way a Scribe feels the shape of an instrument before she reads it — the weight of it, the binding.

She had been feeling the weight of this for six weeks.

Her sister's name was in the entry with a posting date three years prior. Current status: *deployment, active, transit authority suspended by Canon's instrument.* The Canon's instrument reference number was the one she had copied and filed and cross-referenced and cited in three subsequent instruments. She had handled that number thirty-one times.

She stood in the registry room.

She was aware that this was not, strictly speaking, a surprising development. The pattern had been telling her what it was. She had been allowing herself to continue processing accurately rather than reading the pattern into anything she was not yet prepared to name. That was fair and it was also a choice. She was looking at the outcome of that choice.

She thought about the morning the transit suspension had arrived, six weeks ago. She had been eating a roll — the station bread, which her sister had told her not to eat and she had not listened, because her sister told her not to eat the station bread every time she visited Ocipheus Station and it was a habit of advice that Vega had made a habit of not following. The runner had brought three instruments. She had put the roll down and started copying. The transit suspension was the second instrument. She had processed it in under an hour. She had not known. She had sealed the canonical original and filed it with her working copy and moved to the third instrument and not known.

She had not known.

She did not find this as consoling as she had expected it would be.

She replaced the M-volume. She had made no annotations. Her name was in the access log. She returned to the copy office and sat down at her desk.

---

The instruments she had copied that day were dry. She aligned them and moved them to the transfer stack. The runner would collect them in the morning and carry them to the sealed archive, where they would become canonical and unalterable and the official record of what had been decided. She would never see most of them again.

She kept working copies. Every Scribe did: not canonical, not official, not anything the Liturgy needed to acknowledge or could be held accountable for. Just her own hand, her own reference. They went into the box in the lower left drawer.

The transit suspension from six weeks ago was near the bottom. She found it by the texture of the page — she had pressed harder than usual that morning, the nib had been cold, the lines were slightly heavier than her standard hand. She had not noticed this when she made the copy. She noticed it now.

She set it on the desk.

She picked up her pen.

She wrote her sister's name in the margin, in the space between the header and the body text, in the slightly larger hand she had learned before the canonical script, before the certification, the one she still used in letters — a bit more room in the vowels, the first letter held a beat longer. She wrote the name. Then she drew a line through it.

Scribes did not annotate canonical instruments with their feelings. This was not a canonical instrument. This was her working copy, hers to keep or discard, and the line she drew through it did not remove it; the name was still legible underneath, the ink only slightly darkened, the letters still there in the shape she had learned before anyone had told her what precision was for. She could see it. She would always be able to see it.

She put the working copy in the box and closed the drawer.



She was the record.

She had understood this in the abstract at the beginning of the posting. She was understanding it differently now.

She angled the lamp for the last time that day and covered the ink.

[Beat 9]
SPHERE 31 — ROWE FOUND

She lifted the latch.

The bin's lid was heavy — seasoned oak, a thumb's-width thick, with iron hinges that had been oiled recently enough that they gave without complaint. This was a detail she noted and set aside. Someone had maintained these hinges. Someone had been living near them. She held the lid one-handed as it came up, kept her weight on her back foot, and looked into the dark.

The smell was grain. Warm grain, the drowsy heat of settled wheat doing whatever wheat did in a closed container. And underneath it, the specific human smell of someone who had not been near water for longer than they would have chosen.

She waited three seconds. In three seconds, anyone startled awake in a dark enclosed space makes a sound. The sound she heard after three seconds was breathing — steady, carefully steady, the breath of someone who had been awake for longer than she'd been standing at the latch and had decided on quiet.

He was in the back left corner, pressed into the angle where the bin wall met the rear panel. His knees were drawn up and his shoulders were back against the wood and his rifle was across his lap with both hands on it. Not raised. Present.

Thirty years in the Order and the thing she trusted first was her body's read. Her body read: still. Contained. Not going to move first. She took this information the way she took all physical information — through the chest and the forearms and the set of her own standing — and let it settle before she let herself look at anything else.

She looked at his face.

Not Cauld. The proportions were slightly wrong — not wrong, different; she'd seen enough intake photographs to know the range of Sphere-adjacent phenotype variation without being able to name which specific variant he was. The bone structure around the eye sockets was different from anything in the standard Cauld range. The skin tone was a particular kind of brown that she'd seen in Calyx's southern coast populations but without the underlying warmth, something cooler and more even. He was compact — she'd estimated that from the boot prints, and she'd estimated correctly. Not tall. Built like someone who had worked with his hands for a long time and then been given six months of military conditioning, which produced a specific combination of machinist's hands and a soldier's posture that didn't quite fit the same body.

He watched her.

She let him watch. He needed to see her make a decision about him before he could make a decision about her, and the decision she was making, which she needed to make visible, was the one she was in fact making: she was not drawing the dissolution blade.

Her left hand was at her belt. She moved it deliberately away from the blade and held it open at her side.

He held still. He was very good at holding still.

She looked at the rifle. She had to look at it carefully because the light through the service entrance was angled and the bin's shadow fell across it, and what she needed to see was the receiver plate. She'd read enough intake documentation to have a file called *observed Sphere-crossing artifacts, material and technological* and the file had four major categories: metallurgy, textiles, agricultural implements, and weapons. The weapons category was the smallest because weapons transferred between Spheres less often than the guilds preferred to advertise, and Lyra had not contributed to the weapons sub-file because her own research had concentrated on agricultural and material extraction. She had read the weapons sub-file once, two years ago, as a cross-reference verification. She had not expected to need it.

The receiver plate had a notation she had seen in that sub-file.

She looked away from the rifle and back at his face. His expression had not changed. He was watching her in the specific way of someone who had been watching armed people make decisions about him for long enough to have a developed theory of what the decisions looked like before they were enacted, and who was waiting to see which decision she was making.

"I know what you are," she said.

She said it in Cauld. She watched his face to see whether any word in the sentence registered.

Nothing registered. His eyes did not move, which was itself information: in Lyra's experience, even people without shared language responded to human speech with some shift, some change in attention, the physiological response to sound organized in patterns that resembled language. He had no such response. It was not the blankness of someone who had encountered a foreign language before and knew what to do with it. It was the blankness of someone for whom the sounds she was producing had no architectural similarity to any sounds his experience had filed as language.

She had read this in the intake profiles. The description had been: *complete linguistic disjunction upon initial Sphere crossing. No surface-level phonetic bridge with any catalogued Cauld variant.* She had read this in the clinical language of the research literature and had found it interesting in the clinical way that research literature produced interest. She had not known it would look like this.

She went down on one knee.

She did it slowly, because fast movements in small dark spaces were the wrong choice. She did it with her hand still visible and still not at her belt. At knee level she was shorter than him, which was the point — she had fifteen centimeters of height and three infusions and she was in his grain bin without asking, and the one thing she could adjust was the height. So she adjusted it.

She pointed at him. She pointed at the exit she'd come through. She made the gesture that universally meant *come:* hand extended, fingers curled inward, the motion toward her own body.

He looked at her hand. He looked at her face. He did not move, which was also information: he was not accepting the gesture without understanding it, and he was not refusing it from hostility. He was reading it the way she was reading him. Methodically. Gathering before acting.

She held the gesture.

He looked at the rifle in his lap. He looked at her open hand. He looked at the entrance she'd used.

He did something she hadn't anticipated: he looked at the lid of the bin, which she was still holding open with her raised hand. He looked at it for a second, the specific attention of someone noting an object's weight and balance and what that meant for the person holding it.

Then he looked back at her face.

He set the rifle down against the bin wall, very slowly, with both hands visible. Then he stood.

Standing, he was still shorter than her by half a head. He had the quality of someone who was aware of that and was not performing ease about it; he simply had an accurate read of physical facts and was orienting to them. He reached for the rifle again when he was upright and she tensed — he saw her tense, read it accurately — and he stopped, hand on the rifle's sling, and looked at her with an expression that said: *the rifle comes. This is where I will need you to decide.*

She nodded.

He put the sling over his shoulder.

She lowered the bin lid and gestured again toward the entrance. He moved when she moved, which was the correct professional reading of a situation where you were being led by someone with more information than you had. He kept one body-width of space between them. She appreciated this. It was not the spacing of submission — it was the spacing of someone who wanted enough room to do something different if something different became necessary.

In the main warehouse floor, moving between the rows of bins toward the service entrance, she put up one finger. He looked at it. She pointed at the direction they were going, then put up the finger again. One person. Ahead.

His hand didn't go to the rifle. It found the sling and settled there. Ready but not anticipating. She filed this under *combat discipline, trained.* Which was not a surprise given the research literature, but it was useful to confirm.

She knocked twice on the service entrance frame before she pushed it open.

---

Orim was in the passage with his back to the entrance, watching the loading yard. He did not turn around. He said, "We have eleven minutes."

Ardea was two meters down the passage, watching the north end where the formal commercial entrance connected to the district's main road. She turned at the sound of the door. She looked at Rowe. She looked at the rifle. She looked at Lyra.

"You're bringing him," she said. Not a question. The tone of a professional who had received unexpected information and was already adjusting her operating model to accommodate it.

"Yes," Lyra said.

Ardea absorbed this. "The courier can carry four but not comfortably."

"He walks." Lyra looked at Rowe, who was looking at Orim with the expression of someone who had learned to read threat-postures in people of different physical types and was determining which category the old man fell into. "He walks well."

Orim turned around. He looked at Rowe in the way Orim looked at small things: with complete and unhurried attention, the minor scryer's orientation toward the specific rather than the general. "Sphere 31," he said.

He was not asking Lyra. He was stating it for the record, the way he stated things he had already confirmed through means he did not explain.

Rowe looked at Orim. He did not understand the words. He understood the attention, which was a different kind of comprehension.

"We'll need a name," Ardea said. "Something shorter than whatever his designation is in the intake ledger."

The intake ledger used Sphere numbers and intake sequence numbers. The research literature referred to this particular linguistic family — Sphere 31, if that was where he was from, and the rifle's receiver plate said yes, and the complete phonetic disjunction confirmed it — by a catalogue reference that was fifteen characters of research notation. Lyra had been thinking about names since she'd looked at him in the bin, which was a professional departure she'd noted and filed in a different location than she usually filed professional departures.

He had said one sound when she'd held up her hand and said, in Cauld, *you:* a sound she'd recognized as his own word for himself. One syllable, high vowel, soft consonant at the close. She had a phonetic transcription of it in her notebook from the intake profiles. The closest Cauld approximation was two letters.

"Rowe," she said. She said it to Ardea and she said it loud enough that the man who was now standing in the service passage of a grain warehouse in Bressant with a rifle over his shoulder and three strangers around him could hear it.

He looked at her.

She pointed at him. She said it again. "Rowe."

He stood with whatever he was used to standing with — the patience of someone who had spent seven months being processed by systems that did not explain themselves — and then, very carefully, with the precision of someone placing a word in an unfamiliar sentence, he said it back.

Not quite right. The vowel was slightly off, which was the vowel she'd already anticipated being off because the research literature noted that Sphere-31 linguistic families had a different vowel register. Close enough to be a name. She nodded.

"Rowe," she said again.

"Rowe," he said. His inflection was flat, which was not indifference; it was the flat careful repetition of someone who learned exactly one word at a time.

"Right," Ardea said. "Eight minutes."

---

They moved.

The Heloth courier was waiting at the end of the district's south approach, where Ardea had left it under the overhang of a disused loading bay. Getting Rowe onto the courier required three things: demonstrating what the courier was, communicating that he needed to hold on, and confirming that he'd understood both. The first she accomplished by walking up to the machine and putting her hand on its shoulder housing. The second she accomplished by taking his hand and placing it on the grip bar and covering it with her own for a moment. The third she accomplished by looking at him and waiting until he looked back at her and nodded — not the acquiescent nod of someone performing agreement but the considered nod of someone who had confirmed they understood a physical requirement.

He rode it the way a trained person rode unfamiliar transportation: with his weight distributed carefully and both hands on the bar and his eyes on the terrain ahead rather than on the machine. She noted this and filed it.

Eight minutes. Then seven. Then six, when they reached the northern wharf road and the departure barge manifests were posted at the dock authority office and she needed to find the commercial barge going north rather than the formal transit barges, which would ask for papers she was not certain she could produce for Rowe because Rowe did not exist in any registry she had access to.

The commercial barge was at the second dock from the north end. It was loading grain from the warehouse district's overflow lots — the bulk-goods traffic that moved up the Veil River toward the Atrament processing centers, unremarkable, seventeen barges per week at this season, the dock authority stamp on the manifest was a formality that the dockworkers had been performing for so long that the stamp had worn shallow and left partial impressions on the paper. She bought passage for four under the authority stamp of a Calyx commercial guild she held a provisional membership in — the provisional membership had cost eleven quanta in Calyx six years ago and had paid for itself twice over — and paid in credit vouchers, which was normal for commercial passage.

Rowe watched her conduct this transaction with the attention of someone who was learning a new system's visible procedures. He said nothing. He kept one hand on the rifle's sling. The dock workers gave him the look they gave anyone unfamiliar, which was brief and categorical, and then returned to loading grain.

"Three minutes," Ardea said, from behind her.

She handed the passage receipt to the dock authority's junior clerk, who stamped it with the worn stamp and returned it, and she moved toward the gangway.

---

The barge was called the *Houndstooth.* It smelled of river mud and old rope and whatever had spilled from the grain containers in the last crossing and dried into the planking. Below decks there was a cargo hold that had been converted to a passenger space by the addition of rope hammocks along one bulkhead and a bench along the other, none of which were in particularly good condition, all of which were better than standing on the open deck in the cold for however many hours the Veil River required to deliver them to the Atrament border.

Lyra went below and sat on the bench. Ardea took the rope hammock farthest from the hatch. Orim climbed in after her and found a crate near the porthole that suited him, which Lyra had come to understand meant a position where he could see the river and think.

Rowe stood at the base of the steps.

She looked at him. He looked at the space: the hammocks, the bench, the crates, the specific geometry of a cargo hold repurposed for people who were not meant to be comfortable. He was reading it the way she was now accustomed to watching him read unfamiliar spaces — not warily, but with careful thoroughness, the assessment of someone who had developed a practical relationship with the analysis of enclosed spaces over the past three weeks.

He found a spot against the casks farthest from the hatch, which was also farthest from the only exit, which was the choice of someone who had learned that being between strangers and exits was worse than being in a corner. He sat down. He put the rifle across his knees. He closed his eyes.

The barge moved.

Lyra felt the specific shift of water-borne motion in her inner ear, the barely-perceptible unhinging from the shore, and she opened her notebook. She had a phonetic transcription system developed over three years of field documentation — not ideal for this, because the field documentation had been for documenting Cauld linguistic variants, which shared most of her baseline phonetic architecture, and whatever Rowe spoke did not. But it was better than nothing. It was considerably better than nothing, because nothing meant she would have to wait until he had enough Cauld to tell her what she was already certain she needed to know.

She started with the sounds he'd produced in the warehouse. The one syllable he'd said when she'd said *you.* The sound he'd made when he'd looked at the latch — a small sound, involuntary, something between recognition and surprise. The rhythm of his breathing when he'd first understood she wasn't drawing her blade.

She wrote them down as accurately as she could represent them with the alphabet she had.

Then she opened her research satchel and found the intake profiles. The Sphere-31 file was thin — three pages of notes, most of them secondhand from a Vierna field researcher who'd documented a small influx seven years ago. The phonetic sample in the notes was four words. She compared them to her transcription.

The vowel structure matched in two of the four. The consonant clusters were the same family. She looked at her transcription of the sound he'd made when she'd pointed at him and said his name back.

She'd transcribed it as something between an *r* and a *w.* The Vierna researcher's notes had a parallel sound in the phonetic sample, marked with the same uncertainty: *r/w (voiced approximant, non-rhotic).*

She looked at the ceiling of the cargo hold.

She had found a pierced conscript in a grain bin in a Vierna river city. She had read three pages of field notes seven years ago documenting a small influx from the same Sphere. She had, in the last six months, processed approximately forty Scry data blocks derived from observations of that same Sphere. She had not, in any of those forty transactions, connected those observations to a living person who might have watched those observations happen from the other side.

The intake literature called this *contextual professional distance.* She had always found the phrase accurate.

She found it, in this particular moment, somewhat less accurate than she had previously.

She put the intake profiles away and returned to her transcription notes. There was work to be done and she preferred to do it rather than to think about the alternative, which was not doing it, which was not an alternative that served anyone.

---

Orim came to sit beside her at the porthole in the third hour.

"Fourteen red flags since Pontis," she said, before he could ask.

"There's a cluster at Archival Gate." He looked at the river through the porthole. "Named for Arnault d'Archival, who established Vierna's river-rights claim in Year 312. Every flag since has been the same claim in smaller form." He was quiet for a moment. "The man in the corner is asleep."

She looked. Rowe's head had dropped forward. His hands were still on the rifle but the grip had loosened, the specific loosening of someone who had finally let themselves believe that sleep was currently safer than wakefulness.

"He sleeps with his boots on," she said.

"People who've slept in unsafe places do," Orim said.

"Yes."

Orim looked at her transcription notes, which were open on the crate between them. He looked at them the way he looked at things he was reading without appearing to read. "The intake literature," he said finally, "describes the linguistic disjunction as complete. No surface-level phonetic bridge."

"It is complete."

"And yet." He tilted his head slightly in the direction of the phonetic transcription. "You've already started."

"I've documented sounds. That's not a bridge. A bridge requires two ends."

"You've located one end," he said. "He has the other." He returned to looking at the river. "That's how bridges work."

She did not respond to this because it was accurate and did not require response.

The Veil River moved north under them, carrying them toward the Atrament border and the rail junction and the sequence of days and contingencies that lay between here and the Oculus Memoriae. Somewhere ahead of them, four people who had taken what they'd been sent to take were managing a ten-day lead. Somewhere in her research satchel, a three-page field note on Sphere-31 linguistic structures was sharing space with forty cross-referenced Scry data blocks from the same Sphere, which was sharing space with a phonetic transcription she'd begun in a grain warehouse with seventeen minutes on the clock.

She had been, for thirty years, a researcher. She knew the shape of a question. The question she was presently holding had the specific quality of the kind that, once asked, could not be unasked.

She had not yet asked it.

She was building the vocabulary to ask it correctly. This required time. Time was what the river provided.

She turned back to her transcription notes and continued working.

---

The Atrament border appeared on the morning horizon not as architecture but as smoke, which was accurate for Atrament in a way it was not accurate for other Houses. She smelled it before she saw it: the specific mineral sharpness of high-temperature metal processing, which was different from wood smoke, different from the controlled burn of Catalyst residue, different from anything she'd grown up near on the Ocipheus peninsula with its clean mountain approaches and its archive rooms and its vigil lamps that were always kept precisely fueled.

Rowe was awake. He'd been awake for an hour — she'd heard his breathing change three hours past, the specific shift from sleep to watchfulness, and had left him to come back to himself in the way people needed to, when they'd been sleeping somewhere unfamiliar among strangers. He'd come up the companionway stairs to the deck after a while, and she'd heard him up there, and had not followed.

He came back below when the smoke was visible.

He stood at the porthole. He looked at the smoke on the horizon for a long time.

She watched him watch it.

She had been a researcher for thirty years. She had read the intake profiles. She had documented the Scry data blocks. She had noted, in passing, what the files noted in passing — that the Sphere from which Sphere-31 conscripts came had been observed, in the most recent Scry session documented, as *showing evidence of rapid industrial expansion.* She had noted this in the clinical register of the research literature and had not thought about what *rapid industrial expansion* smelled like from the inside of it.

She thought about it now.

She looked at his face while he looked at the smoke. He was not showing anything she could name, which she'd come to understand meant he was showing something he'd decided not to name.

She picked up her notebook. She opened it to the phonetic transcription she'd started in the warehouse. She opened it to a fresh page and wrote one word in Cauld, in her largest research hand, and held it up.

*FACTORY.*

She waited.

He looked at the notebook. He looked at the smoke. He looked back at the notebook.

He pointed at the smoke on the horizon and made a gesture she hadn't seen him use before: both hands, palm-down, fingers spread, moving apart slowly, the way you'd describe something that had once been there and was now wider, larger, more.

Then he pointed at the word she'd written.

She wrote: *factory. Source: Sphere 31. First Cauld word acquired without instruction.*

She put the notebook in her satchel. She would build on it tonight, when the barge was moving in the dark and there was no smoke on the horizon and only the river and the work to be done.

The smoke grew as they came north. It was very large. It was the kind of thing you expected to be large and still found larger than expected, which was a specific category of experience she didn't have a name for. She noted the gap and filed it under *pending.*

She had a great many things in the *pending* file. It was becoming a significant archive.

She had not been a person who maintained a significant pending archive before this. She had always resolved her pending files efficiently, as a matter of professional practice. The pending archive was new.

She let it grow.

The barge moved north and the smoke grew and behind her, in the corner, Ardea was cleaning her dissolution blade with the competent automatic focus of a soldier maintaining equipment in the space between one thing and the next, and Orim was watching the river through the porthole with sixty years of practiced attention, and Rowe was standing at the porthole looking at the smoke on the Atrament horizon in a way that she could not characterize with any precision and was going to have to find the vocabulary for.

One word at a time.

She was good at that.

[Beat 10]
SEVEN MONTHS

The barracks smelled of metal-oil and wet wool and the particular sourness of men who had not been warm enough for long enough.

He learned *kal* first. Stop. He learned it from the gap between walking and impact — from continuing when everyone else had stopped and from the hand that snapped around his collar and jerked him sideways into a wall. The sound the others made. Not laughter. More like recognition. *That one will learn.* He was not certain this was a compliment.

After *kal* came the equipment words. This made sense: equipment had to function or someone's face would reflect the consequence of its not functioning, and that someone was frequently him. *Kest* was the lock on the action housing. *Vurt* was the strap. *Reml* — he thought of it as reml, the r rolled in the throat — was the cleaning kit, the pull-through rod and the oil bottle and the small brush for the breach face. He learned to say these words by learning to use the things they named. The Cauld was built backwards from how language was supposed to work. You didn't learn the word for oil and then find oil. You held oil in your hand and made the sounds associated with oil until the sounds stuck.

By the end of the first week he had perhaps twenty words. All of them were either objects or commands.

---

Three weeks in, he found the intake form.

It wasn't his — it was a stack of them, sitting on a clerk's desk in the outer office, and the clerk was somewhere else, and Rowe was waiting for someone to tell him to stop waiting. He picked up the top form because it was there and because he was beginning to understand that the written form of the language existed and that some of the squiggles resolved into things he could almost parse if he stared at them long enough.

He could read numbers. Numbers were numbers.

The column heading he couldn't make out. But the column contained numbers, and one of them was 31, and 31 was his.

There was a word in a box beside it. He would learn that word four months later. But that day he didn't have it. He had the number. The number was enough. The number meant there was a catalogue. The number meant the catalogue went past 31, because numbers worked that way.

He set the form back on the stack, face-down, the way he'd found it. He waited for someone to tell him to stop waiting.

---

The rifles were a different kind of knowing.

They handed them out on the third range day — bolt-action, magazine-fed, the action smooth from regular maintenance. He picked his up the way the trainer showed the man beside him: right hand here, left hand supporting. Proper grip. The trainer moved on to the next person.

His right hand moved to the bolt.

He didn't think about it first. His hand knew where the bolt was, and his hand knew what the motion was — lift, pull back, seat the round, push forward, lock down — before the trainer had finished demonstrating it on someone else's rifle. He had it loaded. He didn't fire. He waited.

The trainer came back. Looked at him. Said something he didn't fully understand — the Cauld equivalent of *well,* or maybe *so.*

The trainer took the rifle. Showed it to another trainer. They talked. He watched their hands while they talked, because their hands on the rifle were language he already had.

The mechanism was the same. Not the same model — nothing so exact. The lock housing was different; the finish on the bolt was different; the magazine was better, the feeding cleaner. But the *idea* of it was the same family. His world had made an older version. He had seen the catalog entry at the ironmonger's shop on Cress Street, the one that sold industrial equipment alongside kegs of wire-hemp and bolts of sheeting canvas. There had been an illustrated page, a diagram with lines and numbers indicating the lock components.

The Cauld had the finished form.

He had no words for this in Cauld. He had full words for it in his own language — *derivation* and *iteration* and *came from somewhere,* though he didn't know what it had come from or how. He had the words. They were useless here.

The trainer put him in the front row for the rest of range day and called him something — an approving word, he thought. He filed it under things he didn't want to explain.

---

The others who had come from other places were not hard to find once he knew to look.

There was a particular quality to the confusion. Not ordinary confusion — not the confusion of a man who had grown up in the Cauld and was trying to understand why he was being ordered to do something pointless. Different. The confusion of a man whose confusion had no category for itself. He recognized it. He had seen it in his own face in the tin-sheet mirror in the barracks washroom.

Some of them had been here longer. You could tell — they had lost that quality, or buried it deep enough that it only surfaced sometimes, in a specific way, usually at night. There was one man, Sphere 22 on his intake form, who had been in Vierna for two years. He spoke Cauld with almost no accent. He ate the food without looking at it. He was helpful about explanations when Rowe's Cauld was too thin to follow an order. He was also extremely good at being somewhere else when things went wrong.

Rowe did not judge this. He filed it for future use.

---

The one from the close world came in month two, in a transfer batch from the eastern conscript station.

His hands were a machinist's hands — the specific callousing on the web between thumb and forefinger, the palm hardness that came from tools rather than from ground work. He was about thirty, with the look of a man who had spent the last eight weeks confused in a language he didn't have and was now confused in a second language he also didn't have.

They had no Cauld between them. They had a different problem.

The first time they tried to talk, it was in the dark of the barracks after lights. Rowe said something in his own language — not expecting anything, just to hear himself. The man from the transfer batch turned around.

What came out of his mouth was not the same. But parts of it were not entirely different.

They spent a week in the evenings working out which parts. They found about thirty words — or what seemed like thirty words, which might have been fewer if some of them were not actually the same word said differently, and might have been more if some of them were not false cognates that led to long misunderstandings and then to short agreements about not using those particular sounds anymore.

Factory. *Fabrik.* Not the same word. Close enough.

Machine. *Mashin.* Again.

The man had been on a machine floor when it happened. He had not chosen to come. He did not understand the full picture of what he had been brought here for.

This was not a surprise. It was confirmation. Confirmation was different from surprise: it didn't change anything, but it made the thing more solid under the feet. He was not the only one, and the thing that had taken him had not done it to only one world.

They managed conversation at the level of two people trying to agree on what to eat for dinner who happen to be dining in separate countries. It was not nothing.

---

By month three he could follow orders.

This was not the same as understanding orders. But it was sufficient. The twenty-word vocabulary had become sixty words, had become a hundred and something, had become a grammar he was building like a man building a dike: slowly, with wet hands, plugging gaps as they emerged. He had names for things. He had command words. He had the names of ranks, which were important, and the names of positions, which were important.

He had no words for *loyalty* or *betrayal* or *injustice.* No Cauld for *conscription,* though he suspected the word existed somewhere. He had *morning* and *ration* and *advance* and *hold your position* and *fall back.* He had words for three kinds of terrain. He had the name of the rifle.

He had read the proof stamp on the receiver housing, the angular military notation pressed into the metal near the action end: SPHERE-SOURCE PATTERN — DESCENT CORPS AUTHORITY — NOT FOR CIVILIAN REGISTRY. He had needed the words separately before he could read them together. *Sphere* from the intake form context. *Source* from the dock-yard vocabulary. *Not* and *registry* from the command structure. Put together, what they said was: the institution had noted where this weapon came from. Had stamped it into the metal. Had issued it anyway, and written *not for civilian registry* as if the concern were distribution rather than origin.

He kept this in a box he did not open. Some thoughts, in a body running on a limited account, you held without spending.

By month five he could understand most of what was being said around him if people were not speaking fast and if the subject matter was one he had words for.

Reading was slower. The written language followed different rules than the spoken. Some of the sounds he had mapped onto letters were wrong. He could read numerals, which were the same, and he could read his own designation on the unit board, which appeared regularly and was therefore eventually parseable.

In month six, a man at the clerk's desk used a word he had been seeing on forms for months, and pointed at him, not unkindly. He understood from context that it meant something like *from somewhere else.* He did not understand yet that it was a category. He did not understand that the category had a legal definition, a bracket in the intake system, a designation that placed him at a specific distance from the rank ladder and confirmed he would never be on it. He understood that the word applied to him and to the man from the close world and to the man from Sphere 22 who was good at being somewhere else.

He filed this.

---

The engagement in month seven had no name that he heard, or if it had a name, he didn't have the Cauld for it. He was ordered to advance. The column moved south on a road that was not a good road, in weather that was not good weather — low cloud, the smell of coming rain, mud already thick at the margins.

He reached the ridge.

From the ridge he could see the valley below. He could see the force to the east. He could see the force to the south. He could identify neither one by what it was doing, because what both were doing was the same thing from different angles, which was moving toward the middle of the valley, which was where his column was going.

He understood geometry. He understood what happened to anything caught between two things moving toward the same point. His world had not used the exact word, but his world had had machines, and a man who worked machines all his life developed a specific relationship with things that worked in one motion and things that worked in several conflicting motions.

He looked at the men in the column. He looked at the two forces below. He looked at the space where the three motions would converge.

He had no word for any of the faces in either force. He had no word for the flag — if either side was carrying a flag. He did not know what either force was here for. He did not know what he was here for, in any sense larger than *advance, hold your position, fall back.*

He had nothing here. Nothing to stay for.

He turned around.

He walked back up the road. Thirty seconds, maybe. The column was moving forward; the sounds of the column were moving away from him and toward the valley, and then the sounds of the engagement were beginning below, and he was walking away from both. No one stopped him. They were busy.

He walked until the sound was behind him. He walked until the sound was distant. He walked until the sound was gone, and then he kept walking, because the direction he was going was away and away was the correct direction.

---

Bressant was a city the way any city was a city — too many people moving in too many directions for any single person to be notable. He had enough Cauld to move through it quietly. He had enough Cauld to understand *get out of the way,* which was all you needed in a grain district at harvest.

The grain district in autumn was full. Full warehouses meant full loading yards meant full streets meant constant foot traffic and very little attention paid to individuals moving along the margins of it.

He found the warehouses by smell. Grain had a smell — not unpleasant, a warm dusty smell that reminded him of the mill in autumn when the cotton bales came in and the whole floor had that particular dry-textile warmth. Grain was different but the principle was the same. Large quantities of dry material in an enclosed space had a smell that carried. He followed it.

He slept in the first warehouse for three nights before anyone came to the section he was using. Then he moved to the next. He was not good at this yet. He was learning.

Three weeks in a grain district is long enough to learn the specific warehouses with irregular inspection schedules, the yard supervisors who were former military and noticed things, the loading crews who didn't look at idle men as long as the idle men looked plausible. He looked plausible. He had always looked plausible — compact, unremarkable, the face of a man who was probably doing whatever he was supposed to be doing.

He ate when he could. What he could eat was irregular and varied between *adequate* and *barely.* The military rations had been bad. Three weeks of worse than military rations produced a different kind of hunger — the kind that lived in the body as a specific hollowness behind the ribs, not the sharp hunger of a missed meal but the dull hunger of a body running the math on its reserves and coming up short.

He kept the rifle.

This was not practical. It was heavy, had to be kept dry, was not the kind of thing a warehouse worker normally carried and therefore had to be concealed. He kept it anyway. The reason he had was this: it was the one thing he had learned to do here that was entirely his own doing. He had not been handed the skill. He had not been ordered into it. He had recognized something and claimed it.

He was aware this was a poor argument. He kept the rifle.

---

He had four words of Cauld that he trusted.

Not trusted to be correct — he was fairly confident they were correct. Trusted in a different sense. Trusted to be his. The military vocabulary was serviceable and large and all of it was borrowed from necessity. These four were different.

*Faeb.* Factory. He had found this word not in a barracks but in Bressant, painted on the side of a building — a textile concern, he thought, though the machinery visible through the windows was different from his own. He had spent ten minutes reading the sign and come away with one reliable word. The rest might have been right. This one he was certain of.

*Fume.* Smoke. He knew this one because smoke was present and someone in the loading yard had said it — said the word and pointed at the warehouse roof, where something was smoldering wrong. He had not needed anyone to point. He had seen the smoke and heard the word at the same moment and they had joined.

*Morn.* Morning. He had this from the drill schedule, from hearing it every single morning for seven months: *morn-formation, morn-ration, morn-drill.* The word had the quality of inevitability.

*Solen.* Gone. This one he had worked for — he had asked the man from Sphere 22, in careful Cauld, where a specific person had gone, and the man had used a word he could parse, and that word had been *solen,* and the specific person had been gone in a way he understood, and the word had taken.

He repeated them sometimes in the dark of the grain bins. Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone. Not because he was trying to communicate anything. Not because they were more useful than the military words or the transport words or the district words. Because they were his in a specific way. Because he had found them rather than been handed them. Because in his own language — which he was losing, slowly, in the way you lose a skill you don't use, the vocabulary staying but the ease of it beginning to tighten — these were things he had understood before he had words for them in anything.

He still thought in his own language entirely. But there were gaps appearing. Moments where he reached for his own word and found the Cauld word faster, because the Cauld word had been used yesterday and the other one hadn't.

He did not find this comforting.

---

The bin he was in now was the largest. He had found it two days ago, which meant he had been in one place too long and should move again. He would move tomorrow.

The bin was warm from the grain — grain generated warmth as it settled, something to do with the residual moisture in the kernels working itself out, a process he had no name for in any language but recognized as physical fact. The grain was at chest level. He had a clear column of air above him. The bin was dark except for a thin line of light along the roof seam where the planking had warped with age.

Outside: the sounds of the loading yard, which ran in a cycle he had learned. Heavy foot traffic in the morning, lighter through midday, the grinding of the hoist-wheels in late afternoon when the evening deliveries came through. It was mid-morning now. He could tell from the sound.

He had three days of food left. He was counting carefully.

He repeated the four words, not aloud. Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.

The grain pressed against his chest with a warmth that was not comfort exactly but was not nothing either. He was not comfortable. He was warm, which was different, and hidden, which was different again, and those two things were enough for the present moment. He had learned, in seven months, that the present moment was the appropriate unit of time for measuring sufficiency. Not the day. The present moment: warm, hidden, air in the lungs, three days of food.

He heard the boards above the warehouse shift.

He heard, a few seconds after that, the specific sound of someone moving carefully — not the heavy purposeful tread of a supervisor, not the clustered noise of a work crew. The sound of someone trying not to make sound.

He did not move.

His hand, in the dark and in the grain, found the rifle.

[Beat 11]
THE RIVER — FACTORY / SMOKE / MORNING / GONE

The barge was called the *Houndstooth* and smelled accordingly. Below decks, behind the casks, Lyra had found a corner between a stack of oilskin-wrapped bales and the outer hull where river water moved just inches from her ear. She'd been in worse accommodations. She'd been in better. She rolled her coat under her head and tried to think about what she needed to think about, which was a reliable way of ensuring she thought about nothing useful and fell asleep instead.

She slept four hours. She knew this because Orim was still at the porthole when she woke—he kept the same vigils he'd kept for sixty years, which meant he didn't trust darkness to remain darkness without a witness—and when she'd closed her eyes the river had been black and when she opened them it was only a very dark gray.

Her shoulder had locked. Not the right, which had taken the infusion scar badly and always announced itself first with a grinding complaint, but the left, where the courier's sling had worn a groove into the muscle over twenty years of dispatch work before she'd taken her vows and stopped carrying messages and started being one. She worked the joint with her fingers until it grudgingly recalled that it was capable of rotation. The second infusion had given her the height and the density that the Order required and had left her sleeping asymmetrically for a year while the new geometry of her settled. The left shoulder had never entirely forgiven her for it.

"The manifest came," Orim said.

She hadn't heard anyone come or go. The porthole was fogged with breath—his or hers, she couldn't tell—and the light from the river was the kind that told you nothing about the hour except that it wasn't yet morning.

"Leave it," she said, meaning *I'll read it when I can sit up,* and sat up.

He'd set it on the cask nearest her: a sheaf of papers folded around a wax seal that had been broken before it reached her, which was not unusual for commercial cargo and did not mean anything except that the barge's manifest officer had been sloppy or had been paid. She broke the remainder of the seal away and unfolded the sheaf.

The manifest was twenty-three pages. She turned to the back pages first, the way she always did. Commercial manifests ran cargo from the bow aft—whatever paid most was listed earliest, then grain, livestock, textiles, and at the end the small parcels, the things that wanted no notice. The last four pages of this one were standard river traffic: salt fish in wax paper, two crates of mechanical springs from a Calyx smithy, a physician's bag of compound interests that the manifest listed as *sundries, medical* and which were certainly something more specific but would have cost the physician's guild more to itemize. Nothing unusual.

She turned to page eight.

Six Scry data blocks. She counted them twice. Six was not an unusual number for a commercial barge—Scry information was, whatever else it was, commercially valuable, and the guilds had normalized its inclusion in freight documentation the same way they'd normalized the wax seal and the weight declaration. This had happened during her grandmother's grandmother's time. Before that, the data blocks had been kept separate, handled differently, signed by a Templar before transfer. Now they sat between grain and wine like any other cargo, because the guild lawyers had argued successfully that information was information, and the Vigil had not had the stomach for the fight, and here they were.

Lyra had read Scry data blocks in manifests for fifteen years. She had never liked them. She had filed that dislike in the appropriate category—*professional distaste, noted, proceed*—and proceeded, every time, without examining what proceeded meant.

She sat with the manifest in her lap and read the first block.

*Origin Sphere: 14. Method: [contact, surface membrane, 0.3 seconds]. Data class: agricultural, primary. Subject: grain blight variant (see appendix ref 7-A). Observed at production facility. Transfer to: Henkin Grain Trust, letters of credit attached.*

The notation around the brackets was Calyx standard, which she could read faster than she could read her own handwriting at this point. The contact duration—0.3 seconds—was short. Short was better. She had never, in fifteen years, allowed herself to think about what *better* meant in that context, and she did not do so now. She moved to the second block.

Third. Textiles from Sphere 9—a dyeing method, 0.8 seconds, which was longer. She noted that without dwelling on it. The membrane was alive; she knew this the way she knew everything she had been told as a matter of professional orientation, which was to say she had written it into the appropriate ledger in her memory and had not disturbed it since. *Contact wounds the membrane. Duration minimized by guild protocol.* Noted. Filed. The textile guild had presumably found 0.8 seconds necessary for the complexity of the data. The membrane had presumably healed or had not. The manifest did not say.

The fifth block stopped her.

*Origin Sphere: [designation by number only, no catalogue entry]. Method: [contact, surface membrane, 1.4 seconds]. Data class: manufacturing, secondary. Subject: spring-steel alloying method (notation format: see attached sample). Observed at production facility. Transfer to: Henkin Consolidated Arms, Atrament branch.*

The notation format sample was attached: a half-sheet of heavy paper, folded once, with a column of symbols she'd seen before. She had been seeing it, she realized, for twenty years. She'd seen it in commercial code. She'd seen it in Calyx's freight documentation. She'd thought it was Calyx's commercial code because she had never, in twenty years, had reason to think otherwise, and because the category in which she stored *freight notation* had never before intersected with any other category in a way that required her to question its origin.

Rowe was three meters from her, curled against the far hull with his knees drawn up and his face turned toward the planking. He was breathing in the slow, uneven way of someone sleeping badly. His hands, even asleep, were closed around nothing in the specific way of someone who had recently been holding something and expected to need it again.

The notation format on the attached sample matched the notation format she'd seen on his rifle's receiver plate.

She folded the manifest closed. Then she opened it again, because folding it closed did not change what was on page twelve, and she had not become a researcher by refusing to read things. She read all six blocks. By the time she reached the sixth—*Origin Sphere: [same designation, no catalogue entry], 2.1 seconds, manufacturing, primary, large-scale*—she had a category in which to file this. She did not like the category. It did not have clean edges. She filed it anyway, and held the corner of the manifest against her knee, and thought about edges.

"Six," Orim said, from the porthole.

"I counted."

"The fifth and sixth are from the same sphere. The one without a number."

"Yes."

"The notation on the sample sheet." He paused. He said nothing more, in the particular way Orim said nothing more when he had said the thing he meant and was waiting to see if you'd understood it.

She had understood it.

"How long have you known?" she said.

"Since we found him." He turned from the porthole. He had the look he got when he was going to say something that sounded like a joke and wasn't quite. "I've been looking at small things for sixty years. When someone reacts to a notation format, I notice. It's my gift."

His gift was Scrying, minor-class, contractual, which meant he had sat in a room at fifteen years old and pressed his palm against a membrane that he had not been told was alive until afterward, and had done so eleven more times over the next six months until the contractual minimum was met. The Calyx guild paid his pension. He had never volunteered the information about whether it had hurt. She had never asked.

"It might be coincidence," she said.

"It might," he agreed. "So might the rifle."

The rifle was locked in the manifest officer's strong-chest two decks up. She'd had it examined in Calyx by two smiths who between them had sixty years of combined experience and who had looked at the receiver plate and the barrel assembly and the trigger mechanism and had told her, separately and independently, that they had never seen anything like it and that the metal was something they did not have a name for and that the notation on the receiver plate was not any notation they recognized. The second smith had said, *It's very precisely made,* in the tone of someone who had expected to be unimpressed and was not.

"Go to sleep," she told Orim.

"I don't sleep well on rivers," he said. "Something about the sound of the water. It puts me in mind of other sounds." He said this without inflection, which was the worst way to say it.

"Then sit quietly."

He sat quietly.

---

Lyra worked with Rowe for three hours each day. This had been true since Calyx; it had been Orim's suggestion, offered as a professional opinion and understood by all parties to be an order. *If you don't build a shared language,* he'd said, *you will spend the rest of this assignment guessing. I am too old to guess.*

The three hours were not three consecutive hours. They were built from whatever time the ship's schedule, Ardea's watch rotation, and Rowe's unpredictable sleeplessness would allow. She had a research notebook—not a dedicated vocabulary ledger, because she hadn't expected to need one, and a researcher who could not use available materials was a researcher who had missed the point of research—in which she'd begun keeping two parallel columns. The left column held the Cauld word. The right column held her best phonetic rendering of whatever Rowe said when shown the thing the word named.

It was not clean work. He'd come to her with six words when they'd found him: her own name and title, which he'd approximated badly but recognizably; the word for *river;* the word for *write;* and the words for *no* and *yes.* Three of those she'd given him in Calyx, in the first two days. Three she'd found him using on the third morning, without instruction, pointed at things and waiting.

He learned the words for: hull. Water. Cold. Sleep. Eat. Gun—he'd used the Cauld word for *iron-rod-that-speaks,* which was not the correct term but was technically accurate, and she'd given him the correct term and he'd shaken his head slowly, as if deciding something, and used her term from then on. Knife. Fire. Morning. Night. The word for *thank you,* which he'd asked for by pointing at her and making a gesture she'd eventually understood as gratitude, which she'd filed under *social vocabulary, emotional register,* a category she'd not expected to need.

He did not learn the words casually. He held them. She could see the holding—the pause between hearing a word and repeating it, which was not the pause of confusion but the pause of someone placing a thing carefully before releasing it. She'd met three people in her life who learned languages this way. One had become a negotiator for the Templar Compact. The other two were dead under circumstances unrelated to language acquisition, but she noticed the trait and noted it regardless.

He had the notebook page with her phonetic transcription, the one she'd produced in the first session and given to him without thinking too carefully about whether it was standard protocol to give a found man from an unknown Sphere your working research document.
