She'd given it to him on the second day and he'd held it for a long time before he'd looked up and said, in Cauld, very slowly: *You made this for me.* She'd understood him because she'd written the sentence and pointed at it and he'd said it back, but she had not expected the sentence to sound like that, spoken aloud, and she had not expected her response to go anywhere except the *noted, filed, proceed* category.

It had not gone into that category.

She did not examine the alternative category. She noted that it existed. She continued working.

---

At the second hour past midnight the barge's boards announced Rowe's waking with a long creak and then his boots on the planking—he slept in his boots, which was not suspicious, it was what people who'd slept in unsafe places did, and she'd catalogued it but not against him—and she was awake before he reached her corner.

He sat down against the adjacent cask. Not close enough to be a problem. Close enough to be an intention.

She'd left the lamp burning low, which she did when she expected interruption, which she always did when she wasn't somewhere she knew. He looked worse in lamplight than he had in Calyx. The welt along his left cheekbone had gone from red to the yellow-purple of a bruise moving through its stages, and the skin under his eyes had the particular texture of skin that hadn't had enough sleep for long enough that sleep alone wouldn't fix it anymore. He was twenty-nine or thirty-two, she wasn't sure. The paperwork she'd found with him had been damaged. He looked older than either.

He had the notebook. She didn't remember him taking it; she'd been asleep when she'd last had it, which meant he'd taken it quietly, and she filed this the same way she filed the boots.

He pointed at a line she hadn't written.

She held out her hand. He gave her the notebook, and she tipped it toward the lamp.

He'd added a line. The handwriting was precise—machinist's precision, small and even, formed by someone who worked with tolerances—in his own notation. He'd written four symbols and then drawn a line under them and then written them again, with a question mark she recognized as a question mark because it was her question mark, copied from her margin notations. He'd identified her question marks as question marks. She'd missed this.

She looked at him.

He pointed at the notebook, then at his mouth, then made a gesture she'd come to understand meant *I don't have the word.*

"Say it," she said. In Cauld.

He said it. Four syllables, the first two bunched together, the third with a consonant cluster that her alphabet did not have a single character for, the fourth falling away at the end as if he'd started with force and run out of room. She wrote it down the way she wrote everything she didn't understand: exactly, sound by sound, deferring meaning until she had enough architecture to guess at it.

Then she held the paper up and pointed at the first syllable-group.

He pointed, without hesitation, at the cargo manifest.

She went very still.

Not the manifest entire. She looked again. He was pointing at page twelve—the page she'd marked with a sliver of wood, hours ago, habit—and at the notation format on the attached sample sheet.

She said, in Cauld, "You know this."

He shook his head. Not *no.* Something more precise than *no.* He pointed at the symbols and made a gesture she hadn't seen him use before: touching the symbols, then his own eye, then—slowly, as if working through a problem she couldn't fully see—touching them again and his eye again and then pointing outward, at the hull, at the river, at the dark beyond.

"You've seen it before," she said.

He held up both hands. Then he pointed at her vocabulary column, pointed at himself, and held up four fingers.

He wanted to give her four words.

She uncapped her pen.

He looked at the manifest for a long time. Then he looked at the cargo hold—at the casks, the bales, the walls of the thing that contained them—and he said the first word.

She wrote it: three syllables, the first aspirated, the second long, the third a kind of collapse at the back of the throat that she represented with an approximation she'd correct later. She looked up.

He pointed at the wall of casks. At the hull. At the barge around them, at the whole enclosed wooden structure of it and, she thought, at something beyond it that was also enclosed, also structured, also built around a specific function.

*Factory,* she wrote in the left column.

He said the second word.

It was short. One syllable, fricative at the start, open vowel. He pointed upward. She didn't understand. He pointed upward again, then held his hand in front of his face, palm out, fingers curled, and moved it back and forth slowly, as if tracing something rising through air.

She pointed upward. He shook his head. She pointed upward again, added the rising motion with her own hand. He nodded, but not fully. She tried: *smoke, that which rises.* He looked at what she'd written and nodded, slowly, in the way of someone accepting an approximation that will have to do for now.

Third word. Longer. He pointed through the porthole at the gray that was beginning to be something other than absolute darkness. The place between night and morning that didn't have a clean name in most languages she knew.

*Morning,* she wrote.

He looked at it. He looked at her. He said it back—her Cauld word, not his—and then said his word again, and then hers, and then looked at her with an expression she would have filed under *waiting for confirmation* except it had something else in it that she had no file for. Something that had to do with the difference between a word that was yours and a word that was borrowed.

She said, "Morning." She pointed at his transcription and then at hers. "Both," she said.

Something in his face relaxed that she hadn't known was tensed.

He said the fourth word.

She'd expected him to take time with it. He didn't. He said it immediately, flatly, in the tone of something that had been held in the mouth for too long and needed to leave it. One syllable. Hard consonant at the front, vowel falling off the back of it like something released.

She transcribed it.

He didn't point at anything.

He sat with his hands on his knees and looked at the four words on the page—his transcription, her transcription, the two columns running parallel down the paper—and she watched him decide something in the particular way she'd learned to watch him decide things, which was to look at his hands first because his face had more practice at stillness.

She looked at the four words. *Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.*

She looked at him.

He pointed at the words in order: first, second, third, fourth. Then he pointed at the manifest, at the notation format on page twelve. Then he made the gesture she'd come to understand as *there is more:* both hands out, spread, the space between them indicating size.

There was a longer sentence than four words. He was showing her four words the way you hand someone a corner of a document, so they know the document exists.

She wrote: *Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.*

She wrote it again on a separate page and held it up.

She pointed at the first word. "A factory," she said, in Cauld.

He nodded.

"A factory," she repeated, and pointed at him.

His jaw tightened. He nodded again. The tightening was not resistance. It was the specific tension of someone confirming something they've been trying to say for longer than the conversation.

"Smoke." She pointed at the second word.

He pointed at it and looked at the ceiling and said his word for it, and then hers, and she understood—not from logic but from the way his eyes moved between the two—that these were not the same word in two languages. They were two different things that occupied the same transcription because she hadn't had enough vocabulary to distinguish them yet. Her word for smoke was *smoke, industrial, that which rises from process.* His word was something that included process but also included what remained after process ended. Or perhaps what didn't remain. She hadn't heard enough of his language to know.

She drew a small line between the two transcriptions and wrote a question mark.

He looked at it for a long time. Then he took the pen—asking first, carefully, the way he asked for everything—and added a mark beside her question mark. Not an answer. An agreement that there was a question, which was not nothing.

She took the pen back.

She looked at the four words. She looked at the notation on the attached sample sheet. She looked at the Scry data block on page twelve: *Origin Sphere: [designation by number only, no catalogue entry]. Observed at production facility.*

She looked at Rowe.

He was already watching her. He had the careful stillness of someone who has spent a significant amount of time being watched by people who held authority over his circumstances and has learned to be very quiet when that happens, because quiet people are easier to release than people who are noticed.

She said, in Cauld, very slowly: "You came from there."

She did not point at anything. She didn't need to.

He said, "Yes." Her word, not his. Carefully chosen.

---

She didn't sleep again.

She worked in the notebook until the light from the porthole was clear enough to read by without the lamp, and by then she had twelve new words in the framework: the Cauld equivalents and his equivalents and, in four cases, a notation that they were not quite the same thing, that the languages were approaching a concept from different directions and meeting somewhere imprecise in the middle. Language was like that. She'd known three dead languages and two dying ones and the bones of six more, and they all showed the same pattern: the same concept arrived at from different origins, wearing different clothes, recognizable only when you already knew what you were looking for.

She was beginning to know what she was looking for.

Ardea came below at first light to take stock of the provisions, which was her job, and looked at Lyra and then at Rowe, who had fallen asleep somewhere around the fifth hour with his back against the cask and his hands finally open, and then back at Lyra, with the expression of someone who had several questions and had decided, correctly, that none of them were her business yet.

"We'll see Atrament inside of four hours," Ardea said.

"I know."

"You look like you haven't slept."

"I've slept," Lyra said. Not untruthfully.

Ardea accepted this with the professional grace of someone who knew when a superior wanted to be left with her thoughts, and went to count provisions.

Orim appeared at the porthole an hour later with a cup of something he handed down without comment. She drank it. It was not quite tea and not quite anything else; it was the thing Orim made when he thought someone needed warming and didn't want to make a performance of caring about it. She'd had it twice before in her life. Both times had been situations she would have described as bad afterward, once she'd had enough distance to describe them at all.

"Four words," she said.

"I heard."

"You were supposed to be sleeping."

"I was listening. It's different." He settled back into his lean against the hull. His joints cracked when he moved; he'd stopped noticing. "Four words that go together like a sentence."

"The shape of a sentence," she said. "I don't have the full thing yet."

"Factory," he said. "Smoke. Morning. Gone."

"Yes."

He was quiet for a moment. Then: "In my first contracted Scry session, the membrane—the thing I was put in contact with—was approximately the size of my palm. I was told it was a developed specimen. An old one. They didn't tell me what that meant until later." He looked out at the river through the porthole. "I was given a list of questions to hold in my mind during contact. Nineteen items. I managed twelve before the session was called. The information I received was filed immediately by the guild recorder, and I was not permitted to review it." He paused. "This is standard practice. I've never found it strange until recently."

Lyra said nothing.

"The notation on the manifest," he said. "The same as his rifle."

"Yes."

"Someone documented that sphere very thoroughly." He didn't say *before.* He didn't say *before it burned.* He looked at the porthole and then at Rowe's sleeping shape and then at the manifest in Lyra's lap. "Thorough documentation. Filed in the commercial freight system. Sitting between grain and wine in every barge manifest going north for—" He stopped. "How long does a guild manifest archive hold records?"

"Sixty years," she said. "The older ones are at the central repository in Vierna."

"Sixty years," he said. "At minimum." He turned back to the porthole. "Good documentation," he said, in the tone he used for things that were not good at all.

---

Atrament appeared on the horizon as smoke before it appeared as anything else. This was not unusual for Atrament; the smelting districts ran day and night and the prevailing winds from the Cauld's northern territories pushed the output south over the river valley in a long gray smear that navigators used as a heading marker. *When you see the smoke, you're within a day of Atrament.* She'd been told that the first time she'd made this passage, twelve years ago, and had filed it under *practical navigation, note for future reference,* and had referenced it every time since without further thought.

She was looking at the smoke on the horizon when Rowe came to stand beside her at the porthole—he'd been awake for an hour, sitting against his cask, watching her work with the patient attention of someone who had learned not to interrupt when people were doing things he didn't yet understand—and she saw him see it.

His face did the thing it had done over the manifest. Less controlled this time, or perhaps she was better at reading it than she'd been at midnight. The door blown open in the wind. A fraction of a second. Closed again before she could inventory what was behind it. But different this time: before, what she'd glimpsed had been recognition. This was something else. Something older than recognition.

She pointed at the smoke on the horizon. She gave him the Cauld word for it: smoke, industrial, *that which rises from process.*

He looked at her transcription of his word, the one she'd marked with a question mark. He looked at the smoke. He said his word.

She said hers.

He said his again. Not correcting her. Something else—holding both of them the way you hold a name your mother used for something and the name the world uses for the same thing, and they live in the same space without canceling each other out, because they describe different aspects of the same fact.

"It's not the same smoke," she said.

He understood enough to know she meant something by it. He looked at her and waited, which was the thing he did when he was ready to receive information if she had it to give.

She pointed at the smoke on the horizon and said: "Atrament. A city." She gave him the word for *city.* Then she pointed at the notebook, at the page with his four words, and said: "Not that smoke."

He looked at the horizon for a long moment. Long enough that she counted it.

He said, "No." Her word. Then he said his word for smoke—the one that wasn't quite her word, the one she'd marked with a question mark because she'd known, even then, that the question mark was doing real work—and shook his head.

"Not that smoke," she said again.

He said, "Gone." Her word for gone. The fourth word. He'd had it since midnight and had used it precisely twice since then. He used it now with the particular care of someone who has been saving a word for a specific application and has identified the application.

She looked at the smoke over Atrament.

She looked at her notebook.

*Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.*

She could read the shape of the sentence. She could not read all of its contents. She had, she estimated, perhaps a quarter of the words she would need before she could ask him the question she was now certain he'd been trying to answer since before she'd had any language to ask it in. He'd been waiting. He'd found his four words on his own—not handed them, found them, worked for them, held them until he had someone to hand them to—because he'd needed to say something and the sentence required more architecture than she'd yet built.

She would build it.

She wrote the four words again at the bottom of the page. Below them she wrote the words she didn't have yet: a row of blanks in the order she thought they would fall, based on the grammatical patterns she'd observed in the hours since midnight. Five blanks. Possibly six. She'd missed one gap in a language before and it had cost her three weeks of misdirected analysis in Vierna; she added a sixth to be careful.

She held the page up and showed it to him.

He looked at the blanks. He looked at her. Something in him that had been carefully, professionally, long-practiced still went briefly uncontrolled—she was getting better at seeing it—and then controlled again. He picked up the pen.

He filled in one of the blanks.

She looked at it. A single word, his notation, small and precise. She didn't know what it meant. She filed it under *things to learn* and added it to the left column of the notebook and left the right column empty, a gap in the architecture where the Cauld equivalent would go when she'd earned it.

She would have it by Atrament.

Possibly.

*Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.* [Blank.] And one more.

The smoke on the horizon thickened as the barge moved north, and the smell of Atrament reached them before the city did—coal and rendered fat and the sharp mineral edge of hot metal, familiar as anything she'd known for thirty years—and Lyra sat with her notebook and worked on the language the way she worked on everything: methodically, without hurry, noting the things that would not fit into existing categories and making new categories for them, narrow and provisional, to be revised once she had more data.

The new categories were multiplying.

She noted this. She filed it. She continued working.

[Beat 12]
ATRAMENT — THE FORGE KINGDOM

The border crossing was not a building.

Lyra had read the Compact documents before they left Vierna. *Transit facility. Customs authority. Single inspection point on the eastern approach road.* She had imagined something the size of a gatehouse with a magistrate's annex behind it. What the iron-tie road delivered them to after two days of travel was a complex — a word that meant, here, seven buildings and a freight yard and a staff count that would have embarrassed a garrison. She stood at the rail platform and did what she had done since she was nineteen years old and a senior templar had pressed her left hand flat against a practice-yard wall and explained that a soldier who doesn't count will one day be surprised by arithmetic: she counted. Seventeen workers in the immediate freight yard. Four officers at the check stations. Twenty-one freight cars positioned on the side rail, waiting. Three more buildings she couldn't see into.

She had been wrong about the size.

That was not a comfortable thought for someone who had spent thirty years being right about institutions.

"Productive," Orim said, beside her. He had his arms folded and was looking at the freight yard the way old men look at things they have looked at before and found unchanged. "They call customs *productive* here. Not *defensive*. Not *secure*. Every traveler is a resource. Every cargo is a resource. The queue is a harvesting mechanism." He paused. "I am told it was worse before the Compact."

"Worse how," Ardea said.

"Longer," Orim said, which was not quite an answer and he knew it.

The customs commander who received them in the magistrate's annex was a woman of approximately Lyra's age, which made her younger than she seemed. She had the kind of face that lives near paperwork and direct light for decades and contracts accordingly. She reviewed the Meridian Compact authority document with the attention of someone who had seen every kind of fraudulent paper and was cataloging this one against type. Then she reviewed it again. Lyra felt the familiar minor discomfort of authority being verified, which was not something she had felt often, and let it settle.

"Templar," the commander said. "You're pursuing a Pallor-affiliated theft unit."

"Yes."

"They crossed here." She set down a ledger that had been open on her desk — Lyra could see columns, codes, dates, a freight analyst's notation in a different hand. "Nine days ago. One of them carried a pack with a center-of-gravity that my freight analyst logged as inconsistent with the declared contents. We noted it."

The past tense was doing a great deal of work in that sentence.

"You didn't inspect," Lyra said.

The commander's expression did not change. "The queue. We had eighty-three parties backed up on the eastern approach and three analysts on shift. The anomaly was logged. The inspection was flagged for follow-up." She folded her hands over the ledger. "The follow-up occurred fourteen hours after they passed."

Lyra looked at her. The commander looked back. There was nothing defensive in it. This was, apparently, simply what had happened, and the commander had the specific composure of someone who has long since stopped being ashamed of outcomes that were produced by system design rather than personal failure.

"The pack's anomaly," Lyra said. "What was the analyst's note?"

"Dense material concentrated low in the main body, offset from declared distribution. The outer material read as textiles, which was the declared contents. The interior read as something that sat heavier." She opened the ledger and turned it so Lyra could see. "The weight was within tolerances for the declared load. The distribution was not." She paused. "My analyst was correct to flag it. The queue did not allow the flag to resolve."

"The system worked as designed," Lyra said.

"Yes."

"And this outcome was produced by that design."

The commander said nothing, which was also an answer.

Orim, standing behind Lyra's left shoulder, made a small sound that was not quite a laugh and not quite clearing his throat. When Lyra glanced at him he was studying the ceiling with apparent interest.

---

The rail depot was the size of a garrison.

The freight yard was larger than the depot.

Lyra stood at the platform edge and looked at the length of the train they would be boarding, and then she looked at the freight cars on the parallel tracks, and then she looked at the length of those, and she began counting again, because that was the only honest response to something that exceeded the previous frame.

The train was twelve passenger carriages and six freight cars immediately visible. The freight yard alongside held — she counted three times, because the first two numbers disagreed — forty-seven additional freight cars in various states of loading and unloading and waiting.

"Six hours to Schmalburg," Orim said. "The rail runs northwest through the valley. Stops at Hartenmacher, Ullendorf, Sternwerk. Production centers, all of them. Not worth looking at if you're looking for a city. Worth looking at if you're looking for something else."

"What else," Ardea said.

Orim gestured at the freight yard.

They boarded. Lyra found a seat facing forward, which was professional habit from decades of routes where she might need to move quickly, and then acknowledged privately that she was on a passenger rail in another nation's interior and not currently expecting to need to move quickly. The acknowledgment did not change anything. She kept the forward-facing seat.

Rowe took the window seat.

The train moved.

---

The freight car three cars back from theirs was covered with a canvas tarpaulin that did not quite conceal the silhouette beneath it. Lyra saw it when the train curved and she could see down the line through the window, and then it curved back and she couldn't. But the shape had been specific. She had seen that configuration in the Liturgy armory illustrations — the weight distribution of a battle rig laid on its side for transport, the articulated limbs folded and lashed.

She sat with that for a moment.

*One,* she thought.

The train curved again at Hartenmacher, which was the first stop, and she saw the open freight platform and the dozen covered shapes on the loading dock waiting to board the return route east, and she revised.

*Not one.*

She began counting again and stopped when the curve straightened and the platform disappeared.

"How many rigs do they have," Ardea said, from the seat across.

She had been watching through the same window.

"The Compact documents list the treaty number," Lyra said. "The treaty number and the actual number appear to be different." She paused. "This is not unusual. It is usually not this different."

Orim, across the aisle, had his eyes half-closed and appeared to be sleeping, which Lyra had learned in two weeks of travel meant he was paying close attention to everything. "The Atrament Steel Compact of Year 841," he said, eyes still half-closed, "allows for treaty inspection of standing armament at six-month intervals. The intervals are six months. The Atrament production cycle is four." He settled lower in his seat. "I am sure someone has noted this discrepancy somewhere."

"Has anyone acted on it," Ardea said.

Orim said nothing.

The window showed the valley opening below them, the rail running along the ridge, and the river in the bottom of the valley catching the afternoon light in a color that was not quite right. Lyra had read about the river color. She was looking at it now and finding that reading about a color and seeing it were entirely different physical events.

The Veil River in Vierna ran clear over gray stones, or brown-gray after rain, the way rivers look when they are carrying their natural load of silt and history. The river here — the Rhine-analog, the valley's drainage — ran brown. Not mud-brown, not storm-brown. A different shade. Specific. The color of something that has been introduced, not something that has been worn.

She knew what it was. The Catalyst processing facilities used water for cooling and flushing and several stages of the finishing process, and the chemical additives required for those stages passed through the river in concentrations that the Liturgy's environmental research documented in careful numbers. She had read those numbers. She had nodded at those numbers in the way you nod at statistics that are bad but not immediate.

The river running brown below her was immediate.

"The Veil River," she said.

Rowe had not looked up from the window since they boarded. He was watching the valley with an expression she had not seen on him before, or had seen and misidentified. He had been watching the freight cars, the production facilities, the river, the smoke from the chimney stacks at Hartenmacher with a kind of careful attention that was different from Ardea's strategic cataloging and different from Orim's weary familiarity.

"Catalyst discharge," Rowe said, without looking away from the river. "Iron processing produces it as a secondary. They've got nowhere to put it except the water." He paused. "Or they've got somewhere to put it and this is cheaper." He watched the river for another moment. "How far down does it go."

"The research documents suggest fifty leagues of degraded water quality," Lyra said. "At the current processing volume. The documents are eight years old."

Rowe looked at the freight cars they had passed. He looked at the loading dock at Hartenmacher, still visible on the ridge before they rounded the next bend. He looked at the smoke.

"The volume is higher now," he said.

It wasn't a question.

---

Ullendorf appeared and was not a city.

Lyra had stopped expecting cities by then, but Ardea said "Is that all of it" with the genuine surprise of someone who had not yet recalibrated, and the answer was yes, that was all of it. Ullendorf was three production buildings, a storage facility, a dormitory block, a loading platform. Workers visible in the numbers you'd need to keep three large buildings running. No market. No temple. No common space that served no purpose.

"They don't live here," Ardea said.

"They do," Orim said. "That's the dormitory."

"I mean — I mean they don't *live* here. They sleep here. It's different."

"In Atrament," Orim said, "it is possibly less different than you'd think."

He said this in the tone of someone who is not being unkind. Just informative. Just accurate.

The train did not slow for Ullendorf; it had no passenger traffic. The platform passed in under a minute. Lyra saw a woman at the loading dock looking up at the passing carriages with an expression that was hard to read at that distance and speed. She filed the image anyway, because she filed things. It was the expression of someone looking at something from the other side of a window, which was, technically, what it was.

Sternwerk was the same. Different specific buildings, same structure. Same dormitory, same loading platform, same chimneys. Different sign.

Rowe was still at the window.

"It's a machine," he said, at Sternwerk. Not talking to anyone in particular.

"What," Ardea said.

"The whole valley. It's a machine." He was watching the production buildings recede as the train moved on. "Those places aren't towns with factories. The factories have been given a necessary adjacent structure for worker maintenance. It's the same thing, oriented differently." He paused. "You build a factory. The factory needs workers. Workers need sleep, food, minimal amenity to function. You attach the minimum viable worker-maintenance structure to the factory because it's more efficient than importing workers daily." He watched the last of Sternwerk disappear around the ridge. "The towns didn't grow up around the industry. The industry built the minimum necessary towns."

"Yes," Orim said.

"How long has it been like this."

"Longer than anyone living remembers," Orim said. "Since before the old war. Perhaps since the founding." He shifted in his seat. "There are Atrament scholars who argue that this is not dehumanizing. That the model simply prioritizes collective production over individual amenity, and that the workers understand the exchange and consent to it."

A silence settled.

"Do they," Ardea said.

"The scholars," Orim said, "are generally not workers."

He folded his hands in his lap and appeared to go back to sleep.

---

Schmalburg appeared in the late afternoon in the way that cities appear when you are coming from the northwest along a valley rail line: first as smoke, then as reflected light off glass and water and metal, then as specific buildings differentiated from the blur, then as itself, which was larger than the smoke had suggested.

The name meant, Lyra knew, *the small fortress.* This required explanation.

The city had been called *Kleine Festung* — small fortress — by the Fjorheim forces during the siege of Year 701, which had lasted forty-one days. The Fjorheim-Pallor coalition had arrayed themselves on the heights to the north and looked down at the Atrament position on the valley floor and deemed it insufficient. *Small fortress.* They had said this intending contempt. They had not finished saying it before the Atrament garrison demonstrated, through the application of a Catalyst-batch incendiary, that they had underestimated the resources held within.

The Fjorheim forces withdrew on the forty-second day.

Atrament named the city after the insult. This was the kind of institutional humor that did not require laughing.

Lyra filed this under *things that are relevant* and also under *things that suggest something specific about Atrament's relationship with external opinion,* which were occasionally the same file.

---

The city's archive was in the civic center, three streets north of the rail station, and it was staffed by an archivist who looked at the Meridian Compact authority with considerably less patience than the border commander had. Not suspicion. Just efficiency. He wanted the document verified and the request logged so he could return to what he had been doing.

"Date range," he said.

"Eleven days back," Lyra said. "A party of five, possibly four. Pallor-affiliated by documentation or claim. They may have registered transit papers, commerce papers, or both."

He looked. It took longer than she expected, which meant either the records were complex or the party had been thorough about their paper. When he returned he had three sheets.

"Four of them," he said. "Commerce papers. Textile purchasing agents, declared out of the Weymark district. They were here two days."

Two days.

She had lost two more days of distance somewhere between the border and this room, and the back of her neck ached in the specific way of sustained tension held in armor, the left side worse than the right from six hours of rail motion that was not quite smooth, and she processed both facts simultaneously and set the neck pain aside and focused on the two days.

"What did they do for two days," she said.

"What the records show," the archivist said, with the patience of someone who has explained record-keeping scope before, "is that they registered transit papers and did not register departure until the second day."

"They were waiting for something."

He said nothing, because what she had said was not a question and was not addressed to him.

She looked at the records. The handwriting in the register was a transit clerk's hand, functional and clear. Four names, none of which she recognized from the Pallor border documentation, which meant they had changed identity at least once. Four declared occupations. A lodging address — she wrote it down. A declared travel route: west, toward the Lacerta borderlands.

Lacerta. Which meant, eventually, Sal Vento.

"They were waiting for passage," she said. Not to the archivist. To herself, filing as she went. "They needed something that didn't operate on the public schedule." She looked up. "The river trade. Who operates river cargo on the lower Rhine analog, west of Schmalburg."

"Several licensed companies," the archivist said. "The registry —"

"I need the unlicensed ones."

A pause.

"The archive," he said carefully, "does not maintain records of unlicensed river commerce."

"I understand. Who would know."

Another pause. He was deciding something. She watched him decide it with the neutral expression of someone who has learned that pressure applied too early collapses the decision in the wrong direction.

"The Dockhands' Association office," he said finally, "is on the river quay. The secretary has been there for thirty years and is thorough."

"Thank you," Lyra said.

---

The Dockhands' Association office was a single room above a rope-and-tackle store that smelled of linseed oil and old rope and something that had been wet and dried repeatedly until it had given up any pretense of organic origin. The secretary was a man in his seventies with the particular build of someone who had done physical labor for forty of those years and the rest at a desk, which meant he was built like a desk that had once been a wall.

He looked at the Compact authority and then at Lyra and then at Orim and then back at the Compact authority.

"Eleven days ago," he said.

"Or twelve," Lyra said. "They were in the city two days. They arrived twelve days ago, left ten."

He considered this for a moment in a way that suggested he was remembering rather than calculating. "Four of them," he said. "Small load, dense. They were waiting for the Sallander."

"What is the Sallander."

"River trade. Operates the lower Rhine and the border crossing into Lacerta." He looked at the wall to his left, which was covered in schedule sheets. "The Liturgy navigation registry doesn't track it."

She looked at him.

He looked back.

"You know about the Liturgy navigation registry," she said.

"I know that the Sallander isn't on it," he said, which was different from an answer and served the same purpose. "She runs cargo the licensed companies won't carry. Materials in gray classification. Equipment that doesn't have clean origin papers." He returned to looking at the schedule sheets. "I don't track what she carries. The Association's concern is the men loading and unloading, not the manifest."

"She runs on the lower Rhine regularly."

"When she has cargo. Two or three times a season, usually." He paused. "Eleven days ago was unusual. She'd only been in port four days before they arrived. Turned around faster than she usually does."

Lyra filed this. The thieves hadn't waited for a regular schedule. The Sallander had come in and they had moved to meet it. Which meant either they had arranged it in advance, or someone in Schmalburg had arranged it for them, or there was a signal system she hadn't identified yet.

She wrote down the Sallander. She wrote down the secretary's name, which he gave without being asked, which suggested either that he had nothing to hide or that he had decided transparency was cheaper than whatever she might do with reluctance.

"West," she said. "Toward Lacerta."

"Toward Sal Vento," he said. "The Sallander doesn't stop before the border."

Sal Vento.

She had a direction. She had a vessel. She had a border crossing and an arrival point. She was ten days behind them, possibly eleven, and the gap had not narrowed since Vierna.

She put her notebook away. She said thank you to the secretary, which he acknowledged with a nod that suggested the Compact authority had bought her something but not everything. She went back down the stairs into the rope store and out onto the river quay, where Rowe and Ardea and Orim were waiting in the specific arrangement of people who have been waiting for fifteen minutes in a city they don't know and are not sure whether to be concerned.

"West," she said. "Sal Vento. They took a river cargo vessel called the Sallander, unlicensed, Liturgy registry doesn't track it." She looked at the river. The color was worse here, closer to the source of the processing output, the water running the specific brown she had seen from the train and was now seeing from ground level, which was a different relationship with the color. "We need passage west. Tonight if there's anything."

"There's an evening departure," Orim said. "Licensed. Slower than the Sallander would have been. We lose another day."

Lyra looked at the river. She looked at the city around her — Schmalburg, the small fortress that had broken a siege and named itself after the insult, the production center that did not bother to be beautiful, the chimneys visible from the quay, the freight platform she could see from here, the workers moving materials from one point to another with the efficiency of a system that had been built to produce this exact motion.

She thought about the customs commander and her freight analyst and the queue pressure that had converted a noted anomaly into a fourteen-hour delay. She thought about the system working as designed and the design producing this outcome.

She thought about the thieves' pack with its anomalous center-of-gravity, dense in the lower body, heavier than textiles.

"We'll take the licensed vessel," she said. "We make up the day on the other side." She looked at Orim. "The Lacerta crossing — how long."

"Half a day, if the border runs smoothly." He paused. "Lacerta runs their borders more like the old approach. Defensive."

"Meaning slower."

"Meaning interested in who crosses rather than what they carry."

She began making the calculation that she had been making since Vierna — distance, time, vessel speed, border processing — and she was approximately four steps into it when the bell started.

---

It came from the north quarter, from the watch-post on the ridge above the city. Not a civic bell, not a shift-change bell. A watch bell, run in the specific pattern of three long and two short that she had not heard since the Pallor border action three years ago, which meant she recognized it immediately in the way that the body recognizes patterns it has learned to react to before the mind finishes identifying them.

Her hand found the hilt of her sword. She had not decided to do this.

The bell ran again. Three long. Two short.

People on the quay were moving — not panicking, but moving with the specific purposefulness of a population that knew what the bell meant and had a place to be when it sounded.

Rowe was already looking north, toward the ridge.

"Fjorheim," Orim said. He had not moved from where he was standing. He was watching the north ridge with the expression of someone who has lived through enough raids to have opinions about them but not enough alarm to be hasty. "Raiding force, coming from the heights." He looked at Lyra. "The city has protocols. The protocols will move us from where we need to be."

She was already thinking through the architecture of the quay — the cover available, the line to the river, the vessel that was their evening departure and what its captain would do when a raid bell sounded in the city where his vessel was docked.

The bell was still ringing.

The river ran brown below the quay edge, catching the late afternoon light in a color that was not quite right, and the bell rang three long and two short again, and the city that had broken a siege began to respond to another one.

[Beat 13]
THE REVIEW SESSION

---

The bench outside Chamber Three was not designed for waiting. Vega had concluded this somewhere in the first year, before she understood that the bench was not a convenience but a statement — that supplicants to anything above the administrative threshold should feel the stone through the wood and understand their place in the order of things. The Liturgy did not rush its own processes. The Liturgy processed.

She shifted the instruments on her lap. Five folded instruments, each sealed with the red-and-black stamp of the Canonical Registry, each requiring the countersignature of the presiding notary before the session could formally conclude. The presiding notary was her. The session had begun, according to the instrument of convocation she had herself copied and certified three days prior, at the second hour past midmorning. The instrument of convocation did not specify an end time. Instruments of convocation never did.

The bench was cold. The instruments were heavy in the particular way paper was never supposed to be heavy, which was the weight of what they contained pressing through the sealed edges.

Through the chamber doors — old wood, good seals, the kind that had been maintained for generations of institutional conversations that were never meant to be heard by those outside — she could hear voices. Not words. The doors were good enough for that. But she had spent three years outside chambers, or at adjacent desks, or in the adjoining offices where sound traveled in ways architects had not anticipated, and she had learned to read the shape of conversation without its content. The Liturgy was full of people who spoke in institutional cadence. She had become something of an expert.

The Lacerta delegate was frustrated. She could hear it in the intervals. Frustration presented as clipped statements, as controlled pauses where emotion was being processed before it could escape into the record. Three years of copying testimony and deposition had taught her that frustration sounded like restraint — like someone choosing not to say the thing they were saying. The Lacerta delegate had been not-saying something for the last forty minutes.

The Canon's representative was managing. Managing had its own cadence entirely, the particular rhythm of institutional reassurance that was not quite agreement and not quite refusal, the carefully maintained center ground of "the matter has been received and is being considered." She had copied enough Canon's Representative statements to recognize the phrasing from the breathing pattern alone. You learned, after a while. You couldn't not learn.

The Carnyx commander — she assumed it was the Carnyx commander; the convocation instrument listed a Commander Aldec Vorn, Carnyx Territorial Authority, as the second house delegate — was harder to read. He said less, or he said it more quietly, and what she could hear of him was the specific controlled silence of someone who had decided to let frustration do the talking for someone else.

She had written that down this morning in the margin of her working copy: *Carnyx brings observer, lets Lacerta lead. Lacerta burns credibility, Carnyx preserves it.* She had crossed it out because it was not her assignment to interpret the strategic posture of inter-House delegations. Her assignment was the instruments.

The instruments sat on her lap and were heavy.

---

She heard the administrative entrance first — the side approach, the one that processed intake logs and supply requisitions and personnel records for sessions that didn't rise to the formal threshold of the primary entrance. She had used it herself, frequently. It was efficient. It was also, she had noted, the entrance that produced no foot traffic past Chamber Three.

The soldiers came around the corner from the eastern corridor.

She catalogued them without intending to. Seven. Carnyx — not Ocipheus garrison, which she would have recognized; she had processed enough garrison complement logs to know the faces if not all the names, and none of these were faces she had processed. Carnyx equipment. She was certain about the equipment because she had spent eight months copying supply authorizations and requisition instruments and equipment inventory certifications, and Carnyx kit had a specific profile in the registry documentation: heavier weather-treatment on the outer layers, the particular boot construction rated for the Wall sector approach roads, the sidearm configuration that Lacerta and Liturgy central both used but Carnyx had adopted after the border reclassification in the second year of the current Canonical period. Small things. The kind of things you saw in the paperwork before you saw them in the field, if you ever saw them in the field at all.

She was not in the field. She was on the bench.

The Liturgy factor logging them through the administrative entrance was someone she did not know. Not unusual; Ocipheus Station ran a rotating administrative staff above the permanent registry positions, and she only knew the registry staff by name. What she noted was the bearing: someone doing a routine procedure very carefully. The careful routine was not routine. People who did routine things carefully were people who had been told to be careful about this particular thing.

The soldiers had the look of people who had been traveling. She recognized it because she recognized its specific variety — not the exhaustion of long travel, which was soft, but the alert exhaustion of purposeful movement, the kind that came from having a brief and a destination and not yet having been required to execute either. They moved economically. They looked at the chamber doors as they passed, the reflexive situational awareness of people whose training ran below conscious thought, and then looked away.

The factor guided them through the administrative wing, past her bench, and they were gone.

She looked down at the instruments on her lap.

The intake log. She was carrying it because she had processed it this morning — prepared it, certified its form, stamped it with the Registry seal — and she had not yet filed it in the canonical archive because the session instruments had taken priority and she had simply gathered everything and come to wait. She had the session instruments. She also had the intake log.

She read it while waiting.

*SPECIALIST DEPLOYMENT — SINTER ZONE APPROACH PREPARATION.*

She read it again.

The chamber doors were solid old wood, good seals, and through them she could hear the Lacerta delegate not-saying something. The Canon's representative was managing. The Carnyx commander was being quiet.

She refolded the intake log and placed it under the session instruments.

---

The session notation that would eventually reach her desk would read, she anticipated, something in the register of "continued collaborative dialogue" or "productive interhouse information exchange" or possibly, if the Canon's representative had had a particularly difficult afternoon, "mutual confirmation of existing protocols." She had copied enough session notations to predict the vocabulary within two or three adjectives.

She sat with the instruments on her lap for eleven more minutes. She knew it was eleven minutes because she had her own internal clock for this kind of thing, the specific bodily awareness that developed when you spent your working life calibrating intervals. The instruments were still heavy.

The chamber doors opened.

The Lacerta delegate was a woman of perhaps fifty, brown-skinned and grey-haired, with the particular controlled face of someone who had learned not to show the face they were making. Vega recognized the type; they appeared frequently in deposition records, the witnesses who had decided before they arrived what they would and would not say. The delegate's face was controlled. Her hands were not quite still.

Behind her, the Carnyx commander — Aldec Vorn; she matched the face now to the name on the convocation instrument — was unreadable in the way that was itself a kind of reading. He was looking at the chamber behind him as the doors closed, the specific last-glance of someone cataloguing what they were leaving behind.

The Canon's representative was walking too fast. This was the detail she noted most precisely, because the Canon's representative was Subcanon Ireith Malvar, who she had worked with on three previous inter-House sessions, and Subcanon Malvar did not walk fast. Subcanon Malvar processed. The Liturgy did not rush its own processes, and Subcanon Malvar was fully committed to the institutional posture in a way that Vega had found, over three years, to be either admirable or instructive depending on the day. Today he was walking fast. His robes moved wrong for it.

She stood. She presented the instruments.

"Session notarization," she said. "Five instruments requiring countersignature."

Subcanon Malvar took the instruments from her without slowing. He signed them at the corridor pace, which was not correct procedure — correct procedure required a review desk and a reading period — but he was the presiding authority and she was the notary and her job was to present, not to enforce. She watched him sign. She collected the instruments. She looked at the signatures.

He had not misread any of them. Even at speed, Subcanon Malvar's signatures were precise and properly formed. She supposed that was something.

The delegates had already gone. She heard the administrative entrance — the side approach, the efficient one — close behind them.

---

She sat at the registry annex desk just inside the administrative wing and copied the session notation into the canonical record. She did this from the notation she had received from Subcanon Malvar's office assistant seven minutes after the session concluded, which was faster than she usually received session notations, which usually traveled to her desk at a pace that suggested the Liturgy was uncertain the notation needed to exist.

The session notation read: *Interhouse sector review — no immediate action indicated. Continued monitoring protocols authorized.*

She wrote this down in the canonical record.

She wrote it correctly. She used the correct form, the correct ink, the correct notation headers. She dated it precisely. She initialed it in the right lower margin, which was her function, and she sealed it with the Registry stamp, which was also her function, and she placed it in the archival queue.

Then she sat at the desk and looked at the wall.

She was not, she thought, someone who looked at walls. She was someone who looked at documents. She was good at it, which was why she had been given the station posting, which was prestigious in a quiet and non-glamorous way that suited her temperament. She liked precision. She liked the ledger when the ledger balanced. She had been good at this work before she became too good at it, and she was not entirely sure what the difference between those two states was, but she was aware that she had crossed some threshold sometime in the past eight months and had not found a way back.

The wall had nothing to tell her. She put the canonical record in the archival queue and went back to her desk.

---

Her desk was in the registry proper, two corridors from the chamber wing, in a room with two windows that looked out on the interior courtyard — the one where they had been evaluating the war constructs in the autumn. The constructs were gone now. The courtyard was empty most days.

She sat at her desk. She had the intake log in her hands, the session notation fresh in the canonical record, the pattern of eight months in her working copies in the drawer.

She did not open the drawer.

She had accumulated: the canonical property recovery instrument for the Oculus Memoriae (the gap in the registration series that she had noticed and could not un-notice). The transit suspension for T-044, which she had not known then was her sister and had since been unable to un-know. The Lacerta sector reports — "No Action Indicated" — for the three months following the transit suspension. The Carnyx sector reports, same notation, same period. The supply authorizations for the Wall garrison that had increased in aggregate tonnage by twenty-three percent over the same period without any corresponding increase in complement. The equipment certification logs for the war construct evaluations — WC-Eirene and the others, eight of them in the autumn cohort, all rated and processed and noted in the canonical record as "evaluation complete, pending deployment authorization." She had not filed the deployment authorization yet. There had not been a deployment authorization yet.

And now the intake log in her hands: *SPECIALIST DEPLOYMENT — SINTER ZONE APPROACH PREPARATION.*

The Sinter Zone.

She had seen the words before. In maintenance authorizations for the Wall garrison — the specific infrastructure authorizations that covered the approach roads and transit corridors in the contested boundary sector between Ocipheus territorial administration and the ungoverned band that ran along the Wall's southern edge. The Sinter Zone was, in her understanding of it from the maintenance documentation, a characterization of terrain: the specific quality of the approach territory closest to the Wall, where something in the substrate had been altered by proximity to whatever was happening on the other side, and the alteration had made the ground behave differently. She had processed the engineering reports without fully reading them because engineering reports were not her assignment. She had noted the terminology. She had not catalogued it, because it appeared in maintenance authorizations, and maintenance authorizations were routine.

*Sinter Zone Approach Preparation* was not a maintenance authorization category.

She was very good at categories. She had spent three years learning the canonical taxonomy of Liturgy operations by immersion, by handling hundreds of instruments per month, by developing the pattern recognition that came from constant contact with the form and not the content. You learned the shapes before you learned the meanings, and eventually the shapes told you things the meanings hadn't caught up to yet.

She put the intake log in her bag. She went to the library.

---

The library at Ocipheus Station was not large but it was complete, which was a distinction that mattered in the canonical documents infrastructure. A complete library held the canonical codex, the operational taxonomy, the registered precedent records, and the reference documentation for every category of Liturgy instrument that had been formally issued and recorded. It also held, in a secondary archive that was theoretically accessible to all station staff with appropriate clearance, the definitional compendium for canonical categories — the source documents that defined what a given instrument category meant, what authority it required, what documentation it generated.

She had clearance for the secondary archive. She had never needed to use it.

She looked up *approach preparation* under the operational taxonomy, canonical category: specialist deployment.

The definition was not long.

*Approach preparation: pre-staging designation for operations requiring formalized entry authorization for contested or boundary-adjacent territory. Classification: pre-incursion operational. Authorization level required: Canon Immaculate plenary. Documentation required: full canonical instrument set, canonical form series Δ-7 through Δ-14, signed by authorized representatives of all participating Houses and operating authorities. Required countersignature: canonical notary, Ocipheus Station or designated equivalent registry.*

She read it twice.

Pre-incursion operational.

Canon Immaculate plenary.

She knew what Canon Immaculate plenary meant. She had copied enough instruments referencing it to know it was the highest operational authorization in the canonical structure — not a regional authorization, not a sector council authorization, not an interhouse coordination authorization, but the authorization of the full canonical body, which required a formal session of the Canon Immaculate, which had not been convened since the border reclassification six years prior. She had processed the reference instruments for that authorization. She knew the weight of it.

The documentation required a full canonical instrument set, Δ-7 through Δ-14. She knew canonical form series Δ. She had handled them — not frequently, not recently, but she had been trained on the full series and the station held templates for all of them. Eight instruments. Threshold formalities, attestation records, operational mandates, House confirmation instruments, an operational brief filed under seal, a designated authority certification, a deployment roster, and a canonical witness certification.

The canonical witness certification required a notary.

The notary at Ocipheus Station was her.

If the Canon Immaculate authorized a formal incursion or entry operation into the Sinter Zone approach, the canonical instrument set would require a notary. The canonical instrument set would require her signature on the witness certification. She would be required to sign.

She would be required to sign the certification that she had witnessed the formation and execution of a canonical instrument set for a pre-incursion operation.

She had, currently in her possession, the intake log for the specialist deployment that was, per its own documentation, conducting Sinter Zone Approach Preparation.

She sat in the library for a long time.

The library was warm. It was the warmest room at Ocipheus Station, which she had always appreciated, which now felt like an observation from another person's life. Somewhere in the eastern corridor, she could hear the distant close of the administrative entrance — the side approach, the efficient one. The specialists, perhaps. Or the factor. Or someone else conducting routine business efficiently.

She was, she thought, not very good at being the person she was becoming.

She had been, three years ago, very clear on what she was. She was a Scribe. She made the official record true. She did not decide what was true; she recorded what the authorized parties determined and certified it with her mark. This was a good and necessary function. This was the function that made the Liturgy legible to itself. Without scribes, the Liturgy could not see its own actions clearly enough to administer them. She had understood this as a purpose. She still understood it as a purpose. She was not sure when she had begun to feel the gap between the purpose and the practice.

The gap was not her assignment.

The Δ-7 through Δ-14 instrument set was her assignment, if and when it was convened.

She closed the compendium and put it back.

---

She walked back to her desk.

The courtyard was dark through the windows. She had been longer than she had thought, which was the thing about understanding something — it took time she couldn't account for afterward. The time disappeared into the understanding and she emerged from it with less evening than she had entered.

She sat at her desk. The drawer was in front of her. The working copies were in the drawer — the accumulated eight months, the instruments she had processed and noted and cross-referenced in the margins of her own copies, which were not the canonical copies, which were in the archive, which were correct and precise and contained only what they were supposed to contain.

She did not open the drawer.

She sat with her hands in her lap for a moment. She was aware of her hands as objects — the specific hands she had had all her life, which had written what she had been given to write and had not until eight months ago begun to write other things in the margins. She was aware of the pen on her desk and the canonical record open in front of her and the archival queue and the instruments in the queue and all of it waiting with the patience of things that had always waited because things did not know they were waiting.

She opened the drawer.

She did not take out the working copy of T-044's transit suspension. She had done that once, in the registry, when she had found the name. She had not needed to do it again. She knew what it said. She knew the name.

She took out the intake log and placed it on her desk beside the open canonical record. She considered both of them. The canonical record was where the official notation lived — the session notation, properly dated and initialed and sealed, stating that the interhouse sector review had indicated no immediate action and authorized continued monitoring protocols. The intake log was the processing document, now properly filed in the archival queue, stating that seven specialist soldiers had been logged through the administrative entrance for Sinter Zone Approach Preparation.

She picked up her pen.

She began copying the intake log into the record of processed instruments. This was her assignment — her actual assignment, the one she had been given this morning when the instrument arrived at her desk for processing. Instrument type, canonical category, processing date, instrument reference number, presiding notary initials. She did this correctly.

In the disposition column, below the official notation — below the canonical category stamp, below the processing certification — she wrote in very small letters:

*intake factor: unregistered — cross-ref garrison factor log, eastern approach, 14th day. soldier complement: 7. equipment profile: Carnyx territorial, weather-rated, Wall-approach specification. traveling condition: alert mobile. formation: purposeful. brief confirmed. destination undisclosed.*

She looked at what she had written.

She picked up the intake log and looked at the names on the form — the seven names listed in the personnel column, the factor's countersignature, the category designation. She wrote:

*names per form: Vorn complement, unassigned roster (no individual designations on instrument). factor signature: unregistered. category: Sinter Zone Approach Preparation. canonical compendium definition cross-ref: pre-incursion operational, Canon Immaculate plenary auth required, Δ-7 through Δ-14 instrument set.*

She paused.

She wrote: *notary Ocipheus Station: V. Athen-Moor. On notice.*

She looked at those last two words for a moment. They were not a canonical category. They were not a recognized disposition notation. They were, technically, nothing — marginalia, private record, the kind of thing that appeared in working copies and was never supposed to appear in anything else.

She was not in a working copy. She was in the processed instrument record.

She left the notation.

She put the intake log in the archival queue. She took out the session notation from the same queue — she had filed it perhaps two hours ago and it was still in the queue, not yet collected for archival — and she looked at it. *Interhouse sector review — no immediate action indicated. Continued monitoring protocols authorized.*

She had written this correctly. The notation was accurate. It was what the session had produced, as transmitted by Subcanon Malvar's office, in the form specified by canonical convention. She had not falsified it. She had not omitted anything she was required to include.

She put it back in the queue.

She reached into the drawer without looking and took out the working copy. She knew it by feel — the weight of it, the specific fold pattern she had developed without intending to, the tactile difference between this paper and the canonical instruments, which were a different weight and a different grain. Her working copies were her own stock. She bought them herself. She used her own ink.

She opened it.

Her sister's name was in the margin of the third page. She had written it in the registry when she had found the name in the transit suspension: *Lyra Athen-Moor, T-044, transit suspended effective — * and then the date. She had crossed it out with a single horizontal stroke, not hard enough to obscure, just hard enough to mark. The name was legible through the line. She had known when she drew the line that the name would be legible. She had drawn it anyway because crossing it out was not the same as pretending she hadn't written it, which was not the same as pretending she hadn't found it, which was not the same as pretending she hadn't been given, three years ago, work that would eventually require her to find it.

She looked at her sister's name for a moment.

She put the working copy back.

She closed the drawer.

She opened the new instrument on her desk — the blank working copy she had placed there this morning before the intake log arrived, before the session, before the soldiers in the corridor — and she dated the top of the page. She wrote the date very precisely, the way she wrote everything, because precision was either a virtue or a habit and she was no longer certain which it was or whether the distinction was meaningful.

She began copying the intake log.

This was not her assignment. Her assignment was the canonical record, the official column, the notarized instrument and its correct disposition. She had done that. The official column was the Canon's record and it said what it was supposed to say.

The working copy was hers.

*Day 14, month of the Still Watch, 3rd year canonical.* She wrote at the top. *Specialist deployment processed: 7 soldiers, Carnyx territorial complement, Ocipheus Station administrative intake. Category designated: Sinter Zone Approach Preparation. Canonical compendium cross-reference: pre-incursion operational, Canon Immaculate plenary authorization required.*

She wrote carefully, in her small careful hand.

*Session notation, Chamber Three, same date: no immediate action indicated.*

She wrote a note below: *The session notation and the intake log were processed on the same day. They are filed in the same archival queue. They do not reference each other.*

She looked at that last sentence. It was accurate. It was also not her assignment to note it.

She left it.

She wrote: *Cumulative pattern, month 1 through month 8: Oculus Memoriae recovery instrument. T-044 transit suspension. Lacerta and Carnyx sector reports, repeated cycle, "No Action Indicated." Wall garrison supply authorizations, aggregate increase. War construct evaluation cohort, status: deployment authorization pending. Intake log, specialist soldiers, Sinter Zone Approach Preparation. Session notation, interhouse review, "no immediate action indicated."*

She had written these things before, in other working copies, in smaller pieces. She had not written them in sequence on a single page.

She looked at the sequence.

She had been, she thought, trying not to see the shape of it. Not because she had not seen shapes before — she had spent three years learning to read shapes — but because the shapes you read in the documents of other people's decisions were navigable. You could hold them at the distance of the instrument. This shape was not navigable in the same way. This shape had her sister's name in it, crossed out but legible.

She added one more line at the bottom of the page.

*Δ-7 through Δ-14 instrument set: not yet convened. When convened: canonical witness certification required. Notary required. I am the notary.*

She underlined *I am the notary* and then felt that this was excessive and considered crossing it out and did not.

She capped her pen.

She left the working copy open on her desk — open to the air, the ink still slightly wet, the sequence laid out in her small careful hand. She looked at it the way she had been looking at walls tonight, without reading it, which was the other way you read things when you had been doing this work long enough. You looked until the shape resolved into something you could hold.

Eight months. Seven soldiers. No immediate action indicated. Her name on the notary line, when it came.

Outside, the courtyard was dark and the station was quieting toward the administrative close of day. Somewhere in the eastern wing, a door she could not see was closing. Somewhere in the archival queue, the session notation and the intake log sat in adjacent slots, not referencing each other, both of them correct, both of them signed.

She turned the working copy face-down on her desk.

She locked the drawer.

She picked up her satchel, straightened the instruments in the archival queue with one precise motion, and walked out of the registry.

Behind her, on the desk, the working copy lay face-down in the particular dark of an office after closing, making no record of anything at all.

[Beat 14]
SCHMALBURG — THE RAID; THE EATERS; KRESSIDA

Three long. Two short. Then again: three long, two short.

Lyra's hand found her hilt before her mind finished the count.

The Pallor border action, three years past — she had learned the pattern from an Atrament garrison officer who had learned it from a Fjorheim field manual captured eleven years before that, in a skirmish whose name she couldn't recall and whose dead she didn't know because she hadn't been there. She knew the signal the way she knew the notation for a restricted Catalyst preparation: not because she'd made the thing herself, but because she had read enough about its effects to recognize them before they finished arriving.

Fjorheim raid.

"Close," Orim said. He was consulting no instrument. Old men who had spent fifty years scraping their gift across the surfaces of things developed a feel for distance that was more reliable than apparatus and less reliable than luck, and that was still often enough to be worth having. "East quarter. The direction of the rail depot."

The street around them had gone from foot-traffic to empty in the time it took a person to process the sound and move. Schmalburg knew this bell. Had known it for eleven hundred years, or something like it — the gorge-city had been receiving Fjorheim attention since before the battle that gave it its name, and the name itself was the insult the raiders used when they withdrew on day forty-one after the Catalyst incendiary: *small fortress, small people.* The people of Schmalburg had kept the name. Had made armor of it. Had built a civil defense protocol around it that could empty a commercial street in under a minute.

The protocol put civilians in shelters and fighters at garrison points. Both options were wrong for Lyra's party, which was neither.

The first door she tried was already sealed, bar dropped on the inside. The second was locked before she reached it. The third was a stone passage leading downward — the civilian shelter route, which was exactly what the protocol intended.

"Garrison points are east," Ardea said. Her hand was not on her hilt. Ardea Marten kept her hands quiet in a fight, which was different from what most people meant when they said calm. It was a quality Lyra had catalogued in the first week and stopped cataloguing because it became part of the background. "They'll want bodies at the rail depot perimeter. The rigs deploy from the eastern yard."

"The rigs deploy and we're in the way."

"The shelters fill and we lose two hours." This was Orim, who was looking at a narrow passage between two forge-houses — smoke-blackened stone on both sides, wide enough for three people if two of them breathed in. "There is a third option."

Rowe said something in his own language. A short phrase, two words, the kind of thing a person says when they've understood the situation without understanding the words being used to describe it.

"Yes," Orim told him, which was not a translation but was accurate enough. "Come."

---

The gorge-streets of Schmalburg were not designed for combat or for comfort. They had been designed for the forge-industry: high-walled, close, following the ridge geology at angles that made no navigational sense until you understood they were cooling channels, not roads — the city had grown up around the heat-management problem of running twelve hundred years of alchemical-industrial work in the same stone structure. The walls were black at the base and grey above the line where the heat rose, and the air at street level in the forge quarter had a quality of pressure that was not quite sound but not quite smell either — the cumulative residue of Heloth exhaust venting through the same corridors for generations.

She heard the fighting before she reached the junction. The bolt-action rifle had a distinctive report in enclosed stone: sharper than in open ground, the crack cutting back at itself off the walls so what reached your ears was the shot and its own echo arriving half a heartbeat apart. Atrament manufacture. She knew the specific overlap from the Vigil Station's range work.

But the frequency coming around the junction was wrong. Two variants, she catalogued in the first three seconds. One was Atrament. One was not.

"Fjorheim uses a longer action," Ardea said, beside her. "Their source Sphere runs a variant. Same Sphere, different generation."

The same source Sphere. Lyra filed the thought without analyzing it because there was a crossfire developing at the street junction thirty meters ahead and the time for analysis was not this one.

She pulled back. Ardea was already back. She looked for Rowe. He was at the near wall, pressed into a recessed forge door, weapon up. He had not been told to do this. He had read the geometry of the junction and found the position himself — seven months in Vierna, which was real training even if it had been bought with his body without his consent.

The battle rigs arrived before the crossfire resolved.

She felt them before she heard them — the vibration in the stone underfoot, the particular frequency of a Heloth steam-chemical plant working under load. Then the sound: grinding and pneumatic, the controlled hydraulic hiss on the turns, the street-scrape of iron carrying serious weight. Three of them coming up the eastern approach. Three meters of purpose-built Atrament armor, each one designed to be the last thing in an enclosed space still functional when the problem was solved. The BR-designation series. She had reviewed the program summaries for the Vigil Station's threat assessments. The rigs were not fast; they were not designed to be fast. They were designed to be indestructible in the specific architecture of Schmalburg's gorge-streets, which made them exactly as capable as the gorge-streets required.

The lead rig reached the junction and solved the first firing position. Not by any mechanism she could have described precisely — the dust was wrong and the angle was wrong and she was thirty meters back with her spine against stone — but solved it in the way the rigs solved problems in gorge-street work: by being the largest and most armored thing present, and by having a pilot who knew which of those two qualities to deploy first.

The firing from the Fjorheim position changed character. Antipersonnel rounds giving way to something heavier. Anti-armor payload, which was a calculated bet. Anti-armor against an Atrament battle rig required a specific shot angle, a specific distance, and an outcome that had something like luck woven into it.

The lead rig took the round at the wrong angle and at too-close range for the round's design parameters.

Not dead. The rigs didn't die from one anti-armor round, which was the point of their construction. But the impact drove something — she would learn what, later — drove something into the housing, and the rig's movement became asymmetrical. It was still moving. Still solving the crossfire, still doing the work, still functional. But the movement was wrong in a way she could see even at thirty meters and through the smoke.

"Left forearm housing," Ardea said. "Round caught the coupling joint. You can see it in the stride."

She could see it now that it was named. The rig's left arm hung differently. Not loose. Wrong in its load-bearing.

The crossfire resolved, as crossfires do — not with clarity or justice but with the sudden absence of one of the things making noise, replaced by a different kind of noise that was harder to categorize.

---

That was when the Eaters came.

She knew what they were before she saw them clearly. The smell reached her first — the Sinter crawlers' biological Catalyst compound had a specific signature, acrid and organic, the smell of the membrane's own biology being processed through a human system over years. She had read this in the Vigil Station's field reports. She had not expected to identify it by smell, from thirty meters, in the forge-city's exhaust-laden air.

She identified it.

There were four. They moved at a pace that was wrong for the space — too efficient, too certain of the ground, like something that had memorized this architecture without having used it before. They wore the layered work-cloth of Fjorheim's forge-villages, practical, not a statement, but what the cloth covered moved differently than cloth was designed to accommodate.

The leader stopped at the junction.

She was taller than multiple unsanctioned infusions without a certified practitioner should have produced — the body, without guidance, had apparently organized the change around structural necessity rather than Liturgy protocol, and what resulted was this. The Liturgy classified the result as abomination. Lyra had written that classification into her own threat assessments, four times, in the formal notation.

She had written it wrong.

The skin was wrong. Not monstrous. Not corrupted. Wrong in the specific way that something is wrong when it has been reorganized past the point where what it became still belonged to the same category as what it was. The Transmutation, taken without the prescribed attenuation between doses, had rebuilt the surface tissue into something that carried out skin's function — keeping the interior interior — but wasn't skin in the technical sense.
