In motion, particularly at the joint-interfaces, you could see the underlying structural work beneath it. Not organs. Architecture. The thing the body had rebuilt itself around.

But what Lyra's eye kept returning to, even at thirty meters, even through the smoke, was the neck.

The musculature of the neck had been reorganized — additional support structures grown in, visible under the skin where they stood proud in a way the standard anatomy had no room for. You could count them. Four, possibly five, where there should have been two. And the head tracked on a range of motion the human neck did not provide, without strain, without effort, like something that had always worked this way rather than something that had learned to. When the leader turned to look at the far end of the junction, her head moved through an arc that Lyra's hand instinctively wanted to record because the record would be evidence of something the Liturgy's classification system had no category for.

The Eaters had not come for the raid. The raids drew things from the Sinter perimeter's overflow cracks — the membrane monsters that the quarantine never fully contained. That was what the Eaters had tracked here. That was the reason they arrived when they arrived: the raid's noise, the clash of it in the gorge-streets, had drawn whatever had been pressing at the overflow site, and the Eaters had followed their prey through the noise into the city.

The leader moved into the junction, and the other three spread to the walls, and Lyra heard — she would record this later, in the same notation she used for everything — a sound that had no reference in her research archive. Not a cry. Not a body impact. Something between a collapse and a release, the kind of sound a structure makes when the thing holding it together from the inside stops. The sound came from beyond the junction. It came once.

Then it was quiet.

"We should not be between them and where they are going," Orim said, from immediately behind Lyra's left shoulder, which was where he had been for the past three minutes without her having noticed it.

Lyra moved.

---

Ardea died in the Helothworkers' Lane, which ran between the main rig-yard access road and the secondary cooling channel behind the third forge complex. Lyra would record the coordinates later, the specific coordinates, because she was a researcher and recording was what she did. She would record the date, the time, the cause. She would not record what it felt like to hold Ardea Marten while Ardea Marten stopped being a person and became something the stone would keep its own record of.

They were moving for the secondary cooling channel when the Fjorheim position repositioned — not retreating, redirecting, because professional forces redirect rather than break when the rigs push. The shot was intended for the junction where the lane opened onto the yard access road, where a body moving without cover would be in the path of the withdrawal. Rowe moved onto that junction.

He had twenty-eight words of Cauld. He had seven months of Vierna training. He did not have a tactical map of Schmalburg's gorge-streets, and he had understood nothing in the last four minutes as instruction. He moved toward the noise the way a soldier moves toward a problem when the soldier can see the geometry and cannot hear the plan.

Ardea moved faster.

Three years out of the Ocipheus garrison, which was the posting you received when you were the kind of sergeant who kept a research party alive through Vierna entry and ran logistics for three months without losing anyone. Three years out of active combat. Her hand was not on her hilt. Her body went to the right position because thirty years of service had put it there before she had time to think about whether this was the one.

The round took her through the upper chest, left side, below the collar. She was already pulling Rowe back when it found her. The pull became a push. She fell against the forge-house wall and sat down against it, hard, with the specific ungainliness of a body that has stopped being coordinated from the inside.

Lyra was there in — she did not count.

Ardea's eyes were open and tracking. That was the important thing for the first three seconds. She was tracking Lyra's face, and she was not speaking, and Lyra put her hand on the wound without looking at it because looking was not the useful thing and the hand was.

"Sergeant," Lyra said.

Ardea looked at her.

The blood came through Lyra's fingers at a rate that told her what she needed to know without requiring calculation. She had administered enough field tinctures to read the rate. She was reading it now, and what it told her was not something she had a response to, because her kit was in her satchel and getting to it required removing her hand from the wound, and removing her hand from the wound was not going to help.

Ardea said one word, which was not Lyra's name. It was the name of someone Lyra did not know — someone from before the current posting, possibly still alive somewhere east. She said it without urgency, as if she were placing a face she had just recognized. Then she did not say anything else.

She died the way people die, which is not the way accounts say it. No declaration. No moment of clarity. The body finishes what it is doing, and what it was doing was: working, then not working, and the distance between those two states is not marked by any particular event. Lyra had seen it before. She had not been holding the person before.

Thirty seconds. Perhaps forty.

Rowe was at the far wall. He had understood what happened before it finished happening — the sequence was not ambiguous even without the language for it. He was looking at the space where Ardea had been, and his face was doing something that had no file in Lyra's research notation. She noted this. She noted it the way she noted things when she was functioning correctly, which she was. She would return to it when she had the resources to be human again.

She let go of the wound. Her hands were red to the wrist.

The research satchel was over her left shoulder. Ardea Marten's service record was in the document folio, third from the top. It had been there since Bressant. The record needed to be closed by the ranking officer.

She was the ranking officer.

She did not open the satchel. She filed it: *service record, Marten. Closing, pending. Time of death approximate.* She would do it in the hour. She would do it when there was a wall to sit against and a lane that wasn't this lane.

Orim was in the doorway across the lane, watching the yard access road. He said nothing. He had probably understood, from the moment Ardea moved, how the sequence would resolve. Fifty years of watching things end had given him that quality.

Lyra stood. She pulled her field cloth and used it and put it away. The field cloth had a finite number of uses. This was a fact that could be managed.

"We move when the rigs clear the junction," she said.

"The third rig isn't moving," Orim said.

---

The BR-7 was in the secondary yard, rig-wall to the cooling channel. Not where a functioning rig would park, which told her that something about its function had changed.

She came at it from the northeast approach. The BR-7 series had a rotating instrumentation housing at the shoulder that read the environment as thermal and EM gradient. She walked into its range on purpose, clearly, not like someone who needed to be a threat.

The rig did not move toward her. It did not bring its weapon to bear. It was just there in the yard with the left-arm housing showing the round-impact site she had identified from the junction, and the left arm held in a posture that was load-management — the way a person holds a damaged limb, carrying the joint out of load-bearing because the load-bearing was what hurt.

She thought: *the pilot is managing an injury through the machine's posture.* Then: *or the machine is managing the injury for the pilot, which is a different thing.*

The access hatch opened.

The woman who dropped out of it was small in the absolute sense. Not slight — the distinction mattered, Lyra noted, because slight suggested fragility and this person had the same quality Ardea had possessed, the same stillness in the hands, the same way of a body that has been used for serious work long enough that it has organized itself around the work. Dark hair cut short on one side, grown out on the other in the way of someone who'd stopped caring about symmetry six months ago and not noticed. Dockworkers' clothes under a half-unbuttoned tool vest, the kind with deep pockets for maintenance instruments. She dropped from the hatch to the ground — four feet, on stone — and landed without adjusting, the kind of landing that means impact registered as data rather than sensation, because the normal pathway for it had changed.

The rig was three meters of Atrament iron, reaction-plated, built to occupy tactical space the way a wall occupies a wall. The pilot standing in the yard before she walked toward Lyra was the size of a person you would not notice on the dock road. She had been inside that machine. She had been the thing that machine obeyed.

The contrast was — Lyra would note this. Had already noted it.

"BR-7," Lyra said.

"Haun." The flat Atrament-border accent — dropping the final vowel, consonants pushed forward. "Kressida Haun. Formerly." A pause. "The round went into the coupling housing. Left dorsal. The housing drove into the neural pathway — the adjacent pathway." Something crossed her face, brief. "The field surgeon gave me an assessment."

"Is the surgeon correct?"

"He's correct about what happened. He's wrong about what to do about it." She looked at the rig. Not sentimentally. The way a person looks at the thing that has become load-bearing for their continued existence. "The rig is keeping me upright. When the round drove the housing in, it touched the pathway. There was a fusion event. I can feel the rig the way I can feel my hand."

"Can you disengage?"

"Yes." No hesitation in it. "I can get out whenever I want. The rig keeps me alive while I'm in it. I get out, I'm outside it, and then —" She did not finish. She didn't need to. "Atrament has a process for this. A disposal recommendation. They hadn't filed it yet." She said *disposal recommendation* the way Orim said accurate things that were uncomfortable: without decoration. "I didn't wait."

"No," Lyra said.

"You're moving west." Not a question. "I heard what you're after. The Sallander's wake was twelve hours old when I checked with the Dockhands' Association this morning. You're three people now," she said, which landed with the precision of someone who had watched from the rig's sensor range and counted and understood what the count meant. "I need to move. You're moving. West is the only direction that doesn't end with Atrament command finding out I survived the Schmalburg action."

Orim appeared at the yard entrance. He looked at Kressida. He looked at the BR-7. He said: "The rig will not fit through the waterway loading doors."

"It fits through the river-staging gate on the east lock," she said. "I know the yard."

"She knows the yard," Orim said, to Lyra specifically, which was not exactly information but was not nothing.

---

The Eaters pulled off when the Fjorheim raid broke, and the Fjorheim raid broke when the second and third rigs cleared the rail depot junction and the Fjorheim commander did the mathematics that professional forces do when the mathematics have settled. Lyra watched from the cooling channel access point as the Eaters moved northeast — not retreating; withdrawing, in the specific manner of hunters who have finished their business and are not interested in ceremony about it. The thing from the Sinter overflow was somewhere in the east yard, dead. She had heard the sound it made when it died, which resembled nothing in her reference archive, and had filed it: *membrane overflow fauna, unidentified, Eater of Monsters effective countermeasure confirmed.* The Liturgy would want that data. She was not certain what she thought about being the one who carried it back.

The bells had shifted from raid-warning to damage-assessment. The forge-yards were running again — the exhaust-pressure hum was back in the stones underfoot. Two of the three rigs had returned to the yards. The city had the particular quality she had observed once before — the capital, nine years ago, a Fjorheim incursion into the secondary trade district. Not calm. Not controlled. The quality of a population that has done this before and knows the shape of the next four hours and has arranged itself around that knowledge. Schmalburg had been *small fortress* for eleven hundred years. It knew what it was.

She sat down beside Ardea Marten's body.

The service record was in the document folio, third from the top, which was where it had been since Bressant. She took it out. Twelve pages, close notation, Ocipheus garrison format — date of enlistment, posting history, distinguished service marks, the research-secondment authorization that had moved Ardea from garrison duty to Lyra's party. The authorization was dated six months ago. Lyra had signed it. Her signature was on the document, which meant her hand had been present in every step of the chain that had brought Ardea Marten to the Helothworkers' Lane.

She did not think about the chain. Thinking about the chain was not useful to the work of closing the record.

She filled in the date, the location, the cause. *Enemy action, crossfire withdrawal, Fjorheim raid, Schmalburg.* Formal notation. She signed the closing entry with her designation: T-044, Templar rank, Liturgy of the Canon Immaculate.

The form's printed header ran across the top two lines of every service record page, in the canonical font pressed small enough that it did not compete with the content: *In service to the Canon Immaculate and the Liturgy's stewardship mission, the practitioner dedicates their body and their gift to the maintenance of the vigil, the protection of the membrane, and the lawful passage of all that moves between Spheres, for the benefit of the Cauld and all it holds. Their service is their faith. Their faith is the record.*

She had copied this header into two previous closing forms without reading it. She read it now, with the blood still on her hands and the ink of the cause notation drying. The header addressed the practitioner in the third person: *their,* not *your.* The institution did not speak to the person directly. It referred to them. As a category the record held.

She put the record back in the folio. Third from the top.

The Liturgy had a theory about loss and its management and the process by which the living return to function. She had read it in the foundational documents, and the foundational documents were in the Vigil Station archive that was currently empty. She had never found fault with the theory before, because she had never before held the person between the person being alive and the person being a thing the stone kept record of. The theory addressed the aftermath. It had nothing to say about those thirty seconds.

This was not a gap she had noticed before.

She filed it. She would return to it when she had a category for it.

Rowe was across the lane, back against the wall, looking at the place where Ardea had been. The body was not there — Orim had managed this, somewhere in the last hour, with the same quiet efficiency with which he managed things that needed managing without anyone observing him manage them. There was blood on the stone. There was always blood on the stone. The stone kept what it kept.

She looked at Rowe's face. The expression that had no file. A person confronting something he had not been asked to confront, that he had walked into without the language to refuse or the context to understand, and was holding because there was nowhere else to put it. She looked at it and let it be what it was. She would find a file for it eventually, or she would not, and either way she would look at him across the lane on this evening for the rest of her life and know exactly what his face had done.

Kressida Haun was twenty meters away at the yard entrance, the BR-7 standing at the wall behind her. The contrast did not diminish with familiarity. The rig was everything Atrament made things to be: massive, practical, not a single element without function, designed to solve the problems that nothing else in the gorge-streets could solve in the same space. The pilot stood in front of it, compact, undamaged to outward appearance, running her own mathematics with the expression of someone who knows what the numbers say and is waiting for the conversation to catch up.

Lyra closed the document folio. She put it in the research satchel and settled the satchel on her shoulder.

"We move tonight," she said.

Rowe looked up from the lane. His eyes moved to Lyra, then to Kressida, then back. He said one of his twenty-eight words — the one that carried *where,* and *what direction,* and *what comes next,* depending on context. He had learned it early, which was efficient of him.

"West," Lyra said.

He nodded. He had the Cauld nod from the first week.

Orim emerged from the secondary passage where he had not been visible for several minutes, carrying nothing she could identify. "The river-staging gate accepts passage papers or Atrament rig-crew authorization," he said. "One of these we have." He looked at Kressida. "Formerly."

"Still have the rig-crew authorization. They won't cancel it until they process the disposal recommendation, and the recommendation won't be filed until someone notices the BR-7 missing from the yard count." She looked at the rig, then at Lyra. One look, brief, the way you look at the thing that has become load-bearing for your continued existence when you have accepted that it is and have no interest in sentiment about it. "Tonight is the window."

"Third bell," Lyra said. "Have the rig at the staging gate."

Kressida was already walking back to the BR-7 when Lyra stood. The hatch opened before she reached it.

Lyra walked back to the lane entry and picked up Ardea's rifle from the ground where it had fallen. She checked the mechanism from habit and put it over her shoulder. It was a weapon. It was functional. Leaving it served nothing.

The gorge-street was empty of everything except the exhaust-hum in the stone and the quality of a city that had done this before and would do it again and was already making its arrangements. She walked west. Behind her, the BR-7's access hatch sealed with a sound like a bar dropping on the inside of a door.

[Beat 15]
THE FORGE HEARTH — WHAT SHE RECOGNIZES

The ridge path narrowed where the volcanic substrate pushed through the alpine soil. Here the stone had refused to stay underground: it had come up through the topsoil in long dark extrusions, finger-shaped, warm to the touch even in the autumn cold. Lyra pressed her palm against one and left it there. The warmth was geological. She had read about geothermal zones. She knew what the Forge Hearth was before she arrived. Knowing had not prepared her for the particular quality of the warmth, which was not the warmth of heated stone so much as the warmth of something that had not stopped.

Kressida walked beside her. The rig walked three meters back, where the trail was wider.

It moved with a low hydraulic patience, the steam-chemical plant cycling at maintenance pressure between steps, the reaction-plate shoulder housings angling when the path bent to keep the flail housing clear of the overhanging stone. The ember-fungi on the rig's lower exhaust housing had been growing for two days, drawn to the chemical exhaust — orange and bioluminescent, pulsing faintly at the rhythm of the power cycle. It looked like the machine was breathing.

"Hearth-Three is approximately four kilometers south," Kressida said. She said it the way she said most things: as data offered without decoration. "The perimeter station. Hearth-Two is south of that. Hearth-One you can't get to from the ridge without going through the extraction apparatus."

"You've been to the valley."

"Three postings. Valley floor, not up here." She looked at the stone under her boots, then at the country ahead where the ridge opened into a long exposed section with clear sightlines to the south. "The valley crews don't come to the ridge. The ridge crews don't go to the valley. Different operational units. The ridge is Liturgy-chained territory."

Orim made a sound that might have been acknowledgment. He was walking behind them, his travel satchel slung across one shoulder, and he had been watching the country to the south with the specific quality of attention Lyra had come to associate with his work — not the sustained focus of someone performing a scry, but the preliminary attention. Reading the site before he read it.

Rowe was on the other side of Kressida, rifle slung, hands loose. He had been quiet since the descent from the upper approach. He was quiet in the way that had become readable to her over these weeks: not withdrawn, not afraid. Processing. He watched the landscape the way he watched everything that was new — methodically, building a map he had no words yet to describe.

He had forty-seven words now. Fifty, perhaps. She had counted this morning from the notebook.

"Hearth-Four and Hearth-Seven are the reduced yield stations," Kressida said. "Current cycle. I saw the operational reports at Schmalburg before the raid. Reduced yield — that's the notation."

"What does reduced yield mean to the Atrament operational commands?"

"Production down. Extract rate below target. The usual response is apparatus recalibration, personnel rotation, sometimes a geological survey if the geothermal substrate has shifted." She paused. "The survey team finds what it finds and the notation stays in the operational record."

"And the apparatus recalibrates."

"The apparatus recalibrates."

They walked. The ridge path ran along the top of the escarpment with the extraction zone's approach roads visible below on the left, carved into the volcanic substrate, maintaining the switchback geometry that Atrament used for heavy equipment access. The ember-fungi were visible down there too. Orange patches growing around the maintenance stations, clustering wherever the Heloth constructs had idled long enough to leave chemical residue in the stone. At this distance they looked like small fires. They had not been fires for perhaps fifty years, which was how long the constructs had been working this section.

The warmth that should have been geological and wasn't quite came from the south.

Lyra noted it. She catalogued the sensation as a practitioner catalogues sensations near active membrane sites: the chest cavity, below the sternum, a pressure that was not pressure. Not like Sinter — that was directional, specific, the ground's attention landing on you from below. This was something else. Something tired.

She had worked the Sinter perimeter for twelve years. She knew what it meant when the ground was paying attention. This was not that. This was what the ground feels like when it has been worked without rest for a long time and has run out of whatever it was that made the working bearable. Not threatening. Not awake. The specific exhaustion of something that has been made to continue past the point where it understood what it was continuing for.

She filed this.

*

Orim stopped at the overlook where the path widened to a shelf of flat volcanic stone, just wide enough for the party to stand without crowding.

He did not announce what he was doing. He simply stopped, and when Lyra turned to look at him he was already at the preliminary stages: the tincture vial from the side pocket of his satchel, the careful application to his fingertips, the small motion of bringing them together at the sternum. He had done this at the Ocipheus Station archive, reading the south passage. He had done it at the Veil River junction, reading the barge traffic. She had been watching him do it for weeks and she could read the stages now the way you read the stages of any practiced ritual — the preparation, the settling, the two breaths that were not breathing so much as calibrating.

He pressed his fingertips together. He breathed twice. He looked at nothing.

There was a period of perhaps forty seconds. The rig shifted its weight at the path's wider point, steam venting softly at the shoulder joint.

Orim opened his eyes.

"No," he said.

Not the word of protest. Not a word directed at the membrane, or at Lyra, or at any member of the party. A fact. The way you say *no* when someone has asked you to name the thing on the other side of a wall you have been staring at, and when you look there is no other side of the wall — only the wall.

He sat down on the volcanic shelf rock. He sat down carefully, the way old men sit when the joints are particular about it and they have learned not to argue with the joints. He set his satchel on the stone beside him. He looked at the south country for a long time without speaking.

Lyra looked at him.

She had been in the company of Orim Zebulun for six weeks. She had seen him in cold and in motion and in the aftermath of danger and in the long hours of barge transit when there was nothing to do but watch the river and think. She had seen him tired, many times. She had seen him pained, occasionally, in the specific way of a man whose body has opinions about how long it should be asked to ride Heloth couriers over mountain roads. She had not seen him old.

Old was what he looked now. Sixty years of working the membrane at the level available to him — the near and the recent, the small clear impressions that a site gave up to a practiced minor scryer — sixty years of that, and this was the first time a site had refused him. He did not say this. He did not need to say it. The way he was sitting on the rock said it.

Rowe looked at Orim. He looked at Lyra. He said nothing, because he did not have the words, but he understood that something had happened that was not supposed to happen, and his understanding of it was visible in his face, which had gone still and careful in the way of someone who has learned to read situations in the absence of language and has just read something he did not expect.

"Can he tell what kind of no it is?" Kressida said. She asked this the way she asked most questions: with genuine curiosity and no particular assumption about what the answer should be.

"He'd tell us if he could," Lyra said.

She looked at Orim. He had not moved. His hands were on his knees. The quality of his stillness was of a man taking stock of something he was not yet ready to describe.

She did not press him. A scryer who has just experienced an apparatus refusal needs time — she knew this from the practitioner literature on installation sites where the apparatus malfunctioned. The membrane-adjacent shock of the refusal was not the same as a physical shock, but it had a similar effect on the body's regulatory sense. The site had been prepared to receive him, and then it had not received him, and his nervous system needed to understand that the preparation was over.

She turned to Kressida instead.

*

"Show me what the rig is seeing," she said.

The access hatch at the rig's chest housing opened with a sequence of mechanical sounds: the seal engagement releasing, the hydraulic assist on the hatch arm, the particular click of the secondary latch that Kressida had told her meant the pilot interface was active. Through the open hatch, the cockpit was visible — compact, close-walled, every surface covered with either controls or readout glass. Kressida climbed the footing rungs without looking at them and settled into the interface harness in the practiced way of someone who has done this ten thousand times and no longer needed to think about any of it.

The primary display glass lit.

Lyra moved to the access point and looked in at the readout.

Atrament's extraction instrumentation rendered the membrane as it rendered everything: as a resource. The display showed a false-color map of the surrounding terrain with a gradient overlay — blue to orange to red — that tracked what the rig's sensors classified as thermal and electromagnetic pressure variation. The blue was geological baseline. The orange was elevated. The area south of their current position, where Hearth-Three's extraction apparatus was operating, showed red.

Below the map, the readout columns were labeled in Atrament's operational notation:

MEMBRANE CONTACT PRESSURE: 87.4% OPTIMAL YIELD GRADIENT
CATALYST CONCENTRATION: REDUCED — HEARTH-SECTOR 4-7 CORRIDOR
EXTRACTION INDEX: 61.2 (TARGET: 80.0)
SUBSTRATE TEMPERATURE: WITHIN GEOLOGICAL VARIANCE
YIELD PREDICTION (SEASONAL): BELOW THRESHOLD

The numbers were precise. The framework was correct for what it was measuring. The rig had been built to read extraction sites as extraction sites, and it was doing this accurately, and the display was showing her exactly what the machine's sensors observed.

She looked at the columns. She looked at the gradient map. She looked at the designation REDUCED below the concentration entry.

She had read that notation before, in the Scrying installation maintenance literature — the practitioner documentation on membrane site behavior after extended apparatus use. The term there was different. The Liturgy's notation called it *recovery gradient depression.* The meaning was the same: the site was giving back less than it had been giving back, for the same or greater apparatus effort. The extraction index was down. The recovery rate was not matching the extraction rate.

Kressida climbed out and stood beside her at the display.

"The Hearth-Four and Hearth-Seven reduced yield notations," Lyra said.

"Yes."

"When did those start?"

"The operational record goes back thirty years. Those two stations have been below target for eleven and nine years respectively." A pause. "They used to be in the upper production quartile. I saw the historical comparison in a briefing two years ago. The comparison was presented as calibration drift — the apparatus needed realignment."

"Did they realign it?"

"Three times on Hearth-Four. Twice on Hearth-Seven." Kressida looked at the display. "The yield kept declining."

Lyra looked at the display and thought about substrate recovery in biological tissue.

It was not a formal thought. It was the practitioner's reflex — the same reflex that had made her crouch beside the dead night-warden in the archive room and read the angle of his fall. She had read papers on membrane site recovery after Scrying operations. This was part of her research background, the applied biology section, the part of Transmutation study that concerned itself with how the membrane responded to the apparatus's sustained contact. The papers had described the recovery gradient in terms that she now recognized on the display in front of her, translated into Atrament's production vocabulary.

A wound heals inward from its edges. That was the basic principle. The rate depends on the depth of the wound, the frequency of re-opening, the overall condition of the surrounding tissue. In human biology, a wound that is opened and closed repeatedly — sutured, reopened, re-sutured — develops scar tissue at a rate faster than the surrounding tissue can compensate. The scar is not normal tissue. It does not have the same properties. It does not recover at the same rate. Eventually the surgeon's options narrow.

The membrane at Hearth-Four had been opened and held open by apparatus, repeatedly, for decades. The membrane at Hearth-Seven the same. The apparatus was designed to hold the wound open — that was its function, to maintain the aperture against the membrane's natural inclination to close. The aperture was held open through the extraction cycle, then the apparatus was withdrawn, and the membrane was given a recovery interval before the next cycle.

What the papers described — what the researchers had documented in the theoretical literature on membrane biology, which she had read as theory, as data, as the background of a framework she was contributing to with her own research — was that the recovery interval did not produce full recovery. The tissue was not returning to its pre-wound state. The papers had described this in careful, qualified language. They had noted that the documentation at active Liturgy sites was insufficient for strong claims about long-term tissue behavior because the sites had not been monitored at the necessary resolution. They had called for more research. They had been published. They had been filed.

She was watching what the papers had described, in a landscape she could see with her own eyes, rendered in a machine's production language that said *reduced yield* for the thing the papers called *recovery gradient depression* for the thing she was calling, privately, something she did not yet have a word for.

The Cauld's membrane ran under all of it. Under the ridge where she was standing. Under the Sinter zone with its torn places that had stopped healing normally after Year 1079. Under the Forge Hearth zone where the extraction apparatus had been operating since Year 842, which was a hundred and eighty-two years before the Quarantine Compact and four hundred years before the Year of the last authorization renewal. She had learned this in an institutional history course, in the year she was seventeen, in the context of learning how the Canon Immaculate had expanded the Liturgy's administrative reach into Atrament's Catalyst operations. The authorization history had been presented as evidence of the Liturgy's organizational sophistication: Year 842, Year 919, Year 1001. Each renewal was mentioned as an achievement of inter-House coordination.

She had taken notes. She had filed them. She had not thought about the authorization history again until now.

"It is not calibration drift," she said.

Kressida looked at her.

"The apparatus is calibrated correctly," Lyra said. "The yield decline is real. The site is not recovering at the expected rate." She paused. "The apparatus cannot be recalibrated to compensate for that."

"Atrament would want to know this," Kressida said.

"Yes."

"If you have a technical basis for the assessment — if you can document the membrane biology reading — the Atrament extraction authority would accept a Liturgy Templar's assessment. That's within your authority. The report would go through the regional Canon on the Atrament-adjacent filing —" Kressida stopped.

Lyra said: "I know."

A silence.

"You're not going to report it," Kressida said.

Lyra said nothing.

This was not quite true. The mechanism for reporting it existed. She could file a technical assessment with the regional Canon, who would forward it to the Canon Immaculate's assessment committee, which reviewed Templar observations regarding Scrying-adjacent technical anomalies. The mechanism was functioning. The mechanism had been functioning for six hundred years. It was the same mechanism that had received the Forge Hearth authorization request in Year 842 and signed it, and received the Year 919 renewal request and signed it, and received the Year 1001 renewal request and signed it. The Canon Immaculate's assessment committee had a standing financial arrangement with the Atrament Catalyst extraction guilds that was not a secret — it was a formally documented cooperative charter, renewed at the same intervals as the installation authorizations. This was because the installation authorizations and the cooperative charter were the same document, administered from the same authority.

She knew this from the institutional history course, in the same year, the same notes.

A report filed through the assessment committee's review process would reach an institution that had been authorizing the extraction operations for six hundred years and that had an ongoing financial interest in continuing to authorize them. The report would enter the committee's filing system. The committee would review it according to its standard procedure. The standard procedure would produce an outcome consistent with the committee's prior six hundred years of outcomes.

This was not corruption in the way corruption was usually described — not a single dishonest act by a particular dishonest official. The architecture made the report functionally unreceivable by design. The committee was not designed to receive this kind of report. The committee was designed to authorize extraction operations. A report describing harm to the extraction substrate would encounter a review process designed to assess whether authorizations should be renewed. The answer to that question was documented across six centuries.

She was a Templar. Her reporting obligation ran up the chain. The chain led here.

Lyra did not say any of this. She said nothing.

After a moment, Kressida looked away. She did not say anything further. She was Atrament-trained, and she knew — the way Atrament-trained soldiers knew, from the same institutional culture that had produced the extraction operations and the reporting protocols and the seven-generation operational tradition of this site — when a superior had made a decision and indicated it was not open for discussion. The indication was not a statement. The indication was a silence. Kressida recognized it.

But Lyra was not watching Kressida's face when Kressida looked away.

She was watching the display.

She looked at Kressida's face a moment later, when Kressida had turned back to the access footing. And the thing she saw was not visible for long — Kressida was efficient about her own expressions in the way of a person who has learned that the rig is a more useful face than her face — but it was there for the moment between looking away and composing the efficiency back into place. Something that had not expected to matter. Something mattering anyway. The same door she had seen blown open in Rowe's face when he had first been given the word for *factory.* The same moment when a thing that was supposed to stay abstract became specific and heavy.

She filed it. She did not examine it.

*

Orim was still sitting on the volcanic rock.

She went and stood near him. Not close enough to intrude on whatever he was doing, which did not look like doing so much as absorbing. He had his hands flat on his knees and was looking at the south country with the expression of a man who has been going through a door for fifty years and has just found the door gone.

"In the year 1228," he said, without looking at her, "I had a contract at the Eirene's Gate installation. Wall maintenance verification. Four months." A pause. "The tone was present then. The particular Sinter tone — you know it."

"I know it."

"I have crossed the Forge Hearth approach roads six times in the last thirty years. The ambient register here was always different from the Sinter register — lower, slower, more diffuse. The way a bruise is different from a cut." He paused again. "This is not that."

She waited.

"At Sinter, the membrane pays attention. Or something does. Something at this frequency that I cannot distinguish from the membrane." He looked at the stone under his feet. "Here it does not pay attention. It is not present in that way. But it is —" He stopped. He made a small, precise movement with one hand: setting something down. "In fifty years I have never had a site refuse me. A new site will sometimes be slow to receive — it has not been worked, the perceptual channel is less available. I have always been able to press into it and open the surface. Whatever it takes to open the surface, I have always had enough." He was quiet for a moment. "Here there is nothing to press into."

"Not resistance," Lyra said.

"Not resistance. Absence." He looked at her. "The way you could not press your hand through a wall is not the same as the way you could not press your hand through the space where the wall used to be. Different kind of nothing."

The sound came then.

She had been aware of it for some time — the way you are sometimes aware of something you have been hearing before you have noticed you are hearing it. A low sound. Below the wind, below the geological percussion of the steam vents at the valley apparatus stations. Not a sound so much as a register in the chest cavity, below the sternum, where the Sinter tone had its address but where this was not the Sinter tone. This was a different frequency. Slower. Rhythmic, in the way that breathing is rhythmic: not mechanical, not steady in the mechanical sense, but with the particular variation of a live interval. In. The held moment. Out. Longer than it should be.

She had heard this at the Ocipheus Station installation. During the long Scrying sessions, when the apparatus was fully engaged and the operators were maintaining the membrane contact through the full extraction cycle, there was a point — usually around the fourth hour — when the ambient register near the apparatus acquired this character. She had noted it in her research annotations. She had classified it under *membrane-adjacent phenomenology, sustained apparatus use.* She had not thought carefully about what produced it, because the sound was incidental to the research focus and because understanding it fully would have required a kind of inquiry that the institutional vocabulary did not quite have room for.

She had never heard it without apparatus.

There was no apparatus on the ridge. The nearest active apparatus was at Hearth-Three, four kilometers south, behind the extraction perimeter, operating on whatever cycle the current season's authorization specified. Four kilometers. The sound, if it was a sound, was not traveling from there. It was here.

She said nothing. She listened to it for a moment the way you listen to a statement you are not ready to respond to because responding would require admitting that you heard it.

Then she said: "Can we move."

*

Rowe had been waiting near the rig. When the party began moving he moved with them, south around the overlook shelf and then west along the ridge's continuation, the far side of the Forge Hearth zone's boundary, the path descending in long switchbacks toward the Lacerta approach. The country changed as they descended: the volcanic substrate giving way to limestone, the thermal warmth retreating behind them, the air losing the particular quality it had near Catalyst-adjacent sites.

He walked beside her for a portion of the descent and said nothing for most of it. He understood, she thought, that something had happened on the ridge, and he had the particular patience of a man who knew his Cauld was not yet adequate to ask about it and who had learned, in seven months in a country whose language he did not speak, to wait until the moment was right to try.

At the fourth switchback he said: "Old man. No see."

She looked at him.

"No see." He made the gesture he had developed for Orim's scrying — fingers pressed together at the sternum. "No see. Bad?"

"Yes," she said. "Bad."

He nodded. He looked ahead at the switchback's continuation, where the path opened into the broader descent toward the valley and the Lacerta approach roads. He said, carefully: "Like when see, then not see."

She looked at him again.

He was watching her with the attention he gave words when he was not sure whether he had assembled them correctly but had decided to try them anyway. Forty-seven words. He had been building the vocabulary with her for six weeks, word by word, in notebooks and by lamplight and on barge transit and in whatever spaces the journey opened. He had four words in the beginning. The sentence had been building since the grain bin in Bressant.

"Like when you know," he said. Slow, careful. "Then know not enough."

She did not answer immediately. She walked the switchback for a moment and thought about what he had said, and about the papers she had read on membrane biology, and about the particular quality of knowing a thing in a framework and then encountering the thing and discovering that the framework was made of words that pointed at it without touching it.

"Yes," she said. "Like that."

*

The Forge Hearth zone fell behind them.

The descent was long and the Lacerta approach roads were not yet visible, but the landscape was already becoming different in the way that landscapes become different when you have left one regime of stone and entered another: limestone rather than volcanic, cooler, the particular smell of altitude giving way to the smell of altitude combined with sea approach. The channel was west of here. Sal Vento was west of here. The thieves were west of here, and the route they had been following, and the rest of what this journey had to accomplish.

She did not look back at the ridge.

She carried, at present: the Oculus Memoriae in its sealed travel case, packed at the center of her kit with the careful distribution of weight she had learned from six weeks of difficult terrain. The Dissolution Blade and the Vigil Shield, the tincture kits, the sealed authority documents from the Keeper's office that were three weeks expired and that she was carrying anyway because the chain of documented custody mattered regardless of whether the authority it represented was still technically operative. And, filed behind these, two pending matters.

The first: Ardea Marten, Sergeant, Ocipheus Station field unit, twelve years of service. Died in Schmalburg, on a cobblestone street in the commercial quarter, at the beginning of a Fjorheim raid. The death had been quick. The dying had not been. It was the kind of distinction that military service produced, and that Lyra had encountered before in the practical documents of the Vigil — incident reports, casualty notations, the service record entries that summarized in two lines what had taken however long it took. She had written these entries for other soldiers. She would write this one when she had a writing surface and the notation to hand and the time to do it correctly.

She had not done it yet because she had not had the time. This was true. The time had genuinely not been available. She had also not done it because the notation required a next-of-kin contact entry, and Ardea had listed a sister in the Western Atrament valley cities, and writing the notification was the part of the entry that she had been not-thinking-about with the particular care with which you avoid a subject that has not become urgent yet and that you have not quite finished finding a way to approach.

She filed this. Pending. She would resolve it.

The second: the notation she had not made on the ridge.

A Templar's observation of a membrane-adjacent technical anomaly was a documented obligation under the Vigil's standing research protocols. The protocol language was precise: a practitioner with research background who observed conditions consistent with recovery gradient depression at a Liturgy-authorized extraction site was required to submit a technical observation form to the regional Canon within fourteen days of the observation. The form was standard. The routing was standard. She had submitted fourteen of them in twelve years, for minor observations at the Ocipheus Station installation, and they had traveled up the chain and been reviewed and filed.

She was going to submit fifteen instead of fifteen.

She walked the descent. She thought about the fifteen and what she was doing with the fifteenth, and she noted that she was thinking about it in terms of what she was not doing rather than what she was choosing. The distinction was available to her. She observed it and did not press on it, the way you observe the quality of a wound without probing it when the probe would produce less information than the observation alone.

Pending. She had always resolved pending files.

The Lacerta approach roads came into view below as the last switchback opened onto the final descent. The rock here was limestone pale, the road surface compacted and dust-white, and there was the smell of salt in the air that meant the channel was closer than the map's scale suggested. Kressida's rig descended the final grade with the particular gait adjustment it made on loose stone — careful, lower center of gravity, the flail housing raised to counterbalance. Orim walked behind the rig, not because the rig would catch him if he fell but because the rig's wake on the loose stone cleared the surface of the worst of the instability.

Rowe was beside Lyra.

He looked at the road ahead and at the country to the west and at the particular quality of the afternoon light that was beginning to tilt toward the cooler register that meant three hours until dark. He had been building a map of the sky's light for six weeks — the way Cauld light moved, what season it indicated, how it differed from whatever his world's light did. He read the light the way she read the interior of rooms. Carefully and with accumulating context.

He said: "Sal Vento."

"Yes," she said. "Two days."

He nodded. He looked west, at the channel country they were moving toward, at whatever he was constructing in his mind's map of the place he had been for seven months without any of the language for it. He was building the sentence. It had forty-seven words in it now and it was not complete.

She kept walking.

The ridge was behind them. The Forge Hearth was behind them. The warmth that was not quite geological was behind them, and the low sound that she was not going to write down in the notation form she was not going to file, and Orim's face on the volcanic rock, and Kressida's face for the three seconds it was open before it was not open.

The road went west. The light angled. The channel smell strengthened.

She kept walking.

[Beat 16]
SAL VENTO — THE PORT

The path came down through Lacerta limestone and the limestone smelled of the sea even two hundred meters above it, which was the particular quality of coastal cliff country: the sea got into everything before you ever arrived. Salt, kelp, and something sulfurous from the anchorage caves below, rising up through the rock itself as though the rock were sweating. The path switchbacked down through it in the specific way of a path that had not been engineered so much as worn into existence by two centuries of people making the same pragmatic judgment about where the footing held.

The BR-7 went down the switchbacks with eighteen centimeters of clearance on the outer edge. Kressida did not mention the eighteen centimeters. Lyra did not mention it either. They had reached a point, somewhere between the Forge Hearth ridge and the Lacerta borderland, where the discussion of margins had become a private matter between Kressida and the rig and the geometry of whatever passage they were navigating, and Lyra's awareness of the margin was simply that: awareness, filed and set aside.

The carved relief appeared at the third switchback, cut into the cliff face at the level of the sea approach, oriented outward toward the Pallor channel. It had been here a hundred and twenty-seven years. The Council of Corsairs had commissioned it in Year 899 as a diplomatic communication in the specific medium of limestone - a medium that did not require a courier, did not require a response, and did not deteriorate in the way of political sentiment. The relief showed the Pallor envoy fleet of that year: fourteen vessels rendered in meticulous carved detail, the Long Seat pennants at the flagship's prow identifiable if you knew the heraldic conventions, which Lyra did because twelve years in the Vigil meant twelve years of knowing who belonged to what institution's flag. The fleet was approaching the Lacerta coast under treaty convention, which in the carved version meant the ships were arranged in the specific formal pattern of a party arriving to negotiate rather than to contest.

In the right half of the relief, what had happened to them.

The Corsair vessels were rendered somewhat larger than the historical naval record indicated they had been. The Pallor envoys were somewhat smaller. The artisan had been working to a brief. The composition was consistent with the political goals of the commission, which was to say that anyone arriving in Pallor's harbor approach would see this image - the fleet going down, the Corsair vessels standing over them, the Long Seat pennants depicted, with considerable technical skill, upside-down in the carved water - before they saw anything else about Sal Vento or Lacerta or what kind of city they were approaching.

"Every other nation writes letters of grievance," Orim said. He was looking at the carved envoys frozen in what the artisan had decided was the appropriate expression for diplomats in the process of losing a negotiation by drowning. "Lacerta carves grievances into the earth and charges the aggrieved party harbor fees to come read them."

"The Pallor delegation sees it before they see anything else," Lyra said.

"Every time. One hundred and twenty-seven years of Pallor delegations arriving to negotiate and seeing that first." He looked at the fresh-cut tool marks on the lower third of the relief, where weathered stone had been re-carved to keep the detail of the sinking ships sharp. "Someone comes back regularly. To maintain the detail."

Rowe had stopped a few paces back. He was looking at the carving with the expression he used when he was assembling something from insufficient vocabulary - the expression of a man who understands precisely what he is looking at and lacks only the specific words for it. He had approximately fifty words of functional Cauld at this point. He had the word for sea and the word for ship and the words for old and for still-angry, which was a compound he had assembled himself from context and which Orim had confirmed was approximately correct.

"Still," Rowe said.

"Yes," Orim said.

Rowe looked at the fresh tool marks. He looked at the ongoing maintenance of a carved image of diplomatic catastrophe. He made a sound that was not quite a laugh and not quite acknowledgment and contained elements of both.

"Yes," Orim said again, in a different tone.

---

Sal Vento occupied the cliff face and the plateau above it in the specific manner of a city built by people who understood that accessibility was a liability. Every building had a sight line to the harbor approach. Every sight line had been planned. The support pins holding the buildings to the cliff face had been driven so deep into the limestone that the cliff at this point needed the buildings as much as the buildings needed the cliff: two centuries of mutual dependency had produced a relationship that was architectural rather than geological, and the limestone had accommodated this in the specific way that limestone accommodates foreign material, which is to say reluctantly and completely.

The streets were steep, narrow, and arranged on a logic that was not navigational but economic: not where you could move most efficiently, but where you could see most efficiently. Every main approach had a second-level terrace with unobstructed sight lines to the water. The harbor master's office was also, if you knew where to ask, the office that reviewed the letters of commission for the three Corsair intelligence lines. These were not officially the same office. They had been in the same building for eighty years.

The three founding Corsairs were commemorated in a chapel on the upper terrace, between the navigation archive and the pilot registry. The chapel had a nautical chronometer on the altar instead of a saint's relic. The chronometer was accurate to thirty seconds per year, which was more accurate than any saint's intervention in the living memory of the chapel's regular attendants, and it had the additional practical virtue of being calibrated for the local tidal schedule.

Lyra walked the main approach with the party behind her and the smell of machine oil and salt and three-day-old fish in the specific proportions of a working harbor city. Orim was ahead, moving at the pace of a man who has been on his feet for enough consecutive days that his feet have developed opinions about the experience but have not yet arrived at refusal.

Rowe was at the rear. He always positioned himself at the rear in cities he was new to, reading approaches.

The city had the texture - she recognized this texture - of a place where the founding legends were about successful theft and profitable betrayal, and everyone living in it had made a private peace with what that meant for the culture they were participating in. Not dishonest. Not ashamed. Simply the texture of a place that had looked at the available options for how to build a civilization and had made a specific choice and had committed to it long enough that the choice had become the identity.

She had worked in enough of these cities to read the texture without needing to name it.

---

Tavar found them.

This was not surprising. Tavar, it emerged over the following hour, had been expecting someone from Ocipheus for three days, which was approximately how long it would take a Knight with a party and a BR-7 to cover the ground between Fjorheim and Sal Vento via the Forge Hearth ridge. He had an intelligence network and he was using it. That was the correct description of what he had, and the correct description of what he did with it, and the terseness of the description was not because the network was small.

He came down from the third-level terrace to the junction path, moving with the particular economy of a person who has made a decision and is implementing it without decorating the implementation. He was not tall. He was carrying himself in the way of someone who has decided how much space he intends to occupy and is maintaining the decision with complete precision. The coat was expensive in the practical sense rather than the presentational sense - good material, specific cut, the collar and cuff texture of Lacerta shear-thickening shell composite underneath, which would stop four rounds at standard engagement distance and which told her more about how he occupied his professional life than any single fact she might have assembled from the network records that had provided his name.

He was in his middle forties and he had the face of someone who had been outside in variable weather for most of them. The kind of face that tells you about the last twenty years rather than the underlying structure.

"Dame T-044," he said. "I was expecting a cart and a requisition document. You are neither."

"No."

He looked at the rig. He looked at Kressida's position at the pilot hatch, which she had left folded open in the way she always left it folded open in cities she was new to, so that she could read the approaches. He looked at Rowe, who was watching the terrace above them with the particular attention of someone tracking multiple points simultaneously. He looked at Orim, who was looking at him with the expression of a man who has sat across enough tables from enough people with interesting coats to know when the sizing-up ceremony was complete.

"Come in," Tavar said. "The street doesn't have opinions about what it hears. The people on it do."

---

The artificer's shop on the third terrace smelled of machine oil and fine-gauge metalwork and the particular sharp note of a precision lathe operating on hardened alloy. Marine instruments: chronometers, compasses, the deep-channel navigation tools that the Corsair lines used for current-reading in the winter passage. Precision work that required ongoing maintenance, ongoing adjustment, and therefore ongoing legitimate reason for a particular individual to visit on a regular schedule without the visit needing explanation.

The proprietor - a woman of sixty with the hands of someone who had been working with small precision instruments for most of her professional life, which was the particular kind of hand that looked delicate and was not - came in from the back room when they entered, looked at Tavar, looked at the party, and went back to the back room. She did not emerge again. This was the established understanding of this working relationship.

Tavar pulled a chair to the work table and sat in it the way a person sits in a chair they have occupied before. He gestured at the other chairs.

Workshop chairs. Orim sat down with the expression of a man reconciling himself to a surface. Rowe stood near the secondary exit, because Rowe did not sit in rooms he was new to until he had completed his assessment of the room, and he had not completed it yet.

Tavar spread a chart on the table.

"The Oculus Memoriae left Sal Vento's anchorage eleven days ago," he said. "On a vessel called the *Avandrey.* Pallor registry, private commission, three-person crew. They declared the cargo as archival materials under Pallor cultural property documentation." He paused for exactly the amount of time necessary to indicate the following statement was the relevant part. "The documentation was real. Someone in Pallor's archive administration prepared it before the theft occurred, which means the Relic was purchased before it was taken. The theft was a delivery mechanism."

Lyra looked at him. "How do you know what they were carrying?"

"Because the party that hired the *Avandrey* used this harbor as a staging point for three weeks before departure." He said this as a logistical observation, without inflection. "Three weeks is a long time to be in a harbor of this size without developing a profile. They developed one. I have an interest in knowing what passes through Sal Vento's anchorage under sealed commission, and the interest produced the information." He touched a point on the chart without looking at it - the gesture of a man pointing to something he has already looked at enough times not to need to look at again. "The *Avandrey* makes twelve knots in standard channel conditions. Eleven days out of here, with the weather we have had - and I know precisely what weather we have had - she is approximately here. Three days from Pallor's northern coast."

"You know the route."

"They asked me to recommend one." There was something in his tone that was not resentment and was adjacent to it in the specific way of a man who has observed the irony of a situation and has had sufficient time to arrive at a position of calm amusement about it rather than something less useful. "Then they used a different vessel because they had papers and didn't need me. They took the route I recommended because it was the best route. The intelligence is reliable because I provided it."

"What do you want for it," Lyra said. "And what do you want for whatever else you're offering."

He was quiet for a moment - not the pause of a man formulating his answer, but the pause of a man who has had the answer prepared and is deciding how to present it. "There is a Wall Support Vessel, the *Eirene-7,* moored in a cliff anchorage two hours west. Liturgy supply vessel, maintenance rotation for the western garrison. It will be unoccupied except for a two-man mooring watch on overnight rotation. The garrison's departure window for the *Eirene-7* is three days from now. The garrison will not register the vessel's absence until the departure window passes and the vessel does not appear." He looked at Lyra. "A BR-7 pilot nine months into a neural adaptation has integrated the construct's mechanical language into her primary sensorimotor pathways. The same integration allows interface with any standardized Liturgy mechanical architecture. A Wall Support Vessel is standardized Liturgy build."

Kressida's voice came through the rig's speaker housing: "Yes." It was a short word made shorter by the medium - the iron of the housing absorbed the frequencies above a certain range so that what arrived was her voice rendered in the flatter register of bone conduction, the way a sound changes when the body it passes through is not flesh. Still recognizably hers. Still precise. "That's accurate."

"My navigation registry has been embargoed," Tavar continued. "Canon Immaculate level. A Compact Knight of Ocipheus has standing authority that predates the embargo architecture by two centuries - a Compact-level override. The embargo requires Liturgy review for any waiver. Ocipheus standing authority is not a waiver. It is a prior claim."

Canon Immaculate level. She did not let the weight of it reach her face. Canon Immaculate required a canonical tribunal, a finding of significant doctrinal violation, and a three-member review board at the archiving rank. It was not a clerical matter. It was not a procedural inconvenience. Whatever Tavar had done to earn a Canon Immaculate embargo, the Liturgy had assembled institutional resources to respond to it.

He did not explain. She did not press. The explanation would have required him to tell the truth, and she would have had no mechanism to verify it, and she was not certain she wanted to be in possession of the truth about whatever warranted that level of institutional response. What she wanted was the transit papers and the ship. The rest was his.

"Round trip," she said. "Outbound and return. One transit."

"One transit covers both legs. That is all I need."

"One condition. You manage the watch absence yourself — you are at the garrison office while we are at the anchorage. I don't need a proxy who changes his mind at the third hour."

He looked at her. "Agreed." He reached inside his coat and produced a small leather case, the kind used for document seals. He set it on the table. "I'll need the authorization document. The Ocipheus seal, dated and signed. I have the standard language."

She took the document he produced and read it. It was correct. It had been prepared in advance, which told her something about his confidence in this conversation's outcome, or in his preparation for multiple possible versions of this conversation's outcome. She signed it and sealed it.

He put it away with the care of a person handling something they have been waiting to handle.

Then he said: "One other thing." He said it in a different register than everything before it - not transitional, not the register of a man adding an item to an operational list. The register of a man who has been waiting for a particular moment to ask a particular question and has decided the moment is now. "The Oculus Memoriae. The confessional records inside it. What happens to the records of subjects who are no longer living? Do they remain in the archive? Are they sealed? Transmitted to family?"

She looked at him.

His face was doing the thing faces did when a person had decided they were going to say something and had accepted the cost of saying it. Not performing calm. Actually calm, which was different, because actual calm is the state you arrive at after having already paid the cost in private.

"They remain in the archive," she said. "Sealed with the subject's death record. They do not transfer. They do not pass to heirs or family. They are held in perpetuity in the installation where the recording was made."

He nodded once. He did not follow up. He looked at the chart and then at his hands and then at her with the expression of a man who has received a confirmation he had already assumed but needed to hear said aloud, which is different from being surprised by information and different from already knowing it, in a way that she filed and did not press.

There was a person. There was a record. The record was sealed in an installation that was not where they were going. She did not know what he intended to do about this, and she did not need to know tonight.

"Then we agree," he said, and stood, and the conversation was over.

---

The path back to the overnight position was uphill. In Sal Vento the path was always uphill in one direction, which meant that the city always required something from you in the direction of progress. The remaining soldier walked beside Lyra on the curve of the third terrace path, which had a view to the north - the channel, grey and reflecting the low afternoon cloud, and beyond the channel, if you knew the distance and the sight line, the dark coastline of Pallor.

"The *Eirene-7,*" the soldier said.

"Yes."

"I know that vessel's transit record." She said this in the flat register of operational information, the register of a person reciting what they know rather than drawing conclusions from it. "From the Fjorheim garrison archive. It runs supply rotation for the western Wall garrison. Standard manifest. Equipment, rations, maintenance materials." She looked at the channel. "And then the other runs. The ones logged under Descent Corps oversight, northern Vierna jurisdiction."

Lyra said nothing.

"The manifest logs for the Descent Corps runs," the soldier said. "Sealed documentation. Administrative materials. On a vessel making transit between Descent Corps field stations and the Wall's northern processing infrastructure." She was quiet for a moment. "I've been in enough garrison archives to read a manifest log."

The path curved and the north view opened wider: the channel, the distance to Pallor, the grey sky over all of it. Somewhere ahead in the cliff anchorage two hours west, the *Eirene-7* was sitting in its mooring in the dark of the sea-cave, waiting for a scheduled departure.

"We're going to steal it," Lyra said. "A vessel that has been used for that."

"Yes." The soldier reached inside her coat. She took out her field commission - the Ocipheus standing authority issued to the unit six weeks ago. She held it in both hands for a moment, looking at it in the way a person looks at an object they are about to set down. "Dame."

Lyra looked at her.

"I'm going to leave this with you." She set the commission in Lyra's palm. "Because if I take it with me when I walk, I'll have to return it to the garrison registry when I get somewhere with a garrison, and the registry will ask why I'm separated from my party, and I don't want to answer that." She looked at it in Lyra's hand. "You keep it. File it how you need to file it."

"Think carefully -"

"I'm not asking to leave the service," the soldier said. The distinction mattered to her; Lyra could hear the precision with which she drew it, the way she had already worked through the distinction before this conversation. "I know what leaving means. I've done that calculation and I'm not making it tonight. I'm asking to leave this situation. This specific mission. Tonight." She looked at the channel. "I can find a commercial vessel at the lower anchorage heading for Heloth. I have coin. I have family in Heloth I haven't seen since my first rotation."

Lyra looked at her. Twelve years of rotation ahead of her in the service's standard career architecture, which was the architecture as designed and not as it had operated on this particular mission. A garrison manifest log she could read.

She closed her hand around the commission.

The soldier nodded. She looked at Lyra for one moment more, the look of a person checking something they needed to be certain of, and then she turned and walked down the path toward the lower anchorage where the commercial harbor traffic moored and Heloth-bound vessels took on their last Lacerta passengers before the evening departure window.

Lyra watched her go.

She watched her until the path curved and she was gone around the curve.

Orim had come up the terrace path from the overnight site at some point during the conversation. She was not certain when he had arrived. He had not announced himself. He was standing three paces behind her, and she knew he had heard the latter part of the conversation because he had the stillness of a person who has heard a conversation he arrived in the middle of and has chosen not to insert himself into it and has been waiting for it to be over.

Neither of them said anything.

The channel was grey. The path down which the soldier had disappeared showed nothing.

"Heloth," Orim said, finally.

"She has family there."

"Good." He did not look at Lyra. He was looking at the empty path. "The better of the two outcomes." He was quiet for a moment. "The worse outcome would have been next week, when she'd had time to resent it."

Lyra did not respond to this. There was nothing to respond to that would have been accurate. She put the commission in her coat.

---

The artificer's shop again, in the late evening. Tavar spread the chart on the work table. The cliff anchorage two hours west was marked - a cove cut into the limestone, accessible by the path the garrison resupply runs used, with the inner mooring assigned to Liturgy vessels because the inner mooring was out of sight of the channel and the garrison preferred to watch who was moving on the water without being observable in return.

"Two soldiers on the overnight watch," he said. "They rotate every four hours. They are garrison conscripts assigned to mooring watch duty, which is the posting your commanding officer gives you when they want to communicate dissatisfaction without having to say anything directly." He paused. "At the third hour of the watch, people who are not engaged begin to narrow their attention to the number of hours remaining. This is the window."

"You said you could create an absence," Lyra said.

"I have standing in this harbor. The right conversation with the right person creates a situation - a commercial dispute, an inventory discrepancy at the garrison supply station, a matter that requires two watch soldiers to present themselves at the garrison office for a period sufficient to our purposes." He said this with the flat practicality of describing an established technique. "It does not create a record. It creates an absence of approximately forty minutes."

Rowe was following at what she had come to read as eighty percent comprehension - the particular quality of his attention when the vocabulary was sufficient. He was tracking. His Cauld had improved in the six days since the barge, and the situations had become the kind that clarified without vocabulary.

He leaned forward and looked at the chart. He put his finger on the cliff anchorage marker. "In," he said. "Then."

"Then the rig," Kressida said.

She was sitting half-inside the pilot hatch, her feet on the floor, the rig folded open behind her the way she always arranged herself when she wanted to be in a room without leaving the rig entirely. This was the closest she came to sitting at a table with the rest of them, and they had all, by now, stopped thinking of it as a variation and started thinking of it as simply how Kressida sat.

"The BR-7 interface uses the same mechanical language as Liturgy construct architecture," she said. "Navigation control systems on a Wall Support Vessel are standardized Liturgy build - same protocols, same interface layer, same mechanical vocabulary. She reached inside the rig's storage bracket — the shallow tray fitted to the right frame strut — and produced a folded document: the Liturgy's aerostatic architecture specification for the *Eirene-7* class, the Fjorheim garrison issue. There was a House Lacerta intelligence annotation in the margin. She did not explain the annotation. "I have been reading the class specifications," she said, without looking at Tavar. "The interface is direct. Thirty seconds to establish the link. Two minutes to run the departure initialization. The rig does not need to be physically inside the vessel." She paused. "I can navigate the *Eirene-7* from the BR-7's pilot seat. The ship is a construct. I interface with constructs."

Orim looked at her. He was doing the mathematics. "The rig - the pilot hatch, the interface -"

"My nervous system adapted to this rig over nine months," Kressida said. "The adaptation is not specific to this rig. It is an adaptation to mechanical language in general. Liturgy architecture is standardized. I read standardized Liturgy architecture." She looked at the chart. "I can fly anything with a standard Liturgy mechanical interface." She said this in the tone of a person stating a physical fact: not bravado, not performance, the flat accuracy of someone describing what they know their body can do because they have learned it empirically over a sufficient period of time. "I've been thinking about it since the ridge."

Tavar was watching her with the expression he had worn in the previous conversation when she had confirmed his technical assessment of the neural interface adaptation. The expression of a person encountering data that exceeds their current framework in a direction that is useful. He said nothing. He had already decided something, and not saying it was also a decision.

"The departure sequence," Lyra said.

"Standard Liturgy initialization takes four minutes from a cold start," Kressida said. "I can reduce it to two with a warm-interface approach - I establish the link before we need to move, maintain a passive connection through the watch window, and when we need to go, the system is already responsive." She looked at Lyra. "Total time from arrival at the mooring to airborne: six minutes, if the soldiers are absent. Eight if they're not."

"They'll be absent," Tavar said.

"Then six."

The lamp threw its small circle of light on the chart and the instruments and the faces of the people around the table. Outside, Sal Vento was doing what it did at this hour: settling into the particular watchful quiet of a city that had always kept its own counsel at night, every building with its sight line to the harbor, every harbor light noted by someone.

"We leave four hours before dawn," Lyra said. "Two hours to the anchorage, the watch absence at the third hour, six minutes to departure, enough air between us and the cliff before the morning rotation begins." She looked at Rowe. "You understand?"

He nodded. "Go before morning. Fast."

"Yes."

"And then -" He touched the chart above the anchorage, moved his finger north across the channel. "Pallor."

"Three days, if the *Avandrey*'s schedule holds," Tavar said. "The channel in this season favors a direct run. We arrive before they make the northern coast."

Orim had been looking at the chart with the expression of someone doing a different kind of calculation than the navigational one. He looked up. "The *Avandrey's* crew," he said. "Three people. They have the Relic. They have a three-day head start. When we arrive - what exactly are we doing when we arrive?"

"We are locating them," Lyra said. "Before they deliver it."

"And then?"

"And then we are recovering the Relic."

"In Pallor," he said. "With whatever authority you currently have, which is the authority of a Knight of Ocipheus operating outside Ocipheus jurisdiction on a mission that the Vigil has given twelve days and three of those days are gone."

"Yes."

He looked at her for a moment. He had the expression of a man who has heard an accurate description of a problematic situation and is deciding whether to name the problem or whether naming it serves any operational purpose. He decided. "Alright," he said. He settled back in the workshop chair. "I've done worse from a worse starting position."

"How much worse?" Rowe said. It was the most complex construction he had managed in Cauld in two days, and it landed the way he had intended it to land.

Orim considered. "The situation was comparable. The starting position was worse." He thought about it. "Marginally."

"Marginally," Rowe repeated, committing the word.

---
