Four hours before dawn, Sal Vento had the quality of a city that had gone not to sleep exactly but to a version of alertness that did not require witnesses. The lamp in the artificer's shop was dark. The approach paths showed no commercial traffic. The garrison post at the upper terrace had two soldiers who were looking at the channel, which was where they had been trained to look, and were not looking at the cliff-side path that curved west below their sight line.

Lyra stood at the beginning of the path. The sea was below - eighty meters of vertical limestone ending in the anchorage caves and then the open water. The stars were very bright above the channel, and they cast the specific cold light that was not quite illumination and was significantly better than nothing.

The rig's footfall behind her was the sound she had learned to stop registering as separate from her own movement: three meters of iron and Atrament reaction plate, the BR-7 Flail, Kressida inside it now with the hatch sealed for the path, which was the configuration for operational movement. In the rig, Kressida's respiration was already settling into the lower rhythm of deep interface. She was not flying yet. She was preparing to fly. The distinction was internal and invisible from outside the hatch and she had explained it once and did not explain it again.

Orim beside her. Rowe behind, reading the approaches in the way he always read approaches - not for threats specifically, but for information, the texture of a space in the hours before something happened in it.

Tavar was at the cliff-path junction when they arrived. He had come before them and was waiting with a lamp shielded against the wind, and he had the quality she had noticed earlier — not urgency, but its quieter relative. The quality of a man who has needed to arrive at a particular door for longer than this conversation and has now arrived at it without walking through it. He looked at her. He looked at the path descending toward the anchorage. He did not move to follow.

She noted it.

She put one foot in front of the other.

The path curved west along the cliff face, above the open channel, the limestone glowing faintly in the starlight with its own cool luminosity. Below: the sea. Ahead: the anchorage cove, two hours of this path, a mooring watch in the process of developing a professionally inconvenient problem, and a Liturgy supply vessel that had three days of useful life before the garrison noticed it was missing.

Three days was enough.

Three days had to be enough.

The sea was below her and Pallor was across it and the *Avandrey* was somewhere on that water with eleven days' lead and the answer to a question she hadn't known she was asking when she'd left Ocipheus Station fourteen days ago with a soldier and a warden's writ and the expectation that this would be a straightforward recovery operation.

She kept moving.

[Beat 17]
THE ACQUISITION — EIRENE-7

Orim did the scry two hundred meters back from the cave mouth, crouched in the lee of a limestone shelf with his fingertips pressed together at his sternum.

Lyra watched him and did not watch the cave. She had looked at the cave. It was a gap in the cliff face at waterline, wide enough for a barge, the entrance marked by a smear of darkness that was not quite the same as the surrounding darkness. The Eirene-7's envelope was visible from here as a shadow pressed against the stone ceiling inside — long, rigid, the wrong shape for anything natural. She had filed this and turned to watch Orim.

He looked older than he had at the Forge Hearth. He had looked old there too, but that was a different kind of old — accumulated. This was depleted. His face had the quality of something that has been running on a shorter reserve than it normally acknowledges. He had not said anything about the Forge Hearth scry failure since it happened. She had not asked. But the Rod was in his coat and his hands, pressed together at his sternum, were not quite steady.

He opened his eyes after ninety seconds.

"Two soldiers. The one at the gangway foot is seated — he's on the near side of the dock. The one at the booth is upright but his head is down. The ship's hold is clear." He paused. "I didn't go past the hold. There's something between me and the pilot housing I didn't want to push through."

He said this without alarm. He said it the way he said everything he had found in fifty years of scrying: as observed fact, not invitation to interpret.

"The path?" Lyra asked.

"Stairs cut into the cliff on the south side of the mouth — they're slick, watch the third step, the drainage has undercut it. Down to the dock level. The dock is maybe forty meters, most of it planking over the water. The gangway up to the cargo access is at the far end."

"How long before the rotation?" Rowe said.

"Three hours and change. Dawn contact window is longer — four hours. But the courier pass from the garrison post is at dawn." He looked at his hands. "That's what I saw from here. I didn't go closer."

He sat down on the limestone shelf. Not a controlled lowering. He sat down because his body had decided to before he asked it. He looked at the floor and his breathing was deliberate in the way of someone recalling what deliberate breathing is for.

Lyra noted it. She moved on.

Rowe had already produced the ampules. Two of them, small, Lacerta glass — the kind of glasswork that was designed to be invisible in a pocket and break clean when you needed it to. He held them up between two fingers so she could see them and then put them away again.

"Done," he said.

"When?"

"Before we left Sal Vento. Tavar arranged it — the garrison rotation gets a logistical packet from the Wall supply line, dehydrated ration tabs, night-watch standard. The compound is in the water tabs." He checked the angle of the cave mouth against the horizon. "Twenty-minute onset. The packet would have been opened when the watch started, four hours ago."

"And if they didn't use the tablets."

"Then they have two working rifles and we handle it as it comes." He said it without inflection. He was already scanning the cliff for the south-side stairs. "But they used the tablets. The mooring watch is an overnight posting and the garrison does not send warm food to mooring watches. The soldiers have what's in the packet. He checked the protocol."

*Checked the protocol.* She filed this too. Not Rowe's certainty — Tavar's, relayed without apparent awareness of what it implied. He had been on this line three years ago, Rowe had said, in the casual manner of someone passing on what they'd been told. What that meant was that three years ago Tavar had possessed enough access to the Eirene-7's logistics chain to know its garrison supply protocols with the confidence to spike a packet in a Sal Vento staging room and trust the math. She did not know what that meant about him. She had two categories for it: either it was what he said it was, or it was something else. Both categories were still open.

They moved.

The south stairs were cut into the limestone and had been there long enough that the edges had rounded under salt water and foot traffic. The third step was exactly where Orim had said — drainage had worked at the stone beneath it and the step flexed under weight in a way that a normal step did not. Lyra felt it, shifted her weight forward, kept moving. Behind her she heard Kressida's rig navigate it without pause. The rig's footing was deliberate where a human would have been quick — three meters of iron learning the surface as it went.

The dock was planking over water. She could hear the cave water under it, slow and cold — not surf, not current, just the particular movement of water in a contained space, the kind that doesn't go anywhere and knows it. The cold was different here than outside. Outside the cold had been sea cold, which had range. Inside the cave the cold was limestone cold, which had been sitting in the same dark since before the current Houses had names and was not interested in sharing any of it.

The Eirene-7 grew as she walked toward it.

This was a habit of enclosed spaces — the ship had looked large from the cave mouth, and it looked larger now, and by the time she was at the gangway foot it was simply the scale of the thing, which was the scale of a vessel designed to carry supply loads for a Wall garrison across mountain terrain. The hull was deep-bellied and high-shouldered in the way of flying boats, practical without being ugly, built to take water-landings and mean it. The Liturgy's name on the hull was stenciled in block letters: EIRENE-7, and below it the checkpoint designation and a maintenance code, none of it decorated, all of it placed the way you place a tool's identification on the tool.

The two soldiers were where Orim had said.

The one at the gangway foot had been seated on an upturned crate. He was still seated — his body had not fallen, his grip on the rifle butt had not fully opened, so the weapon was still angled against his knee. His chin was on his chest. He was breathing. She could see his breath in the cold.

The one at the booth had his head against the booth frame, arms at his sides, upright only because the frame was holding him. His mouth was slightly open.

Rowe went to the gangway-foot soldier first. He pressed two fingers to the side of the man's neck, checked the time against whatever internal clock he used, and straightened. "Two hours minimum," he said. "Probably more. He's deep under." He looked at the booth soldier without moving toward him. "Same. Move."

He moved with the ease of someone for whom identifying exits was simply the ambient condition of being in a space. He was already at the gangway before she finished observing the soldiers.

The gangway planking held. Kressida had calculated the weight distribution before she put the first foot on it, and she moved the BR-7 up in the careful deliberate rhythm of knowing exactly what you are doing with a machine that could fail something if you were careless. The cave's ceiling was close — too close, at the top of the gangway, where the envelope structure occupied the upper third of the cave's dome. She walked the rig under it with the head angled forward, two inches of clearance above the rig's crown.

Through the cargo hatch.

Rowe found the release handle before Lyra did. It was recessed into the hull plating, manual, a design she recognized from Liturgy transport vessels — the same mechanism in the same position. He had never been on a Liturgy vessel. He had found it anyway, because a cargo hatch handle looked like a cargo hatch handle regardless of what was written on the hull outside. He had the hatch open in the time it would have taken her to locate it and she noted this without comment and went inside.

The hold was wide and high-ceilinged and smelled of petroleum fuel and the particular dry-dust smell of Liturgy warehouse stock, which was uniform whether you were in Ocipheus or at the far end of the Wall. They stored things the same way everywhere. It was a form of institutional consistency she had always found comforting. She noticed she was finding it comforting now and did not examine that too closely.

Kressida walked the rig to the forward bulkhead and positioned it there without instruction — the only location that would give her neural reach into the pilot housing beyond. The rig's hands came to rest against the bulkhead, flat-palmed, the way a person steadies themselves against a wall to feel something through it.

"I need four minutes," Kressida said. Her voice came from inside the rig through the pilot hatch — the small oval viewport that showed her face, steady, looking at something that was not in the room.

"Take them," Lyra said.

Rowe was already at the forward bulkhead on the starboard side, running his hands over the structural framing. Looking for something. Lyra watched him find it — a secondary panel set in the frame, maintenance access. He got it open, looked at the contents, closed it. He went to the port side and repeated the process. He produced a folded document from his coat — a page he had gotten from somewhere in Sal Vento, Tavar's doing, some acquired maintenance schematic — and compared the panel configuration against it. He made a sound of confirmation that was not a word and put the document away.

He moved to the fuel manifold housing on the port side and began running the manual verification sequence. Not the startup sequence, which was Kressida's work. The physical checks that the startup sequence assumed had been done, that a maintenance crew would have done, that nobody on a mooring watch had done because they were mooring watch soldiers and not engineers. His hands were machinist's hands — the specific callus pattern of someone who had spent years working machinery with precision, where the machine's error was your error. He checked the manifold valve seats one by one with the patient accuracy of a man who had been trained that you checked things before they failed, not after.

Kressida said, from inside the rig: "Fuel state is full. Manifold is clear — I can read it from the instrument cluster through the bulkhead." A beat. "Confirming with the physical."

"Port manifold clear," Rowe said. He moved to the starboard side. "Starboard manifold, checking."

They did not discuss why each was doing what they were doing. They distributed the work along its natural lines — the neural interface for the systems that interfaced, the hands for the systems that didn't — and occupied both channels simultaneously without either waiting on the other.

"Starboard clear," Rowe said.

"Starting ignition sequence," Kressida said.

She was a moment of stillness in the pilot housing beyond the bulkhead and then the engines started.

Not simultaneously. In sequence, the way you brought up cold engines: port outboard first, a cough and a catch and then the sustained throb of a working engine building toward its operating register. The sound in the cave was immediate and enormous — compressed against stone and water, reflected back from everywhere. Lyra had been on vessels in enclosed spaces before. She had not been on one in a sea-cave, and the cave's acoustics turned the engine sound into something that pressed on the chest.

The starboard outboard. Then the center pair.

The running lights came on. The instrument cluster in the pilot housing beyond the bulkhead produced a wash of light through the gaps in the structural framing. The ship was running.

Then it stopped moving toward anything.

The engines at idle. The lights on. And the ship still in the water, still moored — but not moored, the lines had been cut before they boarded, this was something else. The ship was running and stationary in the way of a mechanism that is producing output and going nowhere because something upstream of the output was closed.

Rowe was already at the forward bulkhead. He had not hesitated. He had moved before Lyra had finished registering the pause, gone to a secondary panel in the structural framing — a red-painted valve handle inside, a Liturgy placard, the panel set flush with the frame in the way of secondary systems that are not meant to be accessed during normal operations.

He turned the valve handle. She heard the pressure change above — the envelope structure responding, a hiss from somewhere overhead, the ship settling differently in the water as the gas distribution adjusted to the new pressure state. Something that had been closed opened.

Kressida said: "That's it. Movement available."

Rowe closed the panel. He turned and Lyra was looking at him.

He did not offer an explanation. She did not ask for one. She was noting: the location of the panel, the certainty of his movement, the fact that the schematic was still in his coat — he had not checked it before he moved. He had found the valve by reading the housing. She had two possibilities: either Tavar's document had told him exactly where to look, or he had not needed it. Either way, the knowledge that had put him there — Tavar's prior familiarity with this vessel's secondary systems, encoded in a schematic precise enough to navigate by — she filed it. It would stay filed until she needed it.

"How long to get us out?" she said.

"Ballast shift takes four minutes. Then we move."

"The engines are loud."

"The garrison's booth faces the dock. Both soldiers are down and the booth faces the water." He was already checking the hour, looking at the instrument panel through the bulkhead gaps. "I'd rather move than wait for them to potentially wake up."

She agreed. "Kressida. Move when ready."

"Moving," Kressida said.

The ballast shift was a process of the ship deciding where its weight was and adjusting accordingly. The hull moved in the water — not dramatically, but enough to feel underfoot, a slow reorientation. The dock planking groaned against the hull. Then the ship began to back.

Rowe was at the cargo hatch, which he had left cracked for sight lines. He had his hands on the hatch edge and he was watching the dock and not speaking. He did not have Cauld for this situation and he knew it, so he occupied the thing he could do: watching, and reporting if there was something to report. His hands were steady.

The ship backed through the dock space. The noise in the cave was worse as they moved — the engines' output bouncing off the walls they were approaching, the water pushing around the hull, the structural creak of the envelope against the cave ceiling where the clearance was at its minimum.

And then the envelope scraped the ceiling.

A long sound. Metal on stone, dry and sustained, the kind of sound that produced absolute silence from everyone who heard it because everyone who heard it was calculating whether it was a scrape or a failure. It lasted perhaps two seconds. Then it stopped. The ship kept moving.

Rowe let out a breath through his nose. He had been holding it since the sound started.

The cave mouth: she watched it approach from the cargo hatch aperture. The darkness inside giving way to a deeper darkness — open air, open water, the pre-dawn sea with its cloud cover and its smell of salt and cold and the specific quality of pre-dawn water, which was different from water at other hours. Something about still air and low light and the particular silence that preceded things. The cliff face went past: limestone, pale where the moisture hadn't darkened it.

They cleared the mouth.

The acoustic changed the way acoustics changed when you left a cave — everything expanded, the sound found room, the engines became themselves again instead of the cave's version of themselves. The sea air came in through the cracked hatch and it was cold in the way that open cold was cold, which was different from cave cold. Cave cold was historical. Open cold was present.

Kressida began the water-takeoff run. She did not announce it. The engines went to higher power and the hull responded, bow rising as the speed built, the water spraying up at the hatch and wetting Rowe's hands. He pulled the hatch mostly shut and watched through the gap. The spray came in anyway.

The speed. More speed. The bow spray sheeting, the water noise enormous and close, the hull skipping at the threshold between dragging and lifting.

The hull lifted.

First the bow, then the body of the ship — a moment of the water noise still present and then it was not present, the hull was above the water, the sound of the run replaced by the sound of the engines and the wind and the creak of the envelope structure overhead. The ship climbed and banked east along the cliff line. The stone went past the viewport — too close, the kind of close that was the cliff deciding not to kill you rather than the pilot having room to spare. Then open sky.

The ship leveled.

Lyra went forward to the structural gap in the bulkhead and looked through at the pilot housing. The instrument cluster was running — everything reading, everything, as far as she could tell, doing what it should. Through the forward viewport she could see the cliff line falling behind and the open dark of the pre-dawn sea.

She went back to the hold.

She had watched Kressida through the pilot hatch oval while the startup sequence ran — the small face, steady, looking at something that was not in the room. She had asked about it in Sal Vento, in one of the brief moments when the party was in the same space and the logistics of the next twelve hours had been briefly exhausted as a topic. She had asked what the interface was like.

Kressida had looked at her. She had the quality of someone deciding whether the question merited the answer it was asking for, which was not whether she was willing to answer but whether the answer was going to be accurate enough to be worth giving.

She said: "It's a machine. Machines have a language."

She said it to the wall behind Lyra, which was where she was looking. Not the rhetorical subject of the statement — not to her — but the location she had directed the statement, which was nowhere.

Lyra had thought about this and thought about it again later and had not said anything because there was nothing to say that Kressida wanted said about it. The statement had landed as a fact. What the fact implied was something neither of them was going to examine yet, here, in a stolen airship over dark water with three hours to the channel.

Orim was on a cargo crate. He had identified the one crate in the hold that was likely to be structurally sound and occupied it at the earliest opportunity. His hands were in his coat pockets. He did not look like someone who had participated in the theft of a Liturgy supply vessel. He looked like a man on a cargo crate who was thinking about something else and waiting for the journey to conclude.

"You said Eirene is Old Cauld," Lyra said.

"Peace," Orim said. "The cessation of hostilities. The state after fighting has ended." He looked at the hull above them, briefly. "The state, not the cause. Not the victory or the surrender. What's left when neither of those is still happening."

She waited to see if there was more. There wasn't.

Rowe had stayed at the cargo hatch. He was watching the sea through the gap — nothing specifically, not sighting lines or calculating anything, just watching the water move below the hull in the early gray that was not yet light. He had not grown up watching the Cauld's sea. Whatever sea he had grown up watching looked like something else. She did not know if this sea looked like that sea. She did not know how to ask.

The ship's name was stenciled on the hull outside, which she could not see from here but had already read. Eirene. She was aware of it the way you were aware of a borrowed tool — the name that belonged to someone else, the provenance you were currently carrying without having been given it. The Liturgy had named this vessel for the state after fighting. The Liturgy administered peace in the Cauld the way it administered everything else: as a managed resource, distributed through authorized channels to authorized recipients, produced by apparatus that the recipients were not authorized to examine.

She had taken this vessel. The Liturgy had not given it to her. She had arrived in the dark, chemically incapacitated the garrison soldiers responsible for it, and flown it out of its anchorage before the watch rotation could discover them. This was theft. She had no other word for it.

She also had a Relic to recover and four hundred kilometers of water to cross and a Canon who had suspended her transit authority and would be tracking her movement through whatever intelligence apparatus he had available. She had no other option for any of it, and the ship was the most functional option she had found. These facts existed in parallel with the theft and none of them altered what the theft was.

The ship did not have a name that belonged to them. It was still the Eirene-7 and it would be until something changed that, which was not going to happen on this ship over dark water with no particular occasion for renaming. She was aware of this the way you were aware of other things that were slightly wrong with a situation you were in for good reasons — filed, present, not resolved.

Kressida said, through the bulkhead: "Altitude holding. Course set for the channel approach." A pause. "We'll reach open water in forty minutes. After that the courier route breaks west and we won't be in it."

"Any traffic?" Rowe said, from the cargo hatch.

"Nothing in the instrument range. Whatever the rig's sensors are pulling from up here —" She stopped. Amended: "Nothing visible."

Lyra looked at the hull above her. The envelope structure, the rigid frame running fore to aft, the gasbag material she could not see but knew was there. A machine designed by the Liturgy for the Liturgy's purposes, named for a concept the Liturgy administered on behalf of everyone else.

They were in it. They were going somewhere they needed to go. The name on the hull was not their business and the machine was doing its work and in three hours they would be over the channel, which was where Rowe was going to tell her something she needed to hear.

The something was not going to be easier to hear because she'd gotten there on a stolen airship. She had understood this before they left. She was still understanding it. That was what the next three hours were for.

Outside, through the viewport gap, the cliff was gone. The first gray of morning was beginning at the horizon's edge — not light yet, just the sky deciding to be distinguishable from the sea, which it did every morning and had done before the Cauld existed and would do after whatever happened at the channel. The envelope, catching that gray, showed its outline above the hull.

Orim said, from his crate: "I'm going to sleep, if no one needs me to do anything requiring being awake."

Nobody answered him. He took this as permission, which it was.

The ship flew east.

[Beat 18]
THE CHANNEL — ROWE TESTIFIES

The channel was louder than she'd expected.

She knew the theoretical noise profile of a rigid airship at altitude over open water — she had reviewed the Liturgy's transport specifications enough times to have an accurate model. What the specifications did not convey was what it sounded like from inside, which was a continuous conversation between the envelope and the wind, both of them convinced they knew better, neither of them willing to concede. The hull vibrated with it. The floor of the cargo bay vibrated with it. Lyra sat against the starboard bulkhead with her notebook on her knee and her coat across her shoulders and listened to the argument and did not find it conducive to concentration.

She had been trying to concentrate since they cleared the Lacerta coast.

The notebook was open to a blank page that had been blank for two hours. She had started three sentences in it and crossed them all out — not content, just opening structures, the syntactic container she would have filled with Ardea's service record. She needed to write the service record. Ardea's family would receive a formal notification through the Ocipheus garrison administrative office, which meant the administrative office needed the service record, which meant she needed to write it, which meant she needed to find the words. She had been finding words for thirty years. She could not find them for this.

She closed the notebook.

The helm was Kressida's — the Eirene-7's guidance system answered to the neural interface she had found in the hold, the rig's hands flat against the bulkhead, the same reach that had extended to the BR-7's weapons array extended here to rudder and elevator and trim. Rowe had put a hand on the physical wheel once, felt the non-response of something already spoken for, and taken it off. The ship did not need him. She was asleep in the rig now, or something like sleep — the rig was running warm and the readings on its external indicators were stable, which Lyra had come to understand as Kressida's analog of sleep. The machine maintained. The pilot rested.

Orim was at the forward porthole with his tincture bottle, running what he'd called a passive attunement — not a real scry, just presence, keeping his gift oriented in the way that, he'd said, helped him feel whether the air ahead had anything in it worth knowing about. He did this in silence, which was the correct way to do it and also the correct way to give Lyra room to think without appearing to notice that she needed it.

Rowe was standing at the cargo bay hatch — not outside it, just at it, looking out through the small round window at the channel below. He had been there for half an hour. The channel was a particular shade of cold gray that the northern sea produced specifically in this season, and whatever he was thinking while looking at it was not available to her.

She had given up knowing what he was thinking before his face resolved it into something he had decided to let her see. Four months of working on his face had taught her the difference between *thinking* and *deciding to show.* She watched him decide.

He came away from the porthole.

He sat down against the bulkhead across from her. The distance between them was approximately what it had always been in enclosed spaces — one body-width, the spacing of someone who wanted enough room to do something different if something different became necessary. His hands were on his knees and his rifle was slung across his back and he looked at her with the expression she had filed, weeks ago, as *preparation.*

She waited.

He had been preparing this since Schmalburg. She had known it from the specific way his language acquisition had accelerated after the raid — the words he'd asked for, the constructions he'd started practicing, the phrasing he'd been quietly testing in the three-hour daily sessions. She had noted it. She had not told him she'd noted it. This was a judgment call about which of them needed the preparation to complete before the conversation could happen.

He said, in Cauld: "I want to tell you something."

The structure was correct. The pronunciation of *tell* was slightly off, the *l* landing harder than a native speaker would land it, but the construction was there. He had been practicing this sentence. She recognized the practice in it — the specific flatness of a sentence that has been said enough times that the words have settled into their shapes.

She put the notebook down.

She said, "I'm listening."

---

He started with the factory.

She had known he would. He had been building toward it since *factory, smoke, morning, gone* — the four words that were the corners of the room he had been trying to let her into for four months. Now he had the walls.

A city. He gave her the name in his own language first, then paused. "I don't know if it has a Cauld word," he said.

"It doesn't need one," she said.

He nodded. A city. Not the biggest he'd known — he had been to bigger, for work, before. The factory made textiles. Not his factory — his factory made small mechanical components, springs and couplings, the kind that went into larger machines. He had worked there for six years. He said: "I knew the machines." He said it the way you say a thing that has weight in it, a thing you've thought about. "I knew them by sound. Different sound for different problems. You learn." He paused. "I don't know the Cauld word for — the knowing that comes from time with a thing."

"We might not have one," Orim said, from the porthole, without turning.

He'd been listening. Of course he'd been listening. Orim listened the way he scryed — not intrusively, but completely, the attention of someone for whom receiving was a professional orientation.

Rowe looked at Orim for a moment. Then back at Lyra.

A Thursday in autumn. He knew the day because the factory had shift rotations that corresponded to the calendar, and Thursdays were when the morning shift overlapped with the maintenance crew for forty minutes. He had been at his station. He knew the time because the clock on the factory floor — he gave her the phrase for it in his language, she heard the shape of it, wrote it — had a particular sound when it moved past the half-hour. He knew the season because the light from the high windows was at a certain angle. He had been aware of all of these things, which was not unusual for him, because he was someone who had always tracked the conditions of the space he was in.

"Then," he said.

He stopped. He looked at his hands.

"Then," he said again, the word doing the work of all the other words he didn't have yet, the three-hundred words between *and then it was Thursday morning* and *and then the floor was not the floor.* His jaw worked once, the specific jaw-movement of someone hitting the edge of language and stopping.

She said: "Take it in pieces."

He looked at her.

"There is no hurry," she said. This was not quite true — the Pallor coast was somewhere ahead in the gray — but it was true enough, and the rest could wait.

He took it in pieces.

The floor was wrong. Not gone — wrong. A different quality. He said: "I thought I was sick. Or the machine had broken something in the floor." He'd had a moment of checking himself — was he sick? Was the floor structurally compromised? He was someone who checked before reacting. He checked. He was not sick. The floor was not broken.

Then the stone room.

He said it the way he said hard things — flatly, the affect of someone who has learned that flatness is less expensive than the alternative. A room made of dressed stone. Cold. A smell he would later understand as Catalyst-adjacent but did not know at the time. Three figures in robes. Not Atrament — he would understand that later too, when he'd seen enough House colors to read them. Ocipheus, he said, now, looking at her without particular accusation. He said it the way he said accurate things.

"Yes," she said.

He said: "One of them spoke."

She knew the intake protocol. She had read it in her first year. She had read it again as a researcher when she began working on Sphere-intake documentation, three years into her career, when the intake documentation project had seemed like a minor administrative assignment. She had contributed to the literature that defined best practices for intake-oath administration. She had written: *oath administered prior to language acquisition minimizes resistive response in conscript cohort.*

She had written that sentence.

He said: "The words had a rhythm. Like something official. I didn't understand any of it." He looked at his hands. "There was a gesture. The figure with the book made a gesture. I copied it." He demonstrated: a slight inclination of the head, a specific hand position. She recognized the gesture. It was the acknowledgment position from the Compact Oath. "I copied it because — because copying is what you do when you're in a room that holds you and three people in robes are making official sounds. You cooperate. You look cooperative. You think: I will be cooperative until I understand what is happening, and then I will decide." He paused. "I never decided. I never understood fast enough."

She said nothing.

"Later," he said. "When I had enough Cauld. I asked someone what the words meant." A Vierna barracks senior, an Ocipheus-seconded administrator who spoke to conscripts for the intake processing. He had asked the administrator: *what did they say to us, in the stone room?* The administrator had looked at him. Then looked away. Then said: *it was the oath of service. It binds you to the canon law of the Cauld for the duration of your term.*

Rowe said: "I asked him if it was valid if I hadn't understood it."

She already knew the answer.

He said: "He said that was a theological question and he didn't have the training to address it."

---

He gave her the numbers.

Not immediately — they came after he told her about Vierna. The barracks. The language acquisition, the bolt-action drills, the march patterns, the faces of the soldiers they were being trained alongside who were not from his Sphere and could not talk to him and he could not talk to them and after enough weeks of this you started making a map of it, the specific geography of who could be pointed at and who could not.

He said: "Sphere 31. That's what they wrote on my intake form. I saw it." He had been able to read the number. Numbers were numbers. "There was a form. They had us put a mark on it. A signature equivalent — I don't know the Cauld word."

"We would call it a mark," she said. "For those who haven't registered a signature."

"I can write," he said, without offense. "I made a mark because I didn't know the form was a signature."

"Yes," she said.

He said: "Sphere 31. Then I saw others. In the barracks. Different intake markers — they put the sphere number on the collar during processing, some administrative purpose. Sphere 22. I met someone from Sphere 22. We couldn't talk. We tried." He paused. "We had a word we shared. A word that was the same in both languages, or close enough. You know how that happens with languages that are — not related, but adjacent?"

"When two languages independently arrive at the same phoneme for the same concept," Orim said, from the porthole. "It happens when the concept is concrete enough. Simple enough."

"The word was *mother,*" Rowe said.

She heard Orim's tincture bottle click against the porthole housing. Very quietly.

She said nothing.

He said: "I met someone from Sphere 14. One of the Vierna senior staff — a researcher, I was told later — spent four hours with her. Trying to build a contact vocabulary. I watched this. I understood what the researcher was doing because I had watched you do it." He paused. "I didn't understand at the time that the research would be filed. That there were files. That the files —" He stopped. Then: "The notation. On my rifle."

"Yes," she said.

"I've seen that notation," he said. "In Sphere 31. In my world. At the factory. On the machinery." He looked at her steadily. "The patterns in the documents here are derived from patterns in Sphere 31. Someone was watching. Long before I was brought here."

She said, "Yes."

The word cost her nothing to say. That was the worst part of it. It cost her nothing because she had always known it, in the clean abstract way you know something you have filed correctly and never needed to examine. The Liturgy had been Scrying Sphere 31. The Scry data blocks she had processed — forty of them, over six months — had been produced by that observation. The notation in the cargo manifests was the same notation because both came from the same source.

She had known all of this.

She had not known she was going to have to sit in the cargo bay of a stolen Liturgy vessel and hear it from someone who had been on the other side of the membrane when the observation was made.

He said: "How long has this been happening."

She said: "The canonical records begin in Year 831."

He did the mathematics she'd done three days ago when she'd first thought about the specifics. The Liturgy's Scrying operations had been targeting Sphere 31 for approximately four hundred years. He was from a world that had been observed, catalogued, and extracted from for four hundred years. He was not a conscript. He was a resource — a late-stage output from a multi-century extraction program.

He said nothing. This was not unusual for him. He processed in a way that was visible if you knew where to look: the hands, the set of the jaw, the specific quality of stillness. She had learned where to look.

She waited.

He said, finally: "When I was in the factory. Before." He said *before* with a specific weight — the weight of a word that divides a life. "We knew our machines were copies. Old designs, refined. We had—" He used a phrase she didn't recognize; she wrote it phonetically. "Engineers who studied the history of designs. Trying to understand where they came from. Because you could see in the designs — there were gaps. Things that were not quite ours. Things that had come from somewhere else, very long ago, and been adapted."

He looked at her.

"We thought it was an older civilization," he said. "We thought: someone built these first, long ago, and we found their knowledge and built on it. We had whole—" The word again; she'd get it later. "Whole theories about this lost civilization. What they were like. Why they disappeared. What we owed them." He was quiet. "We were proud of that. The search for the origin. The respect for the source."

The channel noise was constant around them. Gray northern water moving fast and cold below.

He said: "We were right that the knowledge wasn't ours originally. We were wrong about the lost civilization. You didn't disappear. You just kept taking."

She held very still.

He said: "I'm not angry." He said it in the flat way he said accurate things. "I don't have the energy for it right now. I'm telling you because you are the person who has the most of the language and you are also the person whose institution made the forms I put my mark on and the files you processed and the research that included me without my name." He paused. "I think you should know that someone who was in those files is telling you this."

She said: "I know."

She said: "I have known, and not known, for longer than I would like to admit."

He looked at her for a moment with an expression she had no file for.

Then he said: "The others. Sphere 22. Sphere 14. However many spheres." He indicated the general vastness of the Cauld's Scrying reach with a gesture that was somehow both small and enormous — two hands, spread, the same gesture he'd used in the warehouse in Bressant when he'd described something larger than the word she had for it. "They are all in files."

"Yes," she said.

He said: "They don't know what the files say."

"No," she said.

He said: "Because the oath is given before the language."

"Yes."

He said: "On purpose."

The word she'd written, years ago, came back to her. *Minimizes resistive response.* She had written that. She had meant it as a professional observation. She had not thought about what it looked like from the resistive side.

She said: "Yes. On purpose."

He sat with this. She sat with it with him. Somewhere ahead of them, Kressida was maintaining the ship's course in the comfortable part of her strange new sleep. Orim was at the porthole, very still, making no sound at all.

Orim said, from the porthole, without turning: "What are we calling the ship."

The question settled. Nobody answered immediately. The envelope and the wind continued their argument. The channel moved below.

Rowe said, in his own language, one phrase. She had his phonetic transcription open and she found the nearest approximation she had. She said it back in Cauld: "The ground undone."

He looked at her. The vowel was wrong — he adjusted it. She said it again, closer.

"The ground that undid," he said. The structure was slightly different in Cauld from whatever the phrase meant in his language, but it was the structure that the Cauld language made available, and it was close enough to carry the weight.

"She goes to Pallor under a new name," Orim said, from the porthole, still watching the water. He had not turned. He said it in the tone of someone filing a report that no one had asked for.

She wrote it in the notebook.

*The Ground Undid.* Then, below it: *Rowe. Sphere 31. Thursday.*

---

The Pallor coast appeared on the northern horizon three hours later — first as a darkness against the gray, then as the specific darkness of rocky coast, then as the Hebrides cliffs she had read about and was now seeing in the specific register of something that has always been theoretical becoming present. The ship moved toward it. The channel noise changed as the land came closer, a different conversation between the envelope and the air, the resistance of a landmass interrupting the ocean's open argument.

Kressida woke — or the analog of waking — and the rig shifted against the cargo-bay wall and the ship's guidance systems responded to her returning attention.

Lyra looked at the coast.

She had recovered the Relic once before from a research situation that had complicated itself beyond the expected parameters — a Vierna archive job, a misidentified artifact, the entire attending mess of proving provenance when provenance had been deliberately obscured. She had been thirty-two years old and completely certain. She had been wrong about two of the three key facts and right about the outcome and she had filed this as a lesson in professional humility and moved on.

She did not feel completely certain now.

She felt the specific condition of someone who has been handed information that restructures everything behind it, and who has to now navigate forward in the restructured landscape without the benefit of having had time to survey it. She was a researcher. She knew how to operate in uncertainty. She had always known. She had always found it easier when the uncertainty was other people's.

Rowe came to stand beside her at the forward porthole.

He didn't say anything. He looked at the coast. She looked at the coast.

After a while he said, in Cauld: "What will you do with it? When you have it."

She knew he meant the Relic.

She said: "I don't know yet."

He said: "But not the thing they want you to do with it."

She looked at him.

He said: "You would have given it to them before Bressant. I don't know who *them* is. But you would have. You were the kind of person who gave things to the right authority."

"And now?" she said.

He said: "Now you know that I am in the authority's files."

She looked at the coast of Pallor, getting closer, darker, more specific.

She said: "Yes."

He nodded. He turned away from the porthole. He went to find a place to settle before they made the descent to the sea-loch below, and she watched him go with the specific attention she had been giving everything, lately, that she had not known how to look at before.

The notebook was open in her hand.

*The Ground Undid.* She looked at it.

She had been, for thirty years, a person who knew who she was. The names she would not answer to were shorter than the names she would. She was an Ocipheus Knight. She was a Templar of the third infusion. She was a Transmutation researcher with a specific publication record and a specific institutional role and a specific frame through which the world organized itself into manageable categories.

She was also the person who had written *minimizes resistive response.*

She was also the person who was writing, now, in a notebook on a stolen Liturgy vessel named The Ground Undid, heading for the coast of Pallor to recover an object that had been watching for 1,200 years.

Both of those people were her. She was not going to be able to file one of them until she understood which one to keep.

She closed the notebook.

Pallor was ahead.

[Beat 19]
SHE GOES TO SINTER

The dispatch note arrived at the sixth hour.

Vega had been at her desk since the fourth, which was not unusual; she arrived at the fourth hour and departed at the fourteenth and had been doing so for three years, and the Liturgy's administrative schedule had arranged itself around this without comment because the Liturgy's administrative schedule arranged itself around reliable people in the same way it arranged itself around good furniture: with gratitude that did not rise to acknowledgment. She had her desk. The desk faced two windows. The windows faced the courtyard. The courtyard was empty most days. This was the structure of her work.

The dispatch note was from the Office of the Senior Scribe. Not Subcanon Malvar's office, not the Canon's administrative office, not anyone in the vertical line she filed things upward to. The Office of the Senior Scribe was a horizontal office — advisory, archival, the function of institutional memory. It had been housed in the same three rooms since Year 872 and was staffed, currently, by one woman who had been in those rooms for forty-one years and had, in that time, made herself as indispensable as the furniture.

Senior Scribe Brentha Osel. Vega had met her twice. Once at the orientation for new Registry appointments, where Osel had delivered a three-minute address about the canonical responsibility of the witness function that Vega had found, at the time, professionally sound and personally uninspiring. Once in the corridor outside the map archive, where Osel had asked Vega, without preamble, whether she had found it interesting.

Vega had said: "Found what interesting?"

Osel had said: "The work." And had continued down the corridor.

The dispatch note was brief.

*V. Athen-Moor — You are requested to present yourself at the Office of the Senior Scribe at the eighth hour. Bring your notary seal and travel instruments. — B. Osel*

She read it twice. She folded it. She placed it in her working-copy folder, which was not where it belonged — it belonged in her correspondence file — but she placed it in the working-copy folder because the working-copy folder was what she had been carrying with her everywhere since the first month she'd started seeing the pattern, and the dispatch note was now part of the pattern, and the pattern was where it belonged.

She had two hours.

She spent them at her desk, working through the routine instrument queue with the methodical focus that had always been her professional strength and had become, lately, something she relied on more heavily than she used to. Methodical focus was the one thing she still had full access to. She could look at an instrument and see its form, assess its completeness, certify its disposition. She could do this even when — especially when — the instrument was part of something larger that she was also trying to see. The two processes ran in parallel. She had learned to let them.

At the eighth hour she picked up her travel bag — she had packed it before coming to work, which meant she had known before the dispatch note arrived, which meant something she did not examine — and went to the Office of the Senior Scribe.

---

Brentha Osel was seventy-three. Vega knew this from the staff records she had access to as a Registry notary. She looked seventy-three in the way that some people looked their ages: accurately, without distress, the years worn in a way that was informative rather than apologetic. Her desk was smaller than Vega's and covered in materials that were not canonical instruments — reference compendiums, historical records, a set of documents in a binding format Vega didn't recognize.

She looked at Vega the way she'd looked at her in the corridor. The same direct attention. The same sense of someone deciding how much of what they knew they were going to say.

"You've been keeping a working copy," Osel said.

It wasn't a question. Vega said: "Yes."

"For how long."

"Eight months."

Osel was quiet for a moment. She was looking at the document in her hands, which appeared to be a historical register of some kind. She said: "The current Canon Immaculate has been in his position for eleven years. Before him, the position was held by Subcanon Treye Falconer, who served for twenty-three years and retired in good standing and is currently living in his family's estate in Calyx's northern province." She set the document down. "Before Falconer, the position was held by Canon Immaculate Amaris Dort, who served for thirty-one years and died in office." She folded her hands. "During Dort's tenure, the Forge Hearth extraction authorization was renewed. During Falconer's tenure, the Sphere-intake quota was increased for the third time. During the current tenure —" She paused. "The working copy you've been keeping. Does it include the deployment roster for the war construct evaluation cohort?"

"No," Vega said. "I have the evaluation certifications. I don't have the deployment roster — it wasn't filed through Registry notation."

Osel said: "It exists. The deployment authorization was convened under the standing order of Canonical Article Eighteen, which permits the Canon Immaculate to authorize force deployment without inter-House consultation when the designated threat is classified as membrane-breach level." She looked at Vega. "The war constructs were authorized under a membrane-breach classification. The breach they were authorized against has not been publicly announced."

Vega said: "The Sinter Zone."

"Yes."

She had known, she supposed. The working copy had been building toward it. The Specialist Deployment intake log. The *approach preparation* classification. The Δ-7 through Δ-14 instrument set that had not yet been convened. The deployment roster that had not come through Registry. All of it pointing at the zone that was also where the recovery instrument pointed, that was also where T-044's transit suspension pointed, that was also where — now — twelve Liturgy military columns were apparently pointing.

She had known. She had been trying not to see the shape of it.

She said: "What do you need me to do."

Osel said: "Go. See what happens. Write it down."

She said this in the tone of someone who has given this instruction before, or who has thought about giving it for long enough that it had the quality of something rehearsed. Not practiced — rehearsed. The difference between a thing you say because you have said it before and a thing you say because you have held it long enough that the saying has become necessary.

"I can't stop it," Osel said. "I have been a notary for forty-one years and a Senior Scribe for twelve of those and the thing I have been given the authority to do is witness and record." She picked up the reference compendium on her desk and set it down again without opening it. "The canonical instrument set will require a notary when it is convened. It has not yet been convened. That means the operation is still — technically — pending canonical authorization." She paused. "When the instruments are convened and sealed, they cannot be unsealed. What the notary witnesses before convening, in the exercise of her professional preparation function, is a different matter."

Vega said: "You're sending me to be a witness."

"I'm sending you to be the record," Osel said. "These are not the same thing."

She let this settle.

Then she said: "Your sister is there, or will be. T-044." She said it without particular affect. "Not because I arranged it. Because the recovery instrument pointed that direction and so did your sister's competence." She paused. "I thought you should know."

---

She went back to her desk.

She had two hours before the morning supply convoy departed from the north gate, which was the transport Osel's dispatch office had booked her passage on — she had read this in the travel instrument before she left Osel's office, the automatic professional reflex of checking the document for errors. There were no errors. The document was correct.

She sat at her desk.

She took out the working copy. She had not intended to — her hands found the drawer without instruction, which was a thing that happened more often now, the body executing decisions the mind had not yet finished making. She opened it.

The accumulated eight months. The pattern laid out on the facing pages in her small careful hand. She read it through from the beginning, which took twelve minutes because she had written it efficiently and efficiency had a tempo. At the end of twelve minutes she had confirmed that the pattern was what she had believed it to be, that she had not invented it, that the connections between the instruments were real and not a function of the anxious way she had been reading everything lately.

She had not invented it.

She closed the working copy. She put it in her travel bag.

She was the Registry notary. She was the witness function. She made the official record true. She did not decide what was true; she recorded what the authorized parties determined and certified it with her mark. This was a good and necessary function. This was the function that made the Liturgy legible to itself.



She had never, in three years, asked herself what the difference was between certifying something and authorizing it. She was asking herself now, in the way you asked yourself things when the answer mattered practically rather than theoretically.

She packed the remainder of her travel instruments. She packed her notary seal. She packed the working copy, which was not a canonical document and had no legal standing and which she was bringing anyway because Osel had said *write it down* and the working copy was where she wrote things down.

She did not say goodbye to anyone. This was not because she did not have people to say it to — she had colleagues in the Registry, a deputy notary she had been training for seven months, a woman at the commissary who had been setting aside the good bread for her on the mornings she arrived early enough to catch it. She knew their names and the shapes of their days. She had not said goodbye because she did not know how to explain where she was going in a way that would not require her to also explain why, and the why was not a thing she could articulate at the present time without the articulation itself becoming a canonical incident.

She walked out of the registry at the ninth hour.

---

The convoy north was four supply wagons, a Heloth construct for heavy freight, and a garrison escort of six soldiers — standard north-road complement. She had a passenger notation on the supply manifest, which the convoy commander reviewed without comment. People from the administrative offices traveled on supply convoys occasionally. It was not unusual.

The road north ran through the alpine approaches and then into the lower mountain passes and then into the territory that the Liturgy's administrative files classified as the Sinter Zone Perimeter Region, which was a designation that covered the area between Ocipheus's northern alpine boundary and the Wall's southern checkpoint. Vega had been north as far as the alpine ridge on three previous occasions, all of them administrative trips related to garrison supply authorization. She had not been to the Wall.

She sat on the wagon bench with her travel bag between her feet and watched the terrain change.

The alpine approaches were familiar — the Ocipheus peninsula's specific quality of mountain light, the clean air, the juniper scrub on the lower slopes. Then the character of the road changed. Not dramatically. Incrementally, the way things changed when they were being changed by something that had been working on them for a long time. The rock formations at the roadside were slightly wrong: the way the strata lay was not quite how Lyra would have described it, she thought, and then stopped thinking about how Lyra would describe things because that was a path that went somewhere she couldn't afford to go yet.

The first military column passed them on the second day.

Going north. Atrament equipment — she recognized the housing pattern on the freight wagons from the canonical inventory formats she had processed. Approximately forty soldiers, supply complement, three battle-rig carriers. The battle-rig carriers were broad flat wagons with specific hardpoint mountings. She had seen the certification documents for this class of carrier. She knew their rated capacity. She counted the hardpoints as the column passed.

The convoy commander noted her counting without comment.

The second column passed four hours later.

Ocipheus garrison colors this time. She knew those very well. Forty soldiers, different freight format — the wagons had the canonical property mark of the Liturgy's permanent contingency reserve. She recognized this mark from the supply authorizations she had processed six months ago, when the reserve stores had been released on a standing order renewal that she had certified and filed and had not thought about again until she had begun accumulating her working copy.

Standing order renewal for the permanent contingency reserve required Canon Immaculate authorization.

She had seen that authorization. She had certified it. She had filed it.

The third column passed at dusk, moving slower, carrying something she couldn't categorize from the wagon covers — the shapes underneath were not battle rigs, not standard freight, something else. She watched until the convoy turned a bend and disappeared.

She sat with her travel bag between her feet and looked at the road ahead.

The Liturgy's permanent contingency reserve had been unsealed three times in recorded canonical history. The first time was the Year 1079 Sinter catastrophe — the event that had destroyed House Sinter and established the quarantine zone. The second time was the Pallor-Atrament border action in Year 1243, which had threatened the Wall's eastern garrison. The third time was now.

She had known this. She had processed the standing order renewal. She had certified it.

She had certified the unsealing of a reserve that had last been unsealed for a catastrophe.



She opened her working copy. She dated the top of the next blank page. She wrote:

*Day 1 of travel north. Three military columns passed our convoy, moving north. Atrament: 40 soldiers, 3 BR carriers. Ocipheus: 40 soldiers, Liturgy contingency reserve mark on freight wagons. Third column: uncategorized freight, unrecognized form profile.*

She paused.

*The contingency reserve mark is canonical form stamp P-7-R. It requires Canon Immaculate authorization to apply. The standing order renewal I certified six months ago authorized P-7-R deployment for an unspecified operational period. The form I certified was correct. The deployment was authorized.*

She wrote: *I am not the person who authorized this. I am the person who certified the authorization.*

She looked at those two sentences.

She wrote: *I am also the person who will certify the canonical instrument set when it is convened at the Zone.*

She paused.

*I am the notary.*

She did not underline it this time. She didn't need to. She left the page open to dry and looked at the road, which was darker now, the mountain dark that was not the absence of light but the presence of a different quality of it, and the road north ran through it toward the Wall and whatever was being prepared on the other side.

The supply wagons moved. The Heloth's steam-chemical exhaust rose white against the dark. Somewhere ahead, past the alpine passes and the Wall checkpoint and the contested boundary region and the Sinter Zone's specific quality of wrongness, her sister was also moving toward this.

She would get there first.

She was not certain this was better.

She closed the working copy. She put it in her bag. She sat with her hands in her lap and watched the road north until the dark made it indistinguishable from the sky, and then she sat with her hands in her lap and watched that.

[Beat 20]
PALLOR REACHED — CAER GLAS MOOR

The sea-loch was the color of cold pewter and it did not forgive the hull's landing.

Lyra had flown in Liturgy transport vessels twelve times in her career and had never landed on water before. The hull hit with a sound she felt in her teeth and then the vessel settled - not gracefully, not immediately, but with the gradual reluctance of something that had been designed for water landings but had opinions about the specific water. The loch water was black under the overcast and cold enough to be visible as cold, which was something she had not known was possible and filed under *things the theoretical literature does not convey.*

Pallor. The northern coast was rock and heather and a horizontal quality to the rain that suggested the rain had been going sideways for so long that it had forgotten any other direction was available. Nothing like Ocipheus's clean alpine approaches or Vierna's dense river-country or Atrament's productive grimness. This was a different category of landscape: one that had been shaped by something long and relentless and indifferent, and that had arrived at its current form through the specific process of losing everything that couldn't hold on.

Kressida brought the ship in with the practiced competence of someone who had been flying for three hours and had developed an understanding of the vessel's specific temperament. The water settled around the hull. The envelope above them shifted in the wind and then steadied.

"Good landing," Rowe said.

"It was functional," Kressida said, through the rig's speaker housing.

---

The moor-hounds were what Orim found first.

Not the squad. The hounds - three of them, six-legged, low to the heather, moving in the specific pattern of animals following a trace they'd held for too long and had begun to associate with something they did not like. They were a kilometer north of the sea-loch, working the ridge above the vault path. He watched them from the airship's hatch for two minutes without saying anything.

"They're not tracking us," Lyra said.

"No." He was still watching. "They're tracking what they've been following since the coast crossing. They don't want to find it. That is a different thing from losing the trace."

The vault was another two kilometers - she had the pre-Compact survey in her kit, a Loera route document Tavar had produced at Sal Vento that showed the approaches, the sight lines, the terrain between the sea-loch and the Caer Glas vault. The squad had two days on them, possibly three. The moor-hounds' track meant the squad had not moved on - they were holding position at the vault, waiting for collection.

"They know we're here," Orim said. He was no longer looking at the hounds.

"When?"

"When the hounds lost interest in anything else." He turned from the hatch. "An hour. Possibly less." He looked at his Rod - not the checking gesture, the one he used when he was doing a specific assessment of what the preparation contained and how much of it remained. "There is one other thing."

He said it in a particular register she had learned to attend to: the register of a man who has been holding a piece of information until the moment when withholding it would begin to cost more than giving it.

"The Relic trace," he said. "It is very warm. It has been handled recently, within the last four hours. Not transported. Held." He paused. "At a scrying aperture, or adjacent to one."

She looked at him.

"Someone has been looking through it," he said.

---

The vault approach came from the west, across two hundred meters of open heather with no cover. There was no other approach. The survey document had noted this - *no tactical approach; vault was designed to be observed from outside* - which was the document's way of saying that whoever held this ground had built it to favor the defense.

She went across anyway. The party went with her.

The moor-hounds caught their scent thirty meters out and broke from their circuit and ran. Not back to the squad - east, into the open heather, away from everything. Orim watched them go. He noted their direction.

"That way," he said, almost to himself. "If we need to know where he went."

The vault door was open.

Not broken - open. The lock mechanism on the pre-Compact door was undamaged; the key had been used, which meant the Caerglas property claim was real enough to have included the key passing to someone who could open it. Inside: the Yggdra box on a stone ledge at eye level. The oilskin wrapping on the floor, recently unwrapped. The case beside it, open.

Empty.

The woman standing at the far wall turned when Lyra entered. She had the look of someone who had been expecting this arrival and had made a decision about it before it happened.

"T-044," she said. Lector's register - formal, no surprise in it.

"Lector Mirren," Lyra said, because the Loera network had given her the name and rank and operational role three weeks ago and there was no operational reason to pretend otherwise.

The second figure moved at the vault's side entrance - the fixer, circling for angle, doing what fixers do when the primary confrontation is engaged. Not trained the way the Lector was trained. More experienced in other ways.

"Where is the Relic," Lyra said.

"Gone," the Lector said. "He folded with it. I imagine your Scryer can work the trace."

"Why."

The Lector was quiet for a moment. She had the face of someone who had already written the accounting of this situation and was reading back from a final entry rather than discovering anything new. "Because the commission was wrong," she said. "I understood that three days ago. He understood it sooner." She looked at the empty case. "The commission was framed as a property dispute. A Relic provenance review. We were told the Ocipheus station had been holding a Calyx ancestral claim in administrative suspension for six generations and the Long Seat had authorized recovery. All of it was real on paper." She paused. "All of it."

"Prelacze."

"We knew the Liturgy was involved. We did not know which Canon. The framing was clean enough that we did not need to." She said it precisely, without apology and without self-justification. The register of someone making an accurate report while there was still time to make it. "The boy was Calyx. He had a real claim. He had a real right to open that door. When he understood what the commission was actually for, he stopped participating in it." She looked at Lyra. "He is not your problem. He is trying to undo it."

The fight was not negotiated. She had not expected it to be - the Lector had a commission she had accepted in good standing, and abandoning it without consequence was not how the Lector's order worked. What followed was clean and specific and neither of them pretended it was anything else. The fixer came in from the side and Rowe handled her - two exchanges, the kind of efficiency that came from a man who had spent seven months at a Vierna conscript line learning exactly how much effort it took to put someone down. The Lector was harder. She was good, genuinely good, and she knew it, and she fought with the particular quality of someone who has accepted the outcome and intends to make it cost what it should cost.

It cost. Lyra paid.

At the end, the Lector was down. Not gone - she had too much training to go easily - but down and staying, and she looked at Lyra with the expression of someone reading a closing entry in the same ledger she had been reading from throughout. "The name he gave us," she said. "For the commission. Write it down."

"I know the name."

"Write it down anyway." She said it with some force left in it. "So it's on paper. Somewhere that isn't Liturgy paper."

Lyra looked at her for a moment. Then she took out her field log and wrote: *Canon Immaculate Tomasz Prelacze.* She showed it to the Lector.

The Lector closed her eyes.

---

Orim found the boy on the northeast face of the ridge, a hundred and fifty meters from the vault.

He was sitting in the heather with the Relic case in his lap and the Relic in his hands and the expression of someone who had been holding a thing that was warm when it should not be warm and had been trying to decide what the warmth meant. He was nineteen, possibly twenty. The Loera network had described him as *skilled, Blink-trained, Calyx-provincial, no commission record.* He looked like all of those things simultaneously.

Orim sat down beside him without asking permission.

They sat in the heather for thirty seconds. The rain moved sideways between them.

"Your uncle sent you," Orim said.

"My uncle sent me because he believed it." He was not trying to sound younger than he was. He simply was younger than the situation. "He had documents. Six-generation property claim. The vault key. Everything proper. He believed the Liturgy had finally acknowledged the Caerglas claim." A pause. "I believed him."

"When did you stop believing him."

"When I looked through it." He looked at the Relic in his hands. "It showed me something. From forty years ago. The vault. My uncle, ten years old, at the vault door with his father, who is my grandfather, who was filing the claim at the Long Seat for the fourth time. Who was telling his son: *we will get it back.* It showed me -" He stopped. "It showed me my grandfather's face while he said that. And I have never met my grandfather. He died before I was born." He was quiet for a moment. "It has been watching this moor for forty years. At least. That is not a Calyx property claim. That is something else entirely."

Orim said nothing. He had a particular quality of silence in these moments - not uncomfortable, not pressing - that Lyra had learned to read as the silence of a man who had arrived at a conclusion decades ago and was watching someone else complete the same journey in real time.

The boy held out the Relic.

"Take it back," he said. "I don't know what it is. I don't think anyone does. But it shouldn't be here."

Orim took it with both hands, the way he handled the Rod when the preparation was live - with full attention, no gesture wasted.

"What's your name," Orim said.

"Wren." He said it without hesitation, which was the answer of someone who had been deciding something and had decided.

"Wren." Orim turned the Relic over in his hands once, reading its warmth, then put it in the case. "Come, then."

---

She saw Vaen before Vaen moved.

That was the tell - that Lyra saw her first, standing at the moor's edge two hundred meters out with the specific stillness of someone who has been there long enough to have become part of the landscape's texture, and who had chosen to become visible at this moment rather than earlier. The distance did not matter. The size and the way it occupied space were sufficient: six infusions changed what the body was at a structural level, and the structural change was visible before the face was, before the register was.

She had been dispatched as the final guarantee. The squad had carried the commission. If the squad failed, the commission had one more layer.

Vaen came across the moor at a walk. No urgency. The ground responded differently to her weight than it did to anyone else's - not softer, the opposite: as if the heather understood the difference between what it usually held and what it was holding now.

"Little Sister," she said, when she was close enough to say it at conversational volume.

"Champion," Lyra said.

"You know what this is."

"Yes."

Vaen looked at the party behind her. She looked at Kressida's rig with the assessment of someone reading a physical situation - three meters of Atrament reaction plate, neural interface adaptation, the specific threat profile of a construct piloted by someone who had grown into its mechanical language. She looked at Orim, who was holding his Rod at his side in the way he held it when he had already decided and was waiting for the moment. She looked at Wren, who had gone very still in the way of someone who had just understood that the situation had escalated past the point where his presence was relevant and was trying to become part of the landscape.

She looked at Lyra.

"I have a commission," Vaen said. "The commission is in good standing. I accepted it in good standing."

"I know."

"Then you know I cannot let you leave with it."

Lyra said: "You can return to Pallor having been bested by a third-infusion Knight who was following a legitimate pursuit authority."

"That requires me to be bested."

The fight was different from anything Lyra had fought. She had known it would be. The infusion differential was not a matter of technique - it was structural, physical, the difference between what the body was built to do at three infusions and what it was built to do at six. Vaen applied force the way a beam applies force: not with skill exactly, with physics. She adjusted her grip. The consequences followed.

Kressida took the opening exchange. The rig absorbed what the math said Lyra could not survive - three-meter plates of Atrament reaction plate against a Champion's adjusted grip, and the plates held because Kressida had grown the rig's sensors into her own nervous system and could read the force distribution before it arrived. She held Vaen's attention for eleven seconds. That was all she had promised herself.

Wren blinked. He came through at Vaen's left flank, behind her sight angle, and what he did was not an attack - it was an anchor point, the youngest and least experienced member of the party appearing in a location that a Champion's spatial awareness could not easily ignore and could not safely dismiss. Vaen turned. That was enough.

Rowe's shot came from the east ridge, three hundred meters out, finding the gap between the rig's plate and Vaen's second exchange with Lyra. He had been reading the geometry since Vaen crossed the two-hundred-meter mark. He had seven months of Vierna conscript rifle training and thirty years of WW1-Europe bone knowledge and the specific marksmanship of a man who had learned to find gaps in a mechanical system because mechanical systems were what kept him alive. The gap was there for half a second. He fired once.

Vaen stopped.

Not down. Not finished. Stopped - the specific halt of someone who has received information their body cannot ignore, processing it, making an assessment of the situation in the clinical way that six infusions produced: not pain-response, not emotion, pure physical accounting.

Orim's Rod was already live. She saw him. She saw what he was pointing it at.

She looked at Lyra.

"Little Sister," she said again, and this time it carried something else - not condescension, not the opening of a fight, the closing of one. The specific address of someone who has been in enough of these to recognize the moment when continuing costs more than the commission is worth. "You have three more."

"I know," Lyra said.

"When you get them." Vaen looked at her for a full three seconds - the honest accounting, the kind she owed - and then she turned and walked back into the moor. The heather closed around her. The fog came in off the loch and erased her in stages.

Nobody said anything.

Wren was standing where he had blinked back to, slightly off-angle in the way of someone who had folded eight times in the last hour and was running a private inventory of what remained. He looked at the moor where Vaen had been. He looked at the party.

"Is that - normal?" he said.

Orim considered this. "No," he said. "And also yes." He looked at the Rod, which had not been used, and wrapped it in his coat with the care of a man who was grateful it had not been needed. "Welcome to the party."

Wren looked at them each in turn. He had the expression of someone assessing a situation he had just permanently joined.

"Right," he said. He looked at the vault path, the sea-loch below, the *Eirene-7* sitting in the pewter water waiting. "Which direction."

"South," Lyra said. "Then east."

He nodded. He fell into position behind Orim, slightly to his left, which was the position of someone who had been moving in a group for three weeks with a different party and understood, without discussion, how a party organized its approach to terrain.

She noted it.

She walked south toward the sea-loch.

[Beat 21]
THE RELIC — WHAT THE EYE HAS SEEN

The rain had been coming in off the channel for the better part of two hours, and somewhere around the first kilometer it stopped being rain in the usual sense and became a condition of the air instead. Horizontal. The kind of rain that gets into the gap between the collar and the neck before you can think to close it.
