She had read about this in the practitioner literature, which called it *zone-proximity affect* and kept the clinical notation intact in a way she recognized as the professional strategy for not saying the simpler thing: that the ground near the Sinter perimeter made soldiers feel like they were being watched by something that had no eyes.

She filed this away. There were four days ahead of her and a pursuit and she did not have time for phenomenology.

The Heloth courier's gait was not designed for mountain passes. It was designed for flat road and moderate grade, for eating distance in the way efficient machines eat distance — evenly, without complaint, with the particular patience of something that does not get tired. The pass's loose stone descent was not flat road and moderate grade. The construct managed it with a technical competence that did not extend to comfort: each step a controlled lurch, the weight transferring through its shoulder joints in a way that telegraphed into her hips in a rhythm she was already learning to hate. Three hours of this descent behind her. The ache had been settling for the last two.

She was tall enough that the Heloth courier's standard saddle configuration required adjustment — they had managed this the morning they left Ocipheus Station, the depot technician making the changes with the focused neutrality of a person making the same modification for the third time that week — and still the machine's gait did not suit her. Lyra had three infusions and a body that the Transmutation had made excellent at many things. Endurance in rocky alpine descents on a freight-optimized construct was not one of them.

She looked down at the pass bottom and saw the checkpoint.

It was smaller than she had imagined from the reports. She had been through Eirene's Gate twice in the past twelve years — once on an institutional assessment in Year 1126, once with a Transmutation research party in Year 1131 — and both times she had been moving fast and focused elsewhere. What she saw now: a low stone building, four centuries old at minimum, built into the eastern rockface where the pass narrowed to its worst point. The mortar had given up and been replaced by a later generation of mortar that was now also in the process of giving up. A newer lean-to extension on the downslope side, rougher than the old stone, the lumber still pale enough that it had not spent many winters at this altitude. Thirty meters further down the road, an outbuilding where the soldiers slept. Smoke from a fire inside it.

The pass itself was the barrier. She had known this from the doctrinal reading but the reading had not prepared her for how absolute the mountains were — two ridgelines compressing toward each other, limestone and hard quartzite layered at angles that had nothing to do with horizontal, the strata running slant as broken ribs. Nothing had made the pass except the geological argument that had produced it over ten thousand years of frost-crack and slow collapse. The checkpoint occupied the narrowest point because that was where the road was narrowest. The architecture followed the terrain. This had always been the case.

On the road in front of the checkpoint, three Heloth freighters stood in a line, each one loaded with dressed limestone in the carry-cradle configuration, each at idle — low exhaust output, that near-silence of a machine holding position between tasks. Beside each one, working from a flatbed wagon, eight or ten people were transferring stone: lifting, carrying, loading, in the efficient rhythm of people who had done this work long enough that thinking about it was no longer part of doing it. She watched them as her Heloth descended the final grade. No House insignia on their clothing. No unit markings, no standard gear, nothing that placed them in any House's catalog. Their work was competent in the specific way that comes from training rather than improvisation.

Two soldiers stood on the lean-to steps. Their attention was on the workers.

She noted this and kept riding.

---

The checkpoint building's interior was what the reports had said and somewhat less than the reports had implied. The desk was iron, bolted to the floor through the stone flags, the bolts new enough to still show bright threads where the wrench had contacted them. The departure log on the desk's left side was open to a page three-quarters through the volume, weighted at the corner by a smooth stone because the pass wind came through the door gap when the door was open. The wind was coming through the door gap now. The window facing the pass had an oilcloth frame currently folded back against the wall, which let the light in and the cold in equally. There was a stamp and an ink block. There was a stool for the officer and a worn spot on the stone floor where the visitor stood.

She stood on the worn spot.

The officer was a Vierna man of approximately fifty, two infusions, the specific patience of someone who had been processing paperwork at stations like this one long enough that the unusual arrival had ceased to produce any response beyond the next procedural step. He stood when she entered. He looked at the Templar designation on her credentials.

"T-044," he said.

"Lyra," she said. "Dame, Templar rank, Ocipheus Station."

"I know what T-044 means." He was not rude about it. He was precise. He took the credentials and the Keeper's sealed letter and held them in the flat window light and read both in sequence. He read the Keeper's letter twice. She watched his face and found nothing in it except attention, which was the quality of a professional who understood that finding things in his face was not his job.

He set the documents down and opened the desk's left drawer.

"I received this three days ago," he said. He set a second document on the desk between them.

She picked it up.

It was a suspension instrument — a canonical authority restriction, issued under the Canon Immaculate's standing review power, citing an active property certification dispute. Field authority suspension, designation T-044, pending canonical review of property recovery procedures related to the Ocipheus Station vigil archive. The Canon Immaculate's seal was in the upper right corner, correct format, correct impression. The filing notation in the upper left cited the central registry instrument number and the date.

Three days ago. The day after the Relic had been taken, or the day of, or close enough that the distinction changed nothing.

The Keeper's sealed letter authorized transit through the Sinter perimeter on pursuit grounds, invoking her field authority as the Templar of record at Ocipheus Station. Field authority was the mechanism. Without it, the letter was a piece of paper with a seal on it. The suspension was the prior instrument. Prior instruments governed.

She set the document back down on the desk.

She had known, she thought now. She had known it was waiting somewhere at the end of the descent, not as a specific conclusion but as a weight, something settled below the sternum that was distinct from the zone's low pressure and older. The body knows things before the mind has worked through the sequence.

"The property dispute that's cited," she said.

"House Pallor. Long-standing certification claim on the vigil archive's Relic holding." His voice was flat and precise — the voice of a professional delivering bad news without inflection because inflection complicates things. "The suspension cites the claim as grounds for restricting independent field action pending review. The claim's age doesn't affect the instrument's validity."

"How long has the claim been filed?"

He looked at the instrument. "One hundred and sixty-six years."

She looked at the departure log. It was still open on the desk from her initial glance. Three days ago's page. "Were there crossings on the day of the filing?"

He turned the log toward her. She found the date and ran her eye down the entries. Two were Descent Corps, the standard rotation notation. The third was a canonical transit authorization: Pallor Templar, Lector rank, authorized under standing property claim transit rights, party of three. The departure time was mid-afternoon.

They had gone through. They had walked through this checkpoint, presented Pallor's property claim authorization, and the officer on that watch had logged them and let them pass. The same legal framework that suspended her authorized their crossing. The property claim in dispute supported both operations simultaneously: it gave the Canon grounds to restrict her field authority, and it gave the Pallor party grounds to invoke transit rights. One document in the central canonical registry had done both things at once.

She thought about this for a moment — about the distance between what such an instrument required: a person with access to the canonical registry, understanding of how property claim disputes could be weaponized as standing instruments, and the foresight to file before the pursuit had even begun. Someone who had known, before the theft, that the theft would happen and that she would be the one sent after it.

This was not improvised.

"I need to note that I am lodging a formal objection to the suspension," she said. "I'll submit it through the review process on my return."

"I'll note that." He took up his pen and wrote something in the log's margin — neat script, brief — and then looked at her with an expression that was not unkind. Not sympathetic, exactly. Realistic. "You're going around."

"Through the Vierna eastern approaches. Do you have the current route conditions?"

He went to the document cabinet and returned with a route notation sheet, old stock, printed in the small press-type that regional offices used. He smoothed it on the desk and traced the roads north and east. "The western approaches are open, but you said Vierna. The eastern entry — Bressant junction is here. Two days from the outer gate at operational pace, three if the high pass has had early snow." He looked at her. "I don't know what the pass conditions are currently. I can tell you they were clear four days ago when the last rotation transfer came through."

She took the route sheet.

At the door she turned back once, though she was not certain why. The officer was already returning the suspension instrument to the left drawer. The stamp sat on the desk, unused. The wind came through the gap in the door frame and moved the edge of the departure log's open page very slightly, not enough to turn it.

"The workers outside," she said.

He looked up.

"Where are they from?"

A pause. "Contracted labor," he said. "Wall maintenance coalition contract. They've been at this section for three months." He said it in the tone of something he was willing to say and nothing more. She had the answer to the question she had asked. She had not asked the right question.

She went out.

---

Orim was waiting at her Heloth's shoulder, the position he took when attending to something she could not see. The Rod was in his coat, not in his hand. He turned when she stepped out.

"South passage," he said. "Three people and two loaded couriers, early afternoon three days ago. I can see the thermal trace of the Heloth exhaust at this range — three days cold but still distinguishable from the construction freighters. They went south." He looked at the document in her hand. He looked at her face. "Or not."

"Not," she said.

He accepted this without a question.

"The eastern route," she said. "Bressant."

He looked north along the road. "The pass at the Vierna junction should be clear. The thermal signature of snowfall — old or fresh — has a particular quality I can read at range. What I saw this morning looked dry. There is a shortcut through the lower ridge line that is not on the official route sheet." He looked at her. "It saves half a day. The road is not maintained and passes through a village in disputed House territory — a dispute between Vierna and two other Houses, ongoing for forty years, and nothing resolved and no action expected. The road is perfectly passable."

"In your experience."

"I have taken that road four times."

"How many without incident?"

"Three." A pause. "The third House was polite about it."

She mounted her courier. The construct shifted its weight to accommodate her — the hydraulic sequence the research literature described as weight-responsive stance correction, which felt from the rider's position exactly like the machine acknowledging you. She had never found this comforting. She found it accurate.

The checkpoint officer was standing in the doorway. Not watching them in an unfriendly way. Watching them the way a man watches something leave his area of jurisdiction and become someone else's problem — not relieved, not troubled, present.

She looked back at the pass. The mountains rose on both sides: limestone and hard quartzite, the layers running at angles that had nothing to do with horizontal, the way stone runs when the pressure has been too much for its original orientation for too long. Somewhere in those mountains the Sinter perimeter ran through the rock itself. Not a fence, not a wall. The rock sealed it. The rock had been sealing it since Year One, which was eleven hundred and thirty-eight years ago, and the Descent Corps patrolled the gaps because mountains did not close every gap and every gap that remained was a gap that could be used.

She felt the zone at the center of her chest: low, directional, the quiet insistence of something very large being very still. The Descent Corps debriefs mentioned this. The ones from officers who had done multiple rotations described it as getting worse. Not dramatically — not in the way of symptoms. Measurably. Officers who came back after an interval noted the change.

She turned her Heloth east.

---

The stone workers had finished loading one Heloth's carry-cradle and had started on the second. She passed close enough on the road out of the checkpoint to see their hands: rough-worked, the particular dryness of people who had been doing physical labor in mountain cold long enough that the condition was permanent. One of them looked up when her Heloth's footfall sound changed direction. The look was not hostile or curious. It was the quality of someone in a specific kind of situation who had learned to observe soldiers and their decisions without appearing to observe them. She recognized the quality of it the way you recognize something you have seen before without remembering where.

She rode past. Ardea had taken the western road to avoid the checkpoint log; they would meet in Schmalburg.

Orim came up beside her when the checkpoint was out of sight. He did not comment on the workers.

"The suspension was expected," he said. "Not by me. But by whoever filed it."

She had been waiting for him to say this, or something like it. He was sixty-odd years old and had worked border approaches for most of that, which was a kind of education in how institutions used their machinery.

"The instrument cites a dispute that's been filed for one hundred and sixty-six years," he said. "You do not reach into a one-hundred-and-sixty-six-year-old dispute for a three-day-old suspension without knowing the dispute exists and understanding precisely how to use it. This was not improvised." He rode for a moment. "Whoever removed the Relic also had, or arranged, the canonical mechanism to ensure the most obvious pursuer was removed from the most direct pursuit path."

She had reached this conclusion at approximately the moment she read the filing date. She had not said it aloud because there were parts of the conclusion she was not ready to articulate to a contractor she had hired eleven days ago in the aftermath of a theft.

"That suggests the same person controls both operations," she said.

"Yes." He adjusted the guide-rein — the habit of a man who had been riding long enough that his hands needed something to do when he was thinking. "Or was used by someone who does."

The Canon Immaculate's seal was on the suspension instrument. The Canon Immaculate commanded her chain. The theft had been committed by, or on behalf of, someone with access to the canonical registry — someone who could file a suspension through the central office without it being flagged as anomalous. Either the Canon was the source of both operations, or someone had used the Canon's authority without the Canon's knowledge, and the second option required a level of access that she did not find credible.

She was a Templar with a thirty-year record. She had never once had a reason to consider that her institutional chain might be the problem.

She filed this. Not as a conclusion — as a working observation that required more data before she could responsibly treat it as a conclusion. That was the researcher's discipline. You observed, you filed, you continued collecting.

"At Bressant," she said. "What do you know about the eastern route from the river?"

"The *L'Accord* barge run." He said this with the ease of a man who had taken a route many times and had opinions about it. "Commercial freight, Vierna compact authority. It runs the Veil River eastward to the Atrament border approach — six days of river, then the rail north. If we miss the current run, there is a two-day wait at the Bressant dock for the next." He paused. "The barge captain has worked that river for thirty years and does not particularly like passengers, but does particularly like the kind of credentials that reduce his inspection time at the Atrament border checkpoint. I have passed through on Liturgy contracted passage before. He will remember."

"And you believe he'll accommodate us."

"I believe he will accommodate the credentials and find me tolerable in the process." He considered. "He found me tolerable before. He will probably have strong opinions about the state of the river that I will be expected to listen to."

She let this sit. Six days by river plus the two-day approach plus whatever interval was lost at the Bressant junction: she was looking at eight days before she reached the Atrament territory the thieves were moving through. They had four days on her at the checkpoint. They would have more at Atrament. The gap was not a gap anymore — it was a distance that would require something other than faster riding to close.

"There will be checkpoints in the Vierna eastern passes," she said.

"Yes." He did not say it with particular worry. "The Vierna eastern entry is not the Wall rotation. The Vierna checkpoints operate under their own compact authority. Your Templar credentials will be logged but not challenged — the suspension covers Wall-transit authority specifically. It does not, as I read it, restrict your movement through civilian territory."

She had read it the same way. She had read it twice to be sure, in the flat window light of the checkpoint building, while the officer waited. The suspension was precisely drafted — it removed the specific field authority she needed to invoke the Keeper's letter, but it did not ground her movement. Whoever had written it knew exactly what it needed to do and had not done more than that. Precision as a form of confidence.

"They're not trying to stop me from pursuing," she said.

"No." He turned this over. "They're making the pursuit difficult enough that the Relic reaches where it's going before you arrive."

She thought about where it was going. Pallor's claim was the legal instrument. The transit authorization logged at the checkpoint was a Pallor Templar. The Relic, or whoever had arranged the theft, was moving it toward Pallor territory. But the Canon was Ocipheus. Ocipheus and Pallor maintained a formal diplomatic distance that made joint operations between them unusual.

An Ocipheus Canon and a Pallor Templar working the same instrument. Either one was using the other, or both had something to gain from the same outcome, or the Pallor party did not know what they were carrying and why.

She had not enough data to determine which. She needed to reach Bressant, she needed to catch the barge, and she needed to find the thread that connected these things together before the thread went too cold to follow.

The road climbed north through the morning. The pass walls receded as the ridgelines drew apart — the geological argument resolving into broader terrain, the mountains still present in all directions but no longer pressing. The cold came off the limestone: clean, specific, a mineral smell that cut through the Heloth exhaust when the wind shifted. Her fingers had gone numb inside the riding gloves. She kept working the wrist articulation of the half-plate to stay ahead of the stiffening.

"The village on the shortcut road," she said.

"Ordinary enough." He glanced at her. "They are accustomed to travelers who do not want to be logged at official checkpoints. They have a particular indifference to such travelers that suggests long practice."

"And the disputed House authority."

"Present in the form of a very old border-marker stone that three Houses have each at various times painted their own insignia on. All three coats are visible. Nobody has replaced the marker." He paused. "The village children use it to keep score."

She rode north. The zone's pressure had eased as the checkpoint fell behind — or it had not eased and she was simply becoming accustomed to it, which was the more troubling interpretation. The Descent Corps debriefs mentioned both. Some officers reported zone-proximity affect diminishing with distance. Others reported it becoming background: the way a sound heard for long enough stops registering as distinct from silence.

She could not determine which was true of her own case and this bothered her more than the sensation itself. A researcher should be able to distinguish her own data from her adaptation to it.

"When we reach Bressant," she said, "I want to know if the Pallor party stopped there."

"I'll be able to tell you within a few hours of arrival," Orim said. "The Veil River junction is a membrane-adjacent site — one of the documented minor Sphere contacts in the eastern lowlands. My range at a site like that is better than at altitude." He considered. "Also the barge captain will know. He notices everything that happens on his dock."

She kept riding. The mountains were the color of overcast limestone: grey-white, almost chalk, the strata running slant in the ridgelines on both sides. Somewhere behind her, south and below, the Sinter zone sat in its sealed basin and the constructs of the Descent Corps walked its perimeter and filed their reports and logged their observations and returned to the patrol stations at the pass approaches. Somewhere ahead of her, four or five days ahead, moving east through a country she had not moved through in six years, was a lens in a carrying-case and the people who had taken it.

The suspension was a message. She had received it. She was not going to behave as if she had not.

She kept riding.

Orim said, without inflection: "The shortcut junction is in approximately three hours. We should stop before it and eat something. Cold will affect judgment at the village if the third House happens to be active."

"Will they be active?"

"I have no reason to think so." He watched the road. "But cold affects judgment regardless."

She acknowledged this and rode on. The pass opened before them into broader alpine terrain, the road running north between the last of the compressed ridgelines, the sky above it colorless and close, the mountains on both sides not threatening and not welcoming, simply there, the way mountains are simply there — older than the institutions that had built checkpoints in their gaps and filed documents about what was permitted to pass through them, indifferent in the way only large geological things are indifferent, which was completely and without effort.

The Relic was ahead of her. The road was ahead of her. Whatever the Canon Immaculate had done with the machinery of his office, and whatever the Pallor Templar had done with the machinery of her House's six-generation grievance, and whatever the relationship was between those two things — that was ahead of her as well.

She did not know what she would find when she reached it.

She rode east.

[Beat 27]
THE MILL — SPHERE 31

The third stair from the bottom had a loose tread, and he stepped over it without thinking.

Left foot to the second, right foot skipping the third to land on the fourth — the body had absorbed this the way it absorbed all the small corrections of the boarding house: the door handle that required pressure in before it would turn, the window catch that left the room cold by morning if he forgot it, the exact width of the side passage that meant he could move through it in the dark without touching either wall. His feet knew the stairs. His hands knew the window. He was on the first shift and the rest of the house was still asleep and he kept himself quiet without deciding to.

Out through the side passage. The coal shed on the right, its door hanging slightly open the way it always hung; the smell of it, coal and wet ash, brief and familiar. The ironmonger kept a terrier on a chain by the front step of the next building — a small alert dog, brown and white, that had never barked at Rowe in three years. He passed it. The dog looked at him from inside its own pool of early-morning attention. He nodded at it, which was the extent of the arrangement. The dog settled back. He turned left at the corner and the canal path opened in front of him.

He had twenty minutes to the mill. Twelve of those minutes ran along the water.

The canal path was the best part of the walk and had been the best part of the walk since he was old enough to use it alone, which was a long time ago. In autumn the barges moved less; the surface went still in the mornings, reflective, holding the gas-lamp light — district-maintained, yellow-white, spaced every forty meters — and giving it back at an angle that made the far bank look like something that had been drawn rather than built. Specific. Clear. Slightly outside itself, the way a familiar place gets when the light is doing something you haven't seen it do in a while.

He had been home from France for eight months. The canal was still, sometimes, a small surprise.

Not a shock. He had known it was here; he had kept it in the back of his mind in the specific way you keep things you mean to return to, which is a form of insurance against the possibility that you won't. He had returned. The canal was exactly as he had left it. But eight months was apparently not enough time for the occasional double-take to stop — the moment when it arrived in his awareness as real rather than recalled, the slight clocking of it, a beat that hadn't existed before he went and was still there now that he was back. He didn't make anything of it. He walked.

At four in the morning the light over the district was no light at all. The autumn dark had a different quality from summer dark; it had settled, committed, settled in for the duration in a way that summer dark never quite managed. The eastern sky over the mill showed nothing. His breath made small clouds. The cold had reached the point in the season where it wasn't a surprise anymore — it was the ground condition, established, and breathing it carelessly meant it lived in the chest for the first hundred meters. He had learned to breathe carefully. He wore his good wool coat, the one his sister had given him the previous Christmas with the observation that he was wearing the other one to death, which he had been.

The canvas work coat had a hole in the left elbow that he had been meaning to address for five months.

He was a compact man who walked like he worked: not quickly, but without pause. He had the particular build of seven years at the loom, which produced a specific distribution of strength — the shoulders and forearms carrying the weight of a day's repetitive pull, the back following suit. Before France he had taken this for granted, the body's ordinary condition. He did not take it for granted now. He was aware of it daily, the specific fact of his hands working, the specific fact of his body operating inside the expected range. He did not think of this as unusual. He had simply become a man who noticed it, in the small itemizing way you notice things you were afraid to lose.

The wind was from the west, which meant the dye-works smell wasn't here. On east-wind mornings the chemical sweetness — not unpleasant exactly, more of a presence, something between bleach and warm cloth — arrived before the coal smoke and preceded him all the way to the mill entrance. This morning he smelled wet stone and coal and the cold itself, which had a smell at this point in autumn that he'd never had a word for but could recognize immediately: the smell of air that had decided. The canal turned it metallic where the water was near.

Further on, the canal path crossed beneath the dray bridge. Early mornings the drayman brought his horse and cart up from the stables at the canal yard, and the horse knew the route as well as Rowe knew his route, and the sound of iron shoes on the bridge's stone — four beats, then silence as the cart passed the apex, then four beats going down — was a thing he heard from fifty meters and recognized without looking. The drayman himself he knew by hat-brim and the specific set of his shoulders in cold weather. They had never spoken. Rowe raised a hand as he passed beneath the bridge. The drayman lifted his chin. This was sufficient.

The city was beginning to wake, not eagerly. A light in a bakery window two streets over, orange in the blue-dark. The smell of bread before you reached it and after you had passed it, the warm grain of it mixed with the coal smoke in a combination that was specific to this hour in this district and that he associated more completely with home than almost anything he could name. He had thought of it in France, occasionally. The smell of the early bakery and the cold canal and the ironmonger's quiet dog — not the canal's appearance, not the faces he knew, but this smell combination at this hour, which was the thing his body had held onto without asking his permission.

He walked the canal path, which was what he did on mornings, and the lamp-light lay on the water, and the water gave it back.

Somewhere over the mill district a pair of waterfowl were moving from one part of the canal to another, low and purposeful in the dark. He could hear them more than see them — the specific sound of wings that know where they're going. He watched the water where they'd been for a moment after they passed, the slight disturbance settling back into the lamp-reflection, and then he continued.

He had walked this path so many times the walk did not require him. It happened around him while he was somewhere else. He was aware of this and considered it one of the better arrangements of his daily life.

—

The boarding house put out tea in the common room between three and four for the mill workers. Strong tea, always hot, in a pot that the cook set on the hob before she went back to sleep and that Rowe and the two other men on the first shift had been using without ever coordinating among themselves because there was nothing to coordinate — the pot was there, you poured it, you drank it. One of the other two men was called Fenn. The other one Rowe had never asked. They nodded at each other most mornings. On rest days they did not nod because they did not see each other.

The bread came from the district bakery two streets over. The boarding house took the early delivery and put it out with the tea, sliced, with a small pot of butter that was always near-empty because whoever had the pot first used more than their share and nobody had ever said anything about this. Rowe had been arriving early enough for two years that he usually had the pot near-full, which he considered one of the material advantages of the first shift.

There was sometimes a hard-boiled egg. The cook's commitment to the egg question was variable and unpredictable in the specific way of things that depend on a single person's inclination rather than on any system. He had never seen a pattern. Some mornings there was an egg, some mornings there wasn't, and no prior evidence predicted either outcome. He had stopped trying to predict it. He ate what was available and was glad for the tea, which was always hot and always strong enough to move him from the state he was in at three forty — operational-but-not-awake, functional, the body present but the mind not yet committed to the day — into the state required to walk to the mill and work the machines for six hours.

This morning there was no egg. He ate the bread with a reasonable portion of butter and drank two cups, standing by the hob for warmth. Outside the common room window the street was empty and dark. Fenn arrived, poured his cup, stood at the other end of the hob, and they did not speak. The clock above the mantel showed twenty to four. In twenty minutes the shift clock at the mill would start its run.

He left the common room, sorted his coat situation in the passage — the wool coat on the hook, the canvas coat on, the wool coat back on over it, the brief frustration of the established error — and stepped out into the cold.

The terrier. The canal path. The twenty minutes.

—

He could hear the loom floor from the street.

That was the first thing about the mill, every morning — you heard it before you reached it, and your body made the small adjustments before you decided to make them. The first shift was arriving and the night shift was finishing and both complements on the floor together made the particular sound of a large thing at full run, sixty-two machines in total, their individual rhythms slightly different from each other but the sum of them more organized than chaos, the way things sound when they are working the way they were built to work. He had learned this sound over seven years until it was background. What he heard, within the background, were the deviations — the sound that meant a tension issue, the sound that meant a shuttle jam, the specific hesitation in the left-side shuttle return of his own machine that the maintenance team had addressed twice without resolving.

He listened for the hesitation from the street. It was there, consistent, the night shift having run it without incident.

The side entrance had a lamp above it, gas, with a reflector that caught the heat and threw it down at the doorway. In cold weather the workers stood in that column of heat for a few seconds before going inside, which was a small and entirely unconscious ritual he had observed for years. This morning he was the first from the first shift to arrive, which put him in the heat alone. He stood in it. The warmth came at his face and hands. He went inside.

The floor hit him with its heat before the sound of it resolved as separate from the outside sound. The wall between them was stone, which the machines had been warming over the course of the night, and stepping through the inner door was like stepping into a different season: the cold coat, the cold breath, all of that releasing as the floor's warmth arrived and the body responded without instruction, the shoulders coming down a fraction, the jaw unclenching from what he hadn't noticed it was doing. Then the smell: machine oil and thread and the warm particular smell of wool being worked at speed, which was like nothing else and which was the smell of his working life more completely than any single image. He changed coats. The wool coat went on the hook. The canvas coat went on, familiar, the sleeve worn thin at the left elbow where the hole had been meaning to be addressed.

His station was clean. The night crew had left it correct. He checked the thread, the tension on the shuttle arm, the left-side mechanism — the hesitation that lived in the machine, which he knew better than the maintenance team did because he had observed it continuously for three years at a range of zero meters. It was consistent, which was the best state for it to be in. A consistent small fault was manageable. An inconsistent small fault was the kind of thing that became a stoppage without warning.

Greiss was on the floor. He was always on the floor before the shift clock, which was fundamental rather than early — the man's relationship to the floor was more complete than his relationship to anywhere else, probably. He moved through it with the economy of deep familiarity: when to duck under the overhead mechanism, when to step sideways rather than forward, how to pass between operating machines in a way that disturbed nothing and nobody. He saw Rowe arrive and gave him the flat-palm sign — *in order, carry on* — and continued his pass down the row.

Hartner arrived beside Rowe at two minutes to the clock. Twenty-two years on the loom floor, and the calm that came with that — not contentment exactly, more like a relationship with the work so complete that the work had become background and his actual attention was free for whatever he wanted to do with it. He thought about his garden. Rowe knew this because Hartner had told him once, briefly, and had not mentioned it again since, and Rowe had understood this as the correct amount of information: one disclosure, sufficient, not requiring follow-up.

"Tension'll be high," Hartner said.

"I know."

"Settles by the second hour." He said this without looking up from his station check. He had said it before, in prior weeks, and had been correct before. He said it the way a person states a known fact in the presence of someone who also knows it, which was a form of conversation Rowe appreciated.

"Good run last night otherwise," Rowe said.

Hartner nodded. They went to the clock.

—

The work had a particular kind of attention at its center.

Not concentration — that was the wrong word. Concentration was what you applied to a problem that exceeded the skill, and this problem did not exceed him. He had been at this machine long enough that the work was not the challenge. The challenge was narrower than that, and more continuous: it was the attention of someone watching for the small deviation that announces itself before it becomes a stoppage, reading the machine, the thread, the material under the shuttle, the specific feel of the tension at each pass. His hands knew the mechanical operation. His attention was on the diagnostic layer above it.

He had learned this kind of narrowed attention before the mill, and it served him the same way here as it had served him then. He was aware of the transfer. He had no particular feeling about it. In France he had learned to narrow to the relevant and clear out the peripheral because the peripheral in France was full of things that would kill you if you attended to them too closely and that you would miss if you didn't attend to them at all, and the skill was the calibration. Here the peripheral was thread-dust and machinery noise and Hartner's presence at the adjacent machine, none of which required the same calibration. The skill still worked. He was grateful for that.

What he was less grateful for, and had been more aware of since coming back, was how easily the body reached for that narrowed state on small provocation. A sound outside the expected range. A movement at the edge of vision that resolved into nothing. His hands would still be running correctly, his attention still correctly on the shuttle and the thread, and the other part would have already noted the deviation and found it ordinary and filed it away, all of this in the time it took to complete a pass. He was aware of the mechanism. He could not stop it operating. He had decided not to find it troubling. It was how the body adapted to what it had been through, and the body was not wrong to have adapted.

There was something else he had brought back. The morning he walked into the mill for the first time, eight months ago, and put the canvas coat on and checked his station and felt his hands settle into the work — the specific moment when the hands committed, when the job became the job and the body had something it understood how to do — there had been a quality of relief in him that had nothing to do with decision. Not relief at the familiar, exactly. Relief at being occupied in a way that was the exact size of the task and no larger. His attention had something to attend to that was not himself. He had not known he needed this until it happened, and the gratitude for it had been out of proportion to the occasion. He had not told anyone. He had gone home that day and eaten supper and slept better than he had slept since arriving back in England.

He thought about this sometimes, when the work was running well and his hands were occupied and the floor was loud and everything was in its ordinary state. He thought about it briefly, without elaboration, and then he went back to the work, which was where he was supposed to be.

The floor was loud in the way of correct operation. He worked.

The material on this contract was heavier than the last — wool-cotton mixed, which ran stiffer under the shuttle and required a higher tension setting to maintain the count. This was what had been producing the elevated tension for the past week and what Hartner had predicted would settle by the second hour. By the second hour Rowe had confirmed the prediction: the stiffness eased as the material warmed from handling, the tension dropped to the expected range, and his shoulders — which had been carrying the extra load since the start of the shift — released the specific ache of overwork and settled into the comfortable ache of the right level of work, the kind that reported honestly and did not demand response.

Hartner's machine ran beside his. He had learned, over seven years, to hear the difference between Hartner's machine at the correct tension and Hartner's machine beginning to drift. Today it was correct. Down the row, the other fifty-eight machines were in their various states of correct. He knew most of them by their character: the one six stations down that ran slightly fast, the two at the far end that shared a mechanical quirk in the shuttle return, the one operated by a younger man called Crewe who was careful and good and would be better than good in another two years. He knew these machines the way you know what you live with. He could not have explained when he had learned them. He just had.

—

The break came at the midpoint: twelve minutes, officially a maintenance interval, practically a chance to stop moving and drink something.

He stood at the east window. The windows ran along the upper third of the outer wall, designed for light rather than view, and from his position he could see the sky and the upper edges of the buildings across the street and, if he leaned slightly, a narrow strip of the canal. He did not lean. He looked at the sky, which had changed since the walk in.

The cloud he'd predicted was arriving from the west — high, grey, the kind that moved quickly and arrived before you'd fully registered it was coming. The sun was still clear to the east, which meant the lateral light was still working on the floor. He watched the light through the window and thought about nothing, which was the skill he'd developed for breaks: to let the twelve minutes be empty rather than fill them, because he came back to the machine from emptiness differently than from planning.

His water tasted of the pipes, which was normal. He drank it.

Hartner stood beside him, also looking out the window. After a few minutes he said: "Garden wants rain."

Rowe looked at the cloud coming in from the west. "This afternoon," he said.

"Won't be any use," Hartner said, in the tone of a man who has observed that rain at the wrong moment is categorically worse than no rain. "Too late in the season."

Rowe considered this. He had not thought carefully about the needs of gardens in autumn. "Next year, then," he said.

Hartner appeared to find this adequate. They finished their water.

—

At the midpoint of the shift the sun came in from the east at the angle that caught the thread-dust.

He had noticed this his first autumn on the floor, years ago. The fine particulate that the machines raised constantly into the air — cotton and wool mixed, the contract material — was invisible in ordinary light, a presence you breathed without seeing, something you knew was there because of the specific quality of the air after a full-run shift, how the throat felt, how the day coat held the smell. In the lateral sun it became visible. A golden haze, chest-high across the floor, moving in the slow currents of the machines' exhalation. Thirty men working inside it, their hands and arms moving through it at the full pace of the shift, none of them attending to it because attending to it required stopping and stopping required a reason.

He had stopped for it once, the first autumn. Greiss had redirected him with the flat palm. He had never stopped again. But he saw it every year when the angle was right, and he saw it now.

It put him in mind of something, the way certain qualities of light did — a brief association, arrived before he could name it, and gone before he needed to. Stone-dust, not thread-dust. Cold, not warm. Early morning, not midmorning, and a different kind of light coming through a different kind of gap. The men moving through that other haze had not been attending to it for reasons he was not going to think about at his machine in the third hour of the shift. He noted this and returned to work.

Five seconds, at the most.

He was back at the machine, his hands on the work, his attention on the shuttle return and the thread count, the left-side mechanism running inside its expected variation. The floor was loud in the good way. The cloud was coming in from the west and would deliver rain by afternoon, and at noon he would put on his wool coat and walk home by the canal in the early stages of the rain — the canal path would be his, the drayman already back at the stables, the ironmonger's terrier under whatever shelter it had for wet days — and the elm above the bench would hold its leaves because it still had a week before it shed all at once, and the canal would be darker under the clouds but still the canal.

He would walk home at noon. The wool coat on, the canvas coat on the hook. Twenty minutes back the way he came — the canal darker under the rain-cloud, the elm holding its leaves, the ironmonger's dog under its shelter, the bakery smell replaced by the smell of noon traffic and whatever the boarding house was putting out for the midday meal. He would eat. He would sleep for two hours in the way he slept in the afternoons, which was a different quality of sleep from the night: shallow, alert at the edges, dreamless. He had slept this way in France and continued doing it at home because the body had not found a reason to stop. In the early evening he might walk. He had the rest day to plan, which required nothing more than knowing what the market had and whether the weather was going to be worth the walk to the canal's far bank, where there was a stretch of path that he liked in autumn and that his sister had once called a very modest ambition for a Sunday afternoon, which he had considered a fair assessment and had not disputed.

He knew this Thursday the way he knew all the Thursdays that had preceded it, which was completely, without drama, the knowledge of a life that was his and whose terms he understood. The morning shift. The canvas coat. Hartner at the adjacent machine, thinking about his garden. The bread from the early bakery and the tea that did its job. Greiss moving through the floor with the economy of a man who lived there. The slight hesitation in the left-side shuttle return that was never going to be fully repaired and that he had long since incorporated as a feature rather than a fault.

He was at his machine and the morning shift was half done.

The sun was at its lateral angle and the thread-dust moved in the light and down the row Hartner's machine ran with the specific rhythm of twenty-two years and across the floor Greiss moved between the machines and the new contract material was running at the correct tension and the left-side hesitation was inside its expected range and his shoulders had the honest ache of work being done and the tea had done its job and his hands knew what they were about.

Nothing was wrong.

The shuttle ran. The thread fed. His hands moved without instruction, and the floor ran on, and the morning was exactly what the morning was.

[Beat 28]
THE AUTHORIZATION

The canonical property recovery instrument arrived on her desk on a Tuesday, in the bottom third of the morning stack, filed by Canon Immaculate Tomasz Prelacze under the standard dispute-resolution authorization number and routed through the Scribe's office for copy and notarization in the ordinary course of business. It was the ninth authorization she had processed that morning. It was not the kind of document that required unusual attention.

Vega read it twice anyway.

---

The Scribe's office occupied the second floor of the east administrative wing — a stone room with two narrow, south-facing windows that admitted the morning sun in strips that crossed the floor and moved as the day did, predictable as the tide. The window embrasures were deep enough to sit in, which she had done once in her first year and not again, because the stone was cold and the angle wrong and the floor was better. The walls held shelves of canonical codebooks, each volume in its assigned position, each position known to her without looking. Seven hundred years of institutional sediment. The stone absorbed light and gave it back reluctantly.

Her desk was organized in the way that three years of the same work organizes a desk: everything in the position that minimized unnecessary motion. Blank instrument forms on the left. Incoming stack centered. Outgoing — completed and sealed — on the right. The canonical codebook open to the section she was currently working in, weighted at the relevant page by a smooth grey stone she had carried since her first posting. Not a talisman. She did not attach meaning to objects. It was the right weight and fit her grip and had never failed to hold a page flat in a draft.

The lamp was one she had replaced herself two days ago, because the maintenance rotation used a smaller wick than she preferred, and the smaller wick produced a light that made her eyes ache by midafternoon, and her eyes were going to be occupied through midafternoon and she could not afford the ache. She kept a stock of the correct wicks in the bottom drawer of the desk. She had asked twice, in her first year, for the rotation to be updated to reflect her preference. Both times the request had been received with great courtesy and no result. She had stopped asking. She kept the stock.

She had developed, in three years of becoming good at this, the thing that accompanied any sufficiently practiced skill past the threshold of requiring conscious management: the capacity to do it without thinking, which freed her attention for the adjacent thing. The adjacent thing was the text.

This was, she understood, not part of the Scribe's official function. The official function was accurate copying and notarization. The text was not her concern.

She had stopped believing this approximately eight months ago.

---

The canonical property recovery instrument for the Oculus Memoriae read as follows:

*By authority of the Canon Immaculate, exercising plenary jurisdiction in matters of Relic provenance and custodial accountability under the Liturgy's founding compact with the House of Ocipheus:*

*Whereas the Oculus Memoriae (Registered Relic, Ocipheus Station, Year 397, Inventory Reference O-001) has been held under a vigil custodian arrangement requiring renewal of custodial certification every fifty years, and*

*Whereas the certification dated Year 1097 (Keeper Fen Aldric, countersigned Canon Marta Veyne, Canonical Registry Reference CV-1097-88) was rendered without active confirming authority upon the death of Canon Marta Veyne in Year 1119, and*

*Whereas the Canon Immaculate, appointed Year 1134, has identified the absence of continuous countersigning authority as a material lapse in the custodial certification chain under provisions governing uninterrupted Relic accountability:*

*Therefore, let this instrument authorize the Canon Immaculate to initiate review of the Oculus Memoriae's current custodial status and, if review finds the certification lapse material to uninterrupted accountability, to take such steps as canonical law provides for the resolution of custodial disputes in Relic provenance.*

*Seal of the Canon Immaculate. This eighteenth day, Month of the High Autumn, Year 1138.*

Vega read it twice.

The Year 1097 certification had been properly executed by Keeper Fen Aldric and countersigned by Canon Marta Veyne and filed in the canonical registry in Year 1097. Canon Marta Veyne had died in Year 1119, nineteen years after the certification. A certifying authority who died after executing a document did not therefore unsign it. The certification was valid from the date of execution. It remained valid. The provisions governing uninterrupted Relic accountability applied to the currency of the certification cycle — whether a new certification was due — not to the continued living availability of whoever had countersigned forty-one years prior.

The next certification was due in Year 1147. Nine years hence.

There was no lapse. What Prelacze's instrument described as a gap was the ordinary period between certifications — the period in which, per the founding compact, no certification was required. The argument required reading continuous countersigning authority as a condition of validity rather than as a requirement at certification time only, which was not what the provisions said. It was a reading the provisions could survive. A careful reading with adequate context could not.

She had been copying the custodial accountability provisions for three years. She knew the relevant section the way you know a road you have walked in every weather: by its specific texture underfoot, not by consulting a map each time. She knew what the provisions said. She knew what this instrument was doing to them.

She did not note this on the instrument. Her function was accurate copying and notarization. She copied the instrument correctly in the precise canonical hand she had spent three years developing, affixed her notary seal in the correct position, and set it in the outgoing stack.

She picked up the next instrument.

---

The transit suspension for T-044 arrived in the afternoon, in the middle of a batch authorization covering operational adjustments to field personnel deployment across the High Autumn period. Eleven pages. She processed batch authorizations in this format frequently enough that she read them with the particular efficiency of a familiar task: moving through the sections at pace, assessing each clause for copy accuracy, not pausing unless something required pausing.

She paused on page eight.

T-designations were Templar field designations. A T-prefix followed by a posting-station identifier followed by a sequential number — the system was simple, which was its value. You could process a deployment record, assess a field authority question, revoke or reinstate a mandate, all without the Knight's given name appearing in the authorization chain until the revision was fully processed and the affected party formally notified. The designation carried all the operational information required. The name was adjacent to it. Her function did not require her to find the name.

T-044. Templar designation. Posting-station identifier consistent with Ocipheus. Three infusions. Field authority suspended pending canonical review of relevant certification.

The review cited was the same review. She recognized the authorization number — she had copied the originating instrument this morning. The property recovery instrument and the transit suspension were facets of the same operation, filed through different authorization tracks to prevent the operational connection from being visible to anyone reading either document in isolation. Someone reading the morning instrument would not, without the afternoon batch, see the suspension. Someone reading the afternoon batch without the morning instrument would see only a routine field authority modification.

She had been doing this for three years. She understood what documents looked like when they were designed to be read separately.

She copied the transit suspension accurately. She affixed her notary seal. She added the batch to the outgoing stack.

She did not know whose designation T-044 was. Cross-referencing a field designation against the Knight's personal record required access to the Templar deployment registry, which sat in the canonical personnel archive rather than the Scribe's reference section. She had not requested access. Her function did not require it.

She picked up the next authorization.

---

At midday, before the afternoon batch arrived, the activity in the courtyard below her window had stopped being routine.

She had been looking down at the courtyard for three years from this window. She knew the ordinary: the maintenance crew's wheelbarrow against the east wall on its scheduled days, the filing clerks taking air during the midmorning break, the Descent Corps courier who came through at the same hour every week and who had mastered, over years of the same route, the exact path through the courtyard that avoided the gate that required a key. She knew the pace and population of the courtyard through every season. In three years she had not seen it set up for a Great Scrying.

The primary apparatus frame was four meters across. She knew the scale of the portable certification units — she had seen those used for vigil-tests, for maintenance activations, for the routine assessment work the Station's smaller installations required. This frame was not those. The Catalyst mineral housing was a different material, denser, darker — the color of deep charcoal rather than the grey-brown of standard frames — and the anchoring crew was driving pinning rods into the flagstone joints of the courtyard with the systematic attention of people who expected significant membrane pressure. You did not anchor that carefully for a demonstration.

Two apparatus crews, eight people total, moving through setup with no ceremony and considerable efficiency. A Descent Corps evaluator she did not recognize, standing to the east side with a clipboard and notation kit. He was not from the regular administrative complement. His kit was not the standard issue — it was a field notation kit, built for use without a stable surface, the kind carried in a pack rather than kept on a desk.

Three Descent Corps soldiers in full field dress, not station secondment. Two of them were holding a transport guide-frame — an iron bracket assembly she recognized from the warehouse transit records she filed occasionally, used for moving large constructs through spaces not designed for them. The guide-frame was pre-positioned. They had known what they were going to need.

She watched from the window, which was the correct thing to do when the courtyard was showing her something that was part of the Station's official activity and which she would need to register accurately when the summary came through. She was observant by training and inclination. She watched.

The apparatus activated.

The air at the frame's center became different in the way she had learned to recognize over three years of watching vigil-test activations from this window. Not a light change, not a sound she could name. Something more fundamental: the quality of the courtyard air at the frame's center losing the characteristic of ordinary courtyard air and becoming instead a surface, membranous, the way a pool's surface is a surface — the difference between the medium above and the medium below visible from the right angle as a distinct plane rather than a continuous space. The membrane's aperture. She had seen it perhaps fifty times. It was never the same twice in small ways, and it was always the same in the essential way: the moment it opened, you knew.

The light that came through was not the same light as the courtyard. This was the quality she found hardest to describe in formal language — the observation reports she processed described it variously as spectral variation, extra-standard illumination, or non-native light source characteristics. What she saw was simpler than any of those: a light that came from somewhere else's morning or afternoon or season, light that had traveled through a membrane from a sun that was not theirs and arrived in this courtyard slightly wrong. The aperture was open for perhaps thirty seconds.

She did not see the construct clearly. The aperture was ground-level and the thing that came through arrived below her angle of sight. She saw the evaluator write something without looking up. She saw the two soldiers with the guide-frame step back and then reposition to the left, which told her the thing was larger than they had been holding the frame for, or had come through offset from the expected position. She saw the third Corps soldier move in a specific direction quickly and then stop, which was the movement of someone who had been given a clear instruction and received new information simultaneously.

Something cold moved through her chest. Not the cold of fear — she was not afraid, she was watching from a window — but the cold of the aperture itself, which was not in the room but which she could feel anyway, the membrane's biology registering in her body the way a change in pressure registers before you understand it as weather. She had felt this occasionally near vigil-test activations. She had never felt it this strongly from a second-floor window.

The thing was being moved through the courtyard toward the south service gate. She could track it now, partially: a shadow crossing the courtyard stone at an angle and scale that did not match any of the standard equipment she had ever seen moved through that space. The guide-frame soldiers had released the bracket assembly and were walking alongside it, hands not touching it now, the posture of people escorting rather than controlling. The evaluator was writing continuously.

The construct moved through the service gate and was gone.

The apparatus crew began the close sequence. She watched the membrane aperture seal — the process reversed, the wrong light replaced by the correct light, the surface plane of the aperture relaxing back into ordinary air. The Catalyst housing on the frame was visibly lighter in color now. The preparation had discharged.

She noted, before she stepped back from the window, where they had taken it. The south service gate accessed the maintenance passage that led to three storage halls on the south side of the administrative complex. Two of those halls were in regular use — she had filed their rotation records. The third had been locked for eleven years.

She had filed the lock authorization in her first year, under the previous senior Scribe's direction: a routine maintenance lock for a facility undergoing structural assessment. The structural assessment had concluded in Year 1133, per the notation on the resolution filing she had processed as a junior apprentice. The hall had not been re-opened.

She went back to her desk.

---

The assessment summary arrived an hour later, standard routing from the Descent Corps evaluator to the Scribe's office for canonical registration as an official Station activity record.

The heading read: *War Construct Evaluation — Sphere 42 Origin — Designation: WC-Eirene (provisional).*

She copied it accurately.

The summary described a construct of substantial physical dimensions — she copied the specific measurements — evaluated under the standard Descent Corps assessment rubric for load capacity, command responsiveness, and field deployment suitability. The evaluator's finding: *suitable for forward staging, pending secondary structural assessment under expanded-force parameters.*

She noted the word *provisional*. War constructs received permanent designations once confirmed for operational deployment — she had filed the full designation instruments for six constructs in three years. Provisional meant the designation was held pending secondary assessment. It also meant the question of quantity was not yet resolved.

WC-Eirene. One entry among many.

She filed it in the outgoing stack.

---

She had been writing *no action indicated* into canonical summaries for three years.

The phrase appeared at the conclusion of review proceedings that had reached a finding — had been considered, assessed, formally evaluated — and had been determined to require no current operational response. It was the correct notation for certain findings. It was also the notation that appeared at the bottom of the Sinter zone's annual perimeter survey, the Wall rotation's quarterly sector report, the vigil monitoring summaries from the eastern installations, and the biological observation assessments from the outer zone observer corps. It appeared, in one form or another, in a portion of everything that crossed her desk from the northern stations.

In three years she had written it approximately nine hundred times. She had developed the specific muscle memory for it — the way you develop muscle memory for any formation of letters you write with sufficient frequency. The pen made the words before she decided to.

She had thought, occasionally, about what the phrase was doing. Not the specific documents — she understood what each document was describing. She had thought about the phrase itself: its function as a canonical notation, the formal weight it carried, what it meant as a conclusion rather than a deferral. *No action indicated* was not the same as *no action available* or *no action possible* or *no action warranted*. It was the notation for something that had been observed, assessed, and returned to file with the finding that the institution did not need to respond to it at this time.

She had thought about what *at this time* was doing in that meaning. She had continued copying.

---

In the afternoon, between the transit suspension batch and the assessment summary, she had carried the morning's outgoing stack to the distribution window in the administrative corridor and handed it to the clerk with the appropriate flagging.

"The property recovery instrument needs a cross-reference notation to the batch authorization from this afternoon's intake," she said. "Same canonical review number. They're the same operation filed separately."

He looked at her for a moment before he wrote it down. Not, she thought, because he doubted her — he had been doing this as long as she had and he knew what he was looking at. He wrote it down because cross-referencing two separate filings in the distribution record was outside the standard intake notation and he wanted to be precise about it.

"Do you want me to flag that to the Canon's filing office?"

"It's informational. The operation will resolve under whichever instrument reaches completion first."

He noted this. She went back upstairs.

---

The amber of late High Autumn light came through the south-facing windows at the angle of five o'clock and lit the papers on her desk sideways, showing her the vellum's texture — the small variations in the surface you could see in the right light but mostly felt with your fingers, the characteristic grain of a high-quality canonical instrument prepared with the proper compound. She had looked at that texture for three years.

The property recovery instrument was in the outgoing stack. The transit suspension was in the outgoing stack. The war construct evaluation was in the outgoing stack.

She picked up her pen and held it without writing.

The custodial certification gap for the Oculus Memoriae did not exist under the provisions the instrument cited. The transit suspension for T-044 covered the same operational period as the property review. The war construct designation was provisional and had been moved to a hall that had been locked for eleven years and was now open.

Eirene. The eastern Wall checkpoint bore that name. It was also the name of the last Sinter champion — the Pallor Knight who had held the eastern pass during the Year 830 emergence, whose account of what she had observed in the zone had been submitted to the canonical record and processed, per the archival reference she had encountered twice in three years, as a standing observation without current response requirements. She did not know the account's full content. It was not in the general archive.

She knew its filing status. She had seen the notation.

*No action indicated.*

She set her pen down.

The constructs Eirene designated were war constructs: a specific classification within the broader construct registry, distinct from the courier constructs and Heloth labor units she saw on the roads, designed for a different purpose under a different operational mandate. She did not process war construct deployment filings frequently. She processed them often enough to know the assessment rubric was not the same as the labor-construct rubric, and that *suitable for forward staging* under the Descent Corps evaluation format meant something the labor-construct equivalent did not: it meant the construct had been assessed specifically for deployment into contested or hazardous conditions, and had been found suitable to survive them.

The hall in the south complex held one, currently.

The designation was provisional. The secondary structural assessment was pending. The quantity was not yet final.

She thought about the way the Corps soldiers had adjusted when the thing came through the aperture — the quick repositioning, the hands-off escort posture — and she thought about how large the shadow had been crossing the courtyard stone, and she thought about *expanded-force parameters* as a phrase in an assessment summary and what the summary would look like if the secondary assessment resolved the way the first one had.

She looked at the outgoing stack. Three documents. One operation.

It was not her function.

---

The note had been on the scribing table at the Station when she left — the portable table she used when on contract there, in the administrative building's copy room, two hundred kilometers north. She had not taken the note when she packed her kit and settled with the Station's clerk and walked out to the courier on the morning of the third day. She was not the kind of person who kept notes. She kept the memory without the paper.

Lyra's handwriting was the handwriting of someone who had spent thirty years taking field notes in small spaces with inadequate light: dense, lateral, the letters compressed in the specific way of a mind accustomed to recording more than the medium easily held. Not a considered hand. A fast one. The pen had barely lifted between strokes.

*Back in three days. Don't eat the station bread.*

The bread at the Station had been underproofed approximately two-thirds of the time for as long as she had been making the contract visit, which was three years. Lyra had registered this formally with the Station kitchen twice, in the measured tone of someone who felt the record should reflect the problem even when the problem would not be addressed. She had eaten the bread anyway. You ate what was available.

It was the fourth day.

This was within normal range for a Descent observation at the eastern sector. The deployment was one night, perhaps two. Lyra had been back from field postings in twenty-four hours before. Four days was within normal range for extended observation. Six days would begin to fall outside it. Six days had not yet happened.

T-044. Posting-station identifier consistent with Ocipheus. Three infusions. Field authority suspended pending canonical review.

She thought about the identifier. The T-044 designation was assigned at the station of the Knight's primary posting. Ocipheus Station was a small installation. The sequential number was forty-four — not a large count. The designation series would have accumulated over years of Templar postings and reassignments, and the current holder of forty-four could not be assumed from the number alone, because designations were reassigned when a Knight left a posting and reissued to the next Templar assigned there. But the active field authority for T-044 had been issued under the current Keeper and was on the suspension instrument with a current operational date.

Whoever T-044 was, they had been at Ocipheus Station recently enough for the suspension to be operationally relevant.

She did not cross-reference field designations against personal records. She was not going to.

She thought about why an operation that required a property review authorization for the Oculus Memoriae would also require ensuring that the Knight responsible for that archive could not be in the field while the review was conducted.

She thought about the answer without writing it down.

---

She ate in the common room at the table she usually sat at and said the things that were said in common rooms — the coming cold, the allocation schedule for the High Autumn provision cycle, the question of whether the third floor's east corridor heating element was going to be repaired before the first frost or, as had happened the previous two winters, afterward. She listened and added observations where she had them and ate the bread, which was dense and a little sour and not what she would have chosen.

She went to her quarters. She lay on her bed with her hands folded on her chest and looked at the ceiling in the dark, which was what she did when she was processing something without a category.

She had good categories. She had developed them over three years of careful, attentive work in an institution that had been generating canonical instruments since before the Houses had their current names, and the categories were sound and had covered everything she had been required to categorize. The problem was not the categories. The problem was that what she had been processing for eight months, and what had arrived this morning and afternoon in specifically illuminating form, did not belong in the categories that existed.

It belonged in a different kind of record. The kind that did not begin with *By authority of the Canon Immaculate* and end with a notary seal. The kind that began with what she had actually seen and what it had actually meant and what she understood when she considered the morning's three documents together rather than separately.

She did not know whose designation T-044 was.

She lay in the dark and thought about the war construct moving through the courtyard in that particular quality of motion — not an animal's navigation, not a person's, but the movement of something built to receive a direction and hold it precisely and not stop unless directed to stop — and she thought about *forward staging* as a phrase in a finding, and she thought about the hall in the south complex that had been locked for eleven years and was locked no longer, and she thought about how the summary she had filed this afternoon had used the word *pending* in its finding rather than the word *concluded*, which meant the question of what came next was not answered yet.

Provisional.

She had filed six permanent war construct designation instruments in three years. The permanent designation was the end of the assessment process. Provisional was not the end. Provisional was what happened before the end.

WC-Eirene. One entry.

She thought about the plural of one entry and what the assessment schedule would look like if the Hall was going to be used for what the summary suggested it would be used for, and she thought about all the authorization she would need to copy to make that happen, and she thought about the property recovery instrument and the transit suspension and the way the three documents had arrived on the same day in the ordinary course of business, filed separately.

She went to sleep, badly, and in the morning she got up and went to work.

[Beat 29]
EAST OF THE WALL — THREE DAYS

The moor-hounds were up first, which Wren had learned to expect.

Three days out from the Wall and the squad had settled into the specific rhythm that comes when the hard decisions have already been made and what remains is execution against landscape. Behind them: the alpine passes, the checkpoint, the stamp in Esvane's canonical transit documents and the duty officer who had looked at a Pallor Lector's papers for perhaps four seconds before waving them through without comment. Ahead: eastern Vierna's lowland country opening out flat and agricultural, the fields stripped and turned for the season, stone boundary walls running to grey horizons and then diverging as if the farmers who'd built them had disagreed about something fundamental in the first generation and their descendants had simply continued the argument in stone.

Fog sat in the hollows. It sat everywhere that had a lower elevation than the road and was not moving. The smell of turned earth and drainage water and the deepvine growing along the channel edges — purple-black leaves catching what morning light there was, the stems showing blue-tinted where the light came at them at the right angle, bioluminescent in a way that was barely visible in daylight and present but not dramatic by dark. Wren had been looking at it for three days and still found the color slightly wrong in the way that all the membrane-origin flora of the Cauld was slightly wrong — not unnatural, exactly, but not what the land would have grown on its own, given the choice.

The moor-hounds moved in their particular way. Six legs in an alternating stride that was nothing like anything native to this road: low to the ground, long-necked, bodies staying level even when the field-road junctions threw the surface into ruts. The oldest one, carrying a ridge of scar tissue along its left shoulder, set the pace with the unhurried certainty of a creature that had been not-native to a great many places and had stopped finding it interesting. The youngest ranged off the road's edge when something in the turned earth attracted it and came back when it didn't. The split-ear one walked between the travelers, occasionally glancing back at Wren as if confirming he was still present, which he was, and had been, and intended to continue to be.

Esvane Mirren walked at the front behind the hounds, the carry-case against her hip, the strap crossing from her right shoulder to her left hip. She was fifty and walked like it — not slowly, but with the specific economy of someone who had been making long roads since before Wren was born and had no fuel to waste on excess motion.
