Her cloak had been repaired in three places and showed the repairs without apology. Her grey-and-dark hair was pinned back with the efficiency of a decision made long ago and not revisited. She had not looked at the carry-case since she'd put it on that morning. This did not mean she was not aware of it. The oldest moor-hound ranged in a loose pattern around her, not guarding exactly but oriented, and had been doing so since Ocipheus.

Petra Dahl walked beside her. Not behind — beside, in the way water runs alongside a canal wall, with a continuous low-level assessment of the wall's condition. She was forty-four and had the walk of someone who had spent fifteen years finding routes that other people had concluded didn't exist, and her body had learned to treat every road as provisional. She had done something with her boots that had resulted in an ongoing disagreement with the road's mud, and Wren had been watching the mud side of this disagreement winning for three days and had said nothing about it, because it was Petra's fault and Petra knew it and didn't need the annotation.

"We should have turned south at the junction," Petra said.

"We'd have hit the garrison road," Esvane said.

"Three hours ahead."

"Two more military checkpoints. A Myrmidon intake station between the junction and the Bressant approach."

"Our papers passed the Wall."

"The Wall is one checkpoint." Esvane's voice held no particular heat. It was precise in the way that a well-constructed canonical argument is precise — no surplus material, nothing to grab as a handle. "Two more checkpoints is two more occasions for a junior duty officer to notice that Pallor Lector transit documents don't match his expected traffic roster for the day and decide to ask a follow-up question."

"Most wouldn't."

"I'm not worried about most."

Petra walked in silence for a moment. The split-ear hound had moved into the field margin and was tracking something in the turned earth, its nose following a line that meant something to it. The oldest one watched it without moving.

"I'm not wrong," Petra said.

"You're not wrong about the hours," Esvane said. "I'm right about the checkpoints."

Wren walked at the back of the column and kept his count of the things he'd noticed and chosen not to say. It was a running count, three days old, and it had not stopped growing.

He'd grown up hearing Owain talk about this road. The retrieval route. The Vierna approaches. The care required. Owain had been planning this for thirty years, refining it, telling it to anyone who would listen in the specific way that a man tells a thing he's been thinking about alone for a long time and has finally been given permission to say aloud. Wren had been a captive audience for most of his life. The road looked like a road. The fog was the fog. The deepvine grew in channels and did not care about the cargo they were carrying.

The road-village came at midday: stone and timber around a central well, a Vierna military post with a flag that hung without commitment, two women at the well watching the moor-hounds pass. The post had a duty soldier outside it with a bolt-action rifle on his shoulder and the particular expression of someone who had been watching this specific road for several months and had formed an opinion about it. He stepped forward when the squad reached him.

Esvane already had the canonical transit document out.

He took it, read the relevant sections, looked at the moor-hounds. The oldest hound looked back at him with the patient assessment of a working animal that had been worked a long time and had no opinion to offer about military posts.

"Pallor Lector authority," Esvane said, in the formal register she used for institutional exchanges — unhurried, with the practiced ease of a woman who had been producing correct paperwork for other people's benefit for twenty-three years. "Canonical property transit, three-four-nine-B. We're registered for the Bressant approach."

He handed the document back. He looked at the hounds once more and then at the horizon behind them, the Wall country invisible in the distance, the fog between.

"Continue," he said.

They continued. The road ran under a silverthorn arch at the village's eastern edge — the hedge's silver-filament leaves reading the sound of their passage and turning it into something that sat between music and the weather, fading behind them as the road opened again into open field. One of the women at the well said something to the other. Wren didn't catch it.

---

Late in the afternoon they crossed a Vierna supply column moving west on the main road: twelve wagons loaded with dressed stone, military escort of eight soldiers with rifles, and in the wagons, working the load-ropes and the chains, men who were not from any Cauld house Wren could name. Their faces were the faces of the Cauld — the same physical inheritance, the same coloring, the same features that the whole northwestern migration had laid down and left — but their clothes were wrong in a specific institutional way, and their movements had the quality of labor performed under a constraint that was not fatigue.

Esvane stepped to the road's verge and let the wagons go by. Petra stepped with her. Neither of them looked at the workers in the wagons. Wren looked, and then looked away, and then looked again because looking away was a choice too and he hadn't decided to make it.

One of the workers was young — possibly younger than him. He looked at Wren from the nearest wagon for one flat second and then looked at the stone he was managing, which was a thing he was responsible for and which did not look back.

The last wagon cleared the road junction. The dust settled. The escort soldiers were already past.

"How long has that road run?" Wren asked.

"Since before the Compact," Petra said, which was not an answer to the question he'd asked.

They moved on.

---

The stream was where Esvane had said it would be, east of the first junction, cutting through a stone-bottomed gulley at a field's edge. Cold water. The moor-hounds went in without waiting — the oldest dipping its long neck to drink, the split-ear crossing to the far bank and back on all six legs, coming out wet and moving immediately to press its soaked side against Wren's leg.

He stood still and let it happen and filled his water skin.

Petra filled the skins efficiently and recapped them and said nothing. The fog had been thickening as the afternoon progressed, softening the field edges and filling the drainage channels. The deepvine glowed bluer in the reduced light. The small things in the hedgerows made their abbreviated-question sounds.

"How far behind is she?" Wren asked.

Both of them looked at him. This happened when he spoke after long silences. He'd stopped taking it personally.

"Several days," Esvane said. "The soft crossing at Eirene's Gate requires Pallor Templar transit credentials or a Liturgy counter-brief. She has neither."

"She's been at the Ocipheus vigil for years. She'll know the approaches."

"Knowing and having credentials are different conditions."

Wren thought about the vigil Templar — the seconds of her in the archive before things moved too fast to take inventory. Tall. Field kit worn the way someone wears armor they've been inside for years, no longer performing it. Dissolution blade. The expression of someone who had arrived at a place she'd left under different circumstances and was accounting for what was different.

"She'll find a crossing," he said. "Whatever it costs her."

Neither of them answered that. The oldest moor-hound had lifted its head from the stream and was looking southeast, into the fog, at nothing visible. It held that for a moment before lowering its head again.

"Move," Esvane said.

---

The road-house east of Bressant was low and stone and had been something official before it became a place for travelers to sleep. The bones of something authoritative showed in the lintel's carved channel — letters worn smooth by weather into a suggestion of inscription, something that had once mattered announced to a road that no longer read that language. The sign above the door was a painted boot, rust-red, touched up at least twice and now a different shape from the original. The yard had paving stones that had settled unevenly over a generation of irregular maintenance, and a stable block with the smell of accumulated occupation, and a water trough with mud rings marking the week's various water levels.

The keeper came out when they entered the yard. He was a big man with the build of someone who had done physical work for decades and the knees to show for it, and he looked at the moor-hounds with an expression that moved through several stages before arriving at something workable.

Esvane handled the conversation in her formal Vierna: stable accommodation, separate pen if available, the hounds had grazed the road and didn't need feeding tonight. A Pallor canonical travel instrument produced before the keeper had finished articulating his request for a damage surety — not the document he'd asked for, but a document from a Pallor Lector with a House seal, which was an institution attesting to the legitimacy of the travelers, which was arguably more useful. He looked at it, understood what it was, handed it back.

He led them inside.

Their room was small and faced the yard. Two beds and a pallet, a table, a lamp burning rendered fat that produced sufficient light at the cost of a particular smell that would be familiar by midnight. The wooden shutter over the window had warped away from its seat and let a thread of cold air in at the gap. The floor was swept clean. Through the shutter gap Wren could see the stable block, and after a few minutes he could see the moor-hounds settling in the hay — the oldest finding its corner and turning once before going down, the split-ear positioning itself at the door-side, watching.

"I want the wall bed," Petra said.

"Take it," Esvane said.

"I'm not asking permission. I'm telling you which bed I'm taking."

"Then take it."

Wren set his pack against the wall and sat on the pallet.

---

They ate in the common room. Three Vierna road-soldiers occupied the other table — between postings from the quality of their ease, belonging temporarily to nobody. Their rifles were stacked in the proper fashion. They ate with the focused application of men who had been on their feet all day and did not need conversation to make the food better.

Petra had ordered for the table in the Vierna that asks no one's permission: grain porridge with rendered fat and dried herb, bread that had been correct some hours ago and was now being gracious about it, preserved vegetable sour in the way of intention rather than accident. The watered drink was a distant relation of wine.

"The bread," Petra said.

"It's the end of the day," Esvane said.

"It was the end of the day yesterday."

The keeper, within earshot, offered a small nod of the kind that means accurate. Esvane ate. Wren ate. One of the road-soldiers glanced at the carry-case that Esvane had set between her feet under the table — glanced, and glanced at the next thing. His face said nothing about either glance. Esvane didn't look at the case. She didn't look at the soldier. She ate her porridge with the efficiency of someone fueling a machine she needed functional tomorrow.

The common room smelled of the lamp and the food and old wood and the particular tobacco that Vierna soldiers carried, which was darker and stronger than what Wren knew from home. Outside, through the shuttered windows, the deepvine channels would be fully luminescent now — the blue-tint strong in the dark, running along the drainage lines through the turned fields, visible from the road as a faint network of cold light. He had watched it every night from the road-house yards they'd stopped in, and it was one of the things he'd looked at and not said anything about, because there was nothing to say about it that would be useful.

Petra argued with the second round of bread. Esvane confirmed the morning departure time. The road-soldiers finished and collected their rifles and went upstairs. The keeper moved through the room banking the secondary lamps.

Back in the room, Petra was asleep within ten minutes. The lamp settled into its second burning cycle. Cold came through the warped shutter and crossed the floor without reaching the table.

---

Esvane set the carry-case on the table.

She hadn't announced it. She'd come back from the brief exterior check she made every night — the yard, the moor-hounds, the road — and put the case on the table and stood looking at it for a moment, not hesitating but deciding something, and then sat down. She opened it with the two-point latch: simultaneous pressure at both contact points, the secondary seal releasing with a small click, the lid coming up.

The lens sat in the custom padding.

Palm-sized. The irregularity of its shape was the kind that belonged to the material — not an imprecision in making but a form that had arrived at itself. One edge slightly more distinct than the others. The face on that side different in surface quality from its reverse, a difference you could perceive without being able to say precisely what the difference was. In the lamplight the lens was amber and gold and carried a depth that resolved differently depending on the angle of attention, appearing both deeper and shallower than a palm-sized object had any reason to be.

It was lighter than it looked. Wren had known this from the archive. He had watched Esvane's hands when she'd first picked it up — the slight overreach as she compensated for expected weight, the recovery, the immediate and complete adjustment.

She picked it up now.

Held it in both hands and examined it — surface, edge treatment, the way the lamplight moved through the material and was altered by it in a way that good glass would not have altered it. She turned it: edge-on, then face-forward, then reversed. She was looking for damage, for the evidence of transit stress, for whatever a practitioner looks for in an object she is responsible for transporting and needs to confirm has survived three days. Her examination was professional and thorough. It lasted perhaps twenty seconds.

The aperture face — the edge more distinct, the face with the different surface quality — passed between her fingers twice during the examination. She did not orient it toward her eye either time. She did not hold it up to the lamp and look through it. She turned it and examined it and set it back in the padding and closed the case with the two-point latch.

"It's fine," she said. "No transit stress."

"Good," Wren said.

She looked at him with the look that meant she'd been aware of him watching and had let it be until he made acknowledgment necessary.

"You didn't look through it," he said.

"I examined it for transit integrity."

"I know. You could have looked through it during the examination. You specifically didn't."

She was quiet. Petra breathed with professional regularity against the wall. The lamp made its sound.

"I know what it accumulates," Esvane said. "I didn't need to see it to confirm transit integrity."

"What does it accumulate?"

She considered. He kept himself still and present the way Owain had always done when he needed to let a conversation run to its own conclusion — a stillness that was not pressure but wasn't nothing either.

"Get some sleep," she said.

"In a minute." He didn't move. "I've been watching you carry that case for three days and you haven't looked through it once. I'm not asking about before the archive. I'm asking about the object itself. What does it actually do? Not the family account. What does it do?"

The case was closed on the table between them. The lamp made a small sound. Wren watched Esvane decide whether she was going to answer.

"That's not our concern," she said. "It belongs to Pallor. We're returning it."

"But what does it do?" Wren said.

She looked at him. He was twenty-two and had been looked at by people who were older and knew more for all twenty-two years, and he had learned that being looked at was not the same as being dismissed and that the correct response was to remain present.

"It watches," Esvane said.

The word settled in the room.

"Watches what?" he asked.

Esvane stood.

She picked up the case and moved it to the corner of the room, away from the table, away from the lamp. She set it against the wall with the particular deliberateness of someone who has decided where a thing is going to be and intends it to be there.

Then she lay down on the remaining bed, pulled her cloak over herself, and turned to face the wall.

"Keep up," she said.

Nothing further.

The lamp made its fat-settling sound. Petra breathed. Outside, in the stable block, the oldest moor-hound made a low sound once, twice, and went quiet.

Wren sat at the table and looked at the corner.

The case was over there. The lens was in the case and had been in this room for three hours, watching the corner of a wall in a road-house east of Bressant — the gap between floor and wall where the mortar had pulled back with age, the spiderweb in the high angle of the ceiling gone grey from being in place too long, the warped shutter and the cold moving through it, and Wren at the table, watching back.

He thought about three days of road. The checkpoint and the duty officer's four-second review. The road-village and the silverthorn arch. The supply column and the young man in the nearest wagon who had looked at him for one flat second and then returned his attention to things that were his responsibility. The stream and the fog. Esvane holding the lens in her hands for twenty seconds and not once putting the aperture face to her eye.

She knew what it might be showing. She'd decided she didn't need to see it.

He had questions that weren't about the lens. He'd been carrying them for three months, since the evening he'd found the canonical transfer documentation from Year 972 in the Pallor property archive — the instrument from after the Battle of Nine Days at Caer Glas Moor, when the Pallor Champion fell and the post-battle canonical settlement had moved the Oculus Memoriae to Ocipheus custody. He'd read it carefully, more than once, and what it said was that both claims were real. Pallor's prior possession had been legitimate. The canonical settlement that transferred custody to Ocipheus had also been legitimate. The Year 972 instrument had resolved the contradiction through the mechanism that operates when two legitimate claims collide: choose one and call it done.

He hadn't told Owain this. He didn't know how to tell Owain this, because Owain had grown up with the claim as the family's ground — six generations of Caerglas certainty, thirty years of Owain's specific certainty — and Wren didn't know what certainty looked like after it broke and couldn't picture the conversation that would start the breaking.

He looked at the carry-case in the corner.

Somewhere on the road behind them, in the eastern passes or pushing through whatever Wall approach she'd found, the vigil Templar was moving. Three infusions. Field kit worn the right way. Whatever thirty years of absolute institutional loyalty had built in a person who had also spent thirty years observing the membrane's biology with a researcher's eye that did not stop noticing things even when noticing was inconvenient. She'd find a crossing. She'd spent enough time at the Ocipheus vigil to know every document that described every Vierna approach. Knowing the document and having the credential were different conditions, as Esvane had said, but the Templar was the kind of person who found a third condition when the first two were unavailable.

Several days was not the margin it sounded like.

And when she came, she would come with thirty years of the same certainty that Owain had, and Esvane had, and she would come believing that the lens belonged to her institution and her House and her thirty years of vigil service, and that belief would be as legitimate as the Pallor claim, as correctly grounded, as real in the dimension where it was right. And that was the thing he'd been carrying for three months and had no one to put down, because you couldn't put it down in front of Owain and you couldn't put it down in front of Esvane and you certainly couldn't put it down in front of Petra, who would call it a professional complication and not be wrong.

The lens was watching the corner of the room.

He thought: she examined it for twenty seconds and then moved it somewhere she didn't have to look at it. She knows what twenty seconds of this room it's already holding. She knows that the next time anyone looks through it, this room will be in there — the lamp, the warped shutter, the case on the table, the carry-case in the corner. Three days of road. Seven hundred and forty-one years before that.

He thought: keep up is not an answer.

He thought: she knows it's not an answer.

He got up from the table and lay down on the pallet and pulled his cloak over himself and looked at the ceiling.

A Vierna patrol passed on the road outside — he tracked them by sound, four soldiers, road-heavy boots, the creak of carried kit. They went past without slowing. The road-house settled back into quiet. In the stable block, the split-ear hound made a brief sound that might have been settling or might have been dreaming, and then stopped.

Wren set the question beside three months of unasked things and closed his eyes.

The lamp burned down to its final measure. The room went dark.

The carry-case sat in the corner and watched it happen.

[Beat 30]
THE TAKING

The left-side shuttle returns clean and Rowe does not register it as clean until it has happened three times in a row. On the fourth he lets himself believe it. The tension adjustment he made this morning — two turns of the secondary feed nut, which Greiss would mark as unauthorized modification but which Greiss was not watching and which the machine had needed since Tuesday — has held for two hours, which is two hours longer than any previous adjustment had held, and the floor under his boots is the floor it has always been, and the light off the high windows is the light he knows.

The thread-dust moves in the columns.

He does not look at it. He has been looking at it for nine years. The canal walk was cold this morning; the coat is on its hook. Hartner at the adjacent machine has been elsewhere in his head for the last hour — the specific quality of Hartner's stillness that means he is thinking about the garden. It is not the growing season. Rowe has never asked Hartner what he thinks about in the off-season because the question would require more words than they normally exchange and because the answer is probably not for him.

The shift is half-done. This particular fact is how he measures the morning: the halfway point, when his body has stopped protesting the early start and has accepted the work as the current condition of the world. Past the halfway point is downhill toward noon. He is past the halfway point by perhaps twenty minutes.

His hands know the shuttle. His hands know the moment before the hesitation and know — now, this morning, for the first time in the history of this particular machine under these particular hands — that the hesitation is not coming.

Then the floor stops being a floor.

This is the only way he will have for it, later, when he is trying to describe it in a language he does not yet know to people he has not yet met: *the floor stops being a floor.* No precursor. No sound that does not belong to the mill. The machine is in his hands and then the machine is not there and his hands are not certain where they are and the floor —

Not down.

Down is wrong. Down has moved. Down is simultaneously to his left and behind him and in a direction that does not have a name in any language he speaks, and his stomach knows this the way it knows falling, except he is not falling. He is not moving. He cannot find the direction in which he is not moving. His legs are attempting to compensate for a bearing they cannot locate and his arms are coming away from his sides automatically, the balance reflex, the body buying itself time while it searches for the information it needs to stand upright, and there is no information, and the reflex runs and finds nothing on the other end of it.

He does not have time to be frightened. His body takes the time.

The cold arrives before anything else. Not the cold of the canal walk, which was the cold of an autumn morning in a city on a latitude that knows what autumn is and submits to it properly. This cold has no business being inside his chest. It is inside his chest. It is inside his mouth and inside the air his lungs are trying to process and something is wrong with the processing — he can feel the wrong at the back of his throat, the particular absence of a thing he has always been breathing without knowing it was there. He takes a breath. His lungs do not understand what they receive. He takes another. His body is running a fast and frightened calculation about how much of this air to take in and the calculation has no right answer because the air is not right and his lungs have never had to determine why before.

The pressure is wrong.

He has a word for this. He has stood at the edge of the quarry on the north side of the city, where the cut drops thirty meters straight down into chalk-white rock, and felt the particular quality of that open air — the pressure-absence of a large empty space, a column of height that does not belong in a place where the ground is supposed to be. This is that. Except it is everywhere. He is inside it and there is no edge to walk back from and no near wall to put his hand on and no chalk face to look at and think *at least that is still there.* The pressure-absence is the room. He cannot find a surface from which to measure it.

Then stone. His knees hit stone. His palms hit stone. Cold and grained, the roughness of dressed stone that has been walked on for a very long time — neither smooth nor sharp, simply the surface of a thing that has had a great deal of use. The knees of his trousers will show this tomorrow. His palms register the cold uniformly, deeply, the cold of a space that has been this temperature for longer than any room he knows stays cold without a remedy.

He is on his hands and his knees on a stone floor that is not the loom floor and he is not in the mill.

His body does what it does next. He stays down until the heaving is finished. He counts the stones in front of him — four of them in his field of view, three cut regularly, one not, with a join between the third and fourth that has been mortared and re-mortared at some point — and by the time he has done this twice and gotten the same count both times the shaking has reduced to something he can manage.

He gets up.

His legs do not offer much help. He gets up anyway.

---

He is in a large stone room. Ceiling three meters, maybe a little more, vaulted simply — each arc the same modest curve, repeated, the logic of builders who knew what they were doing and did not embellish it. The walls are old work: he can read age in stone, having grown up with the old buildings at the edge of the canal, and this is older than those, the coursing slightly irregular in the way of stone that has settled over generations and been lived with rather than corrected. The joins are clean lime mortar, white-grey, and they are not the joins of anything built recently.

Lamps on the walls at intervals. They burn something that smells faintly oily — not machine oil, not the particular smell of the mills or the gas works, something else, something that produces a yellow-warm light and does not require a match to adjust and does not produce the small hiss of a gas line. He cannot identify it. He puts this aside.

Robed figures. Five of them visible from where he is standing. Dark wool, or something that functions as wool, practical cut with a hood pushed back — not ceremonial, not theatrical, the robes of people who need to be able to move in them without difficulty and have made that choice over any other consideration. They are distributed across the room with the distribution of people mid-task. Moving, or standing in the purposeful stillness of someone who is thinking rather than pausing.

One of them glances at him. The specific flat assessment of a floor supervisor checking that a machine has resumed operation. Then that one moves attention elsewhere, to a long table along the near wall.

He is not the urgent matter here. He is a thing that has arrived. They were expecting arrivals. He is one.

The stone in the vaulted ceiling above the south lamp is grey-white, the same shade as the limestone face on the quarry cut above the city, the color of that particular stone in flat morning light. He looks at it for a moment. Then he looks at the room.

Through a door at the far end of the room — open, no one in it — he can see the edge of a wide corridor and the partial outline of another room beyond. In that room: people. People sitting against walls. People standing in the specific posture of not knowing what to do with a body that has no instruction. One man has his hands pressed flat against his thighs, pushing down with his full weight, the way a man attempts to push the shaking out through the floor and into somewhere it cannot be seen. One woman has her back very straight and her eyes fixed on a middle distance that is not the wall she is looking at. A boy of perhaps sixteen is sitting in a corner with both arms wrapped around himself and his chin on his chest.

Rowe does not look at them long. He has been in a room like that. Not this room — not these walls, not this stone — but the arrangement is the same, the silence is the same kind, and he has had enough of that particular silence to last him. He looks at the robed figures instead.

They are completing a job. One of them carries a flat board — wood or something like it, rigid, with paper or what functions as paper lying flat across it, and a long instrument for writing held in the same hand. This one is moving across the room in a direction that will bring her to Rowe eventually. One of the others is at the long table managing something with equipment he cannot see clearly from here. Two more are in low conversation near the back wall with the unhurried tone of people reviewing something that has been reviewed before.

One of the two conversing has a face he can see in three-quarter profile: middle-aged, solid, square jaw, the kind of unremarkable face that does not call attention to itself. The kind of face you pass in a market three days running and retain only vaguely. The face is so thoroughly ordinary that it makes the wrongness of everything else sit harder, the way a familiar smell in an unfamiliar place is worse than an unfamiliar one. He had been expecting the faces to be wrong. They are not wrong. They are, in fact, about what the faces on a mill floor look like at the mid-shift mark.

He goes to the window.

---

The stone surround is half a meter deep — thick walls, old construction, the same logic as the quarry buildings or the canal lock keeper's station, built to resist the weather for a long time rather than to be comfortable. The glass in it is irregular, the quality of glass that distorts slightly at the edges, the kind he has seen in the old church at the road junction east of the canal, the windows that have been there since before any living person remembers. Through it: a courtyard. Stone walls three sides. A door in the far wall, wooden, iron-banded, standing open. Daylight, overcast, a milky morning light that is not electric and not gaslight and is just daylight except that the angle of it relative to the courtyard walls is wrong for the time of day. He has been reading the mill's window-light for nine years and knows what the angle means at any given hour. This angle says something he cannot account for.

Two people in the courtyard. One is carrying something — a crate, or a case — moving with purpose toward the far door. The other is standing at the door's edge and speaking to someone Rowe cannot see, his back half-turned, his posture the posture of someone delivering information that has already been delivered twice this morning and will be delivered again if necessary. The uniform he is wearing is not a uniform Rowe knows. Wrong cut, a grey-green color that does not belong to any service corps Rowe has encountered, though the bearing is perfectly legible: a man with somewhere to be who has been intercepted by someone with a question.

The man has a rifle slung over his shoulder, muzzle down.

Rowe looks at the rifle. Through the old glass he cannot see it sharply, but the shape is a bolt-action shape, and he knows bolt-action shapes well enough to know what he is looking at. It is not what he carried. The stock is cleaner, the bolt housing smoother, the magazine housing integrated in a way that suggests someone kept working on the problem after his world stopped working on it. The same thinking, pushed further down the road. The same design, several generations improved.

He looks at the rifle for perhaps three seconds. Then he stops looking at the rifle and goes back to the center of the room.

---

The board-woman comes to him.

She is not hurrying. She is the kind of person who has done this many times and is not intimidated by any version of this. She stops at a distance that is professional and she looks at him — his face, his hands, the state of his coat and his trousers — briefly, systematically, the inventory of a person making a quick determination.

Then she says something.

He hears the words with his full attention, which is more attention than he has given any sound in his life. He has been to France. He has been in training camps with men from Wales, from the north of Scotland, once a man from somewhere he was never able to identify, whose English had a particular flat quality unlike anything else. He has a handful of words of French, mostly about food and water and the direction toward somewhere that is not currently on fire. None of this is any help. None of what this woman is saying has any relation to any language he has ever heard or overheard or stood next to while other people spoke it. He cannot find the family. He cannot find the root. It sounds like a language built by people who made their choices about sounds a very long time ago on a different set of materials and have been building on those choices for so long that nothing underneath them connects to anything he knows.

She says it again. She slows down. He is already listening as carefully as he knows how.

She tries something shorter. A different phrase. She makes a brief motion with her free hand — palm open, a gesture of something being received or transferred, the same motion anyone makes in any language when they mean *give it over* or *take this* or *this is being offered.* Then she angles the board toward him.

He looks at the board.

Writing on it, organized into rows, each entry a cluster of marks in regular groups. The marks are consistent — the same hand throughout, careful and practiced, the writing of someone who has been doing this long enough that the instrument does what they want. He cannot read a single mark. He cannot find the bottom of the system. It is not simplified or pictographic; it is a fully developed script, internally consistent — he can feel the consistency the way you feel grammar even through a language you don't understand — and he has no edge on any of it.

He looks back up at her.

She is looking at him. Not impatiently. Not with particular concern. The specific look of a person who has a job and is doing it and this particular moment in the job requires standing here while a man fails to respond to a reasonable inquiry. She has done it enough times that his incomprehension is a data point, not a setback.

She says something short. She picks up the writing instrument and makes a mark on the board in the left margin of the current entry — two strokes, one short and one longer. She moves on.

He watches her stop three meters away at a young man he had not noticed. Twenty, maybe, or younger — his face is still wet with the shock of it, the particular brightness in the eyes of a person whose body is still several seconds behind the situation. She speaks to him. He also says nothing. She makes a mark on the board.

Rowe looks at the two marks. From where he is standing they appear to be the same mark.

He files this. There is a category he and the young man are both in. He cannot read the category's name. He can read that it has a name.

---

Two different robed figures come to him after a while. Not the board-woman. Two others, both indicating through gesture that he should follow them, and he follows, because the alternative to following people who are leading somewhere in a building he does not know is standing still in the center of the room until someone decides where to put him anyway, and he would rather be moving.

A short corridor. Stone floor, a lamp at the turn. Into a smaller room: low table, two lamps, a chair. He sits because they indicate he should and because his legs have been carrying him through the wrongness of the last hour on no reserves and are relieved to stop.

These two are interested in his body in a particular way. One takes his right hand and turns it — looks at his palm, the thick pads at the base of the fingers, the calluses on his thumb and the inside of his first two fingers, which are the calluses of nine years at a loom and before that three years of something else entirely, both of them legible if you know what you are reading. The figure runs a thumb along the callused ridge and says something quiet to the other. The other writes something on a smaller board.

They look at his face. One holds a small lamp close and tilts it — looking at his eyes, checking something, the way a man looks at an animal for signs of health or damage. Not unkind. Not personal. This is the look of people who are determining the condition of something that has arrived.

They look at his neck. The skin of his forearms, after his sleeves are gestured up. They do not touch him beyond the minimum the assessment requires, and nothing they do carries deliberate discomfort. It is the absence of deliberate harm, which is a different thing from care, and he makes the distinction carefully.

His breathing has evened out. The air still sits wrong but his lungs have stopped fighting it as hard. They are learning to make do.

He is about to look at his hands when he sees what is on the table.

It has been there since he sat down. He registered it peripherally and filed it as equipment, which it is, and did not look at it directly because there were people to read first. Now there are no more immediate people to read and he looks at it.

Metal housing, mostly. Forty centimeters long, perhaps a bit more. A grip at one end wrapped in cord — old cord, worn smooth from regular use, the cord of something that has been held many times by many different hands. Along the shaft: seven grooves cut at irregular intervals, each one a clean-edged notch, the kind of marking you make in a measuring instrument at the intervals that matter. He cannot work out the logic of the spacing. The intervals are not equal, not random, not any sequence he can find. At the other end, set into the metal housing: a dense dark material the size of a man's fist, roughly cylindrical, matte black in a way that does not reflect the lamp light the way metal reflects it. Not coal, not iron, not anything he has a name for. It sits in the housing the way a stone sits in a setting — not structural, not decorative, something that belongs to the object but is not the same class of thing as the object itself.

One of the figures picks it up by the grip.

The figure holds it two-handed, the dark-tipped end facing toward the corner of the room rather than at Rowe, and closes their eyes. Rowe watches the figure's face.

What he sees is effort. Not the effort of a physical thing — it is not in the hands or the arms, the grip is relaxed, the posture has not changed. The effort is behind the face. The particular tightening at the corners of the eyes that he recognizes as the face of someone searching for something at the edge of their reach: a name, a route in the dark, the exact words of a sentence that has moved just far enough away to be uncertain. He has seen this face on men trying to remember a road junction in the rain. He has made this face himself.

Nothing happens, that he can see. Or something happens that he has no way to observe.

The figure opens their eyes and makes a brief gesture — small, precise, the gesture of someone filing something as confirmed rather than as completed — and puts the instrument down on the table.

The other writes.

The first figure looks at Rowe. The look carries a specific quality that is the opposite of disappointment. It is the look of someone who expected to find what they found and has found it, and will now proceed accordingly. Not warm. Not unkind. The comfortable professionalism of a job that has gone as anticipated.

Rowe looks back at him for a moment, and then looks at the instrument on the table, and then looks at the wall behind the table. There is nothing on the wall behind the table. He looks at it anyway because he is working out how to say something in a language he does not speak, which is to say he is working out that there is nothing to say.

Whatever they determined, it is now on the board. He is where the board says he is.

---

They take him to the room with the others.

It is larger than the intake space — longer, east-west, with more lamps and two north-facing windows with the same deep irregular glass. Against the east wall: straw pallets, twenty or more, most of them rolled and stacked. Eight unrolled. Six of those occupied.

Twenty-five people that he can count without making it obvious. The range of ages is broad. A woman who might be fifty, compact, sitting cross-legged against the far wall with the practiced stillness of someone who knows how to be in their body while they wait. A man of perhaps sixty with the hands of someone who has been doing heavy work since before Rowe was born — the knuckle topography of it, the specific configuration of callus and thickening that comes from decades. A boy trying to read older than he is, doing a reasonable job at it until you looked at his eyes. Several who look like ordinary working people, various ages, the general category of person who has been at something physical long enough that it shows.

Nobody is looking at the door.

He goes to the east wall and finds a space between two people who are not looking at him and sits. The stone is cold through his trousers. He pulls his coat up around his shoulders. His coat is still buttoned from the walk he took this morning, the canal walk, the cold morning, and he is grateful for it in a way he has not been grateful for a coat since France, which is to say gratitude for small physical mercy in circumstances that have moved beyond the manageable.

He puts his back against the wall and his hands on his knees and he looks at the room.

The large man — not the one with the heavy-worker hands, a different large man, younger, with the build of a man who loaded or moved things for a living — has his eyes closed. Not sleeping; the deliberate stillness of someone applying their interior resources to a problem. The woman of fifty is watching the north window and the grey light coming through it. The boy is watching no one in particular and trying to make this look like watching nothing.

The woman who was staring at the wall earlier is now looking at Rowe. When he meets her eyes she looks away, but in the way of someone rationing attention, not someone ashamed. He understands this. He does the same.

From somewhere in the corridor outside — not close, not alarming, simply the ambient sound of a building in operation — comes the sound of voices moving past the door. Three or four of them, speaking quickly, the specific rhythm of people exchanging information under mild urgency. He cannot understand a word of it. But the rhythm is the rhythm of soldiers on a schedule, or people who are managing a process that requires coordination and has a timeline. He has spent enough time around that rhythm to know it even in a language that sounds like nothing he knows. He knows what it sounds like when people are doing a job in a building and the job has stages and they are past the first stage.

He looks at the ceiling. The vaulting above the north window is the same construction as the other rooms — same arcs, same lime mortar, same careful old work. The joins there are the same joins he has seen in the church walls on the road east of the canal, the church whose walls have stood since before anyone's grandfather could remember, the joins of craftsmen who understood what they were building and built it to outlast them by several hundred years.

He is inside something that outlasted those builders. He is inside it and does not know what it is.

He knows the following: he was at his machine. It was Thursday. The shift was half-done. His hands were running right for the first time in weeks and the shuttle hesitation was resolved and the work was clean. And then. And he is here, in a stone room with twenty-five people he does not know, in a building made of the same grey stone as buildings he has always known but not the same buildings, and the air is wrong, and the light is at the wrong angle, and people in dark robes have put him in a category on a board and examined his body and held an instrument near him that they were satisfied by, and he does not know what any of it means.

He cannot find the edges of it. He has tried to find the edges and they are not there. This is not panic — panic has a horizon. This is something steadier and worse, the recognition that there is no corner he can get to where this makes sense yet, and the yet may be very long.

He has been in this kind of room before. Not this room. A different building, different walls, different city, a specific kind of damp he will not forget. The room where you are held while people who know something you don't determine what to do with you. He knows how to be in this room. He sat in it for three months on and off while France was happening to him and found, eventually, that the way to be in it was the same as the way to be in any large difficult thing: one hour at a time, and don't look further than you have to.

He closes his eyes.

The stone is cold at his back. His coat is wool and the wool is slightly damp — something happened to it in the interval between the mill floor and this floor, the brief terrible interval of wrong-down and wrong-air, something in that passage left the wool with the particular damp of very wet cold air, and it has not dried. He pulls it closer.

The lamp on the south wall gutters. A draft from somewhere he cannot place. The shadows in the room shift and then settle.

The lamp rights itself.

Across the room, the large man opens his eyes, looks at the ceiling, and then looks at Rowe. They look at each other for a moment with the careful mutual inventory of men who have nothing to offer each other and know it, and neither of them apologizes for it.

Nobody speaks. Nobody moves toward the door.

After a while, someone at the far end of the room lies down on their pallet with their back to the room and pulls their coat over their shoulders. The sound of settling. Then silence, or what passes for it here — the building around them breathing, lamps burning, the sound of the world outside the windows moving about its business in a language he does not have a word in.

He sits with his hands on his knees and his back against the cold wall and waits for something he does not know the shape of. He has done this before. He will do it until the shape arrives.

[Beat 31]
VIERNA ENTRY — THE LAW DOESN'T APPLY HERE

The third morning on the mountain passes Lyra woke with her jaw clenched because the cold had found the gap between her gorget and her chin-strap in the night and taken up residence there. She did not start fires in the passes. The Wall observation posts extended east as well as north, and whatever her current relationship with Vierna's border authority, she did not need to clarify it with a smoke column visible for twenty kilometers.

She stood in the grey early light and counted the day's water. She had filled four containers at the last stream crossing — a seep-fed pool two days ago, slow and cold, not enough for what she needed but enough for what she had. Two containers were empty. One was down to its last third. The fourth had gone to the Heloth courier's cooling intake, which had priority because without the courier she was walking the western descent in armor with the Rod of a seventy-year-old scryer and whatever remained of her field kit.

One container, one-third remaining. Two days of descent ahead, according to Orim's route memory.

He was already at his courier's side, pressing Catalyst sensitizer into his fingertips with the method she'd now watched twice: palm flat to palm, the contact-sensitizer absorbed through the skin, a twenty-minute window of amplified membrane perception at the cost of nausea that he never mentioned and she'd noticed.

"Nothing within the Rod's range last night," he said without looking at her. "Whoever is ahead of us has a different route or a faster pace."

"Or they crossed the watershed before the snow window closed and they're already in the valley."

"That too." He wiped his fingertips on his coat. "We have a problem."

"Water."

"The pool at the lower crossing will be dry. The last significant precipitation in these passes was the snowmelt in the ninth month. The next is usually the first snowfall in the eleventh. We are in the tenth."

She looked at the sky. It was the white of high altitude and no clouds. "You've walked this route."

"I've walked a route adjacent to this route, in a different season." He looked east along the pass, which was a narrow cut of pale rock with winter-dead grass pressing up through the grit at the edges and nothing else for as far as either of them could see. "The eastern route crosses a watershed divide approximately four kilometers ahead. On the far side the drainage goes toward Vierna. That means there should be water. In the ninth month. In the tenth, the drainage has not yet recharged. The passes have been dry since the melt."

She had known this. She had been building toward knowing it clearly for two days, the knowing shaped by the progressive weight of the water containers going lighter and the increasing specific dryness at the back of her throat that one-third of a container would not address. At altitude the air took moisture out of you before you felt the lack. She had been feeling the lack since yesterday.

"How far to the Vierna valley floor from the divide?"

"Two days, perhaps. At mountain pace." He looked at the courier. "The machines are adequate. We are less so."

She put on her pack. The courier came to alert state when she laid her hand on its housing — the warm vibration of it through her palm, the chemical readiness. Thirty-six hours of reserve, approximately, at mountain pace. She and Orim were less than that.

They moved.

—

The pass was narrow enough in places that the couriers went single-file and Lyra leaned her body inward toward the rock face to keep her pack from catching on the outward edge where the path dropped away into the drainage below. The drainage was dry. She looked down once and noted it and stopped looking.

Orim catalogued things as they walked. This was how she was coming to know him — not in conversation, but in the running commentary of a man who had spent fifty years moving through terrain and had developed a specific habit of noting what he passed. The grooves cut in the rock face to her left were the marks of a rope-guide system, pre-Wall establishment, probably eighth or ninth century by the oxidation pattern. Someone had cut handholds and rope-guides across this face for travelers who needed them. The rope was gone. The grooves remained.

He said: "There was a customs house at the watershed divide in the sixth century. Not Vierna's customs — Vierna didn't exist then in any form we'd recognize. A local arrangement. You paid a family that had held the pass for four generations, and you crossed, and the record of your crossing was kept in a notation system nobody outside the pass has been able to read since the ninth century, when the family died and the notation died with them. There are documents in the Bressant archive citing the pass-crossing fee as precedent for the current transit charge and the notation system as its record. The precedent rests on documents no one can verify. Vierna finds this satisfying."

"Do you know how much the crossing fee was?"

"No one does. The notation system." He paused. "That's rather the point."

She filed this the way she filed everything — not dismissively, but as data she would be able to locate when she needed it — and kept moving.

—

They reached the watershed divide at midday.

It was marked by a stone cairn — recent, no older than fifty years by the weathering — and by the abrupt change in terrain on the far side: the eastern face had been pale rock and dead scrub, the gradient severe and north-facing. The western face was darker stone, more sheltered, south-facing, the scrub still brown-dry but with the quality of soil underneath that would hold water when the rains came. Still dry. The sense of descent ahead. Vierna somewhere below the cloud-line that lay against the valley floor.

She had been watching Orim since the third hour of the morning because she had been watching how he looked at the terrain, and how he had been looking at it had changed when they passed the last seep-fed hollow four kilometers back. Not alarm. A noting. The Rod was slung at his back and he touched it twice in the last two hours without appearing to notice he was doing it.

He stopped at the cairn.

She stopped. The couriers stopped behind them — the two machines standing with the patient readiness of things that did not understand why they were not moving but had no pressing opinion about it.

He unslung the Rod.

Forty centimeters of dense dark mineral compound in a plain iron housing, the grip wound in old cord that had been rewound at some point — she could see where the new winding began, a slightly different shade of wear. Seven grooves cut along the shaft at irregular intervals. He ran his fingers along them without looking, the way a person finds a familiar door handle in the dark. The fourth groove. His thumb stopped, rotated slightly, then moved back.

She said: "What are you looking for?"

"I'm not looking yet." He settled the mineral tip between his fingers. "I know what I'm looking for. I'm finding the right address."

He wet two fingertips from the small Catalyst preparation vial on his field belt. Pressed them together at his sternum. Two deliberate breaths. His eyes went somewhere else — not unfocused but differently focused, the way eyes look when they are seeing something that is not in front of them.

She had seen the full-installation scry at the Ocipheus Station archive. The apparatus crews, the wound held open by thirty years of careful damage to the same site, the membrane's resistance worn down until it was soft and responsive. She had found that comforting the way she found all familiar research methodology comforting — the specificity of it, the controlled conditions, the predictability.

This was nothing like it. This was one person's hands and a portable mineral compound and fifty years of knowing what to look for.

It lasted perhaps three minutes. His eyes came back.

"There is a Sphere-08 location approximately three hundred meters below our current position," he said. "Below the rock face to the west. A lake site — deep, cold, freshwater. The pressure differential at the membrane boundary is consistent with significant depth." He looked at the hollow in the rock face to their left — a natural depression in the stone, waist-deep, perhaps a meter and a half wide, open at the top. "I need you to stand behind the courier."

She looked at the hollow. She looked at the Rod. She looked at the hollow again.

"You're going to open the membrane," she said.

"I am going to open the membrane." He walked to the hollow and crouched. He pressed the Rod's mineral tip against the stone at the hollow's lowest point — the place where any liquid would collect. "The aperture will hold for perhaps twenty seconds. Possibly thirty. I cannot extend it and I cannot close it early." He glanced back at her. "The water will be cold. There will be some force behind it. Please stand behind the courier."

"The Liturgy classifies this as—"

"Unauthorized Membrane Perforation, Class III. Yes." He found the trigger with the flat of his finger. "The Liturgy classifies a great number of things. Please stand behind the courier."

She stood behind the courier.

He depressed the trigger.

The membrane responded the way she had only read about in research notation: there was something that appeared at the mineral tip, a translucency, a window into nothing that was also somehow surface. Threaded through it, dark veins, fine as hairline cracks in old stone, pulsing once. Twice. Three times, as the pressure built from the far side. She could see the membrane material itself — she had read descriptions of it but reading descriptions of biological material is not the same as watching it behave. It was thin and alive and trying to heal and it could not yet because the Rod's Catalyst preparation was still forcing the wound open.

The veins went dark.

The surface bulged.

The surface parted.

Water hit the rock hollow with enough force to splash back against Orim's outstretched arm, and it kept coming — not a trickle, not a flow, the sustained pressure of a lake that has a great deal of depth behind it and has been pressing against the membrane and is now being told that the door is open. Cold water, darker than water usually looks, the darkness of something that does not have a bottom your eyes can find. The smell was immediate and specific: wet stone and mineral cold and the deep-freshwater quality that is different from river water, different from rain, the smell of something that has been still and dark and pressured for a very long time.

She counted under her breath.

The hollow filled.

At twenty-two seconds the membrane closed — not dramatically, no sound, just the translucency thinning and the veins fading and the surface sealing the way a wound closes when the pressure is released. The bulge deflated. The aperture was gone.

Water pooled in the hollow and ran along the natural drainage of the rock to a lower shelf, where it pooled again.

Orim was still crouching at the rock face. He had his arm wrapped in his coat where the water had struck it. He was looking at the hollow with the expression of someone checking an outcome against an expected result.

She moved to the hollow and uncapped her first container. The water was cold enough that she felt it through the metal before she'd filled the container halfway. Her hands ached by the time she'd filled the third. She filled the fourth anyway.

When she'd finished, Orim had moved to the adjacent shelf of rock where the overflow had pooled. He sat against the stone. He drank from his own container, which she had filled without asking. He did not speak.

She filled the couriers' supplemental intake tank, which did not require it but which she did anyway. She drank. The cold went all the way down. The altitude headache that had been building since the morning — the specific throb of dehydration at altitude — began, after perhaps ten minutes, to loosen.

Orim was still sitting.

The Rod's mineral tip was wrapped in his coat. She could see, even through the cloth, that the housing was radiating heat — not dramatically, but the coat lay differently over it than it would have over something that was cold.

She said: "You've done this before."

He said: "I know which lakes are deep."

He drank again, and did not say anything further.

She remained at the rock and let the silence have the time it was owed. A researcher asks a question and receives data. The data was: he has done this before, he knows which Spheres are which, he knows what the pressure differential of a deep lake produces against a membrane aperture, and he has known all of this for fifty years. This was not the first time. It was also, she suspected from the precise way he had said it — *I know which lakes are deep*, not *I have done this* — probably not the first time he had been asked.

She capped the last container. Her hands were still aching from the cold but they were working again.

"Thank you," she said.

"We will need it before the Vierna valley floor." He stood, rewrapped the Rod in its carry-sling, and resettled it across his back with the deliberateness of a man handling something that had cost something to use. Not regret. Accounting. "The western descent begins past the cairn."

—

What changed on the descent: the air first, growing heavier with the altitude loss, each hour's progress rewinding the specific thinness that had been sitting on her chest since the first day in the passes. The dry smell of altitude gave way to something wetter and darker — the beginning of the valley smell, old soil and cold vegetable matter and somewhere below, the fog that lay against the lowlands. The rock changed color from the pale limestone of the eastern face to grey-green with lichen in the sheltered spots, the eastern exposure giving way to the terrain that faced into whatever Vierna's weather usually was.

Vierna's weather was usually fog.

She had known this from the operational records. The previous three times she had crossed into Vierna, with proper Compact authority and no particular reason to notice how the fog was arranged, she had noted it in the way you note weather that is not yet your problem. Now, without proper authority, with all her attention on what moving through a territory without papers felt like in the body, she noticed it differently. The fog sat in the valley floor and climbed the lower slopes and the tree line disappeared into it after the first kilometer of descent.

The silverthorn hedges along the upper field margins caught the fog and held it and made a low sound in the wind — not quite a tone, more a resonance, the kind of thing you felt in your sternum before you heard it with your ears. She had read that trained listeners could interpret the direction and speed of whatever moved through the hedge by the sound it made. She was not a trained listener.

The first buildings were low, stone-constructed, the roofs thatched in a style she recognized from regional archive documentation: not Ocipheus thatch, which ran the reeds one direction, but Vierna high-country thatch, alternating rows, the pattern staggered for drainage. There was smoke from the first building and a cow in the yard and a child who saw the Heloth couriers from the gate and went inside without looking at the riders.

Standard response to Heloth traffic in an eastern Vierna hill village. She and Orim had no authority here and no papers either, but authority and papers were not what the child had been frightened of.

Orim said, without looking at the village: "There will be a Vierna road checkpoint at the valley junction, three kilometers ahead. Single soldier, rotation schedule. Compact authority recognized under the Year 831 transit agreement."

"My transit authority has been suspended."

"The Year 831 agreement predates the suspension mechanism by approximately four hundred years. The soldier at the checkpoint is not authorized to exercise a mechanism that did not exist when his station was established." A pause. "He may have been briefed on it. He is not, technically, empowered to act on the briefing."

She looked at him.

He looked at the road ahead with the expression of a man who had been navigating administrative systems for fifty years and had long since stopped distinguishing between the legitimate and the technically defensible.

"How many days behind does the suspension notification typically run, in the eastern administrative district?"

"Given the current season and the relay schedule through these passes? Two to three days." He finally looked at her. "We crossed this range on foot for three days. The suspension notification came by Heloth relay from Ocipheus. The relay system follows the valley road, which is faster. The notification is probably ahead of us."

"But the Year 831 agreement creates a presumption of good faith."

"It does. It is not the most solid position I have ever assisted someone in maintaining." He tilted his head. "It is the position we have."

It was. She rode on.

—

The checkpoint was a wooden structure at a road junction, roofed against the fog, with a horizontal pole across the road and a stove inside whose heat made the fog behave differently around the door. One soldier. Mid-twenties, grey coat, the Vierna House mark at the shoulder, a bolt-action rifle slung across his back in the way that indicated standard patrol training rather than immediate-engagement readiness.

She had read about the bolt-action rifles in Vierna's military documentation. Reading about a weapon and watching a person carry it as if it weighed nothing — with the natural ease of something you had been trained on before you had any reason to refuse — were different amounts of information.

She showed the sealed authority. The soldier read it with the care of someone reading something for the second time, which meant he had been briefed and was checking the briefing against what he was looking at. He looked at the date. He looked at her. He looked at the road behind her and saw Orim on the second courier, and Orim raised his chin in the neutral greeting of a man who had been through more checkpoints than this soldier had been alive.

The soldier stamped the log. He moved the pole.

She rode through. Orim followed.

Fifty meters beyond the checkpoint she heard the sound of the signal relay beginning — the flat clack of the mechanism, three signals to the valley station.

Three signals was the code for *passed through, continue observation*. Not the code for *detain*. She had, from the sound of those three signals, perhaps six hours before the administrative machinery of Vierna's eastern district finished comparing the stamp on the checkpoint log against the suspension notification, decided what to do about the discrepancy, and began moving cavalry accordingly.

Six hours. The valley road was fast. Six hours was enough.

—

Bressant was a market city on the Veil River — the kind of city that had been built to do commerce and had not stopped doing it. Even in late autumn, even with the fog, the landing district was active: barge traffic on the river, the creak of rope and wood, the smell of grain and the specific vegetable darkness of river-wet stone. She had been here twice before on sanctioned runs, both times with proper papers, and had noted the city's organized busyness without giving it much attention. Now, approaching from the eastern road through the fog, she noticed it differently.

There was a flag-change at the eastern gate. She watched it from the road — the gate officer noting her approach in the log, the notation passing to the flag-keeper, the flag raised.

Red.

She was being logged. She was inside Vierna and she was being logged and there was nothing to be done about the logging because she was not leaving and the logging was the price of being here. She had known this when she crossed the watershed divide. It was simply more specific now, watching the flag go up at the gate of a city that had been keeping river records since the sixth century.

Orim pulled alongside her on the road outside the gate. "The Archival Gate," he said, gesturing toward the river district, where the Veil ran past the city's western face. "Named for Arnault d'Archival."

She had not known d'Archival. "Year 312?"

"He crossed the Veil River in pursuit of a Calyx raiding party and planted his House mark on the far bank and declared the river the border. The Calyx disagreed. The river disagreed by flooding the following spring and moving the bank by approximately fifteen meters. D'Archival's mark is now on the wrong side of the water it was meant to define." Orim surveyed the gate with the mild attention of a man visiting a place that had failed to surprise him. "Vierna charges crossing tolls based on his notation of the mark's position. The mark is underwater. The notation remains."

He did not say it was absurd. He did not need to.

"This is the country we are in," she said.

"This is the country we are in." He moved toward the gate. "The record matters here more than the fact. Bear that in mind."

—

Inside Bressant the fog was thicker than outside it, the city holding moisture against its old stone while the river brought more up from below. She rode through the lower market district, where the stalls were closing for the midday break with the specific choreography of vendors who had been doing this same closure in the same order for twenty years. No one looked at the couriers with particular alarm. Heloth traffic was ordinary in Bressant. The landing district used freight models for the heavy barge work and a courier was unremarkable.

The Myrmidon intake station was in the cathedral-adjacent district, on the wide street that ran between the cathedral's north transept and the river. She had not planned to pass it. The route she was taking went through it.

The station occupied what had once been a canonical administrative annex — stone-walled, high-windowed, the vaulted ceiling that the Liturgy favored when it needed functional space adjacent to ecclesiastical authority, the kind of ceiling that directed light down from clerestory windows onto the work floor below. Whoever had taken it over for Vierna's intake operations had not bothered to change the architecture. They had simply placed trestle tables under the vaulted arches and begun filing.

She rode past slowly enough to see through the open door.

A trestle table under the central arch. A Vierna intake officer with a ledger and an ink register, working through a stack of documents with the efficiency of someone for whom this was the third week of it. On the table beside the ledger: a stamp. The stamp was for the designation block — the M-prefix and the intake serial, applied to every conscript document the moment the notation was complete. Beside the stamp: three completed files in a wooden box, corners aligned, waiting for the clerk who would carry them to the garrison archive.

Three people had been through this table this morning.

Against the left wall: a rack. Five bolt-action rifles, clean and maintained. A sixth space empty — the sixth rifle presumably on the intake officer's back or in the anteroom. The rack was the same manufacture as the checkpoint guard's equipment.

She looked at the completed files in the wooden box. She could not read them from the road. She could see that they were the standard intake format — the paper weight and the fold at the top corner were Vierna military, she had handled enough Compact liaison documents to recognize the stock. She knew what was on them. She had known what was on them administratively since she was twenty-two, which was when she had first encountered the form designation *M-intake authorization, Sphere-origin conscript, Year-stamp* in a Compact coordination brief.

The form designation was what she had encountered. The completed files in the wooden box were what the form designation meant.

She kept riding.

The cathedral's north face rose to her left — Vierna's canonical structure, different from Ocipheus's in the way institutions that serve different purposes look different even when they share an architecture. Ocipheus's vigil archive was designed for long occupancy, for the weight of people who lived there and worked in the same rooms for decades. Bressant's canonical presence was designed for throughput. Records entered and exited. People were processed. The high windows let in the light needed to read documents correctly.

She found the road that ran north along the Veil River and took it.

Orim fell in behind her, and for a time neither of them spoke, which was the particular silence of a man who had been noting things for fifty years and a woman who had just spent twenty minutes noting things she did not quite know what to do with yet.

—

The fog came fully off the river at dusk. She could not see the water to her right but she could hear it — the specific low murmur of the Veil at high autumn depth, carrying more than usual given the season. To her left, the city's residential margins had thinned to the industrial edge: a mill, a warehouse with a commercial seal, a small construction yard with materials covered for winter. Workers in the yard were reinforcing a foundation wall against the coming frost. She watched them without stopping.

She camped two kilometers north of Bressant's last outpost marker, not hidden — hidden was its own kind of signal — but set back from the road in the margin, the couriers in rest-state, the fire small enough to be any traveler's fire.

Orim located the exit angles and the gap in the observation coverage with the murmuring efficiency of a man doing something he had done too many times to hurry. He wrapped the Rod in its cover, slowly, with the deliberateness he always used for it. She had been watching how he handled the Rod and had decided that the deliberateness was not care for the instrument — it was more like the care you took setting down something that could not be set down carelessly, because you knew what it had just cost on the other side of the membrane. Not regret. Accounting, as she had thought before. A balance kept in a place she could not see.

"The administrative district's response will be morning," he said. "They will have matched the checkpoint stamp against the suspension notification by now, but the Bressant garrison does not move cavalry at night in fog on the river road. They move at first light."

"First light," she said.

"We should leave before then."

"Yes."

She ate without tasting it and drank the last of the cold Sphere-08 water, which was still distinctly colder than anything else in her kit — the cold of depth, not weather, not the cold of something that had been sitting in a high-altitude pass since yesterday. She set the container down.

She thought about the intake files in the wooden box and the stamp and the empty space in the rifle rack. The Liturgy called it *resettlement under compact*, which was a terminology she had used in Compact liaison documents without thinking about it since she was twenty-two. She could not remember precisely when she had stopped thinking about what the terminology meant and started using it as if the terminology were the thing itself. She did not examine this long. There was no room for it tonight. The administrative district's cavalry would move at first light and she needed to be three kilometers north by then, and the river road would take her toward the Atrament border, and the Relic was somewhere ahead of her on this same road.

She banked the fire and lay back in her bedroll.

The cold found the gap between her gorget and her chin-strap as it had found it every night in the passes. She let it. She was in Vierna without authorization, which was — she noticed this the way she noticed most things, as a fact that had a certain quality to it — the most precisely honest position she had occupied in three weeks.

She slept.

[Beat 32]
NO ACTION INDICATED

The copy desk faced north, which in winter meant it faced a column of pale light that came off the courtyard stones and produced no warmth and did nothing useful except confirm the time of day. She had spent three years at various desks in Liturgy copy offices, and they all faced somewhere inconvenient. The canonical administration had been built for permanence and ceremony, not for the people who worked in it, and the copy office in the central archive complex was no different from the others — a high-ceilinged room, stone walls that held the cold the way stone did, two windows on the north face, one door, a row of shelves that had been built for someone who expected to file things in a particular order that had been abandoned at some point in the room's history and replaced with a different order that she was still learning. Six weeks. She had spent the first three learning the lamp angle and the second three doing it automatically, the way you accommodate an asymmetry you cannot correct.

Her right shoulder ached by the second hour every day. The middle knuckle on her right hand stiffened by mid-morning and had to be pressed back sharply against the joint — one click, release, done — and then she could reload the nib and continue. She had stopped noticing the ache except as a signal that the morning shift was half-done. These were not complaints. They were conditions. She had been a Scribe for three years and she had learned to tell the difference.

The instruments arrived at the third bell. The runner — a junior canon, fourteen years old, still wearing the expression of someone who had not yet learned what the documents he was carrying said — set the stack on the corner of her desk with the particular care of someone who had been told the documents were important without being told what that meant. They were. They were also delivered with the same care as documents that were not important, because the practice did not permit him to judge.

In the first weeks of the posting he had asked whether she required anything else. He had been sociable about it, the ingrained courtesy of a junior apprentice trained to anticipate needs. He had stopped asking in the third week, in the way you stop asking a question when you understand, without being told, that the answer will be no and that asking it is creating a small performance neither of you has the energy for. She had not asked him why. She was fairly confident she knew.

Six weeks was enough time to learn what a stack of instruments contained by looking at it. The weight; the binding method; whether the lead sheet was in the Canon's hand or a secretary's. The lead sheet this morning was in the Canon's hand. She had learned what that meant by process of accumulation rather than by being told — the Canon's hand meant the instruments below had been reviewed at the highest level before they reached her desk. Not processed by an office. Reviewed, personally. She noted the stack's weight: heavier than yesterday's. She set the notation sheet aside and started with the second instrument.

---

The Lacerta document was formal, carefully constructed, and written by someone who understood that they were arguing upward through an institution that did not share their interests.
