She looked at the smoke with him.

The *Houndstooth* moved north and the column grew and the smell of metals at temperature came in through the porthole gaps and settled into the cold of the hold. Behind her, Orim woke at the change in the air and found his crate and his porthole view and said nothing, which was what Orim did when he had already said what mattered. Ardea slept on. The river moved.

She watched Rowe watch the smoke and thought about what the field archivist's three pages did not contain, which was most of it. The records said: *complete phonetic disjunction upon initial Sphere crossing. No surface-level phonetic bridge with any catalogued Cauld variant.* The records said this in the clinical notation of administrative documentation and she had found it interesting in the way she found most research documentation interesting, which was as a problem.

She found it, in this specific morning, on this specific barge, looking at this specific man standing at a porthole watching smoke that he had seen before in a different country — she found it a different kind of thing than she had found it before.

She opened her notebook. She had work to do.

One word at a time was how bridges were built. She was good at one thing at a time. She was exceptionally good at one thing at a time, and the river was long, and the smoke on the Atrament horizon was going to be on this horizon for the rest of the day, and she had a notebook, and she had made a start.

She went back to work.

[Beat 35]
SEVEN MONTHS

The oath room had the specific cold of a building that has been standing long enough to have decided what temperature it is and refuses further argument on the subject. Stone floors, stone walls, a high narrow window that admitted light from the wrong angle. There was a desk. There was a chair behind the desk. There was a robed figure in the chair and a form on the desk and a pen beside the form.

He had been in rooms organized on this principle for thirty-four years. The principle was: you are here to receive conditions that were determined before you arrived. He had stood at the mill office when he was twelve, at the conscription board when he was twenty-six, at the demob processing table in the autumn. The configuration was the same across rooms, across countries, apparently across whatever distance existed between his world and this one: a desk, a form, a person authorized to make the form mean something.

The figure spoke.

He had been in this place — not this room, but this condition — for three weeks. Three weeks of organized sounds that his ear received as language and his understanding received as nothing. Not the nothing of a foreign language that could become comprehensible on repetition. A different nothing. No root he could reach back to, no sound that mapped onto anything in the four languages he had partial access to. He had tried all of them. He had tried the French that had settled into his bones for two years. He had tried the smattering of German from the camp east of Arras. He had tried the Latin from the three years at St. Mabyn's school before the apprenticeship. Every sound in this language landed and went nowhere.

The figure gestured at the form.

He looked at it. The written form of the language was different from the spoken — he had understood this immediately, which was interesting in one direction and useless in every other. He could not read it. He could read numbers. Numbers were numbers.

His number was in the second column: 31. He had seen this number on documents for three weeks, seen it pointed at him, seen it used in the particular way you used a designation rather than a name. It was his number. He did not know what the column heading said. He knew the number went past 31 because the list on the wall in the processing hall had gone past 31, and numbers worked that way.

There was a line at the bottom of the form.

The figure pointed at the line.

He picked up the pen and marked the line. The ink was thick, the pen cut differently from what he was used to — a different nib geometry, the line it made slightly heavier on the left side of each stroke. He noted this and set the pen down. The figure took the form, stamped it, filed it. The stamp had worn to a partial impression from use, which was evidence of volume rather than carelessness. One of a thousand, or of ten thousand. The form was filed in a drawer that was already full.

He was shown to a door.

The door opened onto a passage that smelled of metal-oil and wet wool and the particular sourness of men who had not been warm enough for long enough. He followed the man in front of him.

---

The great hall had stone arches, the vaulting beginning thirty feet up where the walls gathered into ribs and carried the weight of the roof. Someone had built this hall to last and the hall had lasted and someone else had found another use for it. The rows of narrow bunks went wall to wall, wood-frame, two high, straw mattresses and dark wool blankets. The floor had been cleared of whatever it had originally held and given over to the functional requirements of housing a great many people with minimal expenditure of either space or comfort.

On the far wall: a rack of rifles.

He saw them from the entrance, thirty meters away, and knew what they were before he reached them. He would not reach them until the third day. He had been told to go to the bunk he'd been assigned and to put down his kit and to wait until he was told to stop waiting. He did this. He put down his kit and lay on the bunk and looked at the arches overhead and thought about the rifles on the far wall.

He learned *kal* first.

He learned it from the gap between moving and impact — from continuing when everyone else had stopped, from the hand that snapped around his collar and jerked him sideways into a wall. The sound the others made was not laughter exactly. It was the sound of recognition. *That one will learn.* He was not certain this constituted encouragement.

After *kal* came the equipment words. Equipment words came first because equipment had to function correctly or someone's face would reflect the consequence of its not functioning, and the face that reflected it was reliably his. *Kest* was the lock on the action housing. *Vurt* was the strap. *Reml* — the r carried back in the throat — was the cleaning kit: pull-through rod, oil bottle, small brush for the breach face. He learned these words by learning to use the things they named. He held the thing until he had the word. He held the word until he had the thing. He had learned a Cauld that ran backwards from how language was supposed to work, and he adapted, because the alternative to adapting was not adapting, and he had seen what that produced.

---

On the third day they moved him to the range.

He picked up his rifle from the day issue. His right hand went to the bolt. The bolt went back the way a bolt in a particular catalog drawing at Garside's ironmongers had been trying to go for years, except the man who'd drawn the diagram had not yet solved the feed angle and whoever had made this rifle had.

He did not think about this. He loaded the magazine and settled the stock and waited for the trainer to come and tell him what he was doing.

The trainer came. The trainer looked at him standing with a loaded rifle at a ready position and said something that in any language would have meant *when did this happen.* He looked at the other trainer. They had a brief exchange over Rowe's head, their hands on the rifle, turning it to look at it, handling it with the focused attention of men examining something unexpected. He waited.

They put him in the front row for the rest of range day. The word the trainer used for him had an approving quality. He filed it under things he had no way to explain and moved on.

---

By the end of the first week he had approximately twenty words. Every one of them was an object or a command.

He discovered other numbers in the second week, on a stack of forms on the clerk's outer desk. The clerk was elsewhere. Rowe stood at the desk and looked at the top form. Numbers in a column: 31, 8, 22, 14. His number was not alone. He could not read the column heading. He would have the heading in four months. That day he had the numbers, and the numbers confirmed: the catalogue went past 31, and it had been made by someone, and it contained people, and the people were here.

He set the form back on the stack face-down and returned to the passage where he'd been told to wait.

In the third week the man from the close world arrived in a transfer batch from the eastern intake station. His hands were a machinist's hands — the web between thumb and forefinger callused in the specific way that came from tools rather than ground work, the palm hardness of a lathe or a press or something similar, something with repetitive lateral motion. He was about thirty. He had been confused in a language he didn't have for eight weeks and was going to be confused in this one too.

They had no Cauld between them.

They had a different problem.

In the dark after lights, Rowe said something in his own language. Not expecting anything. Just to hear himself. The man from the transfer batch turned around.

What came back was not the same. But parts of it were not completely different.

They spent a week in the evenings building a map. Approximately thirty words — or fewer, if some of them were the same word said differently, or more, if some of the false ones hadn't announced themselves yet. The false ones announced themselves when one of them used a word he thought meant a thing and the other made the face that said *that is not what that means,* followed by a period of careful reconstruction.

*Factory. Fabrik.* Different words. The same shape of an idea.

*Machine. Mashin.* Again.

*Bread.* This one took four attempts and produced two false starts that made them both laugh, which was the first time Rowe had laughed since he arrived.

The man had been on a machine floor when it happened to him. He had not chosen to come either. He did not understand what he was here for.

This was not a surprise. It was confirmation, which was a different thing. Surprise was when something changed your understanding. Confirmation was when something put weight underneath your understanding, made it firmer to stand on. He had understood, since the forms with the numbers, that this was a system with multiple inputs and consistent methods. The man from the close world confirmed: the inputs came from more than one direction and the methods had been applied more than once. The system had been running long enough to develop intake paperwork with worn stamps.

He thought, for a moment, about the German prisoners in the camp east of Arras. Men from the Ruhr and Brandenburg and wherever armies went for their men, in a country whose language those men had not chosen. He had walked past that camp twice. He had not thought much about it then. He thought about it now.

He thought about it once, and noted what the thought was, and put it somewhere he could find it later.

---

By month three he could follow orders.

Not understand them in the full sense — the gap between following and understanding was real and useful to keep track of. Conflating them produced errors, and errors produced *kal* in its physical form. He had a hundred words, all operational. *Morning, advance, hold, fall back, ready, done.* He had equipment designations and rank names. He had *here* and *now.* He did not have *before* in the temporal sense. He did not have *why.* He had the name of his own rifle, which was the only name in the language he found comfortable to say.

Reading was slower. The written language followed rules the spoken one didn't, and some of the sounds he had mapped onto letters were wrong. He corrected them when he caught them. He read numerals correctly. He could read his own designation on the unit board. He had been reading it there for three months.

The man from Sphere 22 — which was what Rowe had decided to call him, having no Cauld name yet and no shared language — had been in Vierna for two years. He spoke Cauld with almost no accent. He ate the food without looking at it. He was good at being somewhere else when things deteriorated, and he was good at explanations when Rowe's Cauld was too thin to follow an order. Rowe did not judge this. He filed it.

By month four the man from the close world had enough Cauld to hold a three-sentence conversation, which was two sentences more than Rowe had. His ear was better. He had grown up near something similar, he indicated by gesture and tone, though the specifics were inaccessible across the language gap between them. Not the same language. Not far enough apart to be nothing.

By month five Rowe could understand most of what was said around him if the speaker was unhurried and the subject was one he had words for.

By month six, a man at the clerk's desk pointed at him and used a word that Rowe had been seeing on forms since week three. The man said it not unkindly. Rowe understood from context that it meant something like *from somewhere else.* He would learn later that it meant specifically: person brought through the membrane from another Sphere and assigned to Vierna military service. He would learn it carried a legal bracket in the intake system, a designation that sat him permanently at a specific distance from the rank ladder and confirmed a term of service that had no defined endpoint.

He had understood these conditions since month two. Having the word for them made no particular difference.

---

The engagement in month seven had no name he heard. If it had a name, he didn't have the Cauld for it, and by month seven he would have.

The unit moved south on a road that was not a good road, in weather that was not good weather. Low cloud. The rain smell already thickening in the air, the kind of thickness that was not yet rain but had committed. The mud at the road's margins was spreading inward in the way mud spread inward when it had decided to. Quick-march pace, the column contracted and purposeful, moving with the specific quality of a column that has something at the other end of the march rather than nothing.

The road ran through lowland country — dead grass on the slopes, the stone grey underneath it, the trees at the field edges stripped to their essential lines. The quality of the light was a flat winter light, without shadows, the kind of light that fell the same way over the Pas-de-Calais in November and apparently fell the same way here, over this country he had no name for and no flag for, under this cloud that sat low enough to feel like a ceiling. He noted the light and released it.

At the ridge they stopped.

He looked down.

Two forces in the valley. One to the east, moving on the lowland road. One to the south, moving through harvested fields, the crop-stubble brown and wet, the column visible at this distance as dark movement through pale ground.

He had learned to read valleys in France. Not as strategy — he had not been a strategist, had not had the rank or the information for strategy. As geometry. A man who had spent ten years working power looms understood fixed paths and moving parts and what happened at the points where they converged. The valley below had a convergence point. His column was descending toward it. The two forces below were moving toward the same point from different angles.

He did not need to understand the reason in order to understand the geometry.

The officer at the front of the column spoke. The column moved forward.

He stood at the ridge a moment longer than the men around him.

He looked at the east force. He looked at the south force. He looked at the faces in the column moving past him — forward-facing, the set of soldiers who have been given an order and are executing it, a look he recognized not because it was his look but because he had seen it from the outside, had passed men wearing it on roads in France, had worn it himself on days when the order had enough information in it to follow.

He had no information. He had the geometry.

He looked for flags. He could not identify either force by flag or by insignia. He could not identify what either side was here for. He could not identify what he was here for, in any sense larger than the column's current direction. He had seven months of *advance* and *hold position* and *fall back,* and he had a designation on forms he could read, and he had an oath he had made in a room before he had the language to know what he was agreeing to.

He had nothing else here.

Nothing on either side that was his. No officer whose authority he had chosen, no purpose he had understood when he agreed to it, no allegiance he had made with his eyes open.

The sound started from the valley below.

He knew the sound. The bolt mechanism made the same sound regardless of which country had built it. His world had built an earlier version. The Cauld had built this one. The sound was the same because the mechanism was the same and mechanisms did not change the sound they made just because you were somewhere else.

He turned around.

He walked back up the road. The column was below him now, moving forward, the sound of it receding toward the valley and away from him. No one was watching behind. There was no one behind to watch him go; the column was ahead and below and moving away.

He walked until the road was empty behind him and empty ahead of him.

He walked until the sound from the valley was behind him and then distant and then absent, and then he walked until the country was quiet, which took longer than the sound but not longer than an afternoon.

He kept walking north.

---

Bressant was large enough to disappear into. Any city was, if you understood city-logic: too many people moving in too many directions for any one person to be remarkable. He had been in cities before, had understood city-logic before, had learned from the mill district in his own city that anonymity was a product of volume and unremarkability in equal measure. He was compact and unremarkable. He had been unremarkable since birth. It was the most useful thing about him.

He found the grain district by smell. Large quantities of dry grain in enclosed buildings had a specific warmth to the smell — dusty, slightly sweet, the slow exhalation of material settling. Not cotton, which was what he knew from the mill floor in autumn when the big shipments came in. Different from cotton but organized on the same principle: bulk dry goods in a closed space had a smell that carried, and the smell led him to the buildings, and the buildings were large and numerous and full of places a man could be that were not the street.

The loading yards were busy and therefore ignorable. He walked into the district as a man with a purpose, because purpose was posture and posture was often the whole of it.

He slept in the first warehouse three nights. When the section he was using showed signs of regular supervision, he moved. He moved again in the second week, and again in the third. He learned the district by moving through it — which warehouses had irregular inspection schedules, which supervisors watched the perimeter workers, which loading crews were the kind that looked up and which were the kind that didn't. He had been around docks once before, briefly, on a job that required moving materials between a riverside warehouse and a cart before a customs officer arrived. He had understood docks from that one occasion: the logic of water and cargo and the men who moved between them was consistent, and consistency was a tool.

He ate when there was something to eat. There often was, in a grain district in harvest season — spillage was edible if you were not particular, and he had not been particular since France. He drank from the drainage channels that ran along the warehouse rows, which was not ideal but was cold and plentiful.

He kept the rifle.

This was not practical. The rifle was heavy and required maintenance and was not the kind of thing a warehouse district worker normally carried and therefore required concealment, which added difficulty to every entry and exit. He kept it anyway. The reason, examined carefully, was this: it was the one thing in the Cauld that he fully understood. From feeding mechanism to bolt to cleaning kit, he had never been uncertain about the rifle. Everything else here — the language, the system, the intake forms, the oath he had made before he had words for what he was agreeing to — had been managed in conditions of partial comprehension. The rifle was comprehension without conditions. He had recognized it on the first day. He had understood it before he was handed it. He was not going to set it down.

He found the large bin in the eastern warehouse on his seventeenth day in the grain district. Wheat, settled from summer, the grain pressing at chest level inside the bin walls. The bin's lid was heavy, seasoned oak, iron hinges oiled recently enough to give without sound. Someone had maintained this bin. Someone had been living near it, or using it regularly. He noted this and moved in anyway.

He had been in it two days. He should move tomorrow.

---

Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.

He repeated them in the dark, not aloud. The four words of Cauld that were genuinely his — found rather than handed to him, acquired through his own observation rather than assigned by the intake system and the drill cadence.

*Faeb.* He'd worked this one out from a sign on a building in the western quarter, ten minutes of staring at it, the root eventually yielding. A textile concern from the look of the machinery through the windows, different from his own mill but organized on recognizable industrial logic. Factory.

*Fume.* Smoke. He'd heard this in the loading yard when something smoldered in the warehouse rafters — heard the word and seen the smoke in the same moment. They had joined the way things joined when they arrived together.

*Morn.* Morning. Seven months of *morn-formation, morn-ration, morn-drill* had made this word as inevitable as the thing it named.

*Solen.* Gone. He had needed this one, had asked the man from Sphere 22 carefully where a particular person had gone, and had been given the word, and the word had taken because the need had been real.

He said them in order, not to communicate anything. Because in his own language — which was still the language he thought in, still the language his dreams used, still the language that arrived first and then had to step aside — these were things he had understood before he had names for them in anything else. Saying the Cauld names was a way of noting that the Cauld had names for them too. That the things existed here as they existed there.

His own language was still his. But there were gaps appearing. Not in the vocabulary — the vocabulary was intact. Gaps in the ease of it. He reached for his own word and sometimes the Cauld word arrived first, because the Cauld word had been used yesterday and his own word had not been used for seven months, and the gap was small but it was real.

He did not find this comforting.

The bin was warm from the grain — the moisture working out of the settled wheat, some slow process he had no name for in any language but recognized as physical fact. The warmth pressed against his chest and sides. Not comfort. Warmth. He had learned the difference between these in France and had not confused them since.

He had three days of food left. He was counting.

Outside the bin, outside the warehouse: the sounds of the loading yard in its mid-morning cycle. Heavy foot traffic early, lighter through midday, the grinding of the hoist-wheels in late afternoon. He could tell the time of day from the sound now, which was the kind of knowledge that accumulated slowly and without announcement.

He was warm and hidden and had three days and had the rifle. He repeated the four words. He closed his eyes.

The boards above the warehouse shifted.

He felt it before he heard it — the specific low-frequency vibration of seasoned timber taking sudden weight at a discrete point. Not the general settling-and-creak of a building working against wind. Not the running vibration of the hoist-wheels. Something applied. Something located.

He held still.

Two seconds. Three.

The sound came then: careful. The tread of someone trying not to make sound, which produced a sound that was specifically different from the sound of nothing, and which announced itself to anyone who had spent time in the kind of place where the difference mattered. Not a supervisor — supervisors walked with the confidence of official presence. Not a work crew — crews moved in clusters and did not bother with care. Not anyone who belonged here unambiguously.

Single. Careful. Moving toward the section he was in.

In the dark of the bin, in the pressed warmth of the grain, his hand found the rifle.

[Beat 36]
THE RIVER — FACTORY / SMOKE / MORNING / GONE

The barge was called the *Houndstooth* and smelled accordingly. Below decks, behind the casks, Lyra had found a corner between a stack of oilskin-wrapped bales and the outer hull where river water moved just inches from her ear. She rolled her coat under her head and lay in the dark and listened to the river working along the keel.

The *Houndstooth* moved at night and stopped in the day at whatever commercial dock would accept the barge master's arrangement without questions about the hold. Orim had negotiated the passage in Bressant, at a chandler's back room, over a transaction she had not been present for and had not asked about. She had learned, in the three days since they'd found Rowe in the grain bin, that questioning the terms of Orim's arrangements was not strictly prohibited but was consistently unproductive. She stopped on the morning of the second day. Orim noticed. He said nothing. She catalogued this as confirmation.

He was at the porthole when she settled into her corner—standing with his hands inside his coat, looking out at the river in the specific patient way of someone who had decided, long ago, that darkness was not inherently stable and that having a witness cost nothing and had saved him twice. She had read three people in her life with this quality. The others had also been cautious, specific, and very difficult to kill.

Rowe was asleep already, his back against the far hull, boots on, hands half-closed around nothing in the particular way of a man who had been sleeping in inadvisable places for long enough that the position had become a habit of the body. She noted the boots. She noted the hands. She filed both of them beside the other things she'd been accumulating since Bressant: the way he moved through unfamiliar spaces, the way he watched people before he let people watch him, the particular quality of his attention when something surprised him—a door opening briefly in a face that otherwise kept its counsel. She had no comfortable category for the collection. She made a provisional one and put everything in it.

She slept four hours. When she woke, the gray at the porthole had thinned slightly at its edges—not yet morning, but the first hour of a morning that had not committed to being one. Her shoulder had locked. Not the right, which had taken the second infusion badly and always announced itself first with a grinding complaint, but the left, the old courier's groove, the shoulder that had never forgiven her for the new weight and new geometry the infusions had imposed on a body that had not asked for geometry. She worked the joint with her fingers until it grudgingly recalled that rotation was available to it. Then she sat up, found the manifest on the nearest cask, and began to read.

---

The days on the barge established their shapes by the second day.

Orim catalogued the hold. He touched the casks and read their labels and weighed the bales in his hands and set them down again with the expression of someone filing something in a category too small for the object. She did not interfere. It was not interferable.

He also began teaching Rowe.

She missed the beginning of it—she had been working and looked up to find it already established. Orim was pointing at a cask and Rowe was looking at it, and then at Orim, and he said a word from his own language: one syllable, tentative, offered with the slight upward inflection of someone suggesting rather than stating. Orim shook his head, not unkindly, and said the Cauld word. Rowe repeated it. Orim nodded once, without ceremony or warmth, and pointed at the adjacent cask, which was a different size and therefore warranted a different word.

She watched this for ten minutes, then went back to her notebook. She could hear it continuing at the far end of the hold—the point, the pause, the Cauld word, the repetition, the next point—with a rhythm that suggested either long practice or a natural aptitude for it. She suspected both. Orim was curious about everything and needed Rowe to eventually be able to communicate what he knew. These two facts together apparently produced a very patient language teacher.

Her own work: two columns in her research notebook, the left for Cauld words, the right for her phonetic rendering of whatever Rowe produced when shown the thing the word named. The columns diverged in ways she found informative. His language was more compressed than hers in some areas and more specific in others. He had distinct terms for at least three grades of ferrous material where she had one general word for metal. She kept the implication in a subcategory and let it sit. She had learned not to pull at threads before she had enough architecture to survive whatever came loose when she did.

By the time she put the notebook away that first day, he had twenty-three Cauld words. She had twenty-three approximations of his. Three of her subcategories would require revision once she had more data.

---

She found him at the porthole that afternoon while Orim slept against the hull, his breathing slow and even in the way of someone making up for a long time without rest.

Rowe was lying flat with his chin on his forearms, looking at the passing bank through the porthole's lower edge. Entirely still. She found a position at the far end of the hold where the angle let her see both the porthole and the side of his face, and she watched.

The Veil River in its lowland reaches ran through country she knew in the administrative sense: checkpoint positions, road conditions in autumn, water quality at the midpoint wells. The farms on the north bank were old farms—the kind that had been there long enough to have stopped explaining themselves, no house markings, no visible working schedule, only the evidence of habitation in the shape of the land. She had passed this country three times in twelve years and had filed it as *transit, noted, no further action required.*

He was watching it with his whole body.

Not alarm. Not assessment. A sustained attention she found difficult to categorize because it was not the kind of attention she recognized as useful. Not strategic. The kind of attention you paid to something you were trying to reconcile with something you already knew, and couldn't quite. His gaze moved with the bank as the barge moved north, tracking something she could not identify from where she sat. The corner of his mouth changed—she had seen this expression in the first session, when she'd produced a river map and he'd looked at it for a long time without speaking.

He said a word. Quietly, to himself, in his own language. Not addressed to her.

She transcribed it. She marked it: *involuntary, unprompted, possibly a name for the thing observed, source unverified.*

A stand of broadleaved trees passed, the first yellowing of autumn at the tops, their reflection shaking apart in the barge's wake. He watched the reflection for a long moment. She watched him watch it.

Whatever he read there, she did not have the notation for it. She noted that she didn't. She filed this in the provisional category alongside the boots and the hands.

---

That night the sound came first.

The third hour past dark. She'd been sleeping in two-hour intervals and was in the shallow end of the second when the vibration reached the hull—not through air, through water and keel-wood, a low rhythmic grinding that her sleeping body registered before her waking mind did. She sat up. Orim was at the porthole.

"Rail yards," he said, without turning. "A kilometer north. The night freight."

She stood and moved to stand beside him.

The river ahead was dark. Then it was not.

The flash came from the north and moved south: blue-white, sharp at its edges. Not like fire, which climbed and spread. Like a signal passed hand to hand down a long corridor—moving faster than any one thing was moving, because no one thing was moving it. The river yards were lit in those bursts: dock pylons, the shallow-draft barges at anchor, the flat water between them. Each flash selected a different piece of the scene. The next flash showed nothing from the first. Then dark again. Then another pulse, further south, the fish carrying the signal forward.

She did not need to be told what it was. She had read it in the fauna documentation—chromatophore-scaled, established in the Rhine-analog over two hundred years, reactive to vibration. She had read the documentation and had not, until now, understood what it looked like. The documentation had not conveyed what it looked like.

Rowe had come awake somewhere in the first pulses. She hadn't heard him move. She found him standing to her right, close to the porthole, watching the river to the north.

He said, "Fire."

Her word. The one she'd given him on the second day: heat-source, burning thing. He said it quietly, in the specific tone of someone who knows they have the wrong word and has not yet been given the right one.

"No," Orim said.

He reached into his coat—she had learned not to watch this reach with anything except patience, it could produce the Rod, the knife, the contact sensitizer, or, on two occasions, a piece of dried fruit he consumed without offering to share—and produced nothing. He simply said a word.

She wrote it before she was fully aware she was writing. The motion was automatic; the notebook was already open in her lap. Three syllables, the second carrying a consonant cluster she would need a new notation for, the third falling away. A proper noun. Not a description. The name of the thing, which meant the Cauld had decided this thing was worth naming specifically, and she filed this immediately as useful data.

Rowe looked at Orim.

Orim pointed at the water.

Another pulse: blue-white, traveling south, the river yards lit briefly and then returned to dark. Three seconds of light. The hull creaked in the current. The grinding from the north continued, moving away now, the freight clearing the yards.

Rowe said the word back. He got the consonant cluster close—close enough that she understood him, wrong enough that she marked it for later revision—and Orim said nothing about the approximation, neither accepting nor correcting it. He pointed at the hull. Rowe said the word for hull. He pointed at the porthole frame. Rowe said the word for that. He pointed at the rope on the nearest cask, which Rowe didn't have yet, and Orim said it, and Rowe repeated it with the particular care he gave all new words—not the care of someone going slowly because the task is hard, but the care of someone placing a thing where it will need to stay.

The river outside went dark and stayed dark. The low grinding faded. She could hear the current and the creak of the deck above them and the sound of the barge master's breathing through the hatch boards, which was loud enough to suggest he was still asleep.

She closed her notebook. Then she opened it again and added a notation beside the word Orim had produced: *see fauna documentation, Schmalburg river-flash, chromatophore-scaled, Rhine-analog.* A reminder to herself to pull the origin-Sphere documentation when she had access to an archive. There was always origin-Sphere documentation. The Cauld documented everything.

---

The manifest had come the first night, placed on the cask nearest her head while she slept—by the barge master, probably, or by Orim, whose ability to move through enclosed spaces without disturbing anything was, she had concluded, not incidental.

She read it in order, which was not how she read manifests; she always turned to the back pages first. Manifests ran cargo from the bow aft—highest-value first, then grain, livestock, textiles, and at the end the small parcels, the things that wanted no notice. The last four pages of the *Houndstooth's* were unremarkable: salt fish in wax paper, a Calyx smithy's mechanical springs, a physician's bag listed as *sundries, medical* that was certainly something more specific but would have cost the physician's guild more to itemize.

She turned to page eight.

Six Scry data blocks.

She counted them twice. Six was not unusual for a commercial barge—the guilds had normalized data blocks in freight documentation during her grandmother's grandmother's time, arguing successfully that information was information and that the Vigil's earlier requirements, a Templar signature before each transfer and the blocks kept outside the standard manifest, were administrative overhead incompatible with commercial freight velocity. The Vigil had not had the stomach for the fight. Now the data blocks sat between grain and wine in every manifest going north on the Veil River, and the old signature requirement was a historical footnote in a filing system she'd worked in for fifteen years and had never had occasion to look up.

She read the first block. Sphere 14. Agricultural data. Contact duration 0.3 seconds. Standard.

The fifth block stopped her.

*Origin Sphere: [designation by number only, no catalogue entry]. Method: [contact, surface membrane, 1.4 seconds]. Data class: manufacturing, secondary. Subject: spring-steel alloying method (notation format: see attached sample). Observed at production facility. Transfer to: Henkin Consolidated Arms, Atrament branch.*

The notation format sample was attached: a half-sheet of heavy paper, folded once, with a column of symbols she had seen before. She had been seeing it, she realized, for twenty years. In commercial code. In freight documentation. She had thought it was Calyx's standard freight notation because she had never had reason to think otherwise, because the category in which she stored *freight notation* had never intersected with any other category in a way that required her to question its origin.

Rowe was three meters from her, curled against the far hull, breathing the slow uneven rhythm of bad sleep. His hands, even asleep, were closed around nothing in the specific way of a man who had recently been holding something and expected to need it again.

The notation format on the attached sample matched the notation format she had seen on his rifle's receiver plate.

She folded the manifest closed. Then she opened it again, because folding it closed did not change what was on page twelve, and she had not become a researcher by refusing to read things. She read all six blocks. By the time she reached the sixth—*Origin Sphere: [same designation, no catalogue entry], 2.1 seconds, manufacturing, primary, large-scale*—she had a category for it. It did not have clean edges. She filed it anyway, and held the corner of the manifest against her knee, and thought about edges.

"Six," Orim said, from the porthole.

"I counted."

"The fifth and sixth are from the same sphere. The one without a number."

"Yes."

"The notation on the sample sheet." He paused. He said nothing more in the particular way Orim said nothing more when he had said the thing he meant and was waiting to see whether she'd understood it.

She had understood it.

"How long have you known?" she said.

"Since we found him." He turned from the porthole. He had the look he got when he was going to say something that sounded like a joke and wasn't quite. "I've been looking at small things for sixty years. When someone reacts to a notation format, I notice. It's my gift."

His gift was Scrying, minor-class, contractual. Which meant that at fifteen he had pressed his palm against a membrane he had not been told was alive until afterward, and had done so eleven more times over the following six months until the contractual minimum was met. The Calyx guild paid his pension. He had never volunteered whether it had hurt. She had never asked.

"It might be coincidence," she said.

"It might," he agreed. "So might the rifle."

The rifle was in the barge master's strong-chest two decks above. She'd had it looked at in Bressant's harbor quarter by two dockyard smiths — Orim knew the men — who between them had sixty years of combined experience, and both had told her—separately and independently—that they had never seen anything like it, that the metal was something they did not have a name for, that the notation on the receiver plate was not any notation they recognized. The second smith had said, *It's very precisely made,* in the tone of someone who had expected to be unimpressed and was not.

---

She worked with Rowe for three hours each day. This had been Orim's suggestion, delivered as a professional opinion and understood by all three parties to be an order. *If you don't build a shared language,* he'd said, *you will spend the rest of this assignment guessing. I am too old to guess.*

The three hours were not three consecutive hours. They were assembled from whatever the barge's schedule and Rowe's unpredictable sleeplessness would permit. She kept the research notebook—not a vocabulary ledger, because she hadn't expected to need one, and a researcher who could not use available materials was a researcher who had missed the point of research—and in it she maintained two parallel columns: Cauld word on the left, her best phonetic rendering of whatever he said when shown the thing the word named on the right.

He had come to her with six words already built: her own name and title, approximated badly but recognizably; the word for *river;* the word for *write;* and the words for *no* and *yes.* Three she'd given him at Bressant. Three he'd assembled on his own, pointing at things and waiting for her to supply them, and she hadn't noticed until later that he'd been doing this because he'd already identified the methodology before she'd instituted it. She noted this. She filed it.

He learned the words for: hull, water, cold, sleep, eat, gun—he'd tried the Cauld construction for *iron-rod-that-speaks,* which was not the correct term but was technically accurate, and she'd offered him the correct one, and he'd shaken his head slowly and used hers from then on. Knife. Fire. Morning. Night. The word for *thank you,* which he'd asked for by pointing at her and making a gesture she'd eventually understood as gratitude, which she'd filed under *social vocabulary, emotional register,* a category she had not expected to need and which was, she noted, growing faster than she'd anticipated.

He did not learn the words casually. He held them. She could see the holding—the pause between hearing a word and repeating it, the pause of someone placing a thing carefully before releasing it. She had met three people in her life who learned languages this way. One had become a negotiator for the Templar Compact. The others were dead under circumstances unrelated to language acquisition, and she noticed the trait regardless.

---

At the second hour past midnight, on the third night of the passage, Rowe woke with a long creak of boards and his boots on the planking, and she was awake before he reached her corner.

He sat down against the adjacent cask. Not close enough to be a problem. Close enough to be an intention.

She'd left the lamp burning low, which she did when she expected interruption, which she did whenever she was somewhere she didn't know. He looked worse in lamplight than he had in Calyx. The welt along his left cheekbone had moved into the yellow-purple stage of a bruise working through its middle, and the skin under his eyes had the texture of skin that hadn't had adequate sleep for long enough that sleep alone wouldn't recover it. She'd put him between twenty-nine and thirty-two. The intake paperwork she'd found with him in the grain bin had been damaged. He looked older than either estimate.

He had the notebook. She didn't remember him taking it; she'd been asleep when she'd last had it. He'd taken it quietly. She filed this the same way she'd filed the boots.

He pointed at a line she hadn't written.

She held out her hand. He gave her the notebook, and she tipped it toward the lamp.

He'd added a line. The handwriting was small and precise—machinist's precision, formed by someone who worked with tolerances—four symbols in his own notation, and below them a line he'd drawn, and below the line her own question mark, copied from her margin notations. He had identified her question marks as question marks. She had missed this entirely.

She looked at him.

He pointed at the notebook, then at his mouth, then made the gesture she'd come to understand meant *I don't have the word.*

"Say it," she said. In Cauld.

He said it. Four syllables, the first two bunched together, the third with a consonant cluster her alphabet didn't have a single character for, the fourth falling away at the end as if he'd started with force and run out of room for it. She wrote it exactly, sound by sound, deferring meaning until she had enough structure to guess at it.

She held the paper up and pointed at the first syllable-group.

He pointed, without hesitation, at the cargo manifest.

She went very still.

Not the manifest entire. She looked again. He was pointing at page twelve—the page she'd marked with a sliver of wood, hours ago—and at the notation format on the attached sample sheet.

"You know this," she said.

He shook his head. Not *no.* Something more precise than no. He pointed at the symbols, then at his own eye, then—slowly, working through something she couldn't fully see—at the symbols again and his eye again and then outward, at the hull, at the river, at the dark beyond.

"You've seen it before," she said.

He held up both hands. Then he pointed at her vocabulary column, pointed at himself, and held up four fingers.

He wanted to give her four words.

She uncapped her pen.

He looked at the manifest for a long moment. Then he looked at the cargo hold—at the casks, the bales, the walls of the thing that contained them—and he said the first word.

She wrote it: three syllables, the first aspirated, the second long, the third a collapse at the back of the throat she represented with an approximation she'd revise later. She looked up.

He pointed at the wall of casks. At the hull. At the barge around them—the whole enclosed wooden structure, and, she thought, at something beyond it that was also enclosed, also structured, also built around a specific function that wasn't the function of a river barge.

*Factory,* she wrote in the left column.

He said the second word.

One syllable. Fricative at the start, open vowel. He pointed upward. She didn't understand. He pointed upward again, then held his hand in front of his face, palm out, and moved it slowly upward, tracing something rising.

She pointed upward. He shook his head. She tried the rising motion. He nodded, but not fully.

*Smoke, that which rises,* she wrote, with a question mark.

He looked at it. He nodded in the way of someone accepting an approximation that will have to do for now.

Third word. Longer. He pointed through the porthole at the gray that was beginning to be something other than absolute darkness—the place between night and morning that didn't have a clean name in most languages she knew.

*Morning,* she wrote.

He looked at the word. He looked at her. He said it back—her Cauld word, not his—and then said his own word again, and then hers, and looked at her with an expression she would have filed under *waiting for confirmation* except for the other thing in it that she had no file for. Something to do with the difference between a word that belonged to you and a word that was borrowed.

"Morning," she said. She pointed at his transcription and then at hers. "Both," she said.

Something in his face relaxed that she hadn't known was tensed.

He said the fourth word.

He said it immediately, flatly, in the tone of something that had been held in the mouth too long and needed to leave it. One syllable. Hard consonant at the front, the vowel falling off the back of it like something released.

She transcribed it.

He didn't point at anything.

He sat with his hands on his knees and looked at the four words on the page—his transcription, her transcription, the two columns running parallel—and she watched him decide something in the way she'd learned to watch him decide things, which was to look at his hands first because his face had more practice at stillness.

She looked at the four words. *Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.*

She looked at him.

He pointed at the words in order: first, second, third, fourth. Then at the manifest, at the notation format on page twelve. Then he made the gesture she'd come to understand as *there is more:* both hands out, spread, the space between them indicating size.

There was a longer sentence than four words. He was showing her four words the way you hand someone the corner of a document so they know the document exists.

She wrote: *Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.*

She wrote it again on a fresh page and held it up.

She pointed at the first word. "A factory," she said.

He nodded.

"A factory." She pointed at him.

His jaw tightened. He nodded again. Not resistance. The specific tension of someone confirming something they have been trying to say for longer than the conversation has existed.

"Smoke." She pointed at the second word.

He pointed at it and looked at the ceiling, and said his own word for it, and then hers, and she understood—not from reasoning but from the way his eyes moved between the two—that these were not the same word in two languages. They were two different things that occupied the same transcription because she hadn't yet had vocabulary to distinguish them. Her word for smoke was *smoke, industrial, that which rises from process.* His word was something that included process but also included what remained after process ended. Or perhaps what didn't remain. She hadn't heard enough of his language to know which.

She drew a small line between the two transcriptions and wrote a question mark.

He looked at it for a long moment. Then he took the pen—asking first, carefully, the way he always asked for things—and added a mark beside her question mark. Not an answer. An agreement that there was a question.

She took the pen back.

She looked at the four words. She looked at the notation on the attached sample sheet. She looked at the Scry data block on page twelve: *Origin Sphere: [designation by number only, no catalogue entry]. Observed at production facility.*

She looked at Rowe.

He was already watching her. He had the careful stillness of someone who had spent a significant portion of his time in the Cauld being watched by people who held authority over his circumstances, and had learned to be very quiet when that happened, because quiet people were easier to release than people who were noticed.

She said, in Cauld, very slowly: "You came from there."

She did not point at anything. She didn't need to.

He said, "Yes." Her word, not his. Chosen carefully.

---

She didn't sleep again.

She worked in the notebook until the light from the porthole was clear enough to read by without the lamp, and by then she had twelve new words in the framework and three subcategories that would need revision. Languages always did this—the same concept approached from different origins, wearing different clothes, meeting somewhere imprecise in the middle. She was beginning to know what she was looking for in this one, which was different from knowing what she'd find, but it was something.

Ardea came below at first light to count provisions, looked at Lyra, then at Rowe—asleep somewhere around the fifth hour, his hands finally open—and then back at Lyra with the expression of someone who had decided her questions were not yet her business.

"We'll see Atrament inside of four hours," Ardea said.

"I know."

"You look like you haven't slept."

"I've slept," Lyra said. Not untruthfully.

Ardea accepted this and went to count provisions.

Orim appeared an hour later with a cup of something he handed down without comment. She drank it. It was not quite tea and not quite anything else—it was what he made when he thought someone needed warming and didn't want to make a performance of caring about it. She had had it twice before. Both occasions had been situations she would have described, from sufficient distance, as bad.

"Four words," she said.

"I heard."

"You were supposed to be sleeping."

"I was listening. It's different." He settled his back against the hull. His joints cracked when he moved; he'd stopped noticing. "Four words that go together like a sentence."

"The shape of a sentence. I don't have the full thing yet."

"Factory," he said. "Smoke. Morning. Gone."

"Yes."

He was quiet for a moment. Then: "In my first contracted Scry session, the membrane I was placed in contact with was approximately the size of my palm. I was told it was a developed specimen. An old one. They didn't tell me what that meant until later." He looked out at the river through the porthole. "I was given nineteen questions to hold in my mind during contact. I managed twelve before the session ended. The information I retrieved was filed immediately by the guild recorder, and I was not permitted to review it." He paused. "Standard practice. I have never found it strange until recently."

Lyra said nothing.

"The notation on the manifest," he said. "The same as his rifle."

"Yes."

"Someone documented that Sphere very thoroughly." He didn't say *before.* He didn't say *before it burned.* He looked at the porthole, then at Rowe's sleeping shape, then at the manifest in her lap. "Thorough documentation. Filed in the commercial freight system. Sitting between grain and wine in every barge manifest going north for—" He stopped. "How long does a guild archive retain records?"

"Sixty years," she said. "The older ones are at the central repository in Vierna."

"Sixty years," he said. "At minimum." He turned back to the porthole. "Good documentation," he said, in the tone he used for things that were not good at all.

---

The sky changed before the smell did.

She noticed it while Orim slept and Rowe still had his eyes closed—the particular gray of Vierna's lowland cloud-cover, which she had watched for three days, had shifted slightly in tone. Not in temperature. In tone. A faint yellowish quality, as if the air between here and the horizon had been filtered through something warmer, something sustained and industrial, before it reached her. She was at the porthole when she noticed it. She noted it, filed it, did not say anything.

Twenty minutes later the smell arrived.

Coal first—not coal in storage, cold and damp, but coal that had been burning long enough to pass through all its stages and arrive at the particular char-and-mineral quality of a furnace in continuous operation. Behind it, rendered fat, the smell of tallow reduced to its components for candle and lubricant production. Behind that, something sharper: hot metal, the mineral edge she had catalogued the first time she'd made this passage, twelve years ago, and had filed as *Atrament entry signature, industrial, note for future reference.* She was noting it again. It sat in the same category. It did not sit with the same weight.

Rowe came up from his corner when the smell changed.

He was at the porthole before she turned—not crowding, simply present, the way he was present when something required his attention. He was breathing slowly. His face was doing the door-in-the-wind thing: the opening, the fraction of a second in which something underneath was visible, the closing again before she could inventory it. She watched it happen and let it happen without naming it.

The sound came before the stacks appeared.

She felt it in her sternum first. A low continuous vibration—not rhythmic like the night freight, but constant, sustained, the acoustic signature of processes that did not stop for darkness or morning or the turn of the season. Then it separated, as they drew nearer, into its components: the percussion of forges, regular as a pulse; a higher mechanical whine that had been running long enough to find its frequency and settle there; and underneath both a ground-note that was less a sound than a pressure against the chest, the kind of thing you registered as your body registering it rather than your ears.

That was when she knew they were close.

The stacks appeared at the river's bend, dark verticals against the yellowed sky: eight of them, then nine, then more as the bend opened and the full industrial waterfront came into sight. Tall. Taller than she remembered from her last passage, twelve years ago, on a different assignment with different purposes. Or the same height, and she was reading them differently, with different things she'd been carrying for three days. The smoke coming from the stacks was the color of the sky—already absorbed, already indistinguishable from the air around it—and it was moving south, the same direction they'd been moving, and she could not tell, at this distance, where the stacks ended and the air became the sky.

Rowe was very still beside her.

She did not turn to look at his face. She had the shape of the sentence. She did not need confirmation from his face right now—she needed to let the shape be the shape, to hold it in the provisional category alongside the boots and the hands and the word he'd said quietly to himself at the passing bank, and to not look at any of it too directly until she had more architecture.

*Factory. Smoke. Morning. Gone.*

She held the pen in her hand and did not write anything.

The stacks came toward them on the river. The smell was fully present now, coal and fat and hot metal, familiar as anything she'd known for thirty years of this work. The sound was inside the hull. The sky above the stacks was the color of the sky above the stacks, which was the color it had always been when she arrived at Atrament from the south in the morning hours with something she needed to do and not enough time to be careful about how she did it.

She looked at the four words on the open page of the notebook.

She added nothing to them yet. The architecture was still provisional. The subcategories still had loose edges.

She would have more data by nightfall.

[Beat 37]
ATRAMENT — THE FORGE KINGDOM

The sound was wrong before anything else was.

They had been on the highland road three hours, the rail line running below them in the valley where it curved south around the granite bluff before swinging back north toward the Schmalburg basin. The road ran above it, older than the rail, older than the Compact by the evidence of its construction — dressed stone in courses, the mortar long since gone gray and crumbling at the joints, but the stone itself still seated and true. This was the quality of old work on the major approaches: built by people who intended to move armies, not goods, and who had not considered that the armies might eventually be replaced by freight schedules. The road held well under the weight of four people who were not a siege.

Three hours in, Lyra heard the thunder.

Not weather. The sky above the northern highlands was the flat white of high autumn overcast, the kind that holds no storm, only the promise that the temperature will decline further before it improves. Not weather and not a natural sound: it was a deep, continuous vibration that came from somewhere ahead and below, something that the body registered before the ears confirmed it, a sustained bass note that had been going on longer than natural things sustain notes. She had been feeling it in the stone under her boots for perhaps a quarter of an hour before she understood it was not her own fatigue.

"We're getting close," Orim said.

He was ahead of her on the road, moving in the steady unhurried way of a man who has covered a great deal of ground over fifty years and has made his peace with the pace it requires. He had not looked back. He had not slowed.

"You've been here before," she said.

"I have crossed the Atrament border in eight different directions over forty years," he said. "The sound is the same in all of them. You stop hearing it after the second day. Then you leave, and you stop not-hearing it, and the quiet sounds wrong for a week." He stepped around a gap in the stone facing where a small spring had colonized the joint. "Or so I am told. I've never been here long enough for the second part."

The smell came next. Not the specific smell of anything, not yet, but the category of it: something being done to metal at extreme temperature, something being done to stone that stone was not built to survive, something chemical and particular underneath both of those that she could not name but that coated the back of the throat in a way that was not unpleasant and was not pleasant either. It was the smell of a place that had been doing a specific thing for a very long time.

Ardea had moved up beside her. The younger woman said nothing. She had her scarf pulled across the lower part of her face against the highland cold, and she walked with the particular posture of someone who has learned, by experience, that cold weather does less damage if you refuse to acknowledge it. She was watching the road ahead.

Rowe was behind them both. He was watching the smoke.

The smoke had become visible perhaps an hour ago — not from a chimney, not from a specific source, but as a general discoloration in the sky above the next ridge, a permanent grey-brown stain that the overcast absorbed but could not fully account for. He had been watching it since it appeared. He watched it now.

She had stopped trying to read his expressions in the first week. The register they occupied — the degree to which the Cauld's language had settled into his body, the degree to which the world he was walking through matched or didn't match whatever architecture he carried in his head from the one he'd come from — was not available to her through any surface she could read. He was attentive. He was, she had concluded, always attentive. What he was attending to at any given moment was his own business.


The valley opened below them when the road crested the ridge.

Lyra stopped.

She was not a person who stopped for things. She had been trained out of stopping — the vigil's long-watch discipline, the Templar's field doctrine about maintaining movement in unfamiliar territory, thirty years of applying both — and the discipline was sound and she had followed it. You catalogued as you moved. You did not give the landscape a performance of your reaction.

She stopped.

Below the ridge, the valley descended in a series of terraced drops, and on the largest of the terraces, perhaps a league distant, there was a fortification. That was the correct word for the shape of it: the angles of an old defensive structure, the towers at the corners, the curtain wall connecting them, the evidence of centuries of occupation in the thickness of the stone and the way the architecture assumed threat from every direction simultaneously. The builders had known what they were building. The walls had kept something out for a long time, or kept something in, or both at once, which was often the same thing.

The fortification was also, simultaneously, a production facility.

She had read descriptions of this. She had read the Compact documents' architectural language — *integrated manufacturing installation, castle-form adaptive reuse, Atrament Compact Year 837, ongoing modification as per Hearth Council decree* — and she had formed an image from those words: a factory built adjacent to a castle, perhaps, or a castle serving as the foundation for a factory, or some transitional state between the two in which you could still identify where one ended and the other began.

The image was wrong in a specific way.

There was no between. The curtain wall of the fortification was the wall of the factory floor. They were the same wall. The old towers at the four corners had been cored out and fitted with furnace stacks that rose from what had been the battlements, the stone of the parapets now serving as collar-rings for iron chimneys thick as well shafts. Smoke came from three of the four stacks in a sustained dark column that bent southeast in the highland wind, which meant the production cycle was continuous and had been continuous long enough that the smoke had established its own local weather pattern — a permanent discoloration in the sky above the eastern valley that you would not notice if you lived under it.

The fortification walls themselves had been cut through, not once but in six places she could count from the ridge, with apertures large enough to drive a loaded freight wagon through. The apertures were not windows and not gates: they were utility openings for the specific dimensions of what the facility's internal process required to enter and exit. Raw material in on the eastern side. Finished product out on the western. The wall serving its function as factory wall and not pretending to any other function.

There was nothing apologetic about it. That was the thing she had not anticipated. The architecture did not apologize for itself. The castle had been a castle. It was now also a factory. Both of these things were simply true of the same stone, and the stone had no opinion.

"Year 841," Orim said, from beside her. He had, at some point, caught up. "The Hearth Table authorized the first interior conversion under the Compact manufacturing expansion protocols. Before that it was a garrison facility." He looked at the stacks. "Before the garrison it was a watchtower complex against incursion from the valley floor. Before that it was something older that the Atrament historical record doesn't discuss, which usually means there was an argument about who built it that nobody won."

"How old," she said.

"The stone courses in the base walls read as pre-Compact. Probably pre-House settlement period. Someone was keeping watch from this ridge before the Houses existed." He looked at the smoke. "They're keeping a different kind of watch from it now."

The sound was much louder here. The vibration had resolved itself into specific components: the repetitive thud of forging hammers, very large, at a speed that meant automated rather than human; the deeper sustained note of furnaces at operating temperature; a rhythmic compression noise from somewhere inside the walls that she couldn't identify from the outside. All of it running simultaneously. All of it running continuously.

She started moving again.


Below the fortification, in the yards between the outer defensive perimeter and the approach road, the Heloths moved.

She had worked with Heloths at the Ocipheus Station. The vigil's courier models were purpose-built for single-rider long-distance travel: lean, efficient, designed in a Sphere-5 analogue of something that covered open terrain without complaint. You developed a sense of them if you rode them long enough — not fondness, precisely, but familiarity with the specific qualities of a machine that did one thing very well and declined to do anything else. She had ridden the same courier Heloth for three years and felt approximately nothing when it was retired.

The Heloths in the yards below were different in dimension and different in purpose. Heavy-cargo variants, the kind built for production facility logistics rather than messenger work: wider, lower, the articulated arm-housing fitted for cradle loads rather than saddle points. They moved between the factory entrances and the freight staging area in the specific repetitive pattern of constructs running fixed-route tasks, the efficiency of something that had been calibrated for a route and would run that route until the maintenance interval interrupted it. Three of them were stationary at what she recognized, even at this distance, as construct maintenance stations.

The maintenance stations glowed.

Orange, bioluminescent, the specific warm color of embers viewed through smoky glass. The ember-fungi. She had read about it in the Ocipheus archive's ecological annex — *Sphere-9 introduced flora, established in the valley complexes circa Year 1031, grows on surfaces carrying Catalyst-adjacent chemical discharge, colony self-sustaining once established* — but reading about a bioluminescent growth that coated the maintenance stations of an Atrament construct yard was not the same as standing on a ridge above one and seeing the orange wash on stone that had been there before the Compact, before the Houses, before anyone had a name for the thing that was glowing on it now.

In the daylight, the glow was subtle. Visible only because she was looking for it and because the overcast kept the ambient light low. She noted the coverage: dense, not patchy, every maintenance station in the visible yard running orange at its base. Then she filed it and kept moving.

Orim said: "I should mention that at night, from a ridge, you can read the machine yard layout entirely from the fungi. Every station, every maintenance point, every section of wall that takes spatter from the Catalyst discharge during the cleaning cycle." He paused. "This will become relevant."

"When."

"When we need to see the yards at night," he said, with the tone of someone who has already planned several steps ahead and is releasing information at the rate he judges useful.

She looked at him.

He looked at the road ahead.


The approach road through the valley ran through three production settlements between the ridge fortification and the Schmalburg basin, and none of them were towns. She had understood this in the abstract — Orim had described the valley's settlement pattern with the brevity of a man who has delivered the same description enough times to have edited it to its essentials — but understanding the abstract was not the same as walking through it.

The first settlement was three large buildings and a dormitory block. The chimneys produced a yellow-grey smoke that meant catalyst-adjacent chemical processing at stage two, which she knew because she had read the Atrament production register's notation for chimney smoke classification well enough to place it by color. The workers visible in the yard between the buildings moved with the efficiency of a population that had organized itself around a production schedule rather than around meals and sleep, which was itself a kind of organization, not incompatible with meals and sleep, only different in the ordering of them.

Orim said: "They don't call them towns. They call them hearth-stations. The numbering is by production sequence, not geography. Hearth-Station Twelve is not near Stations Eleven and Thirteen. It's in the twelfth stage of the production chain." He looked at the dormitory block. "The dormitory architecture is standard. Same design across all the valley complexes. Efficient use of the floor plan."

Ardea said: "It's very clean."

He looked at her.

"I was expecting it to be dirtier," she said. "Everything that size, making everything it's making. I was expecting more debris."

"Debris costs," Orim said. "Debris is raw material that has left the production cycle prematurely. The Hearth Table worked out approximately four centuries ago that the most cost-effective form of cleanliness is understanding waste as escaped product." He looked at the clean yard. "The yard is clean because every scrap that lands in it has a value assigned to it, and the value is recovered."

Ardea was quiet for a moment.

"That's worse somehow," she said.

"Yes," Orim said.

At the second settlement, they stopped briefly at the edge of a maintenance yard. A heavy-cargo Heloth was being serviced at one of the ember-fungi stations — two workers on its back housing running the Catalyst-channel clearing procedure, the same one she knew from the Ocipheus courier maintenance cycle, adapted here for the larger chassis. The ember-fungi cast its orange wash over the whole surface of the station, the workers visible in it as shapes rather than details. One of them said something to the other, a brief something, and the other responded in a way that produced a short laugh, the ordinary currency of people doing a routine task in a cold yard.

Ardea stood at the edge of the maintenance yard and watched them for a moment. The Heloth stood motionless under the procedure. The workers continued. Ardea looked at them in the particular way she had of looking at things that she intended to remember but was not sure she had a category for yet.

She moved on.


The staging area appeared at the valley junction, where the approach road met the east-west freight road and the valley floor widened enough for the specific geometry of a temporary military formation: flat ground, sufficient area, access to the eastern supply routes, close enough to the valley's rail line for logistics without being on it.

Six supply wagons under canvas. Three infantry columns in formation, equipment stacked at their feet, the arrangement of people who have been told to wait and have been waiting long enough to have developed opinions about the quality of the waiting. Two heavy-cargo Heloths moving between the columns with equipment loads that were not exercise-weight — she could read the load distribution from the Heloth's gait adjustment, the subtle forward compensation of a construct carrying something denser than it was calibrated for.

She counted the wagons twice. The second count confirmed six.

The wagons' canvas was secured with canonical property authorization seals: the circle-and-line impression in red wax on the securing ropes, the Liturgy's administrative mark for goods in transit under inter-House canonical review. Supply wagons under canonical property seal were, under the terms of the Compact, subject to inspection only by the originating authority.

Which meant they were not subject to inspection by anyone on this road.

She looked at the canvas. She looked at the columns. She looked at the heavy-cargo Heloths and the load distribution and the direction of travel — east, toward the highland approach, which was the direction of the Wall rotation resupply route.

In seven years of Transmutation archival research at the Ocipheus Station, she had read every Atrament production record filed with the Liturgy's central office under the Compact's disclosure provisions. She knew the seasonal movement patterns of the valley compounds. She knew when they moved south toward Lacerta for export, when they moved north toward the Wall patrol resupply, when they stayed in the valley complexes for the Heloth maintenance cycles.

What she was looking at was stage-five supply movement.

The Wall deployment supply doctrine ran five sequential stages. You initiated stage five after stages one through four were complete, positioned, and confirmed. Which meant the canonical property sealed wagons she was watching were not the beginning of a supply chain. They were the end of one. Stages one through four had already moved.

She had been counting supply movements since the Atrament border crossing. She had noted them without understanding the sequence. She understood it now.

The formations at the eastern staging ground had no announced exercise in any Compact document she had reviewed. The supply chain they represented had no disclosed transit purpose in the inter-House notification system. And the canonical property authorization class on the wagons required countersignature by the Canon Immaculate — not a routine cross-border authorization, but the class reserved for operations that required the Liturgy's formal presence in the operation's legal architecture.

She stood at the road junction and looked at the columns and the wagons and the Heloths and all of it pointing east, toward the highlands, toward the Wall, and she filed it.

It went into the same space as the theft, as the Relic's absence, as Prelacze's authorization to suspend her transit authority. It went into the same space as things she did not yet have a complete picture for but whose shape was becoming visible at the edges.

She would finish the picture when she had more of the edges.


Rowe was standing at the road edge, slightly apart from the rest of them, watching the staging area.

He had been watching it since they rounded the valley bend. His face had the quality she had seen twice before on the journey — the three-second expression, internal, specific, the expression of a man for whom the present has briefly become a transparency laid over something he already carries in his body. The staging area, the columns, the equipment loads, the faces of the soldiers who had been standing in formation since whatever time this morning they had been told to stand in formation. He was reading something in them that she did not have the same language for.

It lasted longer than three seconds this time. Then he was watching the road ahead again, the way he always watched it.

She did not ask.

He had four words of Cauld. *Wait. No. That way.* And one word that she was fairly sure meant something on the order of *I understand* but that he used in contexts that also suggested *I have seen this before* and possibly *this is the same thing, wearing different clothes.* It was doing a great deal of work for one word.

Whatever the staging area had told him, the word would not cover it. She let it settle.


They descended from the highlands as the afternoon stretched toward evening, the approach road switchbacking through the lower terraces, and below them, at the bottom of the descent, the Schmalburg basin opened.

The city was built on a river confluence: the Veil's main valley tributary meeting the wider floor at a bend that had, over the centuries, silted into a flat harbor bottom suited to the barge traffic that serviced the Lacerta borderlands route. The dockyard was on the western bank. It ran along the river for what looked, from above, like half a league — old stone from the garrison period, the curtain-wall design she recognized from the fortification on the ridge, built to hold a different kind of pressure. Alongside it, Atrament's machine yards had colonized every available ground between the dockyard wall and the rail line, which meant the dockyard wall was now the western edge of an industrial complex that had grown to meet it from the east.

The city proper climbed the eastern bank in the steep-sided way of cities that had been built inside a defensive perimeter and then outgrown it while maintaining the original angles. The houses that had gone up outside the old walls were visibly later — different stone, different coursing, the compressed construction of a population that had more people than perimeter and had decided to stack them rather than spread them. The taverns and market halls were in this outer ring.
