The old city inside was institutional: the dock authority, the production offices, the Hearth Table's local representative building with the Atrament seal above the door.

"The Veil," Orim said, from beside her. He was looking at the river. "Named before the Atrament valley was settled. Whatever the Vierna territory called the river, Atrament translated the name when they took the upper valley in Year 741 and kept the translation because the original had been accurate. It covers. It obscures the movement of things on its surface." He looked at the color of the water, which was visible even at this distance, even in the fading afternoon light, as not quite right. "It has been doing that work very effectively for the last two hundred years."

The water ran brown. Not mud-brown, not storm-brown. The specific brown of something introduced rather than something natural, the color of a river that had been receiving the chemical byproduct of the valley's Catalyst processing for generations and had stopped pretending to be anything other than what it was.

She had read numbers about this. She had nodded at the numbers in the way you nod at statistics that are bad in the abstract.

The river from above was not abstract.

"The processing discharge," she said.

"The processing discharge," he agreed. "The Compact's environmental provisions require containment above ninety percent efficiency. The Atrament production documentation reports ninety-one percent." He looked at the river. "I have stood at this ridge three times in forty years. The river was brown each time."

"The documentation may be accurate," she said. "Ninety-one percent containment of an output this large is still nine percent discharge."

"The documentation may be accurate," he said, in exactly the tone she had used.


The approach road curved along the ridgeline above the city's eastern edge before it descended to the lower gate. From the ridge, in the last of the daylight, she could see the dockyard wall clearly.

There was construction on it.

Not repair work — not the patching of eroded mortar or the replacement of damaged facing, the routine maintenance of old stone. Construction: scaffolding erected at three points along the wall's western face, dressed stone being added above the existing coursing, precision work expanding the height of the wall above the machine yard. The stone being set was dressed to a quality that required a different hand than the original garrison work. The mortar lines, visible at this distance as dark seams in the lighter facing, were even and fine. This was skilled work. This was the kind of work that could not be done by the Heloths.

Below the scaffolding, along the base of the dockyard wall, there were workers.

Not construct operators. Not Atrament production-settlement labor. The workers below the scaffolding were doing the material-handling work of the construction site: moving the dressed stone from the staging area at the wall's base to the scaffold foot, lifting the smaller pieces, managing the rope-and-pulley system that carried the larger ones up to the workers setting the courses above. They worked with the specific steady efficiency of people who had been doing this long enough that the work had become unremarkable to them — not mechanical, not automated, but habituated in the way that difficult repeated labor becomes habituated, the body settling into the rhythm of the task and the mind going somewhere it can be while the task continues.

Lyra looked at them.

She looked at the dressed stone. She looked at the mortar lines on the courses being set, the quality of the fitment, the way the expansion would hold. She looked at the scaffold and the rope-and-pulley system and the staging area at the wall's base, organized with the efficiency of a construction site that had been running long enough to find its own order.

She looked at the workers again.

She looked away.

She looked at the machine yards beyond the dockyard wall — the Heloths, the maintenance stations with their ember-fungi growth that would be more visible in an hour when the light had finished failing. She looked at the staging ground they had passed on the valley floor, the columns in their formations, the supply wagons under the canonical seals. She looked at the approach road below, where the evening foot traffic was thinning as the city pulled inward for the night.

She did not look for a word.

She filed it.


Orim made the decision when she opened her mouth to ask about evening transit into the city.

"No," he said. "Not tonight." He looked at the city below, at the dockyard, at the approach road. "We see it from here first." He moved back from the ridge edge, toward the scrub growth above the road, where the rock provided cover and a fire would not be visible from the valley. "The city knows something is happening. Pre-deployment, your city develops an awareness. It watches who walks in." He set down his pack. "We watch it tonight. We go in tomorrow when we know what it's watching."

She considered arguing with this.

She did not argue with this.

They made the camp in the scrub above the road, low fire, dry wood that Ardea found in the rock crevice where last season's growth had wedged itself and dried. The fire was small enough to produce almost no visible smoke. The cold at this elevation, after the sun finished, was serious — the kind of cold that required acknowledgment rather than refusal, that settled into the joints with the particular attention of a host who knows the guests have no alternative accommodation.

They ate. They said very little.

And then the dark finished coming in, and Schmalburg went from a city visible in its architecture to a city visible in its glow.


The ember-fungi.

She had noted them in the daylight as a subtle orange wash on the machine yard maintenance stations, visible only because she was looking for them. In the dark, from the ridge, they were the machine yards.

Every maintenance station in the dockyard's machine yard complex — she began counting, lost count, started again, reached eleven before the furthest visible points blurred into each other — was outlined in orange-bioluminescent growth that had colonized the Catalyst-discharge surfaces over the years since the Sphere-9 introduction and had not stopped. The yard layout was readable by them. The maintenance routing between stations was readable by the wear-patterns of traffic that had kept the fungi thin in the walked paths. The sections of wall that took spatter during the construct cleaning cycle were outlined in denser growth, the brightest points in the yard.

In the orange light, the construction scaffolding on the dockyard wall was also visible.

The workers were still there.

She could see them by the ember-fungi wash off the maintenance stations below — not directly lit, but visible in the reflected orange that reached the scaffold base, the shapes of people moving material, the rope-and-pulley system still running, the steady unhurried work continuing past the hour when Atrament's production settlements rang their shift bells.

She watched them for a moment. She watched the mortar lines being set in the new courses above, patient, precise, one stone at a time.

She did not have a word for it.

"The staging sequence," she said, to Orim.

He was sitting against the rock, both hands around his cup, watching the city the way he watched things he was not in a hurry about. "Tell me what you have."

She told him. She told him what she had counted at the border crossing and at the valley junction and on the approach road — the sequential supply movements, the stage numbers, the canonical authorization class on the sealed wagons, the Wall deployment doctrine she had read seven years ago and had not thought about since.

He listened. He did not interrupt.

When she finished, he looked at the city for a while.

"They were never looking for the Relic," he said finally.

"No."

"They knew where it was going when they arranged the theft. Pallor's destination was part of the arrangement." He looked at the ember-fungi glow on the machine yards. "The theft was a mechanism for staging a deployment. The Canon required a legal basis for moving supply wagons under canonical property authorization into position for a Wall-approach operation without inter-House notification. The Relic's recovery — a Liturgy asset, under canonical review, requiring the Liturgy's field authority — provided it."

"It also required suspending the field authority of the Templar assigned to the case," she said. "My transit documentation would have intersected the supply routes. I would have read the stage-five sequence eventually."

"As you have."

"I was supposed to be delayed long enough that the deployment was complete before I could report it."

Orim looked at his cup. He looked at the city. He looked at the staged columns on the valley floor, still barely visible in the fading ember-fungi light at the edge of her vision. "That's the charitable version," he said.

She said nothing.

"The less charitable version," he said, "is that you were meant to be the one holding the Relic when this resolves. That a Templar with a thirty-year documented record of absolute loyalty to the Canon Immaculate, found in possession of a stolen artifact recovered from the House that the Liturgy's deployment will implicate, serves a specific function in the institutional record that the deployment produces." He paused. "But I find less charitable versions less useful unless they change what we're doing."

"They don't change what we're doing," she said.

"Then we proceed."

Rowe was at the edge of the firelight, not quite within it. His rifle was against the rock beside him and his hands were in his lap and he was watching the city below with the particular stillness of someone who is making a record without a notebook. The ember-fungi glow reflected faintly off the Veil tributary below the dockyard, orange light on brown water, the specific color of this place at this time of night.

He said nothing.

He had nothing yet to say it with.

But he had been watching the construction on the dockyard wall for a long time, and his face had the quality she was learning to read as *I know what this is.* Not the three-second recognition he showed to geography, to the familiar bend of rivers or the color of specific stone. This was something that had settled in rather than flashed past.

She would not know what it was. Not tonight. Perhaps not until he had enough Cauld to tell her. Perhaps not until then.


She stayed awake after the others slept.

The cold was a reason. The thinking was the reason. She let the fire go low and sat with her back to the rock and looked at the city and the ember-fungi glow and the construction work on the dockyard wall that was still running — she could see the movement on the scaffold, slow and steady, the rope-and-pulley system completing its cycles, one dressed stone at a time.

She worked through the canonical authorization sequence from the beginning.

The stage-five supply movement. The canonical property seals. The authorization class that required the Canon Immaculate's countersignature. She worked through what that countersignature implied about the timing — when it had to have been issued, how far in advance of the stage-five movement, what the earlier stages had looked like and when they had moved and whether she had seen any evidence of them without recognizing them for what they were. She had. She had seen three separate movements that she had noted and not yet filed in the correct category. They filed now. They fit.

The deployment sequence had been running since before the theft.

The theft had been the completion of a supply sequence that was already in motion. The Relic's recovery — her chase, her authorization, her dispatch from the Ocipheus Station — was the fifth stage of something that had been building since before she knew there was anything building.

She worked through this several times. The conclusion did not change.

The deployment was prepared. It was staged. The eastern highland approach was positioned. The canonical authorization chain was in place, countersigned by the Canon Immaculate, sealed under the inter-House canonical review provisions that insulated it from notification requirements until the operation was underway.

All that was required was the order.

She looked at the city. She looked at the ember-fungi glow on the machine yards, steady and orange and indifferent, fed by the Heloth exhaust and the Catalyst discharge and the long manufacturing night that Atrament ran without stopping. She looked at the construction on the dockyard wall — the fine-work stone being set in the dark, the workers moving material at the scaffold base, the mortar drying in the cold air.

She looked at them for a long moment.

She looked at the city.

She looked east, toward the highland approach, where the staged columns were waiting for an order that had not yet arrived.

When the eastern sky began to separate itself from the highland above it — the barely perceptible differential that arrived an hour before dawn, lighter by a degree that the eyes could not quite commit to — she put her hands in her pockets and looked at the valley below and the Veil tributary's brown water and the ember-fungi glow still warm on the machine yards.

First light. The harbor office. What the Sallander's registry showed. What the Dockhands' Association secretary knew. West before noon.

She had ten days behind her and the rest of the road ahead of her, and Schmalburg in the morning, and a staged army pointing in the direction she needed to go.

She began working through the authorization sequence again from the top.

She had not missed anything.

She went through it one more time to be certain.

[Beat 38]
THE REVIEW SESSION

---

She set the instruments in order before the second candle burned down to its mark. Three for the session itself, one for the supplementary materials intake, one for the disposition record, one for the archival certification. The sixth she kept blank until the session's shape was known. She had learned, in three years of canonical scribing, that sessions rarely ended where they began, and a blank instrument was better than the wrong one already written out.

Chamber Three was cold in the way of rooms that held important things infrequently. The stone kept cold against itself like a resource, spent it into the air in slow degrees. The brazier at the far wall was lit but the ceiling ate the warmth before it reached the scribing table. She could feel her fingers, which was good, but she could feel them precisely in the way that meant she would not feel them much longer if she sat still.

She did not sit still. She organized the instruments. She checked the registration stamps. She sharpened a second pen to have it ready, because something always happened to the first one at exactly the wrong moment, and in three years of canonical scribing she had learned to plan for the failure of the first pen.

The session convocation, which she had herself copied three days prior, was stamped and folded and sitting at the head of the table on the Canon Immaculate's side. Not because Prelacze would need to refer to it — she had attended eight sessions presided by the Canon and she had learned that Prelacze did not refer to instruments in sessions; he carried the citations in his head — but because the convocation at its designated position was procedurally correct, and Prelacze ran correct sessions.

The Canon arrived before the delegates.

This was also correct. The Canon Immaculate presided, and presiders did not enter after the people they were presiding over. She had understood this at her first session and it had not changed since. What she had not known the first time was that the Canon arrived specifically at the point in the preparation where everything was nearly ready but the heat had not yet fully reached the room. She was fairly certain this was not deliberate. She was not entirely certain.

"Scribe Athen-Moor," Prelacze said. He said it as acknowledgment of a correctly arranged room, not as greeting. She had heard him say her name in eight sessions and had concluded this was the most his tone would do in her direction, which was fine. She was furniture. Competent furniture.

"Canon." She kept her pen in hand.

He took his place at the table's head and reviewed the convocation instrument without sitting. He was a man of sixty-something years who moved through institutional spaces the way certain rivers moved through stone — not rushing, not wasting effort, occupying whatever channel the room provided. He read the convocation once, which she knew because she had done it herself three days prior, and set it down at precisely its correct position.

"The Lacerta delegate will have prepared a brief," he said. "Allow her to complete the reading before noting the time." A pause. "She has traveled three days for this."

She wrote that down on her working copy — *allow delegate to complete reading* — then crossed it out because it was not her assignment to record what the Canon anticipated, only what the session produced.

The delegates arrived together, which meant they had been waiting in the approach corridor and had been guided in at the same time, standard form for contested review sessions. She knew the Lacerta delegate from her files: Adnora Keist, senior regional attaché, nine years of Lacerta coastal documentation on file in the canonical registry. The Carnyx commander she knew by his intake certification, filed six weeks ago: Aldec Vorn, Carnyx Territorial Authority, Wall sector eastern designation. He carried a scroll case with four rolls inside it. She knew this because she had processed the inventory certification when his materials were logged at the station entrance.

They came in with the careful arrangement of people who had been told to appear collaborative and who had decided, independently, that this was not entirely wrong.

She dated the session instrument. She noted the attendees. She wrote the Canon's name and designation. She prepared to copy what was said.

---

Keist read her brief in twelve minutes. She had, as Prelacze had anticipated, prepared it in writing, and she read it precisely without looking up, which was not what frustrated witnesses usually did. Frustrated witnesses spoke. Keist read, which meant she had decided her frustration was not relevant to the document and that the document was what would stand in the record. A person who had decided this was a person who understood something about canonical archives.

The brief described the western Wall sector deterioration in detail: seventeen survey points along the western perimeter measured at eight-month intervals over three years. In eleven of the seventeen points, the current measurement fell outside the established baseline range. In four of the eleven, the variance exceeded the canonical threshold for "acceptable variation" as defined in the Liturgy's own vigil standards documentation. Keist cited the document number. She cited the page. She cited the threshold value. Her people had done their work.

Vega copied it. She wrote the survey points and the variances. She wrote the document citation. She wrote the threshold value.

Prelacze listened without expression.

Vorn's presentation was shorter. He unrolled the maps on the table — she had anticipated this and cleared the space — and said: "Eastern sector survey. Current against fifteen-year baseline."

That was all he said. The maps were the presentation.

She was not supposed to study materials in the same moment they were being presented; her station was to the side and slightly back, and her assignment was to copy the record of what was said, not to read the documents themselves. But she noted two things from where she sat, because she could not stop herself from noting them: the old survey line was drawn in faded brown ink, and the new survey line was drawn in clean black ink, and between the two lines there was a gap that in the central section of the eastern survey was wider than the station courtyard was long. And: in three places along the southeastern passage, the black ink had moved into territory marked, in the old survey's legend, as *maintained transit corridor, canonical approach authorization required.*

She looked at her scribing table. She wrote: *eastern sector survey presented, four map sheets, submitted for archival. Current measurement against fifteen-year baseline. See submitted materials.*

She wrote what was there. That was her assignment.

"The Carnyx petition will have the maps included in the session record," said Prelacze. He had not looked at them. He had been looking at the window, the high stone window with its inch of grey light at the top where the cold came in. "Scribe."

"Canon."

"Noted in the record."

"Noted."

Keist said, in the flat voice of someone who had given up on eloquence: "The perimeter is not stable."

Prelacze turned from the window. "The Liturgy's vigil record spans seven hundred years," he said. "Over that period, the vigil has documented thirty-one instances of boundary variation exceeding the baseline threshold in one or more sectors. Twenty-eight of those variations self-corrected within twenty-four months. The remaining three showed continued movement over longer periods. All three were within the documented range for cyclical variation, per the vigil's own standards framework." A pause. "The current measurements fall within that range."

He said this without hesitation. He said it with the quality of someone reciting something true. She supposed it was true. She had not consulted the vigil record herself and would not have cause to unless she were assigned its archival processing, which she was not.

Keist said: "The transit corridors—"

"Are under review. The process for contested approach territories in Wall-adjacent sectors requires a formal assessment by the Order of the Wall's sector command, submitted to the canonical registry, and processed through the standard cycle. The process has been initiated."

He did not say *I initiated it.* He said *the process has been initiated.* In three years, she had come to understand that this was not the same thing.

Vorn said nothing. He was rolling one of the maps back up with the careful motion of a person who had decided this was not a room in which the maps would do further work today.

Keist said: "Acknowledged." The word landed flat on the table.

Prelacze looked at her directly for a moment. "The Lacerta petition's documentation is noted in the record and will inform the sector review. This session has received and registered the presented materials." He said it without warmth and without coldness, in the way you say things that are institutional and true and final. "No immediate action is indicated. Continued monitoring protocols are authorized."

She wrote: *no immediate action indicated. Continued monitoring protocols authorized.*

She wrote: *Lacerta and Carnyx concerns noted in the record.*

She did not write: *the maps are in the archival queue and the lines on them say the cavity is larger.*

That was not her assignment. Her assignment was the record of what was determined.

---

The delegates left first. Keist did not look at Prelacze on her way out, which was controlled. Vorn paused at the place where the maps had been spread on the table. He did not pick them up — they were already in Vega's hands, because session materials submitted for archival moved to the notary at close. He looked at the empty table for a moment, then went.

Prelacze signed the session instruments she presented. He signed at the table, not at corridor pace. He read each instrument before signing. He was not in a hurry and had not been in a hurry and she had never once seen him in a hurry about canonical instruments, which was either a virtue or a specific kind of confidence, and she had not yet decided which.

"The Lacerta delegate's documentation," he said, not looking up from the fourth instrument. "Complete archival processing. Sector review intake will require cross-reference."

"I'll set up the cross-reference."

He signed the fourth. He looked at the fifth. "The Carnyx materials."

"I have them."

"Archived without action."

"Yes, Canon."

He signed the fifth. He handed them back. He went.

She stood at the scribing table with the instruments in one hand and the Carnyx map case in the other. The brazier had been burning for three hours and it was warmer now than it had been. She could no longer feel this as warmth because her body had gone numb past a certain point and then reported warmth when the warmth arrived, and she trusted neither report.

She sat down. She put the instruments aside and opened the map case.

The maps were on good parchment. Vorn's cartographers had done careful work — precise people who understood that a map was not useful if you could argue with the line. The old survey was faded brown, hand-drawn, dated in the lower right corner fifteen years back. Before the secondary monitoring protocols, before the last border reclassification, before any of the documentation she had spent three years handling.

The new survey was in clean black ink. Same scale. Same survey points, each marked with a small cross and a notation number that matched the measurement log on the second sheet. She checked the measurement log. Precise: triangulation references, distances in standard canonical units, margin of error explicitly stated. The margin of error was small. Vorn's people had not left room for arguing with the line.

In the northwestern sector of the eastern survey, the current line sat two hundred and thirty meters east of the baseline. She looked at the scale notation in the corner. The station courtyard — she walked it every day, she knew its dimensions — would fit inside that gap once. Comfortably.

In the central sector, the current line was three hundred and eighty meters east of the baseline. She looked at the scale again. The courtyard would fit perhaps twice.

In the southeastern passage — the one marked in the old survey's legend as *maintained transit corridor, canonical approach authorization required* — the current line intersected the corridor edge. Not crossed it. Intersected the inner boundary of the double line that marked the corridor's maintained status.

Touching was not crossing. She noted this. She noted it honestly: the line was touching, not crossing, and that was a meaningful distinction if you were making canonical arguments.

The maps did not make canonical arguments. They had measured what was there and drawn what they found.

She rolled the first map closed. She rolled the second. She placed them in the map case. In the disposition column she wrote: *archived without action, per Canon Immaculate session determination.* She sealed the case with the Registry stamp. She put it in the archival queue.

She picked up her pen and did not write anything for a moment.

She had been good at her work before she became too good at it. She was not sure when those two states had separated — somewhere in the second year, she thought, somewhere around the time she stopped only seeing the instruments and started seeing what the instruments were about. A notary was not supposed to be about the content. A notary was supposed to be about the form: the correct certification, the correct stamp, the correct procedure. She had excellent procedure. She was not the one who decided what was correct to do about maps showing a cavity three hundred and eighty meters larger than fifteen years ago. That was the Canon's function. He had exercised it. She had written it down.

She was very good at this.

---

She was in the corridor outside the administrative wing, heading for the registry with the session instruments for formal filing, when she heard them coming from the eastern approach.

Seven soldiers. Her mind catalogued them before she had decided to do it — three years of processing complement logs and supply authorizations had left her with the specific reflex of reading equipment profiles the way she read certification stamps: automatically, without effort, out of long habit. Heavy weather-treatment on the outer layers: Wall-approach rated, she knew this from supply authorizations. Boot construction: the specific profile she had filed Carnyx requisition instruments for, the design rated for the eastern approach roads. Sidearm configuration: Carnyx territorial, the variant that had appeared in the registry documentation after the border reclassification. Not Ocipheus garrison — she knew the garrison faces and none of these were from that catalogue.

Carnyx. Traveling soldiers from outside the station. Eight of them, counting the factor guiding them through the administrative wing with the deliberate carefulness of someone doing a routine procedure that had been specified to her as non-routine.

She pressed herself to the wall to let them pass. The corridor was narrow. They went by close enough that she could smell the road on them — cold and dust and the dry-cold of high-ground travel, the smell she associated with the eastern approach documentation, the engineering reports and the maintenance authorizations that she processed but did not read closely because they were not her assignment. The last soldier looked at her as he passed. Not suspicion. The reflexive situational awareness of someone trained at a depth where awareness did not require thought. He clocked her, filed her, moved on.

She waited until they turned the corner. Then she continued to the registry.

The intake log for the specialist deployment was in the pending queue on her desk. She had received it this morning, before the session. She picked it up.

*SPECIALIST DEPLOYMENT — SINTER ZONE APPROACH PREPARATION.*

She held the instrument. She read the form fields: seven names in the personnel column, standard roster format. Equipment certification attached. Authorization chain: a single reference number she did not immediately recognize, which meant a series she hadn't encountered before, which happened with restricted category instruments. She wrote the reference number on her working copy for later.

She read the category designation again.

She had seen "Sinter Zone" in maintenance authorizations — the infrastructure documentation for the approach roads, the survey marker upkeep, the periodic replacement of the distance stones that the winter frost split. "Sinter Zone" in that context was a terrain designation. The engineering reports described substrate conductivity anomalies and unusual compaction challenges in the dry language of people writing about ground and not about what the ground was next to.

*Approach Preparation* was not a maintenance category.

She put the intake log in the pending queue and went to the library.

---

The library was warm. It was the warmest room at Ocipheus Station, which she had always appreciated; the braziers were lit at dawn and not let die until closing, and the room held the heat in its shelves in a way stone rooms rarely managed. She had liked this. She now found she could not feel it in quite the same way, which was not the room's fault.

She looked up *approach preparation* in the operational taxonomy, canonical category: specialist deployment.

The definition was precise.

*Approach preparation: pre-staging designation for operations requiring formalized entry authorization for contested or boundary-adjacent territory. Classification: pre-incursion operational. Authorization level required: Canon Immaculate plenary. Documentation required: full canonical instrument set, canonical form series Δ-7 through Δ-14, signed by authorized representatives of all participating Houses and operating authorities. Required countersignature: canonical notary, Ocipheus Station or designated equivalent registry.*

She read it twice. She read it a third time not because it was unclear but because the first reading had started the process of settling, and she knew from three years of handling instruments that understanding something and having it settle into your working knowledge were two different states, and she was still in the first one.

*Canon Immaculate plenary.*

The full canonical authority. No escalation, no appeal, no modification by House councils or regional canonical bodies. The standing from which the Canon Immaculate acted in the Liturgy's name without requiring consensus from the people the Liturgy served. She had processed eight sessions this year, and none of them were Canon Immaculate plenary sessions — not the sector reviews, not the inter-House coordination instruments, not the resource allocation certifications. Those were all advisory standing or co-signed authority, the deliberative machinery of the canonical structure working as it was supposed to work. Plenary authority was something else. She had seen the reference instruments. She had not, until now, needed to look up what the category itself required.

The Δ-7 through Δ-14 instrument set she knew from her certification training. Eight instruments: threshold formalities, attestation records, operational mandates, House confirmation instruments, an operational brief filed under seal, a designated authority certification, a deployment roster. And last, the instrument that made it canonical:

*Δ-14: Canonical witness certification. Required countersignature: canonical notary, Ocipheus Station or designated equivalent registry.*

The notary.

She sat in the library for a long time. The warmth pressed in around her. Outside, through the narrow window near the ceiling, the afternoon was going grey and cold in the particular way of afternoons in the Still Watch month, when the light left early and the cold came back to fill its place.

She thought about what Canon Immaculate plenary authority was built for. Not in the abstract — she had copied enough instruments to know the history, or the version of the history the canonical codex recorded. The plenary standing had been established in Year 412, fifteen years after the first vigil installation at Ocipheus Station. The founding canonical text cited it explicitly: *the authority of the Canon Immaculate shall be sufficient, in those moments when coordinated action is required and deliberative process cannot serve, to act in the name of all Compact Houses and their peoples.* The founding text specified, further, that the authority was established specifically because of the Sinter vigil — because the vigil had shown, in its first fifteen years of operation, that what was in the basin was not resolving, and that the Compact Houses, left to deliberative process, could not agree on a response to something none of them had seen directly.

The plenary authority was built for Sinter. It had been built because the vigil was showing the Houses something they did not want to see, and the founding canons had understood that eventually the something would require a response that the Houses could not coordinate themselves, and so they had built a mechanism.

He was using it.

The session notation in the archival queue said: *no immediate action indicated.*

The intake log on her desk said: *Sinter Zone Approach Preparation.*

Both were correct. Both were signed. They had been processed on the same day by the same notary and they did not reference each other.

Prelacze had looked at the window during the session. He had cited seven hundred years of vigil record. He had said *within acceptable variation* and the session had adopted the counter-brief because the session had not the standing to refuse the Canon's institutional reading. He was not wrong that he had the authority. She had been in the room. She had written it down.

The maps were in the archival queue. The southeastern passage line was at the edge of the maintained transit corridor. The measurement log had a small stated margin of error and had not left room for arguing with the line.

She was not wrong that he had the authority.

She was no longer certain the authority was being used for the thing it was built for. Those were different problems, and she sat for a while with both of them, because the canonical record had a column for the first one and she did not know what to do with the second.

---

She walked back to her desk in the registry. The courtyard through the window was dark — she had been longer than she had thought, which was the thing about understanding something: it took time she could not account for afterward. The time disappeared into the understanding and she emerged from it with less evening than she had entered.

She picked up the intake log. She processed it correctly: instrument type, canonical category, processing date, instrument reference number, notary initials. She wrote in the disposition column: *received for processing, authorization chain pending, filed pending Δ instrument set convocation.*

She placed it in the archival queue.

Then she opened the new working copy — her own stock, her own ink, not the canonical record — and she dated the top of the page with the care she gave everything she dated: precisely, in full, the way she wrote every date because dates were either correct or they were wrong and there was no middle position.

*Day 14, month of the Still Watch, 3rd year canonical.*

She wrote: *Review session, Chamber Three: inter-House delegation, Lacerta and Carnyx. Lacerta delegate Adnora Keist. Carnyx commander Aldec Vorn. Presided: Canon Immaculate Tomasz Prelacze.*

She wrote: *Session determination: no immediate action indicated. Continued monitoring protocols authorized.*

She wrote: *Carnyx maps, eastern sector survey, four sheets, archived without action per session determination. Central sector: current line three hundred and eighty meters east of fifteen-year baseline. Southeastern passage: current line at edge of maintained transit corridor designation. The cavity is larger. The maps say so plainly.*

She looked at that last sentence. She had written it in the register of a fact, in the same manner she wrote measurement values and certification dates. A notary wrote what she saw. She had been in the room. She had seen the maps. The cavity was larger. The maps had said so.

She continued writing.

*Specialist deployment intake processed same date: seven soldiers, Carnyx territorial equipment, Wall-approach rated, traveling condition: purposeful. Category: Sinter Zone Approach Preparation. Canonical compendium cross-reference: pre-incursion operational, Canon Immaculate plenary authorization required. Instrument set: Δ-7 through Δ-14. Required countersignature: canonical notary, Ocipheus Station.*

She wrote: *I am the notary.*

She looked at the sentence. She did not cross it out.

She put the pen down. She capped the ink. She left the working copy open on the desk — ink still drying on the last line — and sat with her hands in her lap for a moment, the way she sometimes sat at the end of very long days when her body was tired and her mind was still turning something it could not yet put down. Outside, the courtyard was dark. Inside, the registry lamp burned at low wick. Somewhere in the archival queue, the session notation and the intake log and the Carnyx map case sat in adjacent slots. Correct. Signed. Not referencing each other.

He was not wrong that he had the authority. The authority was built for Sinter — built for the moment the vigil had been watching for, built so the Cauld could act when it needed to act and the Houses could not agree quickly enough. He was using it. That was what Canon Immaculate plenary authority was for: using, when the moment came.

The maps said the cavity was larger. The intake log said the Sinter approach force was staging an approach. The session notation said no immediate action.

She had written all three things in the correct columns.

She gathered her satchel. She straightened the instruments in the archival queue with the precise single motion of someone doing the last correct thing before a much longer night. She looked at the queue for a moment — the sealed map case at the bottom, the intake log above it, the session notation at the top.

She walked out of the registry.

The corridor was cold. The station was closing toward evening. She passed the administrative entrance on her way to the outer doors and heard it shut behind the last of the factor's rotation for the day, the efficient side entrance that produced no foot traffic past the chamber wing. Through the high window at the corridor's end, the sky above the station's outer wall was the specific dark blue of last light over stone, the color that arrived in the Still Watch month and stayed through the cold season like a bruise that would not resolve.

She did not think about the maps. She thought about the lamp she had left burning on her desk in the registry, which was wasteful, which she had done anyway because there was something she did not want to leave entirely in the dark.

Behind her, on the desk, the working copy lay open to the air. In the registry, the lamp burned. In the archival queue, the documents waited in the patient way of documents that had been processed correctly and had nowhere further to go.

The canonical record said what it was supposed to say.

What the working copy said was still drying.

[Beat 39]
SCHMALBURG ADJACENT — THE ATRAMENT ROAD

The road from the checkpoint town east of Falke Gate carried them three days through farmland that wanted to be beautiful and had been interrupted. Stripped fields, January cold, and every half-league or so a Heloth standing in the road's margin for no reason Wren could determine — not working, not guarding anything, simply standing at a waypoint and waiting for instruction that had not arrived yet. The moor-hounds gave each one a wide berth, and the unnamed one, Owain's youngest that he had not gotten around to naming, still pushed a sound through her teeth as she passed that was not quite a growl.

She was not afraid. Wren had decided this: she was disapproving. There was a difference.

Brant had stopped making noise about the constructs by the second day. Corda, the grey-muzzled one, the one who had been working before Wren could hold a lance, had never made noise about them at all. Corda made noise about things that were moving in a direction she had not anticipated. Stationary constructs were furniture. She understood furniture.

"What are they waiting for?" Wren said, on the third day, about a construct standing alone in a field with its arm extended at nothing.

"Instruction," Petra said.

"From where?"

"From wherever the instruction comes from."

She did not look up from the road. He had been getting answers like this from Petra for three weeks — not dismissive, no malice in them, just the precision of a person who called things what they were and was not troubled by the parts of a question she could not answer. The carpenter's answer: the joint holds because that is how wood holds. The rest of the question is in the looking at it.

Esvane had stopped thinking about Atrament's construction protocols three years into her transit-law work. The roadside Heloths were Atrament's, deployed under Form Seven authorization with sixteen-week processing time and the Hearth Table's quarterly deployment schedule, and she had filed three of those forms on Pallor's behalf years ago when the moor road needed shoring. She was not inclined to find them strange. She was inclined to find the state of the road surface between here and Schmalburg more pressing, and she was watching the road.

The Relic's case rode on her back, inside the outer pack, distributed across her shoulders the way she had learned to carry it in the first two days when she was still adjusting the straps. She had found the right position by the third day and it had not changed since. Wren had watched her find it, the small precise adjustments, and then watched her stop adjusting. She had not opened the case since Bressant. She had examined it once, professionally, for transit stress, and closed it and put it away and had been carrying it ever since with the same attention she gave to everything: forward, methodical, done.

Corda had begun sleeping at a distance from the case. Not far — still in the same room, or the same section of whatever passage they were sheltering in. Just not close to it anymore. Not the pressed-against-Esvane's-pack sleeping she had done in the first week. She slept now with the case at one end of the room and herself at the other, watching it in the particular patient way of an animal that has decided the thing is worth watching and is prepared to watch it for a long time.

Wren had noted it and said nothing. He had written it in the small book in his vest in three words: C. distance. case. Then he had closed the book.

---

He had learned to read Petra by her feet.

She was not a person who showed her assessments in her face or her shoulders. She showed them in where her feet went. When she was satisfied with the road, she walked in its center, a step and a half behind Esvane on Esvane's right. When she was thinking, she moved left, to the soft edge, where her boot found the ground differently. When something required a decision, she paused for half a breath — no pause that an inattentive eye would catch — and then resumed on a new line.

He had seen the pause twice in three weeks. Once at the Falke Gate checkpoint, when the officer's second-in-command had brought out a second log book that was not the first. Petra's feet had moved two steps left, putting Esvane between herself and the officer while Esvane produced the canonical documents. The officer had read them and signed them. Two leagues past the gate, Petra had said: they changed the log system. Six weeks ago. Someone at the Hearth Table wants a second record of what crosses into Atrament.

Esvane had said: is that a problem?

Petra had said: not today. And then: you might tell Owain.

Wren had written it in the book. He had filled seven pages in three weeks. He had not shown the book to either of them.

The second pause was now.

Corda had her neck up on the road ahead, the long neck describing a slow arc to the left, then back, then left again. Not alarm. The other kind — attention finding something at range, something in the air that was not yet in the road. She moved her neck the way Wren had seen her move it when she was working a three-day-old thermal trace: unhurried, certain that the thing was there, taking her time with the shape of it.

Petra's feet paused.

Then she moved off the road's shoulder into the field margin, her line angled approximately ten degrees away from the road's direction.

"Off the road," she said.

That was all she said. Esvane moved without question. The moor-hounds followed Esvane. Corda last, still moving her neck.

Wren followed.

---

The road south of Schmalburg's river quarter was not a road he had any reason to know. Petra did not explain why she had chosen it. She walked them through field margins and the backs of two farm hamlets — timber houses, grey, one stone foundation apiece, nothing alive visible in the cold — and then down a long slope toward the river, where the smell changed.

He had been smelling Atrament's industry from the road for two days. The smoke from the furnace stacks was visible from further than that — a permanent grey-brown addition to the horizon that the winter sky absorbed without difficulty. But the smell was different at road-distance from what it was here, at the river's edge, where the current had been carrying it long enough that it had settled into the water and the mud and the reed-beds and was no longer only smoke. It was smoke and wet stone and something else — a chemical edge, mineral, the product of processes that happened in enclosed spaces at temperatures he had no direct knowledge of. The smell was specific in the way that smells were specific when they came from things burning that were not wood.

The river here was wide. The far bank had the built quality of a city's working edge: stone quays, wooden dock extensions, a road surface that was paved rather than packed. Heloth-scale cranes stood at intervals, iron and cable, the cold making the metal contract in a way you could see if you watched the cable long enough. A rail line ran along the far bank parallel to the water, the tracks visible at this distance, the ties squared by machine, the whole length of it cutting through the bank's edge without apology or accommodation to what had been there before.

Three barge hulls sat at the near quay, unladen, rocking slightly in no wind Wren could feel.

In the grey light, where the rail line ran closest to the water, the river surface moved in a way that had nothing to do with current. Brief pulses of pale light from below the surface — not bright, not dramatic, just the quiet flashing of something that startled when the vibration of the rail passed through the water. He watched it for a moment. The light came and went in the rhythm of something alive trying to put distance between itself and the disruption, and then the vibration passed and the river was dark again.

Corda pressed against Wren's calf.

He put his hand on her neck. She held still under it.

Petra moved along the near bank, keeping the reed-beds between them and the water, finding the line that kept them at this distance from the far bank and not less.

---

Then the road on the far bank bent toward the river, and the reed-beds opened on a stretch of clear water, and Wren saw the workers.

Six of them. Possibly seven — the grey light and the reed-beds interrupted his angle. They were on their knees or crouched over a section of quay wall doing dressed-stone work. The specific concentrated posture of people doing work that would not be accepted at less than exact. Not the heavy work — not hauling, not the iron bar and the block and tackle. The fine part. The small hammer and the measuring line and the tight fit of stone to stone in a repair section of wall that required the joints to be felt for, the angles adjusted by an eye that understood what it was looking at and hands that could respond to what the eye found.

Heloths could not do this work. That was the point of them being there.

They were not moving at the pace of people who had chosen this work and were at a good hour of the day.

The guards were positioned at the land end of the quay, where the road met the dock's edge. Two of them. Rifles on their shoulders, not drawn, not watching the workers with any particular engagement. They were watching the road, and the river, and the far end of the work site, and then the road again. The watch of men whose job was to see what arrived and account for what left and to make clear, by their presence, what authorization looked like on this quay — and what the absence of it looked like.

The particular quality of the silence over the work site was not the silence of concentration. Wren had been in Owain's drill halls at full work and had learned that silence: the breath-and-tool rhythm, the occasional word about technique, the absence of unnecessary sound rather than the absence of all sound. This was not that. This was the silence that was there because the alternative had been made clear at some earlier point, and what remained afterward was the decision to continue inside it.

The cold feeling that moved through him was not the cold of the air.

He slowed.

"Keep walking," Petra said, without looking at him.

He kept walking.

The reed-beds closed the line of sight. The far bank's dock went behind the bend. There was only the river, and the mineral smell, and the grey sky above the roofline.

He did not write it in the book. He did not know yet what he would write.

---

Half a league further south, Petra brought them back to the road. The road here ran along the ridge above the river's flood plain, and from the ridge Wren could see Schmalburg laid out along the far bank — the full city, all of it at once — and he stopped walking because he had simply not prepared for the shape of it.

He had grown up knowing Atrament as a name and a set of canonical facts. Forge Masters. The Hearth Table. Production oligarchy, no single governing authority, majority vote on everything including war. He knew the number of forge complexes — eleven major ones, each under a family head — and the canonical authorization framework for cross-House Heloth deployment. He knew the name of the battle that had named the city below him: the Battle of the Small Fortress, Year 701, which had not been a battle in any conventional sense but a siege-and-clearing event that had opened the river junction for Atrament's purposes and had subsequently given the city its name in the ironic way that naming worked when the naming was done by the people who had won.

He had not known what it looked like.

The castle walls were the factory walls. Not a figure of speech. The fortifications that would have been, in any other House's city, the defensive outer ring — the worked stone curtain, the towers, the gate structures — were the outer skin of the factory complex. Where another city's towers would have held archers and ballistae, Schmalburg's held furnace stacks. The smoke came from the towers. The towers were chimneys. The old fortification had been absorbed into something else so completely that the walls were now indistinguishable from the factory buildings behind them, and the stacks rose from the tower bases at the same spacing as battlements would have, so that the overall silhouette of the thing, from the ridge, was still the silhouette of a fortified city — castle walls, towers at intervals, the high vertical of a keep at the center — and also the silhouette of a place that had been burning without stopping for a very long time.

The ember-fungi were visible even now, in grey afternoon light. Not the vivid orange he had heard described — the machine-yard glow that made Schmalburg readable from the ridge at night, like coals seen through smoke. In this light it was less: a faint warmth at the bases of the Heloth maintenance stations, low orange patches on the station walls and on the lower housings of the constructs themselves, the fungi feeding on whatever the machines discharged and growing where they found the discharge richest. Not fire. Not embers. Something that had learned to look like both and had been doing it long enough that the distinction had stopped mattering, or had never been the point.

The Heloths in the yards were working.

He had seen constructs at Pallor. The moor road machines, six or seven of them, seasonal work on the north approach. The old ones in the Long Seat's gatehouse that had been standing in the same positions since before his father's time, accumulating the particular stillness of things that only move when they are needed. He understood what they were. He had been told explicitly, the way all Pallor children were told, that they were not alive — had been made to understand it, because Pallor had a history with that category, with the weight given to things that were not alive, and it had not gone well the last time.

He understood the distinction.

But he had not seen them at this density.

They moved in the machine yards with the unhurried certainty of things that did not get cold, did not tire, had no part of themselves that needed to be elsewhere. The scale was wrong for individual intention — each one was tall as a house's ground floor, iron-dark, the reaction plating on the shoulder housings catching the grey light in a way that made them look wet even when they weren't. They did not move in lines or patterns. They moved to where they needed to be and did the thing and moved again. The individual motions were purposeful; the aggregate was beyond pattern. It was simply — presence. Unceasing, unintentional, vast.

His breath stopped for a moment. He let it start again.

Esvane was already past him on the ridge road. She had not stopped.

He watched a Heloth in the nearest yard take hold of an iron beam that six men could not have lifted and carry it from a staging area to a half-built structure at the yard's far end. The construct did not slow for the weight. The beam was not a weight. The beam was simply a thing that was in one place and needed to be in another.

He watched a second Heloth bring a second beam.

He watched a third one standing at a maintenance station, motionless, amber ember-fungi growing in the gap between the station wall and the construct's left calf housing — the still machine and the living orange glow against its iron skin, the fungi warm and the iron cold and neither of them caring about the distinction. He did not know what kind of wrong thing this was or whether it was the same kind of wrong thing as the dockyard workers with the guards standing at the land end of the quay, watching the road.

He thought it might be.

Corda had sat. He had not noticed her sit. She was directly beside him, neck low, watching the yards with the patience of an animal that had decided it was not going anywhere until the handler finished what the handler was doing. She was not alarmed. She was attentive in the flat, recording way she had, taking the information in and storing it in the part of her that did not have words.

He put his hand on her neck. The fur was warm under his fingers, damp at the base from the day's walking, alive in the specific way that living things were alive when you pressed your hand against them and felt the quality of the heat.

Brant and the unnamed one were already well ahead, following Esvane. Petra had stopped fifteen paces ahead of Wren, and she was watching him. Not the yards. Him.

He said: "Is this what we look like to someone from outside?"

He did not say: from outside Pallor. He did not have to. He meant the moor-hounds and the ancestral vault and the six-generation claim and the whole weight of a House that had been carrying its certainty for a hundred and sixty-six years. He meant: is this the shape of it, from a ridge, to someone who is not inside looking out. The stacks. The constructs in the yards. The workers on the quay doing the fine work under the guards' rifles, in the silence that was there because the alternative had been made clear.

The question sat in the cold air. The smoke from the stacks turned slowly in the updraft from the river below. A Heloth crossed the yard at its mechanical pace, going somewhere the yard required.

Esvane did not turn.

Petra looked at him for a moment. He had been watching her feet for three weeks and had not learned her face. He looked at it now and found he could not read it, which surprised him. He had expected the closed expression she wore when Esvane made a decision Petra was storing for later. This was not that. This was something he did not have a name for, from a face he had not been looking at.

Then she looked back at the road ahead.

"Keep walking," she said.

---

He kept walking.

Corda rose and moved alongside him without being signaled. He left his hand on her neck for a few steps and then took it away. The road descended from the ridge and Schmalburg's stacks went behind the ridge's profile, and then they were only visible as the smoke above it — not the towers, not the Heloths, not the ember-fungi or the yards, just the smoke rising into the grey sky and becoming part of it.

He walked.

Esvane was thirty paces ahead and had not looked back. Her pace was what it had been all day — steady, road-eating, the pack settled on her back with the specific evenness of a person who had been carrying an important thing long enough that the body had accommodated its weight without needing to think about it. The Relic's case was in the pack. She had not opened it since Bressant. She had closed it and put it away and had been walking toward Caer Glas ever since, and she had not looked back at the river or the dockyard or the workers or the ridge.

It watches, she had said, when he had first asked.

He had asked: watches what?

Keep up, she had said.

He was keeping up. He kept up.

Petra came alongside him. For a time they walked at the same pace without speaking. The farmland opened on either side of the road. The cold was the cold of cleared ground in winter, the particular flatness of a landscape from which everything useful had been taken and which was waiting for the season that would let it produce again.

Petra said: "The checkpoint east of Falke changed its log books six weeks ago. Someone at the Hearth Table wants a second record of what crosses into Atrament."

He said: "You told me that."

"I told you it wasn't a problem today. I'm telling you now that it's part of the same thing you were asking about on the ridge."

He thought about this. "You're saying Atrament is counting things."

"I'm saying someone at the Hearth Table is counting things. The Hearth Table is twelve people. They don't all agree. They rarely agree. But someone among the twelve changed the log system six weeks ago, and that means something is being counted that wasn't being counted before, and I want to know what."

"Do you know?"

"I have a theory." She was watching the road. "I'm not going to share it with you because theories at checkpoints cost the same as information at checkpoints, which is to say they cost whether you want to spend them or not."

Brant ranged ahead and came back. Ranged ahead and came back.

Wren said: "The workers on the quay."

Petra said nothing.

"They were doing fine work," he said. "The kind that needs hands."

"Yes."

"The kind that Heloths can't do."

"Yes."

"The guards were watching the road."

"The workers weren't going anywhere," Petra said. "The road was the concern."

He walked for a moment without speaking. He thought about the canonical property transfer documentation from Year 972, the secondary form in a different handwriting from the main instrument. An older designation system, pre-compact era. He had asked Esvane's archivist contact about it, framing it as a general question about historical notation.

Workforce acquisition, cross-House, membrane-transit origin, the archivist had said.

He had not asked a follow-up question. He had written it in the book and closed the book.

He said: "In the Year 972 documentation. There was a secondary form. Workforce acquisition."

Petra said: "Yes."

"Pallor filed it."

"Every House in the Compact has filed a version of it. Pallor. Atrament. Vierna. Lacerta. When a House acquires membrane-origin workers for fixed-site labor, they file the form. It's older than the canonical property system. Much older."

He said: "Are there Pallor workers on quay walls somewhere."

Petra was quiet for a moment. Then: "I don't know. I've never worked Pallor interior roads."

Wren walked. The road was the road. It went on.

He said: "That's not an answer to the question I asked on the ridge."

"No," Petra said. "It's not." She kept walking, her eyes on the road ahead. "Your question on the ridge doesn't have an answer I'm in a position to give you. What I can tell you is what I've seen in six cities in four Houses, and it is this: from the ridge, the shape is the same. The stacks. The yards. The constructs in the yards and the workers at the fine-work and the guards watching the road." A pause. "The shape is the same. The justification is always different. Ask any of them and they will tell you what makes their version different from the others."

He said: "Is ours different."

She did not answer.

The afternoon continued across the flat farmland. The grey sky kept its grey. The smoke from Schmalburg had gone out of sight entirely, absorbed into the general grey of the horizon behind them. The constructs in the road margins had thinned out — whatever deployment was running in this region had not extended this far, or had extended and been recalled, or simply had not gotten to this stretch of road yet.

The moor-hounds settled into their end-of-day pace. Corda close at his side. Brant ranging and returning. The unnamed one, who had been disapproving of every roadside construct for three days, was walking quietly now with her neck low, spending whatever she had spent on disapproval and moving without it.

She was learning, Wren thought. Or she had run out of disapproval for a world large enough to contain more than she had been prepared for.

That was the question he had asked on the ridge. That was what it had been, underneath.

He had spent his whole life inside Pallor's certainty — the moor-hounds and the ancestral vault and the six-generation claim and Owain's absolute knowledge that what had been taken from them was theirs and that recovering it was right. The certainty was real. The claim was real. He had read the documentation and found the documentation complicated and he had been carrying that complication in the small book in his vest for three months without showing it to Owain or Esvane or anyone, because he did not know what certainty looked like after it broke and he did not want to be holding it when it did.

The question he had asked on the ridge was not whether Pallor was Atrament. He understood that much. The question was whether the person on the ridge could see the difference, and whether the difference was large enough to matter, and who got to decide.

He did not know the answer.

Esvane was thirty paces ahead and had not looked back. The pack with the Relic's case was on her back. The case was closed. The lens inside it was watching whatever it watched when it was closed away in the dark — accumulated membrane-contact, seven hundred and forty-one years of it, whatever that looked like from the inside of a carry-case on a road in Atrament with three weeks still left to walk.

The moor-hounds walked. The afternoon moved toward the Halger Road junction and the stopping-house that took Pallor canonical transit documents, and Caer Glas Moor was somewhere ahead at a distance Wren was counting now in days.

He kept walking.

[Beat 40]
SCHMALBURG — THE RAID; THE EATERS; KRESSIDA

Three long. Two short. Then again: three long, two short.

Lyra's hand found her hilt before her mind finished the count.

The Pallor border action, three years past — she had learned the pattern from an Atrament garrison officer who had learned it from a Fjorheim field manual captured eleven years before that, in a skirmish whose name she couldn't recall and whose dead she didn't know because she hadn't been there. She knew the signal the way she knew the notation for a restricted Catalyst preparation: not because she'd made the thing herself, but because she had read enough about its effects to recognize them before they finished arriving.

Fjorheim raid.

"Close," Orim said. He was consulting no instrument. Old men who had spent fifty years scraping their gift across the surfaces of things developed a feel for distance that was more reliable than apparatus and less reliable than luck, and that was still often enough to be worth having. "East quarter. The direction of the rail depot."

The street around them had gone from foot-traffic to empty in the time it took a person to process the sound and move. Schmalburg knew this bell. Had known it for eleven hundred years, or something like it — the gorge-city had been receiving Fjorheim attention since before the battle that gave it its name, and the name itself was the insult the raiders used when they withdrew on day forty-one after the Catalyst incendiary: *small fortress, small people.* The people of Schmalburg had kept the name. Had made armor of it. Had built a civil defense protocol around it that could empty a commercial street in under a minute.

The protocol put civilians in shelters and fighters at garrison points. Both options were wrong for Lyra's party, which was neither.

The first door she tried was already sealed, bar dropped on the inside. The second was locked before she reached it. The third was a stone passage leading downward — the civilian shelter route, which was exactly what the protocol intended.

"Garrison points are east," Ardea said. Her hand was not on her hilt. Ardea Marten kept her hands quiet in a fight, which was different from what most people meant when they said calm. It was a quality Lyra had catalogued in the first week and stopped cataloguing because it became part of the background. She had been posted to Ocipheus garrison eleven years before Lyra was born. The body carried that the way it carried bone — not visibly but in everything. "They'll want bodies at the rail depot perimeter. The rigs deploy from the eastern yard."

"The rigs deploy and we're in the way."

"The shelters fill and we lose two hours." This was Orim, who was looking at a narrow passage between two forge-houses — smoke-blackened stone on both sides, wide enough for three people if two of them breathed in. "There is a third option."

Rowe said: "The passage goes west." Not the halting two-word constructions she was used to from him — somewhere in the last two weeks something had clicked over. The grammar was still wrong at the edges, the stress on the wrong syllables, but the sentence was complete and delivered with the quiet certainty of someone reporting a fact he had already confirmed. He was watching the passage with the particular attention he gave to ground, reading the geometry the way a soldier reads geometry. "I can see the light at the far end."

"Yes," Orim told him, in the tone of someone who had already planned for the light being there. "Come."

She sent the second soldier with the shelter queue — the fewer names in tonight's garrison log, the better.

---

The gorge-streets of Schmalburg were not designed for combat or for comfort. They had been designed for the forge-industry: high-walled, close, following the ridge geology at angles that made no navigational sense until you understood they were cooling channels, not roads — the city had grown up around the heat-management problem of running twelve hundred years of alchemical-industrial work in the same stone structure. The walls were black at the base and grey above the line where the heat rose, and the air at street level in the forge quarter had a quality of pressure that was not quite sound but not quite smell either — the cumulative residue of Heloth exhaust venting through the same corridors for generations.

She heard the fighting before she reached the junction. The bolt-action rifle had a distinctive report in enclosed stone: sharper than in open ground, the crack cutting back at itself off the walls so what reached your ears was the shot and its own echo arriving half a heartbeat apart. Atrament manufacture. She knew the specific overlap from the Vigil Station's range work.

But the frequency coming around the junction was wrong. Two variants, she catalogued in the first three seconds. One was Atrament. One was not.

"Fjorheim uses a longer action," Ardea said, beside her. "Their source Sphere runs a variant. Same Sphere, different generation."

The same source Sphere. Lyra filed the thought without analyzing it because there was a crossfire developing at the street junction thirty meters ahead and the time for analysis was not this one.

She pulled back. Ardea was already back. She looked for Rowe. He was at the near wall, pressed into a recessed forge door, weapon up. He had not been told to do this. He had read the geometry of the junction and found the position himself — seven months in Vierna, which was real training even if it had been bought with his body without his consent.

The battle rigs arrived before the crossfire resolved.

She felt them before she heard them — the vibration in the stone underfoot, the particular frequency of a Heloth steam-chemical plant working under load. Then the sound: grinding and pneumatic, the controlled hydraulic hiss on the turns, the street-scrape of iron carrying serious weight. Three of them coming up the eastern approach. Three meters of purpose-built Atrament armor, each one designed to be the last thing in an enclosed space still functional when the problem was solved. The BR-designation series. She had reviewed the program summaries for the Vigil Station's threat assessments. The rigs were not fast; they were not designed to be fast. They were designed to be indestructible in the specific architecture of Schmalburg's gorge-streets, which made them exactly as capable as the gorge-streets required.

The lead rig reached the junction and solved the first firing position. Not by any mechanism she could have described precisely — the dust was wrong and the angle was wrong and she was thirty meters back with her spine against stone — but solved it in the way the rigs solved problems in gorge-street work: by being the largest and most armored thing present, and by having a pilot who knew which of those two qualities to deploy first.

The Fjorheim position changed character. Anti-armor payload, which was a calculated bet. The lead rig took the round at the wrong angle and too-close range for the round's design parameters. Not dead — the rigs didn't die from one anti-armor round, which was the point of their construction — but the impact drove something into the housing, and the rig's movement became asymmetrical. Still moving. Still working. But wrong in its left side in a way she could see even at thirty meters and through the smoke.

"Left forearm housing," Ardea said. "Round caught the coupling joint. You can see it in the stride."

She could see it now that it was named. The rig's left arm hung differently — not loose, wrong in its load-bearing.

The crossfire resolved, as crossfires do. Not with clarity or justice but with the sudden absence of one of the things making noise, replaced by a different kind of noise that was harder to categorize.

That was when the smell reached her.

---

She knew what it was before she understood why she knew it.

The Sinter crawlers' biological Catalyst compound had a specific signature — acrid and organic, the smell of the membrane's own biology being processed through a human system over years. She had read this in the Vigil Station's field reports as an academic fact, recorded by a researcher who had observed from sufficient distance to find the fact interesting rather than immediate. She had not expected to identify it by smell, from thirty meters, in the forge-city's exhaust-laden air.

She identified it.

There were four. They moved at a pace that was wrong for the space — too efficient, too certain of the ground, like something that had memorized this architecture without having used it before. They wore the layered work-cloth of Fjorheim's forge-villages, practical, nothing that announced itself, but what the cloth covered moved differently than cloth was designed to accommodate.

The leader stopped at the junction.

She was taller than multiple unsanctioned infusions without a certified practitioner should have produced — the body, without guidance, had apparently organized the change around structural necessity rather than Liturgy protocol, and what resulted was this. The Liturgy classified the result as abomination. Lyra had written that classification into her own threat assessments, four times, in the formal notation.

She had written it wrong.

The skin was wrong. Not monstrous. Not corrupted. Wrong in the specific way that something is wrong when it has been reorganized past the point where what it became still belonged to the same category as what it was. The Transmutation, taken without the prescribed attenuation between doses, had rebuilt the surface tissue into something that carried out skin's function — keeping the interior interior — but wasn't skin in the technical sense. In motion, particularly at the joint-interfaces, you could see the underlying structural work beneath it. Not organs. Architecture. The thing the body had rebuilt itself around.

But what Lyra's eye kept returning to, even at thirty meters, even through the smoke, was the neck.

The musculature of the neck had been reorganized — additional support structures grown in, visible under the skin where they stood proud in a way the standard anatomy had no room for. You could count them. Four, possibly five, where there should have been two. And the head tracked on a range of motion the human neck did not provide, without strain, without effort, like something that had always worked this way rather than something that had learned to. When the leader turned to look at the far end of the junction, her head moved through an arc that Lyra's hand instinctively wanted to record because the record would be evidence of something the Liturgy's classification system had no category for.

The Eaters had not come for the raid. The raids drew things from the Sinter perimeter's overflow cracks — membrane fauna that the quarantine never fully contained. That was what the Eaters had tracked here: the overflow creature the raid's noise had pulled through its boundary and into the city. They had followed their prey through the noise.

Lyra had known this, academically, from the field reports. What the field reports had not conveyed was the silence. The gorge-street was a noisy place — exhaust vents, bell-echo, the bass note of the rigs through the stone — and the four Eaters standing at the junction made the space around them quiet. Not the quiet of shelters filling. A different kind of quiet, the kind made by everything with a brain stem and an intact survival instinct removing itself from consideration.

The leader moved into the junction. The other three spread to the walls. Lyra heard — she would record this later, in the same notation she used for everything — a sound that had no reference in her research archive. Not a cry. Not a body impact. Something between a collapse and a release, the kind of sound a structure makes when the thing holding it together from the inside stops. The sound came from beyond the junction. It came once.

Then quiet.

"We should not be between them and where they are going," Orim said, from immediately behind Lyra's left shoulder, which was where he had been for the past three minutes without her having noticed it.

Lyra moved.

---

Orim had been scrrying during their approach — she had seen him wet his fingertips with the contact sensitizer, press them together at the sternum, look at nothing for twenty seconds. She had not interrupted him. The minor scry took less than half a minute and the results were always more useful than the information she could have given him about the gorge-streets, because Orim did not look at roads but at what had used roads recently.

What he had found was the dockyard corridor: a service passage running between the secondary rig yard and the river loading bays, wide enough for Heloths moving river cargo, roofed over with iron lattice and tarpaulin, long enough that the far end disappeared into industrial haze. The Fjorheim withdrawal had pushed north along the eastern streets when the rigs drove them back. The Eaters had moved northeast, following the overflow creature. The corridor was the only route west that avoided both.
