"There is a position at the far mouth," Orim said, when they reached the corridor entrance. His voice carried no inflection that would have suggested urgency to anyone who did not know him. "Two Fjorheim fighters, possibly three. They found the corridor in the last twelve minutes and they have the distance advantage." He paused. "The corridor is ninety meters long and has no cover."

"We take the position," Ardea said. She was reading the angles. "Move fast, split the approach before they can —"

"Three against three, in a roofed corridor with no cover," Rowe said. He was at her shoulder, looking past her at the far mouth. He had made the count without being asked and had delivered the number with the flat precision of someone who had done this calculation before. "And they hear us coming before we are halfway."

Orim had not moved from the entrance. His hand had found the Rod without her seeing him reach for it — he had the Rod the way other men had a walking stick, present without announcement. He was rotating the mineral tip in the iron housing, feel-first, a locksmith running his thumb down the tumblers. The groove found the notch.

"I catalogued this site eleven years ago," he said. "Sphere eleven. A cave complex in the deep rock of this sector. Colonial fauna, membrane-adjacent." He looked at the floor of the corridor at the point he had identified, which Lyra could not see but understood to be the membrane boundary at its thinnest in this location. "My documentation describes the fauna as: large colonial invertebrates, membrane-sensitive, aggressive on emergence." He stopped rotating the mineral tip. His thumb rested over the trigger. "The word *aggressive* is doing a great deal of work in that documentation."

Lyra looked at the corridor. Ninety meters. The Fjorheim position at the far end. The Eaters somewhere northeast and moving with purpose.

"Orim."

"Step back," he said. "Behind the entrance. Both of you. Specifically, Mr. Rowe, please step back." He said this the way he said everything: without drama, with the exact weight the information required and no more. He had already decided. He was giving them the distance they needed before he enacted the decision.

She stepped back behind the entrance wall. Ardea was beside her. Rowe stepped back without being told twice; he had learned what *step back* meant from Orim in specific.

Orim depressed the trigger.

---

The aperture opened four meters into the corridor, at the near end.

She could see the skin from the entrance — the membrane tissue stretched across the air in the shape of a wound, translucent, threaded with dark veins that pulsed once, twice, three times as the pressure built on the far side. The corridor's industrial haze made it visible in a way that open air would not have: the thing was there, in the middle of the passage, bulging slightly at the center where the pressure was pressing against it from somewhere a great deal darker and deeper than the Schmalburg dockyard.

The veins went dark.

The skin parted.

What came through came through all at once. She had understood from Orim's previous explanations that things came through apertures sequentially, constrained by the opening's diameter. She had understood the aperture was small. Neither of those things prepared her for the way the creature organized itself in the two seconds after emergence — through the opening and oriented before the skin had finished parting behind it, like something that had been waiting at exactly this pressure point and had been very ready for the door to open.

It was pale as chalk all over. Not the pale of something underpigmented but the pale of something that had lived at such depth in complete dark for long enough that pigment had become a wasted resource and the body had reorganized accordingly. The legs — she began to count them and stopped, because the count was not the relevant fact in this moment — were too many for any architecture she had researched, and they moved in a coordination that had no reference in her existing library of locomotion. Not rippling, not alternating, not anything the Cauld's natural history had produced a name for. They moved and the creature moved with them, and what struck her before anything else was the certainty. The certainty of something that had never needed to be afraid. Not aggression — something worse than aggression, because aggression had urgency in it, and this had none. The settled, efficient attention of a thing that occupied the top of its environment so completely that threat was a category it had no practical experience of.

The eyes were on the sides of the broad, flat head, arranged in a curve — three to each side, she counted them, six — and they reflected the corridor's dim light wrong, throwing it back at an angle that was not the angle of reflection her reference material had given her for any compound eye structure she had studied. They found the far end of the corridor the way a surveyor's instrument finds a fixed point: without hurry, without uncertainty, with the quality of a thing that sees the problem and begins moving toward it in the same motion.

It moved toward the far end of the corridor.

Orim had stepped back from the entrance and turned away from it. He was counting under his breath. She could see his lips moving. Not prayers — he was not a praying man. He was counting seconds. He had forty-five of them, and he knew the count, and he had turned away because there was nothing he could do about the creature now and because he had learned, in fifty years, that watching what he opened the door for did not make it clean. It just made him the one who had watched.

The party moved.

"West wall," Ardea said quietly. "Against the stone. Fast and keep pace."

They entered the corridor. Lyra against the west wall, Ardea in front, Rowe behind, Orim last. The creature was thirty meters ahead and closing the distance to the far end with the certainty she had clocked at the entrance. The corridor haze was thicker here — the tarpaulin roof trapped the exhaust heat and it sat at chest height in a warm chemical layer that smelled of decades of Heloth discharge.

At the twenty-meter mark she heard the Fjorheim position react. Not the organized fire she had expected. The sound that came from the far mouth was the sound bodies make when the body and the mind disagree about whether to continue the current process. Then silence, briefly. Then something that was not silence so much as the absence of organized resistance, which was a different thing.

She kept pace.

At the thirty-five-meter mark she heard the sound again — the one she had heard from beyond the junction, the sound her research archive had no entry for, the sound a structure makes when what is holding it together from the inside stops. It came from the far end of the corridor. It was not quick.

She looked at the west wall and kept walking.

At the forty-five-meter mark the creature was at the far mouth of the corridor. Not through it. At it. The tarpaulin overhead snapped once — something in the creature's transit had disturbed the air pressure in the enclosed space. Lyra felt it against her face.

At sixty meters Orim's count stopped.

She heard no sound from the corridor's far end. She did not look back to establish why.

At ninety meters they came out into the rig yard.

Orim came out last. He put the Rod inside his coat, against his chest, where the mineral was warm. He looked at the ground for a moment. Then he looked at Lyra.

"The aperture closed at forty-seven seconds," he said. "Within normal parameters."

She nodded. She was not going to ask about the Fjorheim fighters. She had the data she needed and the data she needed was: the corridor was clear.

Rowe was looking back at the corridor entrance. His face had the expression it had when he was processing something in his own language first and had not yet found the Cauld for it. He looked at Orim. He said: "That creature — it died in there?"

"Yes." Orim's voice was even. "They all do, when they come through. The atmosphere is wrong for them. Everything here is wrong for them. They have forty-five seconds before the biology fails." A pause. "I find that the specific number of seconds is not the detail that stays with people."

Rowe looked at the corridor entrance for another moment. Then he turned and looked at the yard.

"There is still movement, north," he said. "The withdrawal. They have not all gone."

He was right.

---

The rig yard was controlled chaos, which was better than the gorge-street's uncontrolled variety. Two of the three Atrament rigs had returned to refit. Forge-workers were moving equipment out of the rig paths. Someone had lit the ember-fungi lamp posts at the yard's perimeter — the orange bioluminescent glow turned everything into a composition of industrial light and shadow, the machines large and patient in it, the people small and purposeful.

The Fjorheim withdrawal's northern element had pushed through the yard's edge in the last twenty minutes. The evidence was in the brass shell casings scattered near the northern rail guide and in the wide margin the forge-workers gave the northern quarter. Lyra read the yard and read the western approach: clear to the cooling channel, which was what she needed.

Then she saw the small woman.

She was in the eastern part of the yard, near the secondary rig bay's wall, in the wrong geometry. The Fjorheim withdrawal's repositioning had produced this by accident — no one had placed her there deliberately, but the yard's current movement pattern had built a wall around her position without intending to: the northern quarter clearing to the right, the open yard mouth to the left, and one of the withdrawing Fjorheim fighters coming around the eastern rig bay's corner from the direction no one had been watching.

Not a soldier. Someone in dockworkers' clothes, dark hair cut short on one side, a tool vest with deep pockets. Small in the absolute sense — she moved like she was used to being the smallest person in a space and had made accommodations for it long ago. She was watching the Fjorheim fighter with the still attention of someone who was reading the geometry very carefully and had not yet settled on the solution.

The fighter had seen her. He was three meters away and between her and anything useful.

Rowe moved. Lyra moved. Ardea moved.

Then the secondary rig bay doors opened.

Not loudly. The pneumatic hiss of the hydraulic mechanism was substantial but brief, and the doors were designed to open without drama because drama was not what you wanted when you were moving a three-meter iron construct into a confined space. The BR-7 came out of the bay at the pace of something that knew the exact radius of its own clearance and was not interested in misjudging it. Full height, reaction-plate armor in the ember-fungi's orange light, the shoulder's instrumentation housing rotating to orient. The left-arm housing had a repair patch on it — field work, not forge work, iron over the impact site held with hex-bolts and tension cable, the kind of repair you made when you needed the arm functional before the forge could see it properly.

The Fjorheim fighter saw the rig at the same moment as Lyra. He had approximately one useful option at three meters from a BR-7, which was to be somewhere else. The rig's right arm came down in the motion of something settling a technical problem — which is what it was, the technical problem being the specific geometry of one fighter in a clearance zone when the clearance zone's proprietor had returned to active status. The arm movement took less than a second.

The fighter was not in the yard anymore.

The yard was quiet in the radius of the rig.

The small woman was still standing where she had been standing. She looked at the rig. She looked at where the fighter had been. Then she turned and walked toward the rig, with the specific ease of someone who knew the machine's clearance radius because she had measured it herself.

The access hatch opened before she reached it.

She went up the handholds on the rig's left leg housing and through the hatch in twelve seconds. The hatch sealed behind her.

The BR-7 turned to face the western exit of the yard and waited.

Nobody in the party said anything for a moment.

"West," Orim said. He had the Rod back in his coat and his face had returned to the expression it wore when he was noting facts without annotating them. "Now. We can ask questions when we are no longer in the yard."

Rowe was looking at the sealed hatch. Then at where the woman had been standing. His expression had the quality it had when he was assembling something and had not yet established whether the picture was what he expected. He would sort it eventually; he always did.

The BR-7 followed them out of the yard.

Nobody asked the right question.

---

Ardea died in the Helothworkers' Lane, which ran between the main rig-yard access road and the secondary cooling channel behind the third forge complex. Lyra would record the coordinates later, the specific coordinates, because she was a researcher and recording was what she did. She would record the date, the time, the cause. She would not record what it felt like to hold Ardea Marten while Ardea Marten stopped being a person and became something the stone would keep its own record of.

They were moving for the secondary cooling channel when the Fjorheim withdrawal — the organized element, the one with a professional rear-guard — repositioned across the lane's northern end. Not breaking. Redirecting, in the manner of professional forces who redirect when something indestructible pushes into their crossfire. They had found the lane's junction and established a firing line covering the withdrawal's flank.

Rowe saw the geometry before anyone told him it was there. He had enough Cauld now for full sentences and not enough of the tactical language of the city to have received any instruction about what the lane's junction meant. He had seven months of Vierna training and three years of France before that, and both of them had built the same reflex into the understructure of his thinking: a line of fire had a solution, and the solution was someone who moved into the angle that collapsed it.

He moved toward the junction.

Ardea moved faster.

Thirty years of service in the body's memory, which was older and more reliable than the mind's. The body went to the right position before the mind consulted the rest of the available information — which was: this was an outdoor lane, the lane gave the crossfire limited cover, the lane gave the party even less, and there were four of them and two of the party had already had this idea. The body filed none of that and moved.

The round took her through the upper chest, left side, below the collar. She was already pulling Rowe back when it found her. The pull became a push. She went against the forge-house wall and sat down against it, hard, with the specific ungainliness of a body that has stopped being coordinated from the inside.

Lyra was there in — she did not count.

Ardea's eyes were open and tracking. That was the thing that mattered for the first three seconds: she was tracking Lyra's face. She was not speaking. Lyra put her hand on the wound without looking at it because looking was not the useful thing here and the hand was.

"Sergeant," Lyra said.

Ardea looked at her.

The blood came through Lyra's fingers at a rate that told her what she needed to know. She had administered enough field tinctures to read a rate. She was reading it now, and what it told her was not something she had a response to that would be useful, because her kit was in her satchel and getting to it required removing her hand from the wound, and removing her hand from the wound was not going to help with what removing the hand would reveal.

Ardea said one word. Not Lyra's name. It was the name of someone Lyra did not know — someone from before the current posting, from somewhere east, possibly still alive in the ordinary way that people who are not on research expeditions in foreign cities during Fjorheim raids remain alive. She said it without urgency, with the quality of someone placing a face they have just recognized. Then she did not say anything else.

She died the way people die. No declaration. No moment of clarity in the medically instructional sense. The body finishes what it is doing, and what it was doing was: working, then not working, and the distance between those two states is not marked by anything you can point to. Lyra had known this. She had not been holding the person before.

Thirty seconds. Perhaps forty.

Rowe was at the far wall. He had understood what happened before it finished happening — the sequence was not ambiguous in any language — and he was looking at the space where Ardea had been with an expression Lyra had no file for. Not grief in the Liturgy-document sense. Something older. She noted it. She noted it the way she noted things when she was functioning correctly, which she was. She would return to it when she had the resources to be human about it. She would return to it for the rest of her life as it turned out, but that was not information she had yet.

She let go. Her hands were red to the wrist.

The research satchel was over her left shoulder. Ardea Marten's service record was in the document folio, third from the top. It had been there since Bressant. The record needed to be closed by the ranking officer.

She was the ranking officer.

She did not open the satchel. She filed it: *service record, Marten. Closing pending. Time of death approximate.* She would do it in the hour. She would do it when there was a wall to sit against and a lane that wasn't this lane.

Orim was in the doorway across the lane, watching the access road. He said nothing. He had probably understood, from the moment Ardea moved, how the sequence would resolve. Fifty years of watching things end had given him an economy with aftermath.

Lyra stood. She pulled her field cloth and used it and put it away. The field cloth had a finite number of uses. This was a fact that could be managed.

"We move when the rigs clear the junction," she said.

"The third rig isn't moving," Orim said. He meant the BR-7. It had followed them to the lane's entrance and stopped there — three meters of Atrament iron standing in the access road, waiting with the patience of something that did not tire.

---

The BR-7 did not move for four minutes. Then it moved west, toward the cooling channel access, at the pace of something that had made the decision and was done deciding. It stopped at the cooling channel gate and turned its instrumentation housing toward the gorge-street approach.

Covering the retreat. Not because anyone asked.

Lyra walked south to the channel access and then west along the channel wall, and the BR-7 followed when she was through the gate.

She did not look back at the lane.

---

The staging area was three hundred meters down the cooling channel wall, in a secondary yard where the river-staging gate opened onto the Schmalburg river approach. Atrament infrastructure — the gate accepted passage papers or rig-crew authorization, and between those two options the party had the second one, which was not Lyra's and was not in her name. She was holding this carefully as she sat down against the channel wall and opened the document folio.

The Eaters had pulled off when the Fjorheim raid broke, withdrawing northeast in the specific manner of hunters who have finished their business and are not interested in ceremony about it. The thing from the Sinter overflow was somewhere in the east yard, dead. She had heard the sound it made when it died, which resembled nothing in her reference archive, and had filed it: *membrane overflow fauna, unidentified; Eater of Monsters as effective countermeasure, confirmed.* The Liturgy would want that data.

She was not certain what she thought about being the one who carried it back.

The bells had shifted from raid-warning to damage-assessment. The forge-yards were running again — the exhaust-pressure hum was back in the stones underfoot. Schmalburg had the quality she had observed once before, nine years ago, after a different Fjorheim incursion in the capital's secondary trade district: not calm, not controlled, but the quality of a population that has done this before and knows the shape of the next four hours and has arranged itself around that knowledge. Schmalburg had been *small fortress* for eleven hundred years. It knew what it was.

She took out Ardea Marten's service record.

Twelve pages, close notation, Ocipheus garrison format — date of enlistment, posting history, distinguished service marks, the research-secondment authorization that had moved Ardea from garrison duty to Lyra's party. The authorization was dated six months ago. Lyra had signed it. Her signature was at the bottom of the document, which meant her hand had been present at every step of the chain that had brought Ardea Marten to the Helothworkers' Lane.

She did not think about the chain. Thinking about the chain was not useful to the work of closing the record.

She filled in the date, the location, the cause. *Enemy action, crossfire withdrawal, Fjorheim raid, Schmalburg.* Formal notation. She signed the closing entry with her designation: T-044, Templar rank, Liturgy of the Canon Immaculate.

She put the record back in the folio. Third from the top.

The Liturgy had a theory about loss and its management and the process by which the living return to function. She had read it in the foundational documents, and she had never found fault with the theory before, because she had never before held the person between the person being alive and the person being a thing the stone kept record of. The theory addressed the aftermath. It had nothing to say about those thirty seconds. This was not a gap she had noticed before. It was there now. She filed it. She would return to it when she had a category for it.

Rowe was across the channel path, back against the wall, his rifle across his knees. He was looking at the place where Ardea had been, which was three hundred meters east and through the stone, and he was looking at it the way people look at things that are no longer there when looking is the only useful thing left. His face was still doing the thing she had no notation for. She looked at it and let it be what it was.

The BR-7 was at the staging gate entrance, still. The access hatch was sealed.

Orim appeared from the secondary passage he had gone into fifteen minutes ago, carrying nothing visibly different. "The river-staging gate accepts passage papers or rig-crew authorization," he said. "One of these we have." He looked at the BR-7. "If the authorization has not been cancelled."

The hatch opened.

The woman dropped out and landed on the stone without adjusting — four feet down, a landing that read impact as data rather than sensation because the normal pathway for it had been modified by years in a machine that processed the world as thermal and EM gradient before it processed it as anything else. She was small in the absolute sense, which had been true inside a three-meter iron construct and was true now standing in the staging yard with her work vest half-unbuttoned and a smear of rig-lubricant on her left forearm. Not slight — the distinction mattered, because slight suggested a quality she did not have. The same stillness in the hands that Ardea had had. The same quality of a body that had been used for serious work long enough that it had organized itself around the work.

"Haun," she said. "Kressida Haun. Formerly." She said *formerly* in the way that meant the credential before it was the credential and the word after it was the current status. "The round went into the coupling housing. Left dorsal." She said this without opening it up for examination. The round had happened. The drive had happened. These were technical facts with technical consequences. "Atrament has a process for pilots when a field fusion goes wrong. A disposal recommendation. They hadn't filed it yet." She said *disposal recommendation* the way Orim said accurate things that were uncomfortable — without decoration, because decoration was not what you wanted in a technical report. "I didn't wait."

"How long," Lyra said.

"Six weeks." Kressida looked at the rig. Not sentimentally. The way someone looks at the thing that has become load-bearing for their continued existence when they have reached an accommodation with that fact. "I can disengage whenever I want. I get out, I'm outside, and then the pathway begins to destabilize and I have four hours before that becomes the only thing that matters." She paused. "The field surgeon was correct about what happened. He was wrong about what to do about it. His recommendation was the Atrament recommendation. I disagreed."

"You know the yard," Orim said. He had arrived at this from the scry, twelve minutes of observational data accumulated while the party was moving through the gorge-streets.

"I know the yard. I know the staging gate and I know the authorization and I know we have until the third bell before the rig yard count is done and the BR-7 is logged as unaccounted for." She looked at Lyra. Not measuring. Having already measured, inside the sensor housing, and now comparing the measurement to the in-person version. "You're moving west. I heard what you're after. Three of you now." She said it with the flatness of someone who had counted from the corridor entrance and understood what the count meant. "West is the direction that doesn't end with Atrament command learning I survived the Schmalburg action and finding the rig. Tonight is the window."

Lyra looked at the BR-7. The contrast did not diminish with proximity. The rig was everything Atrament made things to be: three meters of reaction-plate iron, purpose-built for the enclosed tactical problem it had just solved in the rig yard without being asked. The pilot stood in front of it with rig-lubricant on her forearm and dockworkers' clothes, and she had done the assessment from inside the sensor housing and come out and named the facts and was waiting for the conversation to catch up to the conclusion she had already reached.

Rowe looked at Kressida. He looked at the rig. His mouth moved through the shape of a question in English that did not make it to Cauld. Then he looked at Lyra.

"The passages west," he said. "They are not large enough. For that." He meant the rig.

"The river-staging gate is four meters," Kressida said. "I know the measurements."

Orim said: "The passage from the gate to the river loading bay has a seven-degree grade. The BR-7's stabilizers, in my reading of the specification documents, manage a maximum of eight degrees. If the stabilizers are functional." He looked at Kressida.

"Six degrees, on the left side. The coupling took damage." She was already looking at the grade in question. "Get to the gate. I'll manage the grade."

Orim looked at Lyra. Not asking permission. Reporting the available information and indicating, with the economy of fifty years, that the decision was hers.

She closed the document folio and put it in the research satchel. Ardea's rifle was across her back where she had put it an hour ago. It was a weapon. It was functional. She would carry it until she had a reason to do something else with it.

"Third bell," she said. "Have the rig at the staging gate."

Kressida was already walking back to the BR-7 when Lyra stood. The hatch opened before she reached it.

---

She walked back to the lane.

Not for long. She had the coordinates and the record was closed and she had already done the work of sitting against a wall and doing the work. She walked back because it was the thing she was going to do before she knew she was going to do it, and she had learned that the body sometimes moved toward what the mind was not yet ready to approach directly, and that the body was sometimes correct about when to do this.

The lane was empty. Orim had managed it, sometime in the last hour, in the quiet way he managed things that needed managing without anyone observing him manage them. There was blood on the stone. There was always blood on the stone in a city that had been *small fortress* for eleven hundred years. The stone kept what it kept.

She stood there for thirty seconds.

Then she walked back.

The gorge-street had the quality of a city already composing itself around what had happened today and what would happen next. Forge-workers moving an alchemical condenser back into its shed. A garrison soldier directing traffic at the eastern access road. A child standing at the entrance to a shelter, watching the yards, deciding whether it was finished. The ember-fungi posts cast their orange light across the cooling channels and the rig paths and the places where things had happened an hour ago that the city was already adjusting its arrangements to account for.

She walked west.

Behind her, at the secondary yard, the BR-7's access hatch sealed with a sound like a bar dropping on the inside of a door.

[Beat 41]
THE FORGE HEARTH ??? WHAT SHE RECOGNIZES

The volcanic substrate had pushed through the alpine soil in long dark extrusions ??? basalt-colored, finger-shaped, warm to the touch even through the cold morning. Lyra pressed her palm against one of them and left it there. The warmth rose through her hand steadily, without the variation of something that had spent a day in daylight. Something below, continuous, moving upward because that was the direction things moved when they had nowhere left to go but up.

She knew what the Forge Hearth zone was before she arrived. She had read the institutional documents ??? the extraction reports, the geothermal surveys, the authorization history that ran in three-year intervals from Year 842 onward. Knowing had not prepared her for the quality of the warmth, which was less like heated stone than like a fever: persistent, patient, unaware of being noticed.

She took her hand away. The warmth stayed on her palm for a breath's worth of time before the autumn air took it.

"Hearth-Three is four kilometers south," Kressida said. She walked beside Lyra with the efficient, ground-eating pace of someone who had stopped finding difficult terrain difficult. "Hearth-Two south of that. Hearth-One you can't approach from the ridge ??? the extraction apparatus runs between the ridge and the valley floor. No clear path that doesn't take you through the Atrament perimeter."

"Three postings here," Lyra said. "Valley floor each time."

"Valley crews and ridge crews don't share operational briefings. Different command chains." She glanced up at the ridge's continuation, where the escarpment edge gave them a clear view over the extraction valley below. "The ridge is Liturgy-chained territory. The valley is Atrament production authorization. They coexist by not talking to each other."

The extraction roads were visible below, carved into the volcanic substrate in the switchback geometry Atrament used for heavy equipment access. Heloth maintenance constructs moved on them ??? the smooth, purposeful gait of machines that had made this route enough times that the route was in them somewhere, not in their minds, because they did not have minds, but in whatever the Catalyst preparation put into the movement. Orange patches of ember-fungi clustered at every maintenance station along the roads. At this distance they looked like small fires. They had looked like small fires for approximately four hundred years, which was how long the constructs had been working the approach.

The rig walked three meters behind them, where the path was wide enough. It moved at the careful, low-gravity cadence it used on narrow terrain ??? flail housing raised, shoulder angle adjusted for the overhang. The ember-fungi on its exhaust housing had been growing for two days, thick enough now that the housing port was half-obscured. In daylight they just looked wrong. At night, she thought, they would look like a lantern carried by something large.

Rowe walked on the right side of the path, rifle slung, hands loose. He was watching the valley below with the quiet methodical attention he gave to everything that had no words yet. Seven weeks since Bressant. She had counted his vocabulary that morning from the notebook. He had enough Cauld now to build a sentence when he needed one. Whether a sentence captured what he was looking at was a different matter. He spent what he had carefully.

She did not know what he compared it to.

Orim was behind them, walking with his hands down and his fingertips loose ??? the posture that meant he was attending to what was below the ground rather than to where he was putting his feet. He had been doing this since they topped the ridge. His satchel rode on one shoulder, the Rod's case visible at the pocket's lip.

She let him read it.

*

The warmth that came from the south was different.

She noticed this by increments. Not a moment of recognition ??? an accumulation of evidence that produced, eventually, something she could not not acknowledge. The stone under her feet was warm because geothermal heat conducted upward through it; she understood that. But the warmth from the south did not travel through stone. It came from a direction the way a sound came from a direction ??? dispersing, arriving with something remaining of its origin's character. She felt it in the chest cavity, below the sternum, in the same register where the Sinter tone had its address.

This was not the Sinter tone. The Sinter perimeter felt like standing in front of something that was awake and had noticed you. This was different. This felt like standing in front of something that had been asked to keep working past the point where it had the capacity to work. Not menace. Not attention. The specific exhaustion of a system running on the wrong side of its limits because stopping required decisions that the people doing the asking had not wanted to make.

She was a Transmutation researcher. Membrane biology ??? the wound surface's tissue properties, the recovery behavior of frequently-opened sites, the long-term changes in substrate condition under sustained apparatus use. Four papers published, two cited in standing operating procedures, one unsubmitted when the theft happened. The unsubmitted one was the one she had been building for two years, assembled from the archive's own recovery logs, from the minor inconsistencies her predecessors had noted under *within acceptable range* and then filed and not returned to.

The feeling in her chest was evidence. She catalogued it and kept walking.

*

The path widened at a flat shelf of volcanic stone ??? wide enough to stop, wide enough to see clearly south. The overlook. From there the approach road was visible as it came around the ridge's base and ran south toward the Hearth-Three perimeter.

Six figures on the road. Atrament-brown coats. Rifles.

Not a maintenance crew.

"Patrol," Kressida said. She said it the way she named most things: flatly, without alarm, because alarm was not information and information was what she dealt in.

Lyra came up beside her and looked.

Six soldiers. Standard ridge configuration ??? two forward, one rear, three mid-formation ??? moving north at the pace of a patrol that had been doing this since early morning. Long coats, bolt-action rifles slung, operational packs that marked them as rotation personnel. Below them on the road, three hundred meters south of the overlook shelf, was the junction where the ridge path met the Lacerta approach road. The junction Lyra's party needed.

"Rotation schedule runs north on odd days," Kressida said. "I saw it at Schmalburg. At their current pace they reach the junction in twenty minutes."

"And us?"

"About the same. Possibly ahead of them by five minutes, possibly not."

Going back over the ridge added two days. The extraction valley below was Atrament perimeter, a different command chain with a different tolerance for unauthorized transit, and Kressida had already explained that *different* in this case meant specifically hostile. The ridge path was the only way south that did not require Lyra to present credentials that had been expired for three weeks and that carried a watch flag next to her designation.

She looked at the patrol.

Orim had not spoken. When she glanced at him he was looking at the patrol too, and he already had the tincture vial in his hand.

He sat down on the volcanic shelf. Fingertips, sternum. He breathed twice. He looked south.

Not a routine read ??? she understood that. He was trying to get ahead of the patrol, to see the junction, to find how the road lay beyond it, to answer whatever tactical question would give them another option. He was pressing into the membrane the way he pressed into it, with fifty years of practiced contact, in the flat deliberate way of a man to whom doors opened.

Forty seconds.

The rig vented softly at the shoulder joint. Kressida watched the patrol.

Orim opened his eyes.

The expression on his face was not one she had seen before.

He stayed where he was, on the volcanic stone, with his hands on his knees and his satchel beside him, and he looked at the south country with the expression of a man who has been going through a door for fifty years and has just found the door gone. Not stuck. Not locked. Gone. The space where the door was ??? that was there. The door was not.

She had seen him tired many times. She had seen him pained, occasionally, in the specific way of a man whose body has opinions about Heloth courier saddles and who has learned not to argue with his joints. She had not seen him old. He looked old now. Not frail ??? old in the way that accumulation makes a person old, when the accumulation reaches a moment it did not expect and has nothing prepared for it.

Rowe looked at Orim. He looked at Lyra.

"Can he say what kind of no it is?" Kressida said.

"He'd tell us if he could," Lyra said.

She did not press him. A membrane refusal was not the same as a physical shock, but it had a similar effect on the body's regulatory sense. Whatever the site had done, or not done, to him ??? his system needed a moment to understand that the preparation was over and the result was what it was.

She turned to Kressida.

*

"Show me what the rig is reading," she said.

Kressida climbed the access footing without looking at it and settled into the harness in the practiced way of someone who had done it ten thousand times. The pilot interface lit. Through the access hatch, Lyra looked in at the display.

Atrament instrumentation rendered everything as a resource. The display showed a false-color terrain map with a gradient overlay ??? blue for geological baseline, orange for elevated, red for anomalous ??? and the zone south of their position, where Hearth-Three's apparatus operated, showed deep red. Below the map, in Atrament's operational notation:

MEMBRANE CONTACT PRESSURE: 87.4% OPTIMAL YIELD GRADIENT
CATALYST CONCENTRATION: REDUCED ??? HEARTH-SECTOR 4-7 CORRIDOR
EXTRACTION INDEX: 61.2 (TARGET: 80.0)
SUBSTRATE TEMPERATURE: WITHIN GEOLOGICAL VARIANCE
YIELD PREDICTION (SEASONAL): BELOW THRESHOLD

The numbers were precise. The framework was correct for what it measured. The rig had been built to read extraction sites as extraction sites, and it was doing this accurately.

She read the columns. She read the word REDUCED under the concentration entry.

She had seen this notation before ??? not in Atrament's production documents but in the Liturgy's practitioner literature on membrane site behavior after extended apparatus use. The Liturgy's term for it was *recovery gradient depression.* The definition was the same thing in different vocabulary: the site was returning less than it had been returning, for the same or greater apparatus effort. The wound was not healing at the rate the apparatus assumed.

A wound heals inward from its edges. The basic principle from the biology sections of her research background. Rate depends on wound depth, frequency of re-opening, condition of the surrounding tissue. A wound that is opened and closed repeatedly ??? sutured, reopened, re-sutured ??? develops scar tissue faster than the surrounding tissue can compensate. The scar does not have the same properties. It does not recover at the same rate. Eventually the surgeon's options narrow.

The membrane at Hearth-Four had been opened and held open, repeatedly, for decades. Hearth-Seven the same. The apparatus was designed to hold the wound open; that was its function. An extraction cycle, then a recovery interval. Then another extraction cycle.

"Hearth-Four has been below target for eleven years," Kressida said from the harness. "Hearth-Seven for nine. Both were in the upper production quartile before that. The response has been apparatus recalibration." She paused. "Three times on Hearth-Four. Twice on Hearth-Seven."

"And the yield kept declining."

"The yield kept declining."

Lyra looked at the word REDUCED.

The papers she had read ??? the theoretical literature on membrane site behavior, which she had read as theory and as the background of a framework she was contributing to ??? had described this carefully, in qualified language, in the way of researchers who have documented something they cannot yet fully claim. The documentation at active Liturgy sites was insufficient for strong conclusions, the papers said, because the monitoring resolution was inadequate for long-term tissue behavior. They had called for more research. They had been published. They had been filed.

She was looking at what the papers had described, in a landscape she could see with her own eyes, rendered in a machine's production language.

Kressida climbed out and stood beside her.

"It is not calibration drift," Lyra said.

Kressida looked at her.

"The apparatus is calibrated correctly," Lyra said. "The decline is the site. It is not recovering at the expected rate." She paused. "The apparatus cannot compensate for that."

A silence.

"There's a reporting mechanism," Kressida said, careful, not pushing. "Liturgy Templar's technical observation, membrane-adjacent anomaly, forwarded through regional Canon ???"

"I know," Lyra said.

Another silence.

The reporting mechanism had received fourteen similar observations from her, over twelve years, for minor anomalies at the Ocipheus Station installation. They had traveled up the chain and been reviewed and filed. The mechanism was functioning. It had been functioning since Year 842, which was the year the first Forge Hearth extraction authorization had been signed, and Year 919, when it was renewed, and Year 1001, and so on across three centuries to the current cycle. The same mechanism that authorized the extraction operations reviewed reports about the extraction operations. It had been doing both things simultaneously for a very long time. The authorization history and the review procedure were issued from the same office under the same canonical charter.

This was not corruption in the way corruption was described when it was described. It was an architecture. The architecture had a logic. The logic had been producing the same outcome for six hundred years because the outcome was what the architecture was for.

She was a Templar. Her reporting obligation ran up the chain.

"I'm not going to report it," she said.

Kressida said nothing. She looked at the display for a moment, and then she looked away, and in the three seconds between looking at the display and composing her face back into its usual economy, something moved there. Not surprise ??? she was not someone who was surprised often. Something that had been held at arm's length and then was not, briefly. The same thing Lyra had seen in Rowe's face the first time she had given him the word for *factory.* The moment when a fact that was supposed to stay abstract finds a body.

Lyra filed it. She did not examine it.

*

Orim was still sitting on the volcanic rock when she turned back to him. He had not moved. His hands were flat on his knees. He was looking at the south country with the expression of a man taking stock of something he did not yet know how to describe.

She went and stood near him. Not close enough to intrude.

"At Sinter," he said, without looking at her, "the tone is directional. Present. Something at that frequency that I have never been certain is the membrane and not the thing that lives below it." He paused. "I have crossed the Forge Hearth approach six times in thirty years. The register here was always different ??? lower, slower, more diffuse. A bruise is different from a cut." He looked at the stone under his feet. "This is not that."

She waited.

"A new site will resist me. Cold, dense ??? it has not been worked, the perceptual surface is harder to read. But I can always find the surface. In fifty years, I have always had enough to press into it and open it." His hands were very still on his knees. "Here there is nothing to press into."

"Not resistance," she said.

"Not resistance. Absence." He looked at her for the first time since the scry. "The way you could not press your hand through a wall is not the same as the way you could not press your hand through the space where the wall used to be. Different kind of nothing."

She heard it then ??? the sound she had been half-aware of since the overlook, the way you become aware of something you have been hearing before you have noticed you are hearing it. A low register, below the wind, below the geological percussion of the steam vents at the valley apparatus stations. Not a sound precisely but a frequency in the chest, below the sternum, where the Sinter tone had its address and where this was not the Sinter tone. Slower. Rhythmic in the way breathing is rhythmic: not the mechanical regularity of a machine but the particular variation of something live. In. The held moment. Out. Longer than it should be.

She had heard this at the Ocipheus Station installation during sustained apparatus use. At the fourth hour of a full Scrying cycle, the ambient register near the apparatus acquired this quality. She had noted it in her research annotations under *membrane-adjacent phenomenology, sustained apparatus use.* She had not pressed on it because pressing on it would have required asking a question that the institutional vocabulary did not quite have room for.

She had never heard it without apparatus.

There was no apparatus on the ridge. The nearest active apparatus was at Hearth-Three, four kilometers south, behind the perimeter. Four kilometers. The sound was here.

She stood and listened to it for a moment. The way you listen to a statement when you are not ready to respond because responding would require admitting that you heard it.

Then she said: "The patrol."

*

Orim turned to look at the approach road.

The patrol was one hundred and fifty meters from the junction now. Eight minutes, perhaps ten.

He looked at the patrol and then he looked at the ridge behind them and then he looked at the Rod's case in the exterior pocket of his satchel. He took the case out. He held it for a moment.

"Stand back," he said.

He did not say it loudly. He said it in the tone of a man who has said it twice before in this company and understands that the people who need to hear it have already learned what it means.

Lyra moved back six meters. Kressida was already behind her. Rowe had been watching Orim since the scry ??? he was watching him now, and he moved back without being told, because Schmalburg was in his memory and *stand back* had a referent.

Orim took the case to the flat stone's far edge, to the point where the overlook gave the clearest sightline to the approach road's base and the eastern thermal vent shimmer visible in the distance beyond it. He sat.

He cleaned the Rod's mineral tip with the dissolution agent from the small kit container ??? methodical, careful, the cleaning of a man who understood that imprecision in this had consequences he would not be the one to survive. He drew fresh Catalyst preparation from the sealed vial and worked it into the grooves along the shaft, into each of the seven graduated channels at irregular intervals. He was thorough about this in a way that slowed his hands. Not nervousness. The care of someone who understood there was no margin here.

He held the Rod and turned the mineral tip between two fingers, reading the grooves the way a locksmith reads tumblers. Past one. Past three. Stopped at the fourth. Tried it. Moved on. Past six. Stopped at seven, which was, she could see from the pattern of his hands, the one he was looking for.

He pressed his fingertips together at the sternum. Two breaths.

He looked at the eastern thermal vent. Not at the patrol. At the vent.

The scry settled. She could read it now, after weeks ??? the quality of his attention narrowing, the particular stillness of a man who had found the surface he was looking for. Fifteen seconds. Twenty.

He opened his eyes.

He was looking at the vent with the particular quality of a man who has seen something he was half-hoping not to see, and who has now decided that the decision has already been made by circumstances, and that he is going to be precise about it.

He set the trigger and depressed it.

*

The aperture appeared at the vent's base ??? she saw it from where she stood, because she knew to look for it now. Translucent membrane tissue stretched across an opening the diameter of the Rod's tip. Dark veins threading through it. They pulsed once, twice. The skin bulged slightly outward, the way it bulged when pressure was building on the far side.

The veins went dark.

What came through was not fire.

She understood this afterward, when she had time. In the moment it simply looked like fire, because it arrived as fire ??? but what she was seeing was a volcano exhaling. Superheated gas. Particulate. The breath of something that had been building pressure for geological time, that was in the middle of doing what it did, and that was not aware ??? could not be aware ??? that a hole had just opened in the surface of its world into somewhere cooler and somewhere else. The gas came through at the temperature and pressure it had accumulated. The Cauld's autumn air was sixty degrees cooler at least, probably more.

The temperature differential ignited at the point of emergence.

Orim had angled the aperture ground-level, tilted south along the road's direction, so that the burning gas left the membrane surface moving toward the junction at approximately road height. The stream was consistent. It did not gust or vary the way wind-driven fire varied. It was the exhalation of a thing with more pressure behind it than a human body could produce in a lifetime, and it traveled the thirty meters from the aperture to the approach road in two seconds, and it was on the road for seventeen seconds, and then the membrane healed and the aperture closed and it was gone.

What remained: smoke. Burning particulate settling. The smell ??? volcanic, acrid, a chemical quality she did not have a prior reference for, superheated gas from a world she had never been to arriving in the autumn air of the Forge Hearth zone and carrying its origin's character into the Cauld.

The approach road was empty.

She stood on the overlook shelf and did not say anything.

On her right, Rowe had not moved. His right hand was at his rifle ??? not gripping it, not drawing it. Just there. His hand had found the stock in the way a body finds what it knows how to reach for when the world changes register without warning. He was looking at the road. His jaw had a quality she had seen before: the quality of a man who is holding his breathing at a particular controlled rate because uncontrolled breathing is what happens when the body panics, and the body knows from experience that panic costs you what you cannot afford to lose.

He knew this smell.

Not this specific smell ??? she understood that later, thinking through it. He had never been near a volcano. He had not come from Sphere 23. But he had been to France, and he had been in the third year of a war, and he knew what it smelled like when explosive-force gases ignited in the open air, when something that had been building pressure discharged into a cooler atmosphere. His body knew that smell at a level that had nothing to do with intellectual recognition. It was older than thought. It was the part that went still when the world changed register, and that stayed still until the world had proved it was done changing.

His hand came away from the rifle.

He exhaled. A slow, deliberate exhale ??? the kind you used when you had been somewhere for a moment and had come back.

He said something quiet in English. Not to her. To himself, she thought. Something short. She did not have the words for it. She had the register: he was naming what he had seen, precisely, so that his own mind understood it had actually happened, and then he was letting the name do its work and dissolve into the morning.

Then he was still again. Watching the road.

On the volcanic shelf, Orim had not looked at the road since the aperture closed. He was looking at the Rod's mineral tip. The tip glowed faintly ??? not fire, but the mineral's thermal response to extreme heat passing through it. The cord wrapping on the grip was smoking at two points where the housing heat had conducted through. He opened his coat ??? the heavy travel coat he had worn since Bressant ??? and folded the lower portion around the case and held it that way, held the warmth against himself, and stood.

He did not say anything.

He did not look at the road, or at any of them, or at the vent where the aperture had been.

Kressida looked at the junction. She looked at the road and the smoke and the clear route south. She looked at the rig, which had not moved from where it stood.

"We should move," she said.

*

They moved.

The junction was clear. The approach road ran south with the smoke dispersing above it in the autumn wind, the road surface scorched in a diagonal line from the vent to the point of contact. The stone would carry that mark for years. Lyra walked past it without slowing.

Orim walked with the wrapped Rod inside his coat. He carried the warmth against him ??? she could see the small adjustments in how he held the coat, the careful management of a thing that was still conducting heat through two layers of fabric. He would have the Rod in that coat until the mineral cooled, and then he would return it to the case, and neither of them would speak about it, because what could be said was already known by everyone in the party, and saying it added nothing but weight to what they were already carrying.

She had a theory about the scry refusal.

She had been building it since the walk up the ridge ??? from the warmth in the stone, from the numbers on Kressida's display, from the frequency in her chest cavity, from the quality of the not-quite-geological warmth from the south. She had the framework: it was assembled from the papers she had read and the four papers she had written and the one paper she had not submitted, and it was adequate to what she was seeing. The membrane at the Forge Hearth extraction sites had been opened and held open under sustained apparatus use for two hundred and ninety-six years. What the membrane did in response to that ??? what it was doing ??? was what the scry refusal had shown Orim from the inside. He had felt it as absence where there should have been surface. She understood, from the research vocabulary she had in her head, what the biological correlate of that absence would be.

She did not say it. The theory, when stated fully, required saying something about the authorization history from Year 842 to the present, about the observation she had not filed, about the Liturgy's review mechanism and what it was designed to do, and she had not yet found the shape of those words. Not the shape of them together. She knew each piece. She did not yet know what sentence they made when they stood beside each other in the open air, in a world with cold autumn light and volcanic stone and the smell of a distant world's exhalation still settling out of the sky.

She filed the theory. Pending.

She had always resolved pending files.

*

The descent took the rest of the morning.

The path went west and south, switchbacking down the escarpment in the long zigzag that loose volcanic stone required. The rig picked its way carefully, gait adjusted, the ember-fungi pulsing slow orange at the exhaust housing. The geological warmth retreated behind them as the limestone emerged from under the volcanic substrate ??? cooler, pale, the smell of altitude giving way to the smell of altitude combined with the sea approach that meant the channel was closer than the map's scale suggested.

Rowe came beside her at the fourth switchback.

He had been quiet since the road. The particular quiet of a man who had been somewhere and had come back and was letting the distance establish. She had learned the difference between his quiets over the weeks: the quiet of translation, the quiet of watching, the quiet of a man holding something that had no words in either language he was working with.

At the fourth switchback he said: "Old man. What he carries."

She looked at him.

"Still hot?" He made a small gesture toward Orim, thirty meters back, still holding the wrapped Rod inside his coat.

"For a while yet," she said.

He nodded. He looked ahead at the path, where the switchback opened onto the next leg of descent, and the limestone paleness of the lower slope, and the road appearance below.

"At Schmalburg," he said. Then he stopped. He was assembling something from the Cauld he had and the pieces were not quite the right shape, but he was going to try them anyway ??? she knew his decision face now. "At Schmalburg. The thing from the door. Old man." He made the gesture they had developed for the force-pierce: something emerging from something small, spreading. "Different thing, same..." He pressed his hand briefly against the back of his other hand, the gesture he used for cost, for the kind of cost that was not coin. "Same."

"Yes," she said. "The same."

He looked at the path. He looked at the road below where it flattened and ran west toward the Lacerta approaches.

"He knows," Rowe said.

It was not a question.

"He knows," she said.

Rowe was quiet for a moment. Then: "And he ???" He tried to find the word. He touched his chest. He touched his eyes. He tried three arrangements of the gesture and found none of them quite right. "He ???"

"He does it anyway," Lyra said. "Because the other thing would be worse."

Rowe thought about this for the length of a switchback.

"Yes," he said.

He did not say anything else. He watched the road below them come into view and watched the channel smell strengthen and watched the afternoon light tilt toward the cooler register of the day's final hours. He was building the map. He was adding to it, carefully, one word and one observed fact at a time.

Sal Vento at the end of it. The channel beyond that. The rest of what this journey had to accomplish.

*

The Lacerta approach roads were white limestone below, compacted and dust-pale, running west toward the channel country and the cliff cities and the *Meridian* moored at whatever Tavar had last called a dock. The channel smell was in the air now ??? salt, cold, the particular quality of depth.

Lyra walked and carried what she was carrying.

Ardea Marten, Sergeant, Ocipheus Station, twelve years. Dead in Schmalburg. The notification form still pending, and the sister in the Western Atrament valley cities, and the particular shape of those words that she had not yet found. She would find it. The hard words always had a shape. You had to be still enough to let it come.

The observation from the ridge. The theory about the membrane. The reporting form she was not going to file, and the understanding of why she was not going to file it, and the further understanding underneath that ??? something she did not yet have a name for, not in the institutional vocabulary she had been using for twenty-two years and not in any other vocabulary she currently owned. It was in the shape of a question. She had not asked the question yet, not even to herself. She was aware of it the way you are aware of a door that is present and that you have not yet decided to open.

The Forge Hearth was behind her. The warmth that was not quite geological. The sound below the wind that she was not going to write down. Orim's face on the volcanic rock ??? the old face, the one she had not seen before ??? and then Orim standing at the aperture site, not looking at the road, holding the warmth inside his coat, saying nothing.

Kressida walked ahead, the rig behind her. Orim, his coat still folded around the cooling Rod. Rowe on her right, watching the light.

The road went west. The road went west and the channel waited and the thieves were somewhere ahead of them, and the work of this journey was not finished, and she was a Templar who had not yet stopped being a Templar.

She kept walking.

[Beat 42]
SAL VENTO — TAVAR

The path down to Sal Vento smelled of the sea two hundred meters before anyone could see it. Salt and worked limestone and something else underneath — the specific cold of rock that had absorbed forty years of spray without ever properly drying, a mineral cold that was different from the cold of air and colder than both. The path switched back through that smell in the particular way of a path worn into being by two centuries of foot traffic rather than designed: each turn placed where someone's footing had held the first time, and everyone after had agreed without discussion that this was where the footing held.

Kressida had parked the rig at the approach road's wide point, where the path accommodated dock equipment transfers before the descent narrowed into something that had its own opinion about what could use it. She turned it into the machine bay there, cut the hydraulics, and came the rest of the way on foot without announcing any of this. Nobody asked. They had been traveling together since Schmalburg and somewhere between the Forge Hearth ridge and the Lacerta borderland the question of what Kressida intended to do with the rig had settled into something that was not quite trust and was more useful than trust: knowledge that the rig's schedule operated on its own reasoning, and the reasoning would be explained when explanation had value, and that the machine would be where it needed to be.

She walked third in the line, her coat collar up and her hands in her pockets. Small. Nothing about her that drew attention in a harbor city full of people who had made careful decisions about how much of themselves to present in public.

Lyra put one foot after the other and thought about the smell of salt in limestone.

On the third switchback, the view opened north: the channel, grey and wide and specific in the way water was specific at this latitude in autumn, the particular opacity of it, the way it held the overcast without reflection. And beyond it, invisible at this distance but present in the way things you were going toward were always present before you could see them — Pallor.

---

The carved relief was at the level of the sea approach, cut into the cliff face and oriented outward toward the channel so that anyone coming up from the water would see it before they saw anything else about Sal Vento. Two and a half centuries old. The Council of Corsairs had commissioned it after the Pallor naval delegation of Year 899 arrived under treaty convention to renegotiate the channel transit agreements and had not left in the form they had arrived in.

The carving was precise and it was unflattering and it had been built to last. Fourteen vessels in the formal Pallor registry pattern, Long Seat pennants at the flagship's prow — Lyra could read the heraldic conventions because twelve years in the Vigil was twelve years of knowing whose institutional flag belonged to whom — arranged in the approaching protocol of a party arriving to negotiate rather than to contest. And then the right half of the composition: what had happened to them. The Corsair vessels were rendered rather larger than the historical naval record indicated. The Pallor envoys were rendered rather smaller. The Long Seat pennants were depicted, with considerable technical skill, upside-down in the carved water.

The lower third had been re-cut recently. The tool marks were still white against the weathered stone, which meant someone had come back to maintain the detail in the sinking ships, which meant Lacerta had been sending someone up here at regular intervals for a hundred and twenty-seven years specifically to keep the drowning diplomats sharp.

Rowe had stopped a few paces behind her. He was looking at the carving with the expression he wore when he was assembling meaning from insufficient vocabulary: complete comprehension on his face, the language for it somewhere else. He had approximately fifty words of Cauld at this stage, of which several he had assembled himself from context and which Orim had confirmed as approximately correct.

He said: "Still."

"Yes," said Orim.

Rowe looked at the fresh tool marks on the lower third. He looked at the artisan's decision about the size of the opposing vessels. He made a sound in his throat — not quite a laugh, not quite something else, something between those two things that contained genuine appreciation for a grievance maintained at this level of commitment.

"Yes," said Orim, in a different register. The register of a man who had been to enough cities to understand what the cities were saying about themselves.

They kept moving. Sal Vento was below and the channel was to the north and the *Avandrey* had eleven days on them.

---

The city occupied the cliff and the plateau above in the manner of a settlement built by people who had decided that accessibility was a form of vulnerability and had arranged their architecture accordingly. Every building had a sight line to the harbor approach. Every main street had an upper terrace with unobstructed views to the water. The support pins holding the buildings to the cliff face had been driven so deep into the limestone over two centuries that the relationship had become mutual: the cliff at this point needed the buildings as much as the buildings needed the cliff, and the limestone had accommodated this in the specific way that limestone accommodated anything — reluctantly, then completely.

The streets were steep and narrow and arranged on a logic that was economic rather than navigational — not where you could move most efficiently, but where you could see most efficiently. Where you could know what was on the water before it knew you were watching.

The Three-Lantern House occupied the second terrace: a long stone building with a narrow entrance and the kind of interior that was larger than the entrance suggested it had any right to be. The founding corsairs were commemorated at the upper end of the terrace in a chapel between the navigation archive and the pilot registry. The chapel had a nautical chronometer on the altar. The chronometer was accurate to thirty seconds per year. It had been on the altar for sixty of the chapel's ninety years of operation, and the congregation had arrived at a form of practical appreciation for it that served the chronometer adequately and required nothing of the chronometer in return.

Lyra walked the harbor approach and let the city settle into her the way cities settled when she gave them the chance. She had worked in cities like this before — cities whose founding stories were about successful theft and profitable betrayal, whose inhabitants had looked at the available models for civilization and had chosen one and held to it long enough that the choice had become the culture. Not dishonest cities. That was not quite the right word. Cities with a clear-eyed understanding of what the word meant in practice, and an equally clear understanding of what it cost, and a pragmatic relationship to that cost that they did not trouble themselves to make look admirable.

She knew how to move through a city like this. She did not need to name what she was reading.

---

The approach to the harbor quarter ran through a set of streets that cut between the second and third terrace buildings. Narrow enough to force single-file movement in several stretches. The upper stories overhung at the third floor, and the gap between facing walls was wide enough for two people walking without touching, which meant anyone who wanted it to be a problem could make it a problem without much preparation. The walls were cold and damp from the sea moisture in the limestone and the smell was lamp oil and fish brine and the specific organic cold of stone that had not been dry since someone built on it.

Three men at the junction where the alley opened toward the dock approach. They had been standing there when the party came around the corner and they did not move to let the party through. Not aggression yet — the assessment before aggression, the particular posture of men who have not fully committed — the weight shifting between them, their angle to the lane-mouth and away from it at the same time. Four seconds, and the one on the left moved first.

Two of them were looking at Lyra. The third was looking at Kressida.

She had observed this before — in a month of travel since Schmalburg she had observed it more than once, this specific sorting. A party of four people in a narrow passage produced a rapid hierarchy in the minds of men considering whether to make the party difficult: Lyra first, for height and the service coat and the Dissolution Blade's scabbard under it; then Orim for the kit and the Rod's housing at his hip; then Rowe for the rifle on his back and the specific way he stood in spaces. And then Kressida, at the rear of the single-file line: the small woman, slight, coat collar up, nothing about her that read as a problem.

The man who had been looking at Kressida moved. Not a lunge. A deliberate lateral step to block the line toward the dock approach — the kind of step that had been used before in corridors like this one to produce a particular kind of compliance, the step that said this conversation was going to happen and the only open question was how long it took the other party to accept that.

Rowe's hand moved toward his coat. Orim did not move, and his stillness was not the stillness of a man surprised — it was the stillness of a man who had encountered this particular configuration before and was waiting to see what version he was in.

Kressida looked at the man who had stepped into her line. She looked at him the way she looked at clearance problems in the machine bay: with attention and without affect. Then she stepped left, out of the single-file line, into the slightly wider space at the terrace wall.

She started walking toward the machine bay.

The party had passed it forty meters back — a deep bay cut into the lower terrace wall, covered and dark inside, a padlocked iron gate standing open on one hinge. They had passed it without examining it closely. Dock infrastructure. Crane equipment. The routine fabric of a harbor terrace. Lyra had registered it and moved on and had not registered what was inside it.

Kressida walked toward it. Not hurrying. Not hesitating.

The man who had blocked the dock approach watched her for two steps and then followed, because she was walking away from the larger threats and toward a dock equipment bay, and this seemed to him like the situation developing in his favor.

The shape inside the bay stood up.

---

It rose from where it had been crouched — knees folded, hull compressed into the bay's working dimensions — in the hydraulic sequence of a machine settling its weight through a controlled series of articulations. Three meters of iron and reaction-plate armor. The BR-7 Flail at rest position, the chain secured for transit, the iron head hanging quiet. It rose to its full height in three seconds and the motion was not violent and it did not need to be. Violence was a specific tool and the rig had not deployed it yet and the motion said so clearly.

The man who had been following Kressida stopped.

He stopped in the way a man stopped when the information his body had been receiving changed faster than he could process its implications. His weight was still forward — he had been walking, had intended to keep walking — and the stopping was a full-body correction, an abort in progress, his feet recognizing what his eyes were still working through.

Kressida reached the pilot hatch. It opened at her approach — she had the sequence on the inside and the outside, the fifteen-second cycle, drilled until the timing was part of her hands rather than her attention. She stepped in. The hatch sealed behind her.

The rig walked out of the bay.

The man looked at it. He looked at the alley behind him where the other two had been standing, and the other two were no longer standing there in any form that required his engagement. He looked at the rig and the rig was four meters from him now and the arm was coming up.

The arm came across at shoulder height. Not fast — not in the way a human arm was fast — but complete, the force hydraulic and expressing itself as a horizontal sweep covering a specific distance in a specific time, and at the end of that distance was the man's coat and the man's center of gravity and the far wall of the alley. He went against the wall and sat down against it. He looked at things that were not in front of him.

The rig stood.

The pilot hatch cycled. Kressida stepped out onto the rig's shoulder, then to the street. Her coat was still closed. Her hands found her pockets with the ease of someone resuming an interrupted movement. She looked at the man against the wall, who was beginning to return to his own company, and then she looked at Lyra.

"The bay dimensions held," she said. "The gate was standing open."

Nobody said anything for a moment.

"We should move," Orim said.

---

The man had been standing outside the building at the alley's upper end for the full duration of it.

Lyra had noted him when she came around the first corner: fifties, expensively dressed under a weathered coat, standing with the quality of a man who was exactly where he had chosen to be and had every reason to stay there. She had filed him as a watcher and moved on, because the alley had required more immediate attention.

He had not moved during any of it. He had watched Kressida step out of the single-file line. He had watched her walk toward the machine bay. He had watched the rig stand up. He had watched the arm movement. He had watched the hatch cycle and Kressida step back to street level and put her hands in her pockets.

He stood there for approximately one minute after that.

The street was quiet except for the harbor sounds below and the water moving in the caves at the cliff's base and the man against the wall, who was breathing carefully.

Then he came down the alley toward them, moving with the economy of a decision already made: not quickly, not slowly, at the pace of a man who knew where he was going and did not require urgency to get there.

He was compact and dark. He had the face of someone who had been outside in variable weather for the past twenty years — not aged by it, not weathered in the picturesque sense, simply marked in the way of a man who had spent more time outdoors than in and had stopped finding this remarkable. The coat was expensive in the practical way, not the presentational way. She could read the Lacerta shell composite in the collar and cuff texture — the shear-thickening material that stopped four rounds at standard engagement distance — and that told her something more useful than whatever story he might choose to tell about himself.

He moved like a man who thought about exits. In this alley that meant he had identified four before he had started walking toward them.

He was looking at Kressida when he arrived. He looked at her for one more moment — at the small woman standing in the street, at the rig behind her, at the space between them — and then he moved his attention to Lyra. Not dismissing Kressida. Filing her. The filing was not the same as dismissal.

"Dame T-044," he said. "Tavar Leal. I have been expecting you since yesterday." He said this as though it were a complete statement of position, which it was. He looked at Rowe with a brief professional assessment. He looked at Orim with the longer gaze of a man who knew how to read equipment and was reading the Rod at his hip with something like recognition. He did not look at the rig again. He had already looked at the rig enough.

"You know who I am," Lyra said.

"Your approach from the Forge Hearth to Sal Vento has one viable path for Atrament-build machinery. I have sources at the Lacerta borderland post. I have known the composition of your party for three days." He said this without apology. It was information. "The embargo on my navigation registry requires Canon Immaculate review or Ocipheus standing authority. I understand your institutional standing includes the latter. I would prefer to discuss a working arrangement somewhere with a shorter acoustic range."

"The bay," Orim said.

---

Inside the bay, with the rig standing at rest outside the open gate and Kressida sitting on the gate's bottom rail with her coat still closed, Tavar unfolded a chart from his coat's interior pocket and laid it on the flat face of the crane housing.

The Pallor channel. The eastern shipping approaches. A point marked in the north — the approximate position of a specific vessel, based on departure records from the Sal Vento anchorage eleven days prior.

"The Relic left this harbor on a vessel called the *Avandrey,*" he said. "Pallor registry, private commission, three-person crew. Cargo declared as archival materials under Pallor cultural property documentation. I could not confirm the contents — the declaration may not have been honest." He paused for the length of time necessary to let the next sentence stand on its own. "The documentation was prepared before the theft occurred. Someone in Pallor's administrative archive had the instrument written and sealed before the Relic was moved. The theft was a delivery mechanism for a property claim that already existed on paper."

Lyra looked at the chart. "How do you know what they were carrying."

"They used this harbor as a staging point for three weeks before departure." He said this with the matter-of-fact tone of someone explaining how his living worked. "Three weeks develops a profile in an anchorage of this size. My professional interest in this harbor's sealed commissions produced the profile." He touched the marked point on the chart without looking at it, the gesture of a man pointing to something he had already looked at enough times. "They asked me to recommend a channel route and then used a different vessel because they had documentation and did not need me. They took the route I recommended because it was the best route and they were not stupid. The intelligence is reliable in proportion to the competence of the source." He looked at the point.
