"The *Avandrey* makes twelve knots in standard channel conditions. Given the weather of the past eleven days, which I track, she is approximately here. Three days from Pallor's northern coast. Perhaps less."

"What do you want," Lyra said.

He was not performing patience. He had the answer already and he was deciding how to present it.

"My navigation registry has been under Canon Immaculate embargo for fourteen months," he said. "I cannot run established routes without Liturgy review at each waypoint." He said this in the tone of a man reciting a constraint rather than complaining about one. "Canon Immaculate review in my current circumstances would produce an outcome I prefer to avoid. Ocipheus standing authority is not a waiver through the review process — it is a prior claim, two centuries older than the embargo architecture that constrains me. One documented transit under that authority does not remove the embargo. It establishes that the embargo does not apply to a route conducted under Ocipheus standing authority, which creates a precedent useful to me in subsequent proceedings." He looked at her. "In plain terms: an authorization document, Ocipheus seal, dated, signed. Outbound and return passage from Sal Vento to Pallor waters. One transit, both legs."

Canon Immaculate embargo. She held the weight of it for a moment. Canon Immaculate required a canonical tribunal, a finding of significant doctrinal violation, a three-member review board at archiving rank. It was not a procedural inconvenience. Whatever Tavar had done — whatever he had done or refused to do — the Liturgy had assembled the appropriate machinery to respond to it.

She set the question down. She did not need the answer tonight and she might not need it at all. What she needed was the channel.

"You come back with us," she said. "Outbound and return. You navigate the crossing and you provide the vessel."

"Agreed."

"I don't authorize a transit and lose track of where it goes."

"I have no interest in losing track of myself," he said. He reached inside the coat and produced a small leather document case. The authorization language was prepared — she had expected this, because a man who had been running calculations on this conversation for three days would have prepared the language. She took it and read it. It was correct in every particular. She signed it and pressed her Ocipheus field seal into the wax and handed it back.

He put it away with the specific, unhurried care of a person handling something they have spent fourteen months waiting to handle.

Then a pause. Different in register from the pauses before it — those had been operational pauses, the breath between clauses of a negotiation. This one was something else.

"The Oculus Memoriae," he said. He was looking at the chart. "The confessional records it holds. When the subject is no longer living — what becomes of their record."

She looked at him.

His face was doing the thing it did when a man had already decided to ask a question and had already accepted the cost of asking it. Not performing calm. Actually calm, which was different, because actual calm was the state you arrived at after paying the cost privately in the time before the question.

"They remain in the archive," she said. "Sealed with the subject's death record. They do not transfer to heirs or family. They are held in perpetuity at the installation where the recording was made."

He nodded once. He looked at his hands. Something settled in his expression that was not relief and was not grief and was in the territory of things that existed between those two — the particular acceptance of information you had assumed you knew and had needed to hear spoken aloud anyway. For the confirmation. Because there was a difference between assuming a thing and having a Templar of Ocipheus say it to you directly.

There was a person. There was a record at Ocipheus Station. He was not going to Ocipheus Station and neither was she, not yet, not for weeks.

She did not press it. It was his.

"Then we are agreed," he said, and stood, and the conversation was over in the way conversations ended with him: not concluded, simply at its end.

---

Lyra found herself on the upper terrace path above the harbor, the north view open, the channel grey below and Pallor behind the grey. She did not remember deciding to walk there. She had walked there and now she was there and the remaining soldier fell in beside her on the path.

The soldier had been with them since Ocipheus Station. One of the two still living after Schmalburg. She was in her middle thirties, competent in the quieter way, the kind of competence that expressed itself in good judgment rather than noise, and Lyra had relied on it without making an occasion of it for fourteen days.

They walked for twenty paces before the soldier said anything.

"The authorization you signed," she said. "Canon Immaculate level embargo."

"Yes."

"We're taking passage from him to intercept a retrieval party operating under Pallor property documentation, using your Ocipheus standing authority to cover the transit."

"Yes."

Two vessel shapes in the middle distance, heading south. The channel had the specific quality of water that was always slightly dark even in the middle of the day, the depth of it.

"I was commissioned for a recovery operation," the soldier said. "Active duration three weeks. We're on day fourteen." She said this without inflection — not accusation, not complaint, the flat tone of a navigator stating a bearing and its implications. "The operation is now something else. I'm not qualified for what it's become." She paused. "And I don't mean that as a statement about capability."

"I understand what you mean," Lyra said.

The soldier reached inside her coat and produced her field commission — the Ocipheus standing document that had been issued to the unit at the beginning of this, before Schmalburg, before Ardea, before the Forge Hearth's refusal and the three-day crossing of Lacerta country with the rig's footfall on the road behind them every morning. She held the commission for a moment, not reading it. Then she put it in Lyra's hand.

"You keep it," she said. "File it how you need to."

Lyra looked at her.

"I'm not leaving the service," the soldier said. She had drawn this distinction carefully before this conversation — Lyra could hear the precision with which she maintained it, the line between a thing she was prepared to do and a thing she was not. "I know what leaving means. I have done the calculation and I'm not making it tonight. I'm asking to leave this mission. Tonight." She looked at the channel. "There's a cousin in the Heloth commercial fleet. He runs cargo out of the lower anchorage. I have coin. I haven't seen him since my first rotation."

Twelve years of service ahead of her in the standard career architecture. A garrison manifest log she had been able to read. A professional judgment about the distance between a recovery operation and what this had become.

Lyra closed her hand around the commission.

The soldier looked at her once more — the look of a person checking something they needed to be certain of — and turned and walked down the path toward the lower anchorage, where the commercial harbor traffic moored and the Heloth freight lines took on their last Lacerta passengers before the evening departure window.

Lyra watched her until the path curved and she was gone.

Orim had come up the path from somewhere below at some point during the conversation. She was not certain when he had arrived. He was standing three paces behind her, and he had the stillness of a man who had heard enough to understand the shape of it and had chosen not to interrupt until it was over.

Neither of them said anything.

The channel was grey. The path showed nothing.

"Heloth," Orim said.

"She has family there."

"Good." He did not look at Lyra. He was looking at the empty path. "The worse outcome would have been next week, when she had had time to think of a reason to resent it."

There was nothing to say to this that would have been more accurate. She put the commission in her coat pocket and stopped touching it.

---

That evening, Tavar took them to the dock.

A quarter-mile south of the city's main harbor, accessible by a path that descended through the limestone on iron-cleated steps worn smooth by thirty years of use. The path was private in the Lacerta way — not locked, not guarded, simply arranged so that a person unfamiliar with the cliff face would not find it without being told where to look. Tavar had not been told where to look for a long time.

The dock had been built for sailing galleys. The iron mooring rings were hand-forged and set at the scale of that work — two-meter intervals, heavy iron, driven into the limestone and set in lead sealant that had been there for sixty years and was not going anywhere. They had been sized for the mooring lines of a three-masted trading vessel, for the weight and tension of ropes that needed to hold something with draft and displacement, and the dock was long and deep for the same reason.

The *Meridian* occupied the dock in the manner of something designed for a different kind of water.

Her hull was aluminum and riveted steel — the aeronautical construction, tighter riveting than any shipwright would use, a different material logic: built to be light enough for air and strong enough for sea, the engineering compromise of something that needed to do both. She sat low at the waterline with the draft of a vessel designed for open-water landings, broad in the beam for stability in channel chop, the hull's proportions those of a machine that had decided the sea was a surface to land on rather than a medium to move through. Above the hull, the rigid envelope: a framework of pale metal ribs covered in gas-bag fabric, sixty meters of it, the airship section, the reason the *Meridian* could cross the channel in conditions that would strand a conventional vessel and cover the distance in hours rather than days.

The mooring lines were nylon. They ran from the hand-forged iron rings to the hull's cleats in the practiced curves of lines that had been tied and retied in many anchorages, in many weathers. Nylon on iron. The dock had been built for a different century and the vessel had arrived in it from a different world and neither had found the other incongruous, which was a fact about both of them.

Tavar stood at the foot of the gangway and looked at her. He was not performing the looking — he had no need to perform it, she was there regardless of how he presented. He had the quality of a man with a high opinion of the thing he was showing you, an opinion that required nothing from you, that would persist whether you shared it or did not. He pointed it at the *Meridian* and let the *Meridian* do the rest.

"Forty knots in flat air on envelope gas," he said. "Twenty-five sustained against a strong channel headwind. Scried petroleum fuel, Lacerta alchemy-refined accelerants. The cargo hold accommodates the rig." He said the last part toward Kressida, who was reading the hull with the focused attention she applied to machines — not admiring it, reading it. "Navigation systems are Lacerta-modified Liturgy standard from Year 1103. There is some variance from current production architecture."

"How much variance," Kressida said.

"Enough that the initialization takes six minutes instead of three."

She looked at him. "How long have you been running this system."

"Eleven years."

"Then six minutes is accurate and the system is stable," she said. She looked at the hull for a moment more — at the riveting specifically, at the tolerances. "The engineering space. Accessible from the cargo hold?"

"Standard Liturgy access panel. Modified fit but the interface is compatible."

She nodded and looked at the envelope ribs and appeared to be satisfied with what she found there.

Rowe was standing at the foot of the gangway, looking at the *Meridian*'s full length. Not reading her the way Kressida read her — not from engineering knowledge, from something else. He stood there with the quality of stillness that he used when he was encountering something that required him to revise a held belief, and he was doing it fast because he had learned to do it fast. The riveting. The hull's proportions. The aeronautical logic of a construction built to be in air and water both.

He had seen something like this once — not this, not at this scale or this development, but the family of it. A coastal naval air station in the spring of 1917. A flying-boat hull being repaired after a patrol, the mechanics working on the rivet lines, the machine enormous and ungainly out of its element on the hard stand and completely coherent in the air above the harbor. This hull was not that hull. This was a later development of that logic, finished in a way that hull had not been, the way the bolt-action rifles in the Vierna barracks were a later development of something his world had been working out. His world had built the early form. The Cauld used the finished one.

He looked at the nylon mooring lines on the hand-forged iron rings.

He looked at the Meridian for one more moment.

Then he walked up the gangway without looking back.

Tavar watched him board and said nothing and looked at Lyra.

"He recognizes the hull type," she said.

"Does he."

"I believe so."

He considered this for a moment with the expression he had worn since the alley — the expression of a man who has added a new piece to his framework and is allowing the framework to accommodate it, without announcement, without discussion. Then he walked up the gangway and the dock was quiet except for the water moving against the limestone and the nylon lines making the sound of nylon under regular tension, which was a different sound from rope under the same tension and which the dock's hand-forged iron rings had been hearing for long enough by now not to find it unusual.

Orim stood beside Lyra at the foot of the gangway and looked at the *Meridian* the way he looked at everything he was about to rely on: completely, without sentiment, reserving judgment for the performance rather than the promise.

"She'll do," he said. "Against the channel in this season."

It was the most optimistic assessment she had heard him offer since the Forge Hearth approach.

---

They left Sal Vento four hours before dawn.

The city had contracted to its own watchfulness at that hour, the harbor lights below, the Three-Lantern House dark on the second terrace, the garrison post at the upper cliff edge with its two soldiers looking at the water in the direction they had been positioned to look. The stars above the channel were the particular brightness of autumn stars over open water — very sharp, very cold, the specific quality of light that was not quite illumination and was significantly better than nothing for a cliff path in the dark.

The rig's footfall on the dock stones was what it was. Iron on limestone, three meters and reaction-plate armor, the BR-7 Flail at transit rest, Kressida inside with the hatch sealed and her respiration settling into the deep rhythm of active interface. She was already in conversation with the *Meridian*'s navigation systems through the rig's mechanical language, the initialization sequence running, the six-minute estimate becoming four because the system was as stable as she had assessed and the interface was finding her faster than the formal protocol required it to.

Orim went up the gangway with the kit on his back and the Rod at his hip and the expression of a man who had made a professional decision and was implementing it.

Rowe followed — the rifle on his shoulder, the bayonet at his hip, the spare rounds in the coat's inner pocket where he could reach without looking. He had been loading in low light since Schmalburg and the motion lived in his hands now. He did not look back at Sal Vento as he boarded. He looked forward at the Meridian's navigation compartment and the instruments inside it.

Tavar was already at the console when Lyra came aboard. He was running the departure sequence. He did not look up. The instruments on the console were the accumulated customization of eleven years aboard a specific vessel: a Liturgy standard compass rose with Lacerta bearing marks scratched in by hand, the navigation clock retrofitted into a housing for a different instrument, three modifications she recognized and two she did not. The kind of instrument board that told you more about the pilot than any formal specification could.

She went to the bow rail.

The channel was dark. The stars were over the envelope's outline, very sharp. Pallor was across the water. The *Avandrey* was three days ahead of them with the Relic sealed in its cargo hold and a retrieval party that believed, with some legal basis, that they were doing the right thing. In Ocipheus, the vigil archive was empty of the Relic for the first time in seven hundred and forty-one years, and the note she had left Vega on the scribing table fourteen days ago said back in three days and she had not been back. In Schmalburg, Ardea was under circumstances that would not be resolved by the completion of this mission or any mission.

She stood at the bow rail and let the cold come in off the channel. It was the autumn cold of water at this latitude and at this hour, not the cold of the Forge Hearth approach's volcanic stone, not the cold of the Vierna mountain passes, but the specific cold of open water moving through still air, and it found the gaps in her half-plate and settled in them with complete patience. She had learned the gaps because she had needed to learn them. She knew exactly where she would bleed if the wrong blade found the right angle, and that knowledge was a form of intimacy with her own body that she had arrived at through the specific education of the past fourteen days and the thirty years that had prepared her for it.

The *Meridian* moved out of the dock. The mooring lines slipped from the iron rings and trailed in the water for a moment and were drawn aboard and coiled. The dock disappeared behind them, and the cliff, and the relief carved into the limestone with its hundred and twenty-seven years of maintained grievance. The channel opened ahead.

Three days.

Orim settled behind her against the rail with the quiet of a man who had found his position and did not plan to argue with it. Rowe was somewhere aft, reading the water the way he read everything — from the outside, finding the logic of it in the way it behaved rather than in any language anyone had given him for it.

Tavar said nothing from the console. The *Meridian* was talking to him through the interface and he was listening and the channel was ahead of them and he knew this water in the way a person knew water they had crossed many times in many conditions, which was not romantically but specifically — this current, this season, the particular behavior of the channel in the hour before dawn when the wind had not yet decided what it was going to be that day.

The cold was the cold. Her hands were working. The problem was in front of her.

She kept her hands on the bow rail and watched Pallor come to meet them.

[Beat 43]
THE CHANNEL — HOURS, NOT DAYS

The Serracas was built to haul salt fish and lamp oil and worked slate and not to carry passengers, a distinction the cargo master had made clear in the arrangement and continued to make clear through the particular quality of the space she had assigned them in the forward hold. The hold was functional. So was the smell.

Two weeks since the theft. Three weeks since Esvane had briefed Owain in his planning room at Caer Glas and watched him nod with the careful concentration of a man who had been waiting thirty years for someone to say what she was saying. Three weeks of checkpoints and road-houses and one very long crossing through Atrament's industrial approaches, and now this: a night crossing on a commercial trader, the channel rough enough to matter, the lantern oil guttering in the cold that came up through the hull planking. The Pallor coast was twelve hours out. Perhaps ten, in these winds.

The moor-hounds were at the far end of the hold.

They had been settling there for four days — since Sal Vento, or just before — and Esvane had noticed it the way she noticed most things: without comment, filed alongside the other things she had noticed and set aside. There were three of them: Owain's hounds, trained trackers with the long necks and six-legged gait of their heathland lineage, low to the ground in the way of creatures that spent their lives following scent through grass. They did not sleep. They had the posture of sleep — flanks slow, eyes half-closed — but they were watching the case.

The case sat where Esvane had placed it when they came below: against the forward bulkhead, between a rack of salt-fish casks and the spare anchor chain, secured with a length of rope to the nearest ring so the channel swells could not shift it. Palm-sized lens in a field transport case. Lighter than she had expected when she first handled it. The membrane-adjacent warmth she had filed under known phenomenon and moved on.

The hounds had tracked thermal traces for two weeks. She had watched them read the road the way they always did — sampling the air, orienting to gradient, efficient in the way of animals bred to one precise purpose. What they were doing now was not that. What they were doing now was watching. Not with the urgency of animals that had identified prey. With something more patient and less easy to name: the quality of attention you saw in a creature that had been given a problem it could not resolve and had decided to wait it out.

She had not touched the lens again since the road-house outside Bressant. She had considered it once — a practitioner's assessment, the same careful professional examination she would apply to any membrane-adjacent object in transit. She had thought about it and then she had closed the case and moved on. Whether that was discipline or something else, she had not pressed the question.

Petra was awake on the far side of a salt-fish cask, sitting with her back against the hull planks and her arms around her knees. The channel swell moved through the hull in slow rhythmic pushes. She was not sleeping. She had the quality of someone who had stopped trying some time ago.

Wren was somewhere behind them in the hold's darkness, in the space behind the spare tackle where he had assembled himself a kind of corner. He had been there since they came below. Esvane could not see him but she had not heard the specific quiet of actual sleep. She had heard, instead, the controlled breathing of someone managing his own presence in a closed space.

A sailor's boots crossed the deck above them. Paused. Moved on.

Esvane said: "I need to tell you something before we make Pallor."

Petra did not move. After a moment she said: "All right."

"Not a problem with the documentation. The documentation is sound." Esvane shifted her weight against the hull. The plank behind her was cold through the wool. "The Canon's purpose."

Petra waited.

"I have known since the fourth month," Esvane said. "Working the authorization chain. You develop a sense, in this work — for the shape of what a document is actually doing versus what it says it is doing. The shape of this one was not a property dispute recovery, though the property dispute is real." She looked at the carry-case. The hounds were still watching it. "He wanted the Relic's memory."

"What does that mean."

"The Oculus observes. It accumulates what it has seen at each location it occupies. Seven hundred and forty-one years at the Ocipheus vigil station. Seven hundred and forty-one years of whatever the vigil membrane has shown it." She paused. "Prelacze wanted that record. Not to restore Pallor's right — the right was the vehicle. He wanted proof that the Liturgy's founders had foreknowledge of something they chose to suppress. Something they have been filing under no action indicated for generations. He cannot extract it through legitimate channels because the extraction would require disclosing what he wants to find. So he needed someone with a genuine claim to front the recovery."

Petra said: "Owain."

"Yes."

The vessel shuddered through a larger swell. The carry-case held against its rope. The moor-hounds did not look at the swell. They looked at the case.

"Owain believed he was conducting a sanctioned retrieval under Pallor's historical property right," Esvane said. "He was correct about the right. He does not know about the Canon's purpose. He does not know the Canon chose him specifically because a six-generation grievance makes better institutional cover than a Canon's personal leverage program." She said this without inflection, in the way she said things she had rehearsed until the feeling was worn smooth. "When we reach Caer Glas — after the Relic is in the vault, after we have done what we came to do — I will have to tell him that."

The hold absorbed the sentence and gave nothing back.

"The secondary client," Esvane said. "Your Lacerta contact."

"Yes."

"They want to know where the Relic goes after it reaches Pallor."

"That was the arrangement."

"If Prelacze has an agent in that chain — or if the contact is working for a competing interest, something that wants the leverage for themselves — then a confirmed delivery report from Pallor becomes a targeting instrument. Someone who knows the Relic is in the ancestral vault at Caer Glas, with a specific window, has options I would prefer they not have." Esvane pulled her coat tighter. "I need the secondary client to receive no confirmation. I need that arrangement to be dead before we dock."

Petra looked at the carry-case. She looked at it for long enough that Esvane had time to notice the cask nearest to her left shoulder, the grain of the rope she was sitting near, the way the lantern cut the hold into two registers of visibility.

Petra said: "I threw the token two nights ago."

Esvane's hands, which had been resting in her lap, went still. She felt the cold planking under her through the wool of her coat. The channel moved through the hull.

She said: "Where."

"Harbor at Sal Vento. Eastern end, past the commercial docks, where the cliff comes down to the water. There's a walkway out to the water line. I walked to the end of it." Petra did not look up. "I threw it in."

"Two nights ago."

"Before we booked passage. Before you said anything about the Canon's purpose." A pause. "It was a professional call. The secondary client isn't worth the exposure."

The Serracas took a wave at an angle and rolled through it. The lantern swayed on its hook and steadied. A cask settled somewhere behind them with a slow scrape.

Esvane watched Petra not look at her.

There was something she was not saying. Esvane had spent twenty-three years watching people not say things — in canonical offices and road-house negotiations and the particular silences that followed accurate statements that were also, precisely, not the whole truth. Petra had made a professional call. That was true. The professional call was also not the whole of what had happened at the end of that walkway.

She did not press it. She had not earned the right to press it, and she was not sure pressing it would do anything except make Petra name something she was not ready to name, and Petra naming things she was not ready to name on a night channel crossing was not useful to anyone.

She said: "All right."

Petra nodded once.

From the darkness behind the spare tackle, Wren said nothing.

The hold settled. The Serracas worked through the rough patch and came out the other side, the motion changing register to a slower roll, and the lantern stopped swinging and burned steady.

At the far end of the hold, one of the moor-hounds shifted its weight — not rising, just redistributing — and fixed on the carry-case with the focused stillness of an animal that has identified something it cannot resolve and has decided to wait it out. The other two tracked the same point. Their long necks were low. They were not frightened. They were paying attention in the way they paid attention to a quarry that had not yet moved.

---

What Petra was not saying:

Two nights ago she had walked to the eastern harbor at Sal Vento at an hour when the cliff streets were quiet and the last working boats had already put out. The commercial end of the harbor was dark. She had passed two men coiling line on a dock without looking at them, and they had not looked at her, and she had walked past the last of the commercial lanterns and out along the walkway to where the planks ended and the water was underneath.

The token was a small piece of carved bone, Lacerta manufacture, three-symbol indicator on one face. When the arrangement was activated, she was supposed to send it by courier to a contact address in Pallor's coastal port. The contact would arrange for the information to travel further. She had been paid four months ago. The rest on delivery.

She had stood at the end of the walkway and turned the token over in her fingers the way she turned everything over in her fingers when she was deciding something — not examining it, just keeping her hands occupied while the rest of her did the actual work. It was dark. The water was dark. The harbor smell was fish and pitch and the particular salt cold of late autumn, and she had stood there longer than the act required.

She had spent four months telling herself it was nothing. Insurance. An option she might not take, assessed at the time of completion, the same professional framing she applied to any arrangement that ran parallel to a primary contract. She had taken secondary payments before. It was common practice in this work. The primary client knew the world she operated in. It was not deception. It was layered interest, and layered interest was the cost of doing business with someone who worked the border approaches.

The job had complicated in ways she had not anticipated.

Not the checkpoints. Not the transit documents or the Canon's institutional machinery or the very long leg through Atrament. She had anticipated all of that. What she had not anticipated was Owain's certainty applied with the sustained, unconditional quality of a man who had been carrying a belief for thirty years and had never had a reason to set it down. She had argued with him in the planning phase the way she argued with everyone — checking whether something was real by pushing against it. He had not argued back. He had simply continued to believe it, and waited for her to finish, and then explained why he was going to do it anyway, and the explanation had not been different from what he said before she argued. It was the same explanation. He was not performing conviction. He had it.

She had thought: this is what people who have never had their certainty tested look like.

She had thought this and then she had spent six weeks watching him be right about every material assessment he made about the operation. The timing was right. The documentation was sound. The route was clean. Esvane's authorization chain was precise. The things Owain had faith in were, operationally, correct.

She had not had a word for what it was like to watch someone be correct and certain at the same time.

Wren was different. Wren had the certainty from the same source — the Caerglas family, six generations of the same story told as obligation, the same emotional inheritance that Owain carried. But Wren had read something, somewhere in the three months before the operation, that had put a question in his face he could not get out. She had seen it from the beginning. He had not said what it was. He asked questions instead, and Esvane deflected them, and Petra told him to keep walking, and the question stayed in his face like a stone in a boot.

She had not told him to keep walking because she was impatient. She had told him because she recognized what he was carrying and she did not want to be asked to carry it too.

She had stood at the end of the walkway and she had known, with the specific clarity of a person who has been lying to themselves and has run out of road, that it was not insurance. That it had stopped being insurance somewhere in the second month of the planning phase and had become a weight she was carrying alongside the primary contract, and the weight was not money. The money was straightforward. The weight was the specific feeling of holding a document that said: when this is over, here is how you profit from these people's belief.

She had opened her hand.

She had watched the token hit the water and go under. There was no splash worth describing. A small carved bone dropped into harbor water at low tide made very little sound.

She had walked back along the walkway.

She had gone back to her bunk in the road-house and she had lain on the mattress, which was the kind of mattress that left a record of everyone who had slept on it before, and she had looked at the ceiling. The going-to-sleep had taken a long time. She had not expected this. The decision had been clean. Professional. The secondary client was not worth the exposure — that was accurate, that was the framing, and framing had always been the whole of it before. She did not know why this one was different.

She did not examine why. She was going to continue not examining why. There were things you let settle if you intended to keep working, and this was one of them.

---

The lantern oil was getting low. Esvane could see it in the way the flame had compressed to a smaller, whiter point, burning harder to maintain itself against the cold air coming through the hull seams.

She looked toward the darkness where Wren was.

She said, quietly: "You have been listening."

A pause.

"Yes," Wren said.

"And."

Another pause, longer. The channel worked against the hull.

"Nothing," he said.

She waited to see if there was more to it. There was not. He had heard everything she said to Petra — the shape of the Canon's purpose, the secondary client, the token thrown in the harbor. He had heard all of it and he was sitting with it in the dark and he had nothing to add.

That was probably the right response. She was not sure she had anything to add either.

"Get some sleep," she said.

"Probably not."

"No."

The hold moved around them in the slow rocking of deep water. The hounds were still. The salt-fish casks settled.

She thought: I have known about the Canon's purpose for six weeks, and I came anyway.

She thought: Owain does not know, and he came anyway, because the claim is real, because six generations is long enough, and because I did not tell him the thing I knew would change how he understood what he was doing.

She thought: whether that was protecting him or using him is a question I have not asked myself at any length, and I am not going to ask it on a channel crossing at four in the morning, with the moor-hounds watching a lens in a case and Petra staring at hull planks and Wren sitting in the dark behind spare tackle, being twenty-two.

She was going to have to tell him.

That was the fixed point. The documentation would stand — Pallor's claim was real, the recovery instrument was sound, post-retrieval canonical review would find the authorization chain intact. The Relic would be in the vault. Owain would have done the thing. And then she was going to find a room with a door and she was going to tell him that the Canon who authorized the operation had a purpose that was not Pallor's purpose, and that Prelacze had chosen them because they were convenient, and that the six-generation right had been used the way you use a road — not for its own sake but because it ran in the direction he was already going.

She did not know what he was going to do with that.

She had known Owain since he was a Knight two years past his first infusion: certain and earnest and accurate in the specific way of people who have not yet had the thing they believe in tested by the people who claimed to share the belief. She had watched him become the man who could do this — who could see his House's grievance and his own certainty and the Canon's offered authority as three things in alignment, pointing the same direction. She had watched it happening over the years, and she had thought: he is going to have to live past this someday.

She had not known she would be standing next to him when it happened.

The reason she had gone through with it was Owain.

Not the Canon's leverage program. Not institutional cover. Not the authorization chain she had spent three months building to precise specification. She had gone through with it because Owain had spent thirty years believing the claim should be honored, and he was right, and he was also going to find out that the thing he believed in had been used, and she was the person who had known and had not told him, and she was going to be there when that happened. Being there was something she owed him. She did not know another way to pay it.

She did not know how to name what that was. She had a vocabulary for institutional failure and personal betrayal and the specific compromises that a career in the Liturgy's mechanism required. She did not have a word for: I chose to go into this knowing the Canon's purpose was not what it said, because the underlying right was real, and because Owain needed to do this, and because being the person who tells him afterward is the price of knowing and not saying.

She filed it as: the channel is dark and we are hours from Pallor.

That was sufficient. That was what was true.

The moor-hounds had not moved. Their eyes were pale in the lantern's compressed light, fixed on the carry-case with a patience that looked, from a distance, like devotion. She had seen this quality in them when they tracked — the specific commitment of an animal that has identified what it is following and has decided to follow it wherever it leads.

She thought, once, in the way you think things in the dark of a cargo hold at four in the morning when you are not sleeping: it has been everywhere we have been. It has been in every road-house and checkpoint room and river barge and checkpoint queue. It has accumulated all of it.

She thought: the hounds are not wrong to watch it.

Then she did not think about it further, because they were ten hours from Pallor and what was in the case was in the case, and the work of the next ten hours was getting there.

Somewhere behind her, Wren shifted in the dark. Not toward sleep — just the adjustment of a body that has been held in one position for too long. He was twenty-two and he had heard what he had heard and he was going to have to carry it into the morning at Caer Glas, where Owain had been waiting in the moor dark for four days, walking the approach to the ancestral vault and not walking it, standing at the field edge and looking south and east the way a man looks in the direction of something he has been waiting for. He was going to hand Owain the case and watch Owain's face when he took it, and he was going to know what he knew, and he was going to wait for the right time.

The right time was something nobody on this boat could tell him.

Petra had her eyes closed. Probably not sleeping. She had the held-still quality of someone who has made a decision and is now simply on the other side of it, in the terrain where the decision has consequences and you walk through them and see what they are.

The lantern gave what it had left. Outside the hull the channel moved, and ahead of them the Pallor coast was in the dark, and behind them — hours behind them, working through some stage of whatever she was working through, fast enough to close distance but not yet fast enough — Lyra T-044 was on the water.

Hours. Not days.

That would have to be enough.

[Beat 44]
THE ACQUISITION — EIRENE-7

The cliff path ran south along the coast at an elevation where the wind was indifferent to them but the cold was not. It came off the water in the particular way of sea cold at the end of the night — not the dramatic cold of an hour earlier, which had conviction, but the tired cold that preceded dawn, which had given up on announcement and simply continued.

Lyra had been lying on the limestone overhang above the cave mouth for ninety minutes, watching the dock through the vigil-glass scope. The scope did other things — read membrane anomalies at range, logged thermal signatures, performed functions she had appreciated when she had salvaged it from the Schmalburg dockyard and appreciated differently now — but what she was using it for was the straightforward purpose of seeing in the dark, which it managed acceptably. The cave mouth was sixty meters below and the dock inside it was forty meters in and the ship was inside the dock and she had confirmed the hull markings before the last light failed.

EIRENE-7. Checkpoint designation and maintenance code in the Liturgy's block letters, stenciled without decoration because decoration was not what the designation was for.

She had come down from the overhang when the watch changed. The watch change told her three things: the rotation schedule was correct, the soldiers on post were real soldiers doing a real garrison duty and not some other configuration, and the window Tavar had described was the window they had. Three hours, possibly four, before the dawn courier pass from the garrison post.

Now she was below the overhang on the cliff path, the party in a rough line behind a limestone shelf that was big enough to hide them if no one from the garrison was actively looking and small enough to guarantee the kind of cold that came from standing still in a wind that had not gotten any warmer.

Tavar was looking at the cave mouth. He had the clipboard. He had produced it from inside his coat in the way of someone who had packed it for the purpose and saw no reason to produce it before the purpose arrived.

"The plan," Lyra said.

He had already said it once, two hours ago, in the road-house outside the garrison town where they had eaten the kind of meal that was hot and bad and made the cold manageable. She was saying it again because Orim had not been listening the first time with the part of his attention that listened for exits and because Rowe needed the version with more Cauld in it.

Tavar turned from the cave mouth. He said it again.

"The garrison dock is inside the cave mouth," he said. "Land access through the gate on the north cliff face — stairs cut down from the garrison post. The gate watch is two soldiers, one post. The dock watch is two more — one at the gangway foot, one at the ship's forward hatch." He paused. "The rotation's logistics officer is a woman named Vera. Six years in that post. Before that, supply crew on the *Eirene-4*, which was this vessel's predecessor." He indicated the cave with the clipboard. "She knows me. I was running the wall-supply route three years ago and she processed every manifest I filed. She is professional, she is capable, and she will open the dock gate for a reasonable story."

"What is the story," Orim said.

"The Eirene-7's manifold was certified six days ago. The inspection window lapsed because someone in the supply chain failed to file the re-certification request before the garrison rotation began. The vessel can't receive cargo until the window is renewed, which means the garrison's supply delivery this rotation may hold up the Wall schedule." He produced the document from inside the clipboard's pages. "This is the re-certification notice. It's genuine. I generated it through the Liturgy's supply documentation office three days ago."

Lyra looked at the document. She had not known about it. She had asked about the documentation and he had said *handled* and she had filed this under the same category she had been filing things about Tavar since Sal Vento: real, verified, origin unclear, keep the category open.

"Rowe," she said.

He was on her left. He had the rifle on his shoulder and his hands on the stock in a particular way that was not readiness exactly but was the position preceding readiness — the grip you took when you knew what the next position was going to be and were giving the present moment its appropriate space.

She looked at the overhang above the cave entrance. The limestone formed a natural shelf thirty meters above the cave mouth, angle northeast, sightline into the cave's interior through the upper gap where the ceiling opened before it narrowed back to the dock end. She had identified it from below.

She pointed at it.

He looked at it for three seconds. He said: "Ja."

He had more Cauld than *ja* now. He used it when he was saying yes to something he had already understood.

"Two targets," she said. "The gangway soldier and the dock watch forward."

"Yes," he said, in Cauld, and then added: "I see them."

He could not see them yet. He meant he would see them. The distinction was not ambiguity — it was the specific confidence of someone who had looked at terrain and understood what would be visible from which position. She had been in the field with him long enough to know what his certainties looked like, and this was a certainty.

"Kressida," she said.

The small woman was beside the rig, which was not visible from the path because she had walked it into the inlet shadow two hours ago and it had been there since. Kressida was in the same dark that the rig occupied. She had the quality of someone who had been standing in this cold for two hours and had stopped noticing the cold somewhere in the first hour, because noticing the cold was not a use of attention that paid back.

"The dock watch forward is on the ship's starboard side," she said. "That's my side. I'll come over the hull aft of the wing root." She considered. "I need him not at the forward hatch when I top the rail."

"The gate approach draws both watches," Tavar said. "The dock watch turns to look. You have twenty seconds."

"Twenty is enough if I'm already on the hull."

"You'll be on the hull."

She looked at the water. The cave mouth from below was a gap in the cliff face at waterline, the entrance marked by the dock's running lights as a faint smear of warmth against the surrounding rock. The cave water was visible — black, slow, moving with the tide's long breath.

Kressida looked at it with no expression. She made whatever assessment she made. Then she said: "I'll need a two-minute lead."

"You have it," Lyra said.

---

Orim scried from the limestone shelf, crouched with his fingertips pressed at his sternum and his eyes finding the middle distance. He did not use the Rod. The range was not the problem and his minor gift was sufficient for crew positions at this distance, with the cave funneling his attention toward the vessel. He took ninety seconds.

His eyes opened.

"Two soldiers as you said. The gangway watch is seated — starboard side, base of the gangway, rifle across the knees, watching the gate side." He stopped briefly. "The forward watch is moving. He was below when I caught him, coming back up from the hold. He's on deck now with a clipboard — checking the mooring lines along the starboard rail." Another stop. "He'll be at the forward hatch when he finishes the starboard rail. That's approximately three minutes."

"Crew in the ship?"

"The hold is clear. The pilot housing I didn't push through — there's something between me and that space I didn't want to press." He looked at his hands. "It may be nothing. It may be the instrument cluster's output. I've felt similar from Liturgy apparatus before."

"Engine thermals," Tavar said.

"Possibly." He did not sound convinced. He did not push it. He sat on the rock and his breathing was the deliberate breathing of someone who had spent forty years learning what deliberate breathing was for.

Lyra looked at the cave.

The clipboard soldier was three minutes from the forward hatch. Kressida needed two minutes to reach the water and position the rig for the hull approach. The sequences could be made to overlap.

"Now," she said to Kressida.

---

The small woman went down the cliff path toward the inlet below the cave mouth without sound. She did not run. She moved the way she moved through most things: efficiently, with the complete attention of someone who had considered every step before she took it. The rig followed her into the dark because she had the neural link active and the rig followed the link the way a thing that has been learned follows the one who learned it.

Lyra watched the shape of her disappear below the cave mouth level, the rig's outline dissolving against the cliff's shadow. Then she looked at the rest of them.

"Two minutes," she said. "Then Tavar goes."

She looked at Rowe. He was already moving toward the path that would take him up to the overhang, circling south along the cliff to come at the limestone shelf from above. He did not look back. He knew where he was going and he went to it.

Lyra moved to the cave path herself and waited.

---

The cave entrance from the water level was a different thing than the cave entrance from sixty meters above. The ceiling was close — she could see the rock's wet texture where the tide had worked at it over decades, the irregular marks of stone worn patient and slow by salt water that had no urgency about it. The dock inside was lit by running lights, low, the garrison's version of minimum visibility for an overnight watch, which was the minimum that let you see and not much more.

She was at the cave mouth edge, outside the light, in the acoustic transition between open sea and enclosed space. She could hear the difference — the water inside the cave had its own movement, contained, going back and forth against the dock planking and the hull and not going anywhere.

The Eirene-7 was thirty meters ahead of her.

She could see the shape of it now: deep-bellied, high-shouldered, the hull designed for water-landings and meaning it, built with the practical unsentimental aesthetic of something that had work to do and did it. The Liturgy's name on the hull in block letters. The envelope structure visible as a darker solid against the cave ceiling, the rigid frame fore to aft, the gas envelope invisible in the dark above the hull.

The gangway soldier was where Orim had said — seated, rifle across his knees, head turned toward the gate end of the cave. He was watching the gate because there was nothing else to watch. The dock was forty meters of planking over black water with a ship at one end and a gate at the other and he had been watching this combination for the better part of the night.

She could not see the forward dock watch. Starboard side of the hull, over the hull, which was where Kressida was going to come.

She had not heard the rig go into the water. She had not expected to. Kressida's understanding of what made sound was precise — the rig could move quietly when she wanted it to because she had learned what noise the rig made and what caused each kind of noise and how to move through water such that the water came second. Three meters of armored iron going into the sea in the dark could be quiet. Kressida had decided that it would be.

What she heard instead was, eventually, the faint sound of the rig on the hull — not machinery, not metal-on-metal in the aggressive sense, but the deliberate measured grip-and-shift of three meters of purpose-built iron climbing a ship's hull in absolute measured patience. Each movement checked before weight transferred. The machine learning the hull the way machines learned things: one point at a time, nothing assumed.

Tavar's voice reached her from the gate end — pleasant, carrying, the particular tone of a man who was explaining something technical and regrettable and whose regret was entirely genuine in the way that made administrative people feel understood.

She heard the gate.

Both soldiers turned to look at the gate. She could see the gangway soldier's head move — the small rotation of a bored man responding to anything that was not what he'd been watching. Somewhere on the starboard hull above her, the forward dock watch would be turning.

Twenty seconds.

She was moving.

---

Forty meters of planking. Her boots knew the wet texture of it before she was consciously aware of the surface — the body anticipating, adjusting, keeping balance without requiring the decision that keeping balance required. She passed the gangway soldier and he was seated and his chin was going toward his chest and the rifle was still at rest across his knees.

Not unconscious. Not drugged. Shot.

She had known this and she moved past him and she did not look back.

The gangway: up it in the time it took to go up a gangway when you were moving. The cargo hatch was in the standard position and she undogged it with the recessed handle and she was in.

The hold: the smell of Liturgy logistics, the same everywhere. Petroleum fuel, dry warehouse stock, the particular dust of institutional storage. She went forward.

The pilot housing door. Handle, step up.

The instrument cluster was on standby power. She knew this cluster — she had certified on this class six years ago, eight weeks in the administrative period after her second infusion, and the certification had lodged in her hands in the way that physical knowledge lodged. Her hands found the startup panel without searching for it.

She ran the sequence.

Port outboard: the cough and catch, the engine finding its register. The cave took the sound and amplified it, sent it back from everywhere, turned the engine's voice into something that was less about the engine than about the cave's understanding of the engine. She ran the sequence without stopping.

Starboard outboard. Center pair.

The ship was running.

Outside, through the forward viewport: the dock in the running lights, the gate at the far end, the small figure of Tavar's contact standing very still with a document in her hands and the beginning of an understanding of the situation that was going to become complete in approximately the time it took her to look at the gangway foot.

Tavar was still talking. He had his hand at the contact's shoulder — not holding, guiding, maintaining the direction of her attention. He was explaining something with the sustained focus of a man who needed thirty seconds more of her attention than she currently wanted to give him.

But she was going to look.

Lyra checked the manifold readings, confirmed fuel state, ran the ballast initialization. The ship shifted in the water — the slow reorientation of a vessel finding where its weight was.

The contact looked.

---

From the pilot housing viewport she watched Tavar leave Vera cleanly — backing away in the direction of the dock at pace, still concluding the conversation in the direction of the ship rather than toward what came next. He had the clipboard. He had whatever expression he had, which she could not see from this angle. He was moving.

She hit the internal intercom.

"Tavar. One minute."

She did not know if the intercom carried outside the vessel. She started the stern fitting release without waiting to find out. The bow fitting. The dock lines had been cut before she boarded — she had seen the loose rope floating at the waterline when she came up the gangway, which had been Kressida's work, the rig's hands capable of that kind of precision without guidance.

She looked at Vera through the viewport.

Vera had moved to the gangway foot. She was looking at the gangway soldier. She was looking at the ship. She was holding the document with both hands in the way of someone who does not know what to do with the thing they are holding. She had understood the situation. The situation was considerably more than the document.

She turned and called up the garrison path.

Tavar came through the cargo hatch. She heard him hit the hold and call forward: "Move."

She moved.

The thrust levers at taxi. The hull moved away from the dock planking — slowly, feeling the water's resistance, the cave walls going past the viewport as the ship backed toward the entrance. The running lights of the dock shrank. The cave air was cold through the viewport seal's slight gaps. Outside, the acoustic was already changing — the engines' sound beginning to find the larger space it was being drawn toward.

Orim appeared from the hold corridor with the expression of someone who had identified the most structurally sound cargo crate and occupied it for the duration and was now arriving at a transitional phase.

"The cave mouth," he said, "is approximately the same width as the envelope at maximum inflation."

"I know," she said.

"I'm saying this so that you know that I know it."

"Are you alarmed?"

He considered. "The situation is clarifying quickly," he said. This was not an answer to her question and was also his complete assessment of the situation. He went back to the crate.

The cave walls in the viewport. The ceiling coming close — the slight bend in the cave's axis, the envelope structure at minimum clearance, the rock wet and pale where the tide reached it. She held the heading. Outside on the hull she could hear the rig's grip adjusting — Kressida repositioning her hold as the ship's angle changed.

One long sound: envelope on stone. Metal and rock and the sustained dry quality of clearance become contact. It lasted two seconds. Then it stopped. The ship kept moving.

The cave mouth arrived in the forward viewport — the darkness of open sky against the cave's running-light dark. The cliff walls went past on both sides, pale, and then there was open air.

She increased thrust.

The hull hit the swell: two knocks, the vessel adjusting its trim to open water. The spray came up the bow. The cave was gone behind her. She pulled to takeoff power and the bow came up and the hull skipped once, twice on the swell — not errors, just the water being water at night, the surface unpredictable from inside a hull — and she held the heading and held the power and the hull lifted.

Bow first. Then the body of the ship. The water sound dropping away, the spray dropping away, the specific silence of no longer being in contact with the sea.

She climbed east along the cliff line and the stone fell away below and then there was only open sky.

The ship leveled. The Eirene-7 flew.

She checked the chronometer.

Eleven minutes.

---

Twenty seconds later, from the starboard hull exterior: the rig settling into its hold position. Kressida had moved the machine back outside through the main hatch after the cave mouth, which Lyra had tried not to watch through the viewport because the watching would have made her want to say something and there was nothing she could say about it that Kressida had not already considered. The rig was on the hull. Kressida had decided it would be on the hull and it was on the hull and the hull was holding them both at altitude above the channel approach.

The horizon was beginning to gray at its lowest edge — not light yet, just the sky establishing that it was distinct from the sea, which it did every morning with the particular patience of something that did not need anyone's attention to do it.

Orim came forward.

He stood in the pilot housing doorway and looked at the instrument cluster and looked at the viewport for a while and said: "Eirene."

She waited.

"Old Cauld," he said. "Peace. The cessation of hostilities — the state after fighting has ended, not the cause. Not the victory or the surrender." He looked at the hull above them, briefly. "The state that remains when neither of those is still happening."

She said nothing. He went back to the crate.

She thought about the word. The Liturgy administered peace in the Cauld the way it administered everything else: as a managed resource, distributed through authorized channels to those authorized to receive it, produced by the apparatus the recipients were not authorized to examine. She had taken this vessel. She had arrived in the dark, chemically incapacitated — she stopped. She had not chemically incapacitated anyone. Rowe had shot two garrison soldiers on a mooring watch, and those soldiers were dead in the cave, and the contact named Vera was on the garrison path calling for whoever she was calling for, and the ship was flying east with the rig on the hull and all of that was the operational truth of what had happened.

She had filed it as no casualties.

The filing was what it was. She had not yet found a different word for it.

Tavar came forward. He had the clipboard in one hand and a whetstone in the other, which he had produced from his coat in the way he produced everything — already carrying the thing he needed, having never mentioned that he had it. He was not sharpening anything. He was holding both objects as though deciding between them.

"Vera," Lyra said.

"She'll be all right." He set the whetstone down on the instrument shelf and looked at the viewport. "She'll report exactly what happened: a supply documentation officer presented genuine paperwork and requested dock access for a manifold inspection. The gate was opened per protocol. The vessel departed without completing the inspection." He picked up the whetstone again. "The documentation is genuine. It will review as genuine. The irregularity is the vessel's departure, not her admitting me. She did her job."

"The garrison will send a report."

"The report will reach the Liturgy's supply chain office in two days. Three." He looked at the sea. "We'll be in Pallor water."

She nodded.

She also noted: his access to the Liturgy's supply documentation system. The genuine certification notice. The contact who had processed his manifests for three years. The valve panel in the hold that he had gone to without reading the placard. These were facts she held without yet knowing what they were facts about. She was aware that she did not know. She was aware that not knowing was the current state of things and that the current state of things was acceptable for now, and that *for now* was doing significant work in that sentence, and that the work would eventually need to be accounted for.

She left the accounting where it was.

Rowe came forward last.

He stood in the pilot housing doorway and looked at the viewport and did not say anything. He had cleaned the rifle. She had heard him cleaning it in the hold during the startup sequence — the precise small sounds of a man maintaining a weapon after it had been used, which was the correct thing to do if you wanted it to be ready the next time. He had done it without being told and without discussing it and he had done it correctly.

He stood in the doorway and looked at the sea.

After a while he said: "Two."

The word for what they were was not a word he had yet in Cauld. He had the number. He gave her the number because it was what he could give her, and he gave it with the directness of someone who was not asking permission and was not asking absolution. He was stating a fact and making her the person who received it.

She said: "It was the operation."

She heard herself say it. She heard the frame closing around what he had told her. This was institutional language — the thing that took a fact and placed it in a category that made the fact manageable. She knew it was this. She used it anyway.

He looked at her. Not accusatory. Not anything particular. He was deciding something about what he was seeing, and she was watching him decide it.

He said, quietly: "I know."

He went back to the hold.

She sat with what she had said and what he had answered. He knew. He knew the frame. He had come forward to give her the fact and she had given him the frame and he had confirmed he understood the frame for what it was. This was not comfort. It was not absolution. It was the exchange between two people who had both done what the operation required and who were both going to live in the company of what the operation required for whatever time they had left.

She did not change the filing.

The horizon went from gray to the first suggestion of color — not dawn yet, just the pre-dawn hour when the sky committed to the process. The Eirene-7 flew east. The rig held the hull with the patient certainty of something that had been built to hold things. The cave was thirty kilometers behind them and the channel was five hours ahead and somewhere in those five hours Rowe was going to tell her something she needed to hear, and she was not prepared for it, and there was no preparing for it, and she had five hours of flying to find out whether the fact of that affected how she flew.

It did not.

She was a researcher. She was a Templar. She was currently a thief who had filed her theft as a logistics completion. She was flying a stolen Liturgy supply vessel toward a channel she did not have authorization to cross, with a Lacerta intelligence operative in the hold and a battle rig on the hull and a man from another Sphere sitting aft who had just shot two people and given her the number.

She noted all of this. She filed all of this. She flew.

Outside, the sea moved the way the sea moved, without opinion and without pause, gray and cold and going dark-to-light the way it always did and would do regardless of what she was doing above it. She watched the horizon clarify. She adjusted the trim for the first thermals of the morning, which came as the sea temperature and the air temperature began to diverge, and she flew the ship into the day.

Behind her, somewhere in the hold, Orim said to no one: "I'm going to sleep, if no one needs me for anything requiring being awake."

No one answered him. He took this as permission, which it was.

The ship flew east.

[Beat 45]
THE CHANNEL — ROWE TESTIFIES

The channel at altitude smelled of nothing — that was the first surprise. She had expected salt. The sea was below them, the northern channel in the gray before dawn, and the hull of the Eirene-7 was doing the thing hulls do over open water, which was a continuous argument with the pressure differential, and she could hear it, but there was no smell. The membrane of the hull sealed everything out. The cargo hold smelled of its own history: machine oil, old rope, the faint metallic particular of institutional supply transport. Liturgy-issue everything, from the stenciled crate markings to the iron handholds bolted at intervals along the bulkhead. The envelope made its noise. Below them, somewhere she couldn't see, the channel moved.

She had been awake since before they left the Lacerta cliff dock. She had not been going to sleep.

The notebook was open on her knee. The page was blank. She had been trying, for two hours, to write Ardea's service record — the administrative instrument that would allow the Ocipheus garrison to send a formal notification to Ardea's family — and the words were not arriving in any useful order. She knew all the facts. She had Ardea's intake year, her posting history, her tincture certifications, the action-in-field that had ended her. These were not the words that were failing to come. The words that were failing were the ones at the beginning of the record: what you wrote about a person before you wrote the facts, the sentence that established the person as the instrument of their service record rather than a collection of administrative entries. She had written those sentences before. She could not write this one.

She closed the notebook.

She did not put it away.

Kressida was asleep in the rig. Or something like asleep — the BR-7's external indicators showed running-warm, steady draw, the particular profile she had come to understand as Kressida's version of rest. The machine did what the machine did. The pilot rested inside it. The ship held its course because the rig's neural pathway had reached up into the Eirene-7's guidance channels the way it reached everywhere, and now the course was Kressida's in the same way the rig was Kressida's, held without her having to hold it.

Tavar was at the helm. He was not doing much at the helm beyond being present, which was the appropriate amount given Kressida's involvement, and he knew this and was occupying himself with something that looked like maintenance on one of his hatchets. He had the stone out and was making small precise passes along the edge. The sound was very quiet. He was doing it to have something to do with his hands, which Lyra understood, because she had the notebook.

Orim had gone to sleep when they cleared the Lacerta cliff. He was awake again now, which did not surprise her — he slept in short complete intervals and returned to full attention quickly, the sleep of someone who had spent fifty years operating in situations where not returning to attention had consequences. He was at the forward porthole, standing, his fingertips not pressed together at his sternum but resting flat against the porthole glass in the passive attunement position. The light coming through was the blue-gray of northern sea-dawn. His face was tired. He had been tired since the Forge Hearth. That was a different tired from the accumulated road-tired, and it had not resolved.

Rowe was at the starboard porthole. He had been there for half an hour.

He was looking at the channel below with the stillness of someone who is deciding something and has reached the part of deciding where the thing is already decided but the body hasn't caught up yet. She had learned this particular stillness. She had been watching him decide things for four months.

The channel below was the specific gray of northern sea in early morning — not quite silver, not quite green, the color of something that has been cold for a very long time and does not expect to change. There would be drift-bells down there, she thought, the kind Tavar kept a processing tool for. The kind that made the sound fishermen called the tide singing. She could not hear them from here. She could only hear the envelope's argument with the wind.

Rowe came away from the porthole.

He sat down against the bulkhead across from her. Not close. The distance he always maintained in enclosed spaces — enough room to do something different if something different became necessary. His hands were on his knees. His rifle was slung across his back. He had the expression she had filed, weeks ago, as preparation.

She waited.

He said, in Cauld: "I want to tell you something."

The structure was correct. The pronunciation of *tell* had the hard landing of a word said many times during preparation, the specific flatness of a sentence that has been practiced into its correct shape. He had been building toward this since Schmalburg. She had known it from the particular vocabulary he'd asked for in the weeks after — not the survival words, not the direction and food and threat vocabulary, but the words for time, for sequence, for the expression of things that had already happened.

She looked at the notebook on her knee. She put it down, behind her, against the bulkhead. She did not open it.

She said: "I'm listening."

---

He started with the factory.

A city. He gave her the name in his own language first, and paused. She recognized the pause — he was checking whether she needed Cauld, and she did not, she had heard enough of his own language over four months to know she should simply listen.

"It doesn't need one," she said.

He nodded. A textile city. Not enormous. He had been to bigger ones for work — there had been larger factories in places he had traveled. His factory made small mechanical components: springs, couplings, the parts that went into larger machines. He had worked there for six years. He said: "I knew the machines." There was weight in it — the particular weight of a fact that is also a grief for the fact. "By sound. Different sound for different problems. You learned."

He stopped. He looked at his hands.

"I was good at my job," he said. "I want you to know that. I'm not—" The Cauld word was not coming; he worked around it. "I am not telling you that I was nobody. I was someone. I had a name and a place and people who knew me."

"I know," she said.

"I don't think you do," he said, without offense. "You know I was Scried from somewhere. But you don't know I was someone there first."

She held still with this. He was right.

"Tell me," she said.

A Thursday in autumn. He knew it was Thursday because the morning shift overlapped with the maintenance crew on Thursdays for forty minutes, and the overlap meant the floor noise was different, the particular conversation of two crews occupying the same machinery at slightly different purposes. He knew the time because the clock on the factory floor — he gave her the words for it in his own language and she heard the shape without understanding — moved past the half-hour with a sound he knew. He knew the season from the angle of light through the high windows. He tracked these things. He had always tracked the conditions of the space he was in.

"Then," he said.

He stopped.

He said *then* again, the word doing the work of everything he still did not have the Cauld for — everything between *Thursday morning, half-hour past the start of the shift* and *and then the floor was not the floor.* His jaw worked once, the specific movement of a man who has arrived at the edge of available language and is standing at the edge looking at what he needs to cross.

"Take it in pieces," she said.

He looked at her for a moment. Then he nodded.

The floor was wrong. Not gone — changed. The quality of it was different under his feet in a way he recognized immediately as significant, the way you recognize significant things when you have been trained to recognize the difference between normal and not-normal in the machinery you work in every day. He had a moment of checking: was he sick? Had something in the floor failed structurally? He was not sick. The floor was not broken.

Then the stone room.

He said it the way he said hard things — evenly, the affect of a man who has learned what it costs to say things with feeling and has chosen, for now, the other way. A room of dressed stone. Cold — not cold the way the factory was cold in winter, which was the cold of imperfect heating, but the cold of stone that had been cold for centuries and was not going to be otherwise. A smell he would not identify until months later when he had enough Cauld to ask what Catalyst-adjacent compounds smelled like and then he said *that is the smell of that room.*

Three figures in robes. He gave her the colors and she recognized them: Ocipheus white with the canonical gold hem. He said: "Ocipheus," now, with his months of language behind him, and he said it the way he said accurate things. Not as an accusation. As a fact.

"Yes," she said.

He said: "One of them had a book."

He was quiet for a moment. Not the quiet of having nothing to say — the quiet of having too much, and choosing the piece that bore the most weight per word.

He said: "I was not — I was not afraid. I want you to understand that. I have been afraid. I know what it feels like. I was in France for fourteen months and I know what afraid does to a body." He paused. "This was something different. This was the feeling of having entered a situation whose rules I had not been given. A room. Three people in robes. No context for any of it. I did what you do in that situation: I made myself as — legible as possible. Cooperative. Unthreatening. I thought: if I cooperate, someone will explain what is happening."

He looked at his hands.

"No one explained what was happening," he said.

She knew the intake protocol. She had read it in her first year at the Station, the way new practitioners read the foundational instruments. She had read it again as a researcher, three years into her career, when the intake documentation project had seemed like a minor administrative job that would fill one season's writing. She had read the oath text. She had contributed to the literature of best-practice administration. She had written: *oath administered prior to language acquisition minimizes resistive response in conscript cohort.* She had meant it as a professional observation about intake procedure efficiency.

He said: "The words had a rhythm. Like something official. I didn't understand any of it." He looked at his hands. "There was a gesture. The figure with the book made a gesture toward me. I copied it." He showed her: a slight inclination of the head, a specific position of the right hand. She recognized it. It was the acknowledgment position from the Compact Oath, the position of formal assent to canonical authority. "I copied it because — because copying is what you do when you're in a room with people in robes making official sounds and you don't know the language. You look cooperative. You think: I will be cooperative until I understand, and then I will decide."

He paused.

"I never decided," he said. "I never understood fast enough."

Orim had not moved from the porthole. His fingertips were still against the glass. He said nothing.

She said nothing.

---

He gave her Vierna in pieces, the way he gave everything.

The barracks were in a great hall — he described the architecture and she assembled it: the stone vaulting, the high narrow windows, the size of the space, the way sound moved in it. He had been in buildings like that before, she understood — not the same, but the same category of old and stone and built to last. He had found it recognizable in a way he did not know how to explain and had stopped trying to explain after the first days, when the recognizable and the completely foreign were too mixed to separate.

The rifles were on the racks.

He had seen rifles. He said this simply — not with the specific weight he gave to other things, just as a fact that followed from his world's history. He said: "We had them in the war." Four months of shared vocabulary had established between them that *the war* meant a particular thing in his experience, the particular duration of organized killing that had taken approximately four years and most of his world's young men and all of the good certainty about what a country was for. "I recognized the action." He mimed the bolt, the cycling motion. "Not exactly. Later. More—" He searched for the word. "More finished. Like a later version of a thing you know in an earlier form."

She knew what this meant. She let him arrive at it.

He said: "In my world, there were men who spent their careers tracing the development of mechanisms. The bolt-action cycle. The feed system. The tolerances in the receiver housing. It has a history that you can follow — who made the prototype, who improved it, who licensed the design. You could trace it back through forty years of incremental change to the original." He paused. "The rifles here do not appear in that history. They are — past the end of it. Further along than anything my world has made. But the lineage is there if you know how to read the mechanism. The parentage." He looked at her. "Someone here had access to my world's designs and had time to develop them further. More time than my world has had."

"Someone here," he said, slowly, "had been watching. Long before I was brought here."

He waited.

"Yes," she said.

He nodded. This was the Cauld pattern she had noticed in him — he gave her the hard thing and waited for her to confirm it before he continued, because the confirming told him he had understood it correctly, and he needed to understand it correctly before he could say the next part.
