The barracks held conscripts from, he had counted, at minimum twelve different points of origin. Most couldn't communicate. The House had developed a minimal contact language for intake operations — a set of common commands that could be demonstrated and then followed without requiring any shared vocabulary. *Stand. Walk. Carry. Wait.* He had learned those in the first two weeks. They were the first Cauld words he learned.

The collar markers were administrative: a stamped brass disc on the intake-issue collar, a number. He had seen Sphere 31 on his own. He had seen Sphere 22. Sphere 14. Sphere 8 on a man who had been there longer and who worked in the maintenance crews now, and who had a competent intake vocabulary, and who looked at Rowe in the first week with an expression that said: *I know what you are going through, and it gets better in some ways, and worse in other ways, and I cannot tell you which way you are headed.*

Orim's fingertips pressed slightly harder against the glass.

Rowe said: "What is the highest number you know."

She said: "The canonical records reference Sphere 61. Some practitioners believe the enumeration goes further."

He was quiet for a moment.

"I saw Sphere 31 on my form," he said. "And I counted, in the barracks and in the training yard. I met — or saw — conscripts from approximately nine Spheres. I don't know if there were others I didn't see. There were probably others I didn't see." He paused. "How many people are in those files."

She said: "I don't know."

She said: "The records I processed were forty-three distinct intake cohorts over a six-month period. Each cohort averaged fourteen persons."

He worked through the number she had not worked through for him. Six hundred and two, approximately, for that one six-month window. The intake program had been running, in its current documented form, since Year 831. Three hundred and seven years of documented operation. The undocumented period before that — the Scrying practice that predated systematic intake records, the experimental phases the early canonical scholars wrote about in terms that would only be recognized as intake documentation by someone who had seen intake documentation later — she did not know how far back that went. Nobody did. That was the point of not documenting it clearly.

He said: "How many people know what happens in the stone room."

She said: "The intake staff. The canonical records division. Practitioners who have studied the foundational instruments."

"And everyone else," he said, "knows that Myrmidons exist. That they serve. Where they come from in the general sense — the membrane, another world." He paused. "But not what the stone room looks like. Not the cold. Not the robes. Not what the gesture means."

"No," she said.

"Because the oath is given before the language," he said.

She waited.

"On purpose," he said.

"Yes," she said. "On purpose."

He said nothing. He looked at the floor of the cargo hold, which was painted grey-green, the Liturgy's institutional color for utility surfaces.

She looked at the floor too.

The envelope made its noise. The channel moved below.

---

He told her about the man from Sphere 22.

He had been in the barracks four months. Enough Cauld to follow orders and not enough Cauld to do anything else. The man from Sphere 22 had been there two months longer and had the same sparse vocabulary and a different version of the same face, which Rowe had understood as: *I was someone where I came from too.* He was older — mid-forties, the specific age at which people who have done physical work for twenty years begin to show it in the particular way that physical work leaves its marks, in the set of the shoulders, in the deliberate way of moving that comes from having learned to conserve. He had a missing fingertip on the right hand, the kind of absence that came from machinery, from something that had closed too fast or too far. A mechanic, possibly, or a craftsman of some kind. They had never established what.

They had tried, over the weeks, to find overlap in their languages. Not systematically — just the way people try when they have nothing else they can do. You pointed at things. You said the word in your language. You waited to see if there was anything. There mostly wasn't. The languages were unrelated; whatever the man from Sphere 22 spoke, it did not share roots with what Rowe had grown up saying, and the sounds were different in the particular ways that made them hard to approximate. He had never been good with foreign languages. He had known one phrase of French — something learned from the war, from a family in a village near the front, a phrase that had never been useful in the way the family had probably intended it to be useful.

He said: "We found one word."

He paused.

"The word was *mother,*" he said.

Orim's tincture bottle made a quiet sound against the porthole housing. A small sound, barely audible over the envelope's argument with the wind.

Rowe said: "In both languages, the word for mother was nearly the same. Close enough to know. You said it, you heard the other person's version, and you both knew what had been said." He looked at his hands. "I don't know what that means. Whether that says something about language, or about what is the same in all worlds." He paused. "I thought about it a great deal in the following months. I thought about what the word was doing there, in both of us, without either of us having put it there."

Nobody spoke.

The envelope. The wind. The sound of the channel, somewhere below.

He said: "Later. When I had enough Cauld. I asked the intake administrator what the words of the oath meant."

She knew the administrator. Not the specific person — the specific role. The Ocipheus-seconded administrative staff, the ones who processed the paperwork that she herself had contributed documentation to.

He said: "He told me it was the oath of service. That it bound me to the canon law of the Cauld for the duration of my term." He paused. "I asked him if the oath was valid if I hadn't understood it."

She was already waiting for the answer.

He said: "He said that was a theological question and he didn't have the training to address it."

---

She had written that sentence. *Minimizes resistive response in conscript cohort.* She had written it in a professional document. She had meant it as an observation about procedure. She had not thought, when she wrote it, about what *resistive response* looked like from the inside of the resistance. She was thinking about it now. The thought had the quality of a thing that has been waiting in a room she knew the location of for years, and is still in the same room when you finally open the door.

Rowe said: "The notation. On the rifle."

"Yes," she said.

He said: "I've seen the pattern before. In my world. The engineers — the people who study the history of designs, who trace where technology comes from, because you can see in the designs when something came from outside and was adapted. There are gaps. Things that are not quite ours. Things that arrived from somewhere else and were built into our designs."

He looked at her steadily.

"We had a whole— a whole set of theories about this. A lost civilization. Ancient, gone, we had inherited their knowledge without understanding who they were. We thought about them the way you think about something you owe a debt to but cannot name. We were proud of the search." He paused. "We called them the lost people. The ones who built the first things. We had theories about where they'd gone. Whole scholarly traditions dedicated to them. Some people thought they had destroyed themselves. Some people thought they had — moved on. Transcended something, and left the world to us as inheritors. The most hopeful theory."

He looked at his hands.

"We were proud of the inheritance," he said. "The knowledge was ours now. We had earned it by building on it. By developing it further than the lost ones had. That's what we told ourselves." He was quiet for a moment. "Every time someone made something new, in the back of the mind was: *the old ones made something like this first, and we are their continuation.* It was—" He searched for the word. "It made us feel like heirs."

The channel noise went on without them.

"We were right that the knowledge wasn't ours originally," he said. "We were wrong about the lost civilization. You didn't disappear. You just kept taking."

She held very still.

He said: "I'm not angry."

He said it in the even way he said accurate things. Not flattened by distance — simply stated without excess weight, because the statement was already heavy and needed no additional weight from the voice.

"I'm telling you," he said, "because you are the person with the most of the language, and because your institution made the forms I put my mark on, and the files you processed, and the research that included me before I knew what the Cauld was. I think you should know that one of the people in those files is telling you this."

She said: "I know."

She said: "I have known, and not known, for longer than I would like to admit."

He looked at her for a moment with an expression she did not have a file for.

---

Orim turned from the porthole.

It was a small movement — he turned, and then he stood with his back against the hull, looking at neither of them specifically. His face had the quality she had seen, once, on a senior practitioner who had reviewed Transmutation records and found something that had been misfiled for twenty years: the quality of a person confronting a fact they have always known was there and are now confronted with it directly and cannot return to having only known it abstractly.

He said: "I have read intake reports for forty years."

His voice was even. Not flat — even, the way a precise instrument reads even: accurate to both sides.

He said: "The ones I worked from were Vierna commissioning requests. They did not use names. They used the sphere designation and the skill classification and the intake number. Forty years." He looked at the cargo hold floor. "I knew what I was reading. I knew what *M-cohort, Sphere 31, intake 097* meant in terms of what had been done to the person listed as *M-cohort, Sphere 31, intake 097.* I knew it the way a surgeon knows what *casualty, blunt instrument, cranial* means without needing to see the patient." He paused. "I told myself I was being accurate. That someone else would have done the work if I hadn't. That I knew the cost and therefore the cost was somehow—" He stopped. "I don't have the word either. Not in Cauld. Probably not in any language."

Rowe looked at him.

Orim said: "I can no longer say I did not hear it. I'm telling you that so you know that I know."

He did not say more. He turned back to the porthole, and his fingertips went back to the glass, and the passive attunement position settled over him like something he had been doing for fifty years because it was the posture that went with hearing things accurately, and accuracy was the only thing he had left to offer.

Rowe looked at the back of Orim's head for a moment. Then he looked at Lyra.

She said nothing. There was nothing adequate to say and she had stopped reaching for it. The channel kept moving below. The envelope kept arguing with the wind.

After a while Rowe said, quietly: "I'm not asking you to fix it."

"I know," she said.

He said: "I'm asking you to know it. There's a difference."

"Yes," she said. "There is."

The silence that followed was different from the silence before. It was not comfortable — it was not meant to be comfortable — but it was the silence of a thing that had been said and could not be unsaid, which was a different kind of weight from the weight of a thing that was pending. The pending weight pressed forward. This weight simply sat. She sat with it.

She would sit with it for the rest of the crossing.

Lyra sat in it.

She had the notebook behind her, against the bulkhead, unopened. She had not opened it once during the testimony. She was aware of not having opened it the way you are aware of something you have not done that you have always done before — the absence with a shape. She had been a researcher for thirty years. She catalogued. She documented. She noted the specific vocabulary of events so that the events could be recovered. She had spent the last half hour listening to a man tell the truth without writing anything down, and the truth was the same truth it would have been if she had written it down, and she was going to have to live with that.

The channel moved below.

---

Tavar said, quietly, from the helm: "What are we calling the ship."

The question landed into the silence like a small stone into still water.

Nobody answered immediately. Kressida's rig maintained its work. The envelope disagreed with the wind at its usual volume. The gray light through the portholes had shifted from night-gray to dawn-gray, the quality of light that appeared when the sea had decided to let itself be seen.

Rowe said something in his own language. One phrase, short. She did not have all of it, but she had enough of his phonetic patterns by now to get the shape of it. She said the closest Cauld equivalent she had: "The ground undone."

He looked at her. The vowel was wrong. He adjusted it. She said it again.

"The ground that undid," he said. The construction was slightly different from whatever the phrase meant in his language — the Cauld grammar required a different arrangement — but it was close enough to carry the weight. She could feel the weight in it. Something that had been solid and had stopped being solid. Something that had been reliable and then wasn't. A Thursday morning in a textile city. The floor, then the stone room.

"She goes to Pallor under a new name," Tavar said, still looking at the instruments. He did not look at Rowe or at Lyra. He said it in the tone of someone making a notation in a manifest. "The ground that undid it. Better than whatever the Liturgy called her."

Lyra found her notebook. She opened it. She wrote:

*The Ground Undid.*

And below it, not as a research entry but as something else, something she did not have the institutional category for yet:

*Rowe. Sphere 31. Thursday.*

She closed it.

---

The Pallor coast appeared on the northern horizon three hours later.

First as a darkening of the gray — a different quality of dark from the sky, more solid, the dark of something that had been standing in the same place for a very long time and was not going to move because the sea changed around it. Then as the particular darkness of rocky coast, the Hebrides limestone she had studied in cartographic documents and was now seeing in the specific register of a thing that has been theoretical for a long time and is now simply there. The cliff country. The moors above it, which she could not yet see but knew were there, night-heather somewhere in the dark above the cliffs, not yet in bloom.

Kressida woke — or the analog of waking — and the rig shifted its weight against the cargo-bay wall and the ship's guidance felt it, the course adjusting slightly as her attention returned to the channels it held. Tavar stepped back from the helm. He had the look of someone who has been keeping a watch they were not entirely qualified for and is relieved to hand it to the person who is.

Lyra looked at the coast.

She had recovered the Relic once before from a situation that had complicated itself beyond reasonable parameters — a Vierna provenance dispute, a mislabeled artifact, the particular bureaucratic tangle of proving a claim when the claim had been deliberately obscured. She had been thirty-two. She had been entirely certain. She had been wrong about two of the three key facts and right about the outcome, and she had filed it as a lesson in professional humility and moved on with the next job.

She did not feel certain now.

She felt the particular condition of someone who has been handed information that restructures everything behind it, and who must now navigate forward in the restructured landscape without having had time to survey it properly. She was trained for uncertainty. She had always been trained for it. She had always found it easier when the uncertainty concerned something other than herself.

Rowe came to stand beside her at the forward porthole.

He did not speak. He looked at the coast. She looked at the coast.

After a time he said, in Cauld: "What will you do with it. When you have it."

She knew he meant the Relic.

She said: "I don't know yet."

He said: "But not what they want you to do with it."

She looked at him.

He said: "You would have given it to them before Bressant. I don't know who *them* is. But you would have. You were the kind of person who gave things to the right authority."

"And now?" she said.

He said: "Now you know that I am in the authority's files."

She looked at the coast of Pallor getting closer. The cliff country. The moor above it. Somewhere on those moors, the people who had taken the Relic were already there, and her party was coming to take it back, and she still did not know, when she had it, whether *take it back* meant what she had understood it to mean four months ago.

She said: "Yes."

He nodded. He turned away from the porthole. He went to find a place to settle before the descent to the sea-loch, and she watched him go.

The notebook was in her hand.

*The Ground Undid. Rowe. Sphere 31. Thursday.*

She had been, for thirty years, someone who knew who she was. The names she would not answer to were shorter than the names she would. She was a Templar. She was a researcher with a publication record and an institutional role and a frame through which the world organized itself into recoverable categories. She was the person who had written *minimizes resistive response in conscript cohort* in a document that was now in the same archive as every intake form bearing the notation *M-cohort, Sphere 31.*

She was also the person sitting in the cargo hold of a stolen Liturgy vessel named The Ground Undid, heading for the coast of Pallor with four months of restructured landscape behind her and an uncertain coastline ahead.

Both of those people were her. She was not going to be able to put one of them away until she understood which one she was keeping.

She closed the notebook.

Pallor was ahead. The cliffs were getting specific — she could see the individual faces of the rock now, the color of old bone in the dawn light. Somewhere above those cliffs, the moors were waking to whatever morning the moors had, and the Relic was somewhere on them in a carry-case, and the people who had it believed, at least most of them, that they were doing the right thing.

She knew what that felt like.

She had believed it for thirty years. She intended to remember what it felt like, going in.

[Beat 46]
CHAPTER 22: CAER GLAS — THE HOURS BEFORE

They came in off the drove road at the second hour past midnight, and the first thing Wren saw was the heather.

He'd been told. Esvane had said — weeks ago, in a Pallor briefing room that smelled of pine resin and the particular lamp oil they used in the Long Seat's dependencies — she'd said the Caer Glas moors bloomed at night. He'd nodded the way you nod at something you cannot yet picture.

He could picture it now.

The moor opened before them and the heather was lit from inside. Not fire — nothing like fire, because fire was orange and hot and these blooms were pink-white and cold, lit from below the way stone isn't and somehow the heather was, and the light was low and wide and it turned the ground into something that did not look like ground. It looked like the shallow end of something larger. It looked like the world had developed a slow pulse while they weren't watching.

Wren stopped walking.

Petra walked into him from behind. She stepped around him without comment. He heard her boots through the heather, that particular sound of wet stem and dry peat and the crunch of something half-frozen underneath.

Esvane had stopped two paces ahead. She was not looking at the heather.

She was looking at the vault.

---

It was a stone structure, old and older than old, the kind of old that looks tired of standing. No House insignia on it anywhere. That was the thing Wren noticed first, because he'd trained himself to look for House marks — every structure in Pallor territory had at least a notation, a carved glyph, something that said *this is ours and here is whose*. This one had nothing. It sat in the middle of the heather like a fact that preceded arguments about ownership. Pre-Compact, Esvane had said. Before the Houses existed to put their marks on things.

Forty meters in front of the vault, at the place where the drove road ended and the heather began, a man was standing.

He was alone. He'd been alone for four days. Wren could see it in the way he stood — not alert, not anxious. Still in the way that comes from waiting long enough that waiting becomes the baseline state, becomes simply who you are at rest.

Owain.

Wren had not seen him in three months. He looked older. Not tired — something else. He looked like a man who had been alone with a large thought and had made his peace with it not resolving. His beard was longer than when Wren had last seen him, wind-roughened, and his wool coat was the one he wore in the Long Seat's outer yards, practical and dark and carrying four days of moor weather in its weave.

He did not move toward them. He watched them cross the heather, and when Esvane reached him he said her name once, quietly, and she said his.

Then he held out his hand.

---

Esvane had carried the case under her arm the entire way from Ocipheus. Three weeks of road and water and the hold of a trading vessel, through checkpoints and road towns and the channel's cold dark, and she had kept the case the same way she kept everything she was responsible for — close and unobserved and protected by her body's proximity.

She put it in Owain's hand without ceremony. He took it without ceremony.

The case was plain wood and plain iron fittings, the kind of transit case used for canonical instruments and lens-ground equipment, designed to be unremarkable because unremarkable things don't get opened at checkpoints. It weighed almost nothing. Owain turned it in his hands once and then held it still.

He did not open it.

They stood in the heather's cold light and Wren watched his uncle's face, waiting for something. He had been rehearsing this moment in his head since before the run began — since the night Owain sat him down in the Caerglas hall and said *we're going to bring it home, and you're going to help*, and the word *home* had settled in Wren's chest like a dropped stone. He had been carrying a version of this moment for weeks in which Owain's face, when he held the case, would hold thirty years of family weight finally set down.

Owain's face held nothing in particular. He was looking at the case the way he would look at a case.

"Four days," he said. Not to anyone.

"Four days," Esvane agreed.

"The handlers have the hounds settled. The vault's been cleared." He tilted his head south, toward the moor's interior. "There was a crawler two nights ago, east edge. I put it down."

"Alone?"

"It wasn't a large one."

Esvane did not say anything to that, but Wren could see something shift in the set of her shoulders — not relief, not exactly. Something more like the adjustment you make when the weight you've been braced against finally settles without driving you down.

"Is the lock clear?" she said.

"I've been working it every morning. It's two hundred years old and it knows it." He looked up from the case. "It opens."

---

The moor-hound handlers' tent was canvas and practical — long tent pegs, guy-lines knotted at the proper interval, the kind of camp set up by someone who expected to hold it through weather and meant it to hold. One handler was awake when they arrived, a broad-shouldered woman from the Pallor northern dependencies with three of the six-legged hounds on a shared lead. The other handler was asleep in the tent and Owain let him stay asleep.

The hounds came awake when the squad crossed into the camp's radius. Not alarmed — they knew Owain's scent by now, and Esvane they recognized from before the run because she'd been part of the operational planning for six months. Wren they accepted in the way they accepted things Owain brought into their orbit: not warmly, but without hostility.

Petra they watched.

Petra watched them back. She had a professional neutrality about animals that was not fondness and was not fear. She assessed the hounds the way she assessed everything — distance, weight, likely speed, what they would do in a restricted space — and then she went to the tent's windward side and sat with her back against a tent pole and her knees drawn up and her eyes on the moor.

"Sleep," Esvane told her.

"Not tired."

"You've been awake for thirty hours."

"Twenty-six." Petra tilted her chin toward the moor's dark. "And we're forty meters from a vault with something in it. I'll sleep after."

Esvane looked at her for a moment and then did not argue, because Petra was right about everything operational and they both knew it.

---

Owain went to the vault an hour before dawn.

Wren was not asleep either, though he'd tried. He'd lain down on his bedroll in the tent and watched the canvas overhead and listened to the hounds' slow breathing and thought about nothing at great length, which meant he thought about everything. The moor-heather light came dimly through the canvas seams, pink-white, changing quality as the breeze moved the bloom. He'd never seen anything like it. In six months of planning and three weeks of running, he'd somehow not fully pictured the moor itself, only the vault and the handoff and the thing that came after. The moor had arrived anyway, unmoved by what he'd expected of it.

He heard Owain's boots on the frost-hardened ground outside. He heard the vault's approach — the particular silence of a stone building in the cold, the way it absorbs sound differently than air does. He heard nothing from the vault itself, because the vault was old and its walls were thick and its door was iron-bound oak and two hundred years old.

He lay there for a while. Then he got up.

Esvane was where she'd been when he'd lain down — sitting at the tent entrance, not quite inside and not quite out, watching the moor. She had the canonical transport log open across her knees, not reading it. She'd been not-reading it since they arrived. Her fingers rested on the pages without attention.

"He's at the vault," Wren said.

"I know."

He sat down beside her. The heather was different this close to dawn — a little less luminous, or maybe the sky was beginning to lighten just enough at the eastern edge to compete with it. The moor went south and east and north, undifferentiated and vast and cold, and the vault sat in the middle of it like a period at the end of an old sentence.

He didn't know how to start the thing he needed to say. He had been not-saying it for three weeks on the road, two weeks before that, and three months before that when he'd first read the documentation and understood what he was reading. He'd had a long time to develop the habit of not saying it.

"Tell me," Esvane said, without looking at him.

---

Wren looked at the vault.

"The canonical property transfer from Year 972," he said. "The Battle of Nine Days instrument. I read it. The original, not the Pallor registry copy."

He heard Esvane breathe in and out, steady, unrevealing.

"The instrument is legitimate," he said. "Canonical authority at the time, both signatories in proper standing. I checked. The Ocipheus receiving notation is complete and properly witnessed." He paused. "But the instrument's basis is the post-battle settlement, and the post-battle settlement drew on the combat outcome as its primary determination. Which means the Relic passed to Ocipheus because Pallor lost. Not because Ocipheus had a prior ownership claim. Not because there was a preexisting Liturgy stake. Because the Champion fell and the canonical process moved the Relic to the victor's ally under terms that were correct in form and — " He stopped.

"And also the price of a lost battle," Esvane said.

"Yes."

"I know."

Wren turned to look at her.

Her face was the same as it had been. Not still, exactly — not suppressed. Just already settled. The way a person's face looks when they've been carrying a thing long enough that carrying it has stopped having an expression.

"I've always known," she said. "Not the details you found — I haven't read that specific instrument in the original. But the shape. Yes. The shape of it." She turned a page in the transport log she wasn't reading. "Pallor's claim is real. That part of the family story is true. The Relic was Pallor's before the battle, in use and in custody and recorded in every canonical register going back to Year 854. The battle outcome moved it. The canonical process ratified the movement. Both things are true and they have always been true together."

Wren tried to find the thing he'd been trying to say for three months. "Then the Relic doesn't unambiguously belong to Pallor."

"No."

"And it doesn't unambiguously belong to Ocipheus either."

"No."

"Then why — " He stopped himself.

"Ask it," she said.

"Why are we here?"

Esvane set the transport log aside on the frozen ground. She looked at the vault. The stone of it was dark — it absorbed the heather light differently than the ground did, greyer and older.

"Because the claim is real," she said. "It is not resolved — it never has been — but it is real. Six generations of the Caerglas family have filed the petition and been told to file it again. The Liturgy's canonical review process has no mechanism for adjudicating a case this old that both sides can document. It does not move. It accumulates." She paused. "The claim is not made more real by six more generations of filing. Nor less real."

Wren waited. She had more to say; he could hear it.

"Because six generations," she said, "is long enough to wait."

She said it the way she said things she meant exactly as she said them — no particular weight, no performance, just the word and the word and the word in sequence.

"And because Owain needed to do this to become whoever he is after."

Wren looked at her. He looked at the vault.

He did not know what that meant. He could feel the shape of it — the edge of something too large to see straight at — but it didn't resolve. He tried to find the question that would pull it into focus and couldn't.

"After what?" he said.

Esvane was quiet for a moment.

"Come morning," she said, "you may understand it without being told."

---

Inside the vault, Owain worked the lock by lamplight.

The lamp was the one thing he'd brought in himself, two days ago, before he attempted the mechanism — because the vault's interior was full dark and had been full dark for some period of decades he couldn't determine, and you did not work a two-hundred-year-old lock by feel if you had the choice. He'd set the lamp on the floor to his left and spent four mornings learning what the mechanism wanted.

It was a four-tumbler iron lock, the kind that required the correct key in the correct orientation to advance through each tumbler in sequence, and each tumbler had a different resistance from the others because two hundred years of disuse had done different things to different parts of the mechanism. The first tumbler turned smoothly — it had always turned smoothly; someone had maintained this lock more recently than the others, or the oil trapped in its seat had held. The second required pressure from below, a slight upward torque while turning that was counterintuitive and took him three mornings to find. The third wanted to be left alone for thirty seconds between the second and its own engagement; he didn't understand why this was true but it was consistently true and he no longer questioned it. The fourth turned with a click that felt too small for what it meant.

The door opened inward, on hinges that had been maintained more recently than the lock's position in the door warranted, and the vault exhaled.

Cold air. The specific cold of enclosed stone that has not been open in years — dry and still and holding the temperature of the bedrock below the moor rather than the wind on its surface. It smelled of nothing except that cold. No rot. No damp. The vault had been built by people who understood what they were sealing inside it.

Owain set the lamp inside the entrance and let it burn a while before he went in.

The vault's interior was a single room: stone walls, stone floor, a low barrel vault ceiling. No furnishings. No carved insignia, just as the exterior held none. The pre-Compact builders had not believed in marking their spaces — or they had marked them in a way that centuries of heather and weather had removed, or they had not considered that the knowledge of what this place was required any writing down. It was twelve paces across and eight paces deep and it had been built to hold something.

He set the case in the center of the floor.

He stood over it and looked at it.

He had been thinking about this moment for thirty years. Not the vault specifically — he hadn't known about the vault, hadn't known the location of this retrieval site, until Esvane briefed him and his family's records confirmed the ancestral holding. But the moment of having the Relic on Pallor soil, Pallor custody, Pallor-held and Pallor-named — he had been thinking about that since he was fourteen years old and his grandmother had sat him down in the Caerglas hall and told him the story for the first time. The story of the Champion who fell. The story of the canonical settlement. The story of six petitions filed and six times returned unresolved. The story of the wrong that was also somehow the law, that was also somehow correct, that had somehow been both of those things for a hundred and sixty-six years without either one resolving into the other.

He crouched and opened the case.

The lens lay in its padded interior. Palm-sized. The glass — not quite glass, not quite the lens-ground he'd handled in the Pallor archive's instrument cabinet — was clear and slightly warm in a way that his hand reported as temperature without his understanding why it should have temperature. It was a lens. It had been a lens for seven hundred and forty-one years in the Ocipheus vigil archive and before that, at its origin, whenever that origin was and whatever Sphere had produced it.

He picked it up.

He held it in his palm with his fingers not quite closed around it. He felt the warmth of it. He felt its weight, which was not what he'd expected — lighter than stone of that size but heavier than glass. He felt the thirty years of family story in his hands, and the six petitions, and his grandmother's voice, and the Caer Glas heather outside in the dark, and the specific cold weight of having finally done the thing you were supposed to do.

He felt almost nothing.

Not emptiness — not the aftermath of something that had failed. He searched himself for what was missing and found that nothing was missing. It was simply that he was holding a lens in a cold room and the lens was warm and he could not yet make the leap from *having it* to *what having it meant*. He'd thought the meaning would arrive with the object. It was possible the meaning was slower than the object.

He stayed in the vault a long time.

---

The sky above the moor was greying at its eastern edge when he came back to the vault entrance. The heather was dimmer now — the sky light competing with it, winning slowly as dawn built — but it was still there, still lit from inside, and it made the moor look like a country he'd only partly entered.

Wren was no longer sitting with Esvane. He was standing at the camp's edge, his back to the tent, watching the moor. He had the posture of a man who had just been told something he didn't know what to do with yet.

Esvane was watching Owain from where she sat.

He looked at her for a moment. He had known her for twenty-three years. He knew the look on her face — the particular economy of expression she used when she had said the necessary thing and was waiting to see what it grew into.

"What did you tell him?" Owain said.

"What he needed to hear. Not all of it — not yet."

Owain looked at the case in his hand. "It doesn't feel like anything yet."

"I know."

"I thought it would."

"It will," she said. "It's slower than you expected. That's not a failure of the moment."

He looked at her again. Esvane had been in his life longer than any decision he'd made as a Knight, longer than either of his infusions, longer than most of what he considered the architecture of himself. She had agreed to this run knowing what it cost, knowing the institutional exposure, knowing that the canonical process she'd spent twenty-three years operating inside of was not going to bless what she'd done even if it didn't actively condemn it. She had done it anyway. He had never found the right word for what that was. He had stopped trying to find it.

"Thank you," he said. "For bringing it."

"You sent good people to carry it."

"I sent you."

She looked at him with the warmth she only showed when no one was watching except people who already knew it was there.

"Go wait by the vault," she said. "Let it settle."

---

He went.

He stood at the vault entrance with the case and watched the heather dim as the sky came up. The moor was enormous and old and it didn't know or care who held what in its middle — the pre-Compact stone didn't care, the six-legged heather didn't care, the crawler he'd put down two nights ago had not cared about the Caerglas family's hundred and sixty-six years of petition. The moor was not a place that held grievance. It simply was, in the way that enduring things simply are.

He thought about his grandmother. He thought about the story told in the Caerglas hall. He thought about the fourteen-year-old he'd been, and the weight the story had settled in him, and the shape the weight had given to the next thirty years of service — not controlling his choices but informing them, the way a stone in a river doesn't stop the river but changes the way it moves.

The case was in his hands. The lens was in the case. The vault was open behind him.

He would lock the lens inside, and go back to the others, and wait for whatever was coming.

---

The hounds woke before the handlers did.

Not alarmed. This was the thing Owain had learned in twenty years with moor-hounds: when they were alarmed they made noise, low and continuous and with their long necks extended and their six legs set wide beneath them. When they were tracking they were silent but their attention was mobile — heads moving, following something he couldn't see. What they were doing now was neither of those things.

They were awake, all three, and they were still. Completely still.

They were facing south and east.

Not toward the drove road — not toward the direction the squad had come from. South and east was the interior of the moor, the deep part, the ground that ran for seven kilometers before it reached the coastal cliffs above the channel. There was nothing south and east. There was heather and cold and the beginning of the morning light and nothing.

The hounds did not look at Owain when he moved to the vault entrance.

He looked at them for a moment. He had worked with moor-hounds for twenty years. He knew the difference between a thermal trace they were reading and a presence signature. The difference between those two things was direction and stillness. Thermal traces made the hounds move their heads to track. Presence signatures made the hounds hold.

They were holding.

The heather was completely still. The wind had dropped in the last quarter hour, as it sometimes did before dawn on an open moor. The sky was lighter now, pewter and pale, the last of the night-heather's phosphorescent bloom almost invisible against it. South and east was grey and flat and silent.

Owain looked at the three hounds looking south and east for a long moment.

He went back into the vault. He set the case inside, on the stone floor where he'd placed it an hour ago. He did not lock it — he pulled the door to but he didn't lock it, because locked doors were for when you intended to leave and he was not leaving. He straightened up and his hand was on the door's iron surface, the cold metal of it, and he held it there one moment.

Then he stepped back out.

He picked up the case.

He walked to the camp. Wren had turned from the moor's edge and was looking at the hounds. Esvane had risen from where she'd been sitting, the transport log closed and set aside. Petra, who was apparently not asleep despite what Owain assumed, was standing in the tent's entrance with her hand on the tent pole and her eyes on the moor.

The handlers were awake now too. The broad-shouldered woman had her hand on the lead but she hadn't tightened it yet — she was reading the hounds the same way Owain had. Waiting to see if there was more information coming.

There was not more information coming. There didn't need to be.

Owain looked at Esvane.

"She's on the moor," he said.

---

The word settled differently in each of them.

For Esvane it settled like confirmation — the shape of something she had been waiting for since the channel crossing, since she'd looked at the moor-hounds refusing to lie down and known that the distance between the squad and the Templar had closed to hours and was still closing. She had known it the way she knew canonical instruments that were properly formed and still wrong in their purpose — not through a flaw in the structure but through a clear reading of what the structure was aimed at. Lyra T-044 was a Templar who had crossed the Wall from the wrong side and come through Vierna and Atrament and Lacerta and a channel crossing and she was four hours behind them and she was on the moor.

For Petra it settled like a number she'd already been running. She moved from the tent entrance to the camp's supply point — packs, the two cases of equipment she'd been managing since Vierna — and she started checking closures with the quick competent attention she gave to things that needed to be ready in ten minutes.

For Wren it settled in his chest, below thought. He had not understood what Esvane meant when she said Owain needed to do this to become whoever he was after. He had turned the sentence over in the hours since she'd said it and found no purchase on it. He looked at his uncle standing at the camp's edge with the case in his hand and the moor behind him going south and east and flat and enormous, and the hounds were still.

He didn't understand it yet.

He would, in approximately four hours. He would understand it when the Templar arrived and what Owain had done — the claim, the run, the thirty years of family obligation made real — collided with what Prelacze had made of it. When his uncle named the Canon for what he was, in the reckoning afterward. When the certainty cracked open and something else was inside.

He didn't understand it yet because the four hours hadn't happened. He only felt the shape of it, distantly, the way you feel the approaching cold before you see the weather coming.

The heather was still glowing at the moor's edge, faintly, the last of the night's light bleeding out of the blooms as the sky continued to come up. Pink-white, lit from below. Persistent, the way the moor was persistent — not dramatic, not announcing itself, simply present across the cold ground as far as the light let you see and further than that.

Owain looked south and east.

Somewhere on that flat cold ground, a Templar was coming.

He put the case under his arm and held it the way Esvane had held it for three weeks: close, unremarkable, protected by proximity.

"Stow the equipment," he said. "Don't break the camp. She'll want to see we haven't run."

Petra looked up from what she was doing. Something passed across her face that was not quite humor and was not quite respect.

"She'll want to see the vault," Esvane said.

"Yes."

"Owain." She waited until he looked at her. "The lock."

He looked at the vault. The door was pulled to. The mechanism was two hundred years old and it had given him four days of mornings before it learned to open. He thought about the Templar on the moor, and the hounds facing south and east, and the four hours they had before the two threads of this story arrived at the same place on the same ground.

"I'll lock it," he said. "Let her come to a locked door."

He did not say: *and then I'll open it*. He didn't have to. They had come this far. The lock knew the key now. The hounds were reading what was on the moor. The heather was nearly gone in the morning light, pink-white retreating to grey stem and cold bloom that looked, in daylight, like heather and nothing more.

He walked back to the vault.

Behind him he heard Petra and Esvane moving through the camp with the particular efficiency of people who had been doing this for three weeks and had a rhythm for it. He heard Wren's steps in the frost — young steps, still learning their own weight on this kind of ground. He heard the hound handlers murmuring to the animals, low and steady, keeping them calm.

The vault door's iron fittings were cold under his hands. He worked the first tumbler, the second with its counterintuitive upward pressure, the thirty seconds of patience before the third. The fourth clicked home. He had not locked the lens inside — the case was at camp. What he sealed was the empty stone.

He put the key away.

He stood with his hand flat against the door for a moment — the cold of it, the specific texture of old iron — and then he turned back to the moor.

The heather was not lit from below anymore. In the early grey of it the moor was just a moor: flat, wet-cold, vast. The vault was stone. The camp was canvas. The hounds were six-legged shapes standing still against the light.

He picked up the case and waited for the morning to come in.

[Beat 47]
PALLOR REACHED — OWAIN CAERGLAS

The sea-loch received the Eirene-7 the way the cold receives the hand you put into it: completely, without ceremony, and with no concern for your experience of the event.

Kressida brought the hull down and it hit the water with a sound Lyra felt in her back teeth and then the vessel settled—not gracefully, not quickly, but with the particular reluctance of something designed for open water that had opinions about this specific sample of it. The loch was black under the overcast, the color of pewter before it cools, and cold in a way that was immediately visible as cold even in the dark. She had flown in Liturgy vessels twelve times in her career. She had never landed on water. The theoretical literature had not adequately conveyed that the sound would be wrong—wrong in the specific way of something that functions correctly but feels nothing like the operating manual suggested.

"Good landing," Tavar said, from somewhere aft.

"It was functional," Kressida said, through the rig's speaker housing. The BR-7 had been folded into the hold for the channel crossing; the speaker housing was the only part of it visible from the forward cabin, a grilled oval mounted at shoulder height that Lyra had spent eleven days learning to address instead of Kressida's actual face. The face was somewhere behind the iron and the reaction plate. The voice was the same either way: short, functional, accurate.

The hull settled. Through the forward port: the shore. Rock and heather, and above the rock, moorland—a darkness textured differently from the water, moving slightly in the wind. Horizontal rain. The Pallor coastal approach in late autumn looked like everything she had been told and also significantly worse.

She came up through the forward hatch into the air and the cold arrived with the specific intention of making her hands into something less than hands. She had three infusions; the structural changes extended into the vascular system, which meant she ran warmer than she had at twenty and had more tolerance for the practical consequences of cold. This was still very cold. Her breath came out visible. The rock shelf ahead glistened.

She came off the hull and onto the rock and crossed toward the shore. Behind her: Orim first, then Rowe with the rifle slung, then Tavar. The rig came last, the hold hatch releasing, the BR-7 unfolding onto the hull's surface and stepping across to the rock with the particular careful weight of something that weighed three tons and knew it.

---

The moor began at the ridge line forty meters above the high-tide mark, and once she crested it she stopped and looked.

The night-heather was phosphorescent.

She had read the natural history notes. The Sphere-origin catalogue for Pallor's cross-membrane botanical contamination, the registered ecosystem survey from Year 1087. She had read that Pallor night-heather bloomed after dark and that the hybrid colonial variety produced bioluminescent cold-light as an emergent property of its Sphere-origin genetic inheritance. She had read all of this and still the actual experience stopped her for a full two seconds.

The moor was lit from below. Pink-white, soft-edged, the light distributed through the heather across the full width of the moorland like ground phosphorescence, like something in the earth was still warm. The night above was cloud-dark and featureless. The moor was not dark at all. It glowed. It glowed everywhere, in all directions, to the visible horizon where the moorland broke against darker ridge lines, and the effect was of a country lit by something that did not care whether you were there.

She filed it. She moved.

Behind her she heard Rowe make a sound that was not a word—a sharp intake through the nose that meant recognition rather than surprise. She did not look back. She had learned to read the difference.

Orim had done a minor scry from the shore before they disembarked. She had watched him wet his fingertips from his kit, press them together at his sternum, look at nothing for thirty seconds. He had reported without preamble: three moor-hounds, two handlers visible at the ridge above the vault site, a third handler possibly at the eastern approach. And something he could not read cleanly. Something in the heather that was not the handlers and was not the hounds.

She had known what the opacity was. She had known since the channel crossing, when the particular quality of the dark water and the particular sound of the hull had settled something she had been trying to not yet know. But she had let Orim say it as he chose to say it, which was by the edge he could see and no further.

They walked with the knowledge that they were being watched.

The moor-hounds were tracking from the left before they had gone two hundred meters. You could not see them—they were low to the ground, the heather came up to a meter, and six-legged moorland hunters moved through cover differently from anything she had training to spot at distance. You could feel them, though. The feeling was not mystical; it was practical. The heather movements were wrong. Too regular, too deliberate. The pattern of disturbance was moving parallel to the party's line of advance and then slowly converging, and nothing that grew or blew made that specific pattern.

"They know we're here," Tavar said. He was not alarmed. He found it interesting. He found most things interesting rather than alarming, which was either a philosophical position or a failure of imagination, and Lyra had stopped being certain which.

"Yes," she said. She kept moving.

To her right, lower on the slope, one of the hounds made a sound—not a hunting sound, something lower and more patient. The sound of something that had been doing this for three days and expected to keep doing it. She walked toward the vault site and the hounds stayed in the heather and the heather stayed lit from below and the horizontal rain came in off the channel and did not improve.

---

The vault site appeared at the limit of the heather glow.

A pre-Compact structure—older than the Houses by centuries, possibly much older, pre-dating the canonical period entirely. The stone was the dark Pallor coastal type, dressed at the base but rougher above, the construction honest about what it was: shelter that had been here long enough that no one alive remembered building it. No House insignia. No canonical mark. A tower without ownership, which meant ownership so old and settled that it required no declaration.

A fire burned outside the tower base. Small, correct, the Pallor field way: sufficient heat, minimum visibility. She had seen enough of the Pallor way by now to read the intention in a fire the same way she read it in a report. This fire said: we are here, and we have been here long enough to settle, and we are not afraid of the cold.

Seven people in the firelight.

Three with crossbows already up at forty meters, positioned at the triangle of a defensive perimeter she would have drawn the same way, accounting for the approach angles and the elevated corner at the vault's east face. Two more standing back from the fire: a woman in Pallor Templar traveling clothes, the rank markings at collar and cuffs visible even at this distance; and a younger person, twenty-two perhaps, standing slightly behind her with the posture of someone who had not yet decided what his body was supposed to do at this particular moment. He had been deciding for three months, from what she knew of him, and had not arrived at a resolution.

One person standing in front.

He was taller than the trackers and had the distributed weight of two infusions: the density you felt before you saw it, the particular stillness that came from a structural relationship to the ground that the uninitiated did not share. He wore a Pallor gray coat with no House markings. He stood ahead of the fire, which put his face in shadow and hers in the light, and he had positioned himself this way deliberately.

Owain Caerglas. Pallor Knight, seconded to Canon Prelacze's discretionary commission, at Caer Glas Moor for four days. She had known the name since the Schmalburg cross-reference files. She had known the face would look like this—not specifically, but in type. The face of someone who had arrived at something he had been moving toward for thirty years and had found it exactly as heavy as expected and was carrying it exactly as well.

She stopped at fifty meters.

Kressida halted behind her, the BR-7's footfall going quiet in the heather. Tavar took a position to her left, hands loose. Rowe moved to the elevated ground at her right—a low rock shelf, three meters up, nothing obviously tactical about it except that it was the only cover on this approach and he had found it without being directed. Eight months in France and seven months in Vierna and four months with her party, and he still read terrain before he read orders.

She said: "Owain Caerglas."

He said: "T-044."

His voice was level. Not threatening. Not welcoming. The voice of someone who had spent four days settling into what he intended to be when this moment arrived and had finished settling.

She said: "You know why I'm here."

He said: "Yes."

She said: "Then you know how this ends."

He did not answer immediately. The horizontal rain moved between them. One of the moor-hounds made a patient sound in the heather.

He said: "Three infusions against two. It's not mathematics. It's physics."

She said: "I know."

"I still have to hold."

She said: "You don't."

He looked at her with the expression of someone who had been waiting for this specific sentence and had decided before it arrived what he was going to do when it came. It was the expression of a decision that looked like stubbornness from outside and felt, from inside, like the only thing left that belonged entirely to you.

He said: "The object was lawfully recovered under a six-generation standing property claim. I was commissioned in good faith. I executed the commission correctly. I cannot return to Pallor service having abandoned a commission in good standing."

She said: "You can return having been bested by a third-infusion Liturgy Templar conducting a legitimate pursuit. That's not abandonment. It's physics, which you just told me this was."

He said: "That requires me to be bested."

She said: "Yes."

He looked at the rig. At Rowe on the shelf. At Tavar, who was not doing anything visible but whose hands were positioned correctly. He looked back at her.

He said, half-turned toward the trackers: "Hold."

Then he attacked.

---

He was fast.

She had not underestimated him—she had been practicing not underestimating people for thirty years and she was good at it—but the actual quality of his speed made her reassess the space between two infusions and three, which was a space she had crossed herself and which she had apparently been misremembering. The first strike was aimed at her left shoulder, high, where the half-plate had its joint seam. He had assessed her kit at fifty meters in firelight and remembered it correctly.

She took it on the Vigil Shield instead—dropped her shoulder, redirected the arm. The impact ran through the shield and up into her elbow and past the joint and she noted it: real force. He had the density to back the speed and the technique to put them together.

The second strike she redirected rather than absorbed. Her height gave her the leverage—fourteen centimeters and the structural work the third infusion had done on the long muscle groups, which changed what the body could do with its own weight. She redirected and moved inside, because at close distance the height advantage compressed and the leverage differential appeared, and she wanted him to learn that.

He adjusted. Good. He was genuinely good. He converted the downward redirect into a roll, took two steps sideways, and came at her from the right at a lower angle than she had predicted—he was accounting for the height now. He was learning inside the exchange. That meant he had ten years minimum of consistent practice, probably more.

She gave him the ground. Stepped back. Made him commit to the advance.

He did not commit. He held position.

They stood in the heather-glow with the rain coming horizontal between them and she recognized something in him: the patience of a person who had been trained to use waiting as a weapon. He would stand here all night if it gave him the edge. He did not need to win quickly. He needed to not lose in a way that could not be explained with dignity.

She did not have all night.

She moved.

What followed was three exchanges and a conclusion. She took two strikes and landed two and none of the four landed cleanly—this was the reading interval, both of them learning the other's weight and timing. He was better than a two-infusion practitioner should have been at this age, which meant consistent training across decades and a willingness to take hits as a learning tool that not everyone had. By the end of the second exchange she had his measure and knew what the third was going to look like.

The third exchange she closed the distance fully and put her weight across his back and his arm behind him and the Dissolution Blade at his neck and he held very still.

He was still. Professional. He understood exactly what had happened.

She said: "The object."

He said nothing.

She said: "I don't need you to hand it to me. I need to know where it is."

He was quiet for a moment that was not stalling—she knew what stalling felt like in a body and this was not it—but weighing the specific cost of telling her against the specific cost of not.

He said: "Twr Brennid. The pre-Compact tower, two kilometers northeast. Third floor, north wall recess. Take the path from the western ridge high point."

She held the position. The heather glowed under them both. The rain was very cold.

She said: "Who gave you the commission."

He was quiet for a longer moment.

He said: "Canon Immaculate Tomasz Prelacze."

She had known the name since Rowe's testimony, when it had arrived as confirmation rather than revelation. Three months of a paper trail pointing at a Canon, and the name fitting the space that had been waiting for it. But hearing it spoken here, on this moor, with Owain Caerglas face-down in the phosphorescent heather, made it real in a different way. Real enough to touch.

She said: "What did he tell you the commission was for."

He said: "Recovery of a misappropriated Relic. Canonical property dispute, six-generation standing. He told me the dispute had been pending for thirty years and that he was prepared to authorize the retrieval under the Canon's discretionary jurisdiction."

She said: "You believed it."

He was quiet.

He said: "I thought I was doing right. I don't know anymore."

She felt something in her chest that was not pity and not contempt and was not the clean cold of a pursuit concluded. It was closer to recognition. The same quality Orim had had, watching her across six weeks of travel, processing information she had already been given and could not yet say she had. The same inventory, the same careful accumulation, the same moment of finally not being able to file the exception.

She released him.

She stood. He came up slowly, in the controlled way of someone still managing a physical situation and intending to keep managing it. He stood in the rain and looked at her with the expression of someone who had expected something specific to follow a confession and was not sure whether this was better or worse.

She said: "Go to the Long Seat. Not Pallor administration. The Long Seat directly. Tell them everything: how the commission was conveyed, who was present, what you were told and what you were told to tell the squad." She waited. "The claim is real. Six generations is a real grievance. What Prelacze did with it is something else. The Long Seat will hear the distinction."

He said: "You're not reporting me."

She said: "No."

He said: "Why."

She said: "Because I understand who you were before tonight. And I can see you're not that anymore. I don't have a file for what you are now." She looked at him steadily. "The Long Seat does."

He stood with this. The horizontal rain moved between them.

He said: "T-044."

She had already turned. She stopped.

He said: "Whatever Prelacze wants the object to show him—it requires the Relic at a specific location. The place where the membrane is thinnest. The commission was the last piece."

She said: "I know."

She walked northeast.

---

She had taken perhaps ten steps.

A voice came from the moor that had not been in any of the positions she had catalogued.

It said: "Little Sister."

---

Lyra turned.

There was a woman standing in the heather who had not been there. Which was not possible—she had catalogued the moor's visible positions on approach, tracked the three handlers, noted the hound movements. This woman had not been in any of those positions. She had stepped out of the moor-dark with no transition she had registered, no movement in the heather before the voice, and she was standing at thirty meters with her hands empty and looking at Lyra with the expression of someone who had been patient all night.

Six infusions.

You read it the same way you read two versus three—not with the eyes first, with the body's awareness of density. The distributed weight. The structural changes accumulated across decades of Transmutation practice until the body was something different at the foundation. She was shorter than Lyra. Compact and broad in the shoulders, her hair silver-white in the heather-glow. She wore Pallor gray with no insignia and wore it the way old soldiers wore everything: as weather protection and nothing more. She was unhurried in the specific way of someone who had not needed to prove anything in twenty years.

Six infusions and forty years behind them. The rank beyond Paladin. Champion—the last rank before the theoretical ceiling no living practitioner had confirmed existed.

Behind Lyra the rig's footfalls changed character and she knew without looking that Kressida had shifted to combat positioning. She heard the chain flail engage on the BR-7's right arm, the soft mechanical sound of it.

She heard Rowe's bolt work. One round, chambered in the cold. He had been on the rock shelf for twenty minutes and had been still enough in that time that his hands were probably half-numb. He chambered the round without fumbling.

The woman said: "I know what the ratio is. You know what the ratio is. Let's not perform." The same flat accuracy as the heather-glow: real and indifferent. "I am going to ask you to stop where you are and leave the object behind."

Lyra said: "You know I won't do that."

"Yes," the woman said. "That's why I said I was going to ask."

She was called Vaen. Four sentences in the Schmalburg cross-reference files: *Vaen, Pallor service, Champion rank, attached to the house of the Warrior King, deployment history classified at Champion level.* She had wondered, reading those four sentences, why only four. Now she understood. You did not need more than four sentences for something this old and this settled.

Lyra moved.

---

Vaen moved to meet her, and the gap between three infusions and six was not a gap. It was a wall.

The first exchange: Vaen's right arm came across faster than the eye resolved correctly and Lyra took it on the Vigil Shield and felt the impact run through the shoulder socket, past the joint, into the bone of the upper arm. Not broken—the third infusion had done something to bone density—but wrong. The kind of wrong that accumulated. She moved back hard.

Vaen did not pursue. She was reading something.

Kressida brought the rig in from the left.

The BR-7 was three meters of Atrament iron moving at speed, the chain flail already in motion, the spiked head swinging at the full extension—four meters of clear arc. Vaen read it coming and moved, and the movement happened in the interval between the moments the eye catches, and the flail head caught the rig's left shoulder housing instead of what Kressida had intended. The hit staggered the rig—three tons of iron stumbling sideways in the heather, reaction plate shearing. Kressida corrected, fighting the weight. The rig found its footing again.

"Knee housing is intact," Kressida said through the speaker housing, which was her equivalent of an assessment and a warning at once.

Vaen had already changed direction.

Tavar threw.

The hatchet was not aimed to wound—aimed to move, to put Vaen behind cover that did not exist and force her to address a threat. The second hatchet came three heartbeats later at a different angle, opening a different choice about direction. Vaen made the choice—inside, toward the rig—and Tavar was already moving to the angle that opened up. He was good at this. He had been doing this long enough that his body made the adjustments before he did.

Lyra came at Vaen from the right while Kressida's rig came from the left, which was the correct geometry, and it made no difference. Vaen took Lyra's blade strike on her forearm—six infusions of bone density receiving what the Dissolution Blade's ceramic channels could deliver—and turned the contact into a throw that put Lyra four meters back in the heather. Then she addressed the rig with the same undivided attention, and the rig's flail came down and Vaen stepped inside the arc and hit the rig's left knee housing with the heel of her open hand.

The hydraulic assembly in the knee went wrong.

"Still intact," Kressida said, in the tone of someone lying about the extent of the damage to avoid alarming the people who needed to not be alarmed right now. The rig staggered and held itself upright by stubbornness.

Lyra got up.

Her left shoulder was wrong. Not broken. Wrong in the way that would be a problem for three days and a memory for three years. She got up and moved and did not let the wrong shoulder change her visible profile in any way she could manage, because Vaen would read a changed profile.

The third exchange was worse than the second.

Vaen was reading the party now—all five positions, the rig's remaining capabilities, Tavar's angles, Orim's apparent non-position at the rear—processing them with the same unhurried attention of something that accepted whatever the current gave it. Lyra got two strikes past the guard and neither of them mattered at the depth they reached. What she received in exchange was one strike to the left side that made her ribs introduce themselves to each other and one to the right forearm that made holding the Vigil Shield a question she had not expected to be asking. She held it. Her right forearm was bleeding. She had not noticed the cut opening and noted this as information about how the exchange had moved.

Through it all Orim had not moved.

He had been standing at the party's rear since Vaen appeared, the Rod in his hands with the mineral tip pointed down. He had not scried. He had not moved forward. He was watching Vaen with the specific attention of a man looking for something he had not yet found. She understood what he was doing. He had told her once, crossing the Atrament ridge, that the force-pierce was not a solution. It was what you used when the alternative was worse. He needed to know what was behind the membrane before he opened it, and he needed the certainty that opening it was better than not opening it, and he was making that determination methodically, which was the only way to make it that she trusted.

---

Tavar had moved to daggers. He was creating angles from Vaen's left—two blades, point-work, in and out faster than it looked safe to move. Not trying to wound. Trying to multiply the threats she had to track. This was effective in the way that sufficient is useful but insufficient: it kept her processing split without resolving anything.

Rowe chambered the second round from his position on the shelf.

Lyra moved in again. Vaen's response was a palm strike to the Vigil Shield that sent it and her arm sideways and opened her left side for a follow-through that she took on the pauldron, and the pauldron held but the force behind it made her step wrong and she went down to one knee in the heather. She was up before Vaen closed. She was breathing harder than she wanted to be breathing.

Kressida brought the rig in.

The chain-lock engaged on the flail—the spring collar snapping shut, the chain stiffening into the flanged mace configuration, the ball's spikes deploying into six flanged ridges—and the converted head hit Vaen across the left side of her torso. Vaen took it the way the ground takes a tree: absorbing, not breaking. She went three meters sideways and kept her feet. She turned to look at Rowe's position on the shelf with a quality of attention that was not threatening and was very precise.

The second shot came before she finished turning.

Rowe had been watching Vaen move for seven minutes from the elevated position. He had been watching the pattern—the specific rhythm of how a six-infusion body moved in the intervals between commitment, which was a different problem from tracking any fast target he had been trained against. He was not a practitioner. He had no training in how Transmutation affected human movement. He had one relevant experience, which was eight months in France before the membrane took him, and France had taught him—had put it into his hands the way training does—how to lead a target that moved faster than the eye fully tracked, how to aim at the space rather than the person, how to put a round through the gap in the coverage that existed for half a second between two committed positions.

He shot through the gap between the rig's right shoulder housing and the angle Tavar had taken at Vaen's left. The round went in above the left collarbone and it was not a wound that would stop her—six infusions had too much structural redundancy for one round—but it changed what her left arm would do in the next two seconds, and the next two seconds were when Kressida's rig came back around again, the flanged mace at full arm extension, and it hit Vaen on the side she had been favoring.

She staggered.

She recovered. But it had taken her a half-second.

She looked at Lyra.

"Little Sister," she said again. Still the same two words. The second time was quieter, more honest. Not naming the fight—naming the thing underneath it, which was: *I know what you are. I was where you are. One day if you are still alive you will be where I am, and you will say this to someone else, and they will understand it the same way you understand it now, which is imperfectly, and that will be correct.*

Lyra said: "Orim."

He said: "Almost."

---

She bought him time.

She bought it the way you buy things you cannot afford: by spending what you have and paying the rest later. The left shoulder was wrong and the right forearm was cut and her ribs were presenting their inventory on every breath and Vaen had not taken equivalent damage from any of it, but Lyra was moving and moving was still something that needed to be addressed.

Tavar was out of range hatchets. He had moved to daggers and was working the angles with them—not trying for wounds, working the tactical geometry, keeping Vaen's processing split between too many targets to address in sequence. He was already inside the outer range when Vaen committed to Lyra, and outside it when Vaen turned back to him, and this was a kind of skill that looked effortless from the outside and was the result of years of not having a third option. He had two hatchets in his coat lining and two more daggers in his boot and had not yet needed the reserves. He noted this privately and found it less reassuring than he would have liked.

The fourth exchange: Vaen hit Lyra hard enough that she felt the ground under her knees again and was up again and there was a moment—a specific, physical, undeniable moment—when her body registered that the gap between three infusions and six was not a wall you broke through with enough time and ingenuity. It was a wall. You did not break through walls. You found the door.

The door was Orim.

He was still standing at the rear with the mineral tip pointed down and his eyes open and she could see him working. Not scrying—the Rod's minor-scry function was not the function he was looking for. He was looking for the right membrane site, the right Sphere, the right pressure state. He was cross-referencing fifty years of catalogue knowledge against what he needed the aperture to do. He was being methodical because he could not afford to be anything else.

Vaen moved toward the tower.

Not a charge—deliberate. She had read the party's capabilities and exhausted the tactical scenarios that ended with the object remaining in Pallor, and there was one scenario left, which was to retrieve the object herself. The object was in the pre-Compact tower. She walked toward it.

The rig intercepted.

Kressida drove the BR-7 into Vaen's path at full stride—three tons of iron, the damaged knee housing dragging, the chain flail back in swing configuration because the flanged mace had done what it could. Vaen did not stop. She addressed the rig with the full weight of six infusions and forty years and hit the rig's chest housing three times in rapid succession and the third hit collapsed the left reaction plate entirely and sent it into the heather in two pieces.

"That," Kressida said through the speaker housing, with the specific economy of someone assessing damage they have already decided to accept, "is going to be a week's work."

The rig held its footing. Kressida held it upright by will and iron. The right arm was still functional and she put it between Vaen and the tower.

Lyra moved in from the right.

The fifth exchange she did not come for a strike. She came to hold. She got Vaen's right arm with both hands and pulled, changing the direction of her commitment, and Tavar was already moving from the left with both daggers and Rowe was chambering the third round and for three seconds all of it was pressed tight together—the rig and the daggers and Lyra holding on and the shot waiting for the gap—and then Esvane broke from where she had been standing near the fire and walked into the engagement because thirty years of institutional instinct said you inserted yourself into a situation this close to catastrophic and you cited the canonical authority you had and you made it stop.

She got one sentence out before the physics of the engagement arrived at her position. Vaen's left arm was free and moving and Esvane took the edge of it—not the full force, but the edge—and went down hard to her right, her arm folding wrong at the elbow, and lay still with the quality of someone who had hit the ground hard and had made the decision that the ground was where she should remain.

Wren took one step forward.

He stopped. He stood in the heather with his service knife in his hand and he did not know what he was doing there or what his body intended to do with the knife, and the answer—as it had been for three months—was that he did not know, and the not-knowing was the truest thing about him.

Orim said: "Now."

He turned to his left, away from the engagement, which was the direction he always turned before he used the Rod. He wet the mineral tip from the preparation vial at his belt. He touched the preparation to his fingertips, pressed them together at his sternum, held one breath — saw what he needed to see. He dialed the correct groove by feel—the forty-year catalogue in his hands, tactile, the way a locksmith reads tumblers in the dark. He pointed the Rod at the heather four meters behind Vaen's position.

He depressed the trigger.

The membrane opened.

The skin stretched first—translucent, dark veins threading through it, lit briefly from the pressure building on the far side. The veins pulsed once. Twice. Went dark. The skin bulged outward.

Then it parted and the dark things came through.

They had the wingspan of an Atrament kite—two meters at the shoulders, possibly more, the wings folding and unfolding as they came through with the uncertainty of things that had never been anywhere with this much open air. They were dark across the back, pale at the throat and chest, and what they had where feet should have been were not feet.

Hands.

Flat, five-fingered, bone-pale human hands hanging from the ends of each wing, flexing reflexively as they emerged into wrong air, wrong temperature, wrong everything. The first one came through and the second and then six more in the next eight seconds and then the aperture sealed—membrane closing, the skin deflating, the veins fading—and Lyra's mind noted, in the same register it noted the horizontal rain and the wrong sound of the hull landing, that Orim's field catalogue had apparently been missing a relevant anatomical detail about Sphere-44.

They did not know what Vaen was.

They did not know what the rig was, or Lyra, or Tavar, or Rowe, or the glowing heather or the horizontal Pallor rain.
