They had been on the other side of a membrane that had been sealed for the entire duration of their existence and now they were here and the wrong air was already working on their biology and they were going to be dead in twenty seconds and in those twenty seconds they addressed the entire situation with the flat democratic intensity of things that had never needed to learn the difference between threats.

Two went for the rig, which was the largest moving object and colonial fauna across all the Spheres Orim had catalogued preferred the largest moving object. Two went for Vaen, because Vaen was standing and standing things were addressed next. The remaining four distributed themselves across the available space with the efficiency of things that did not make decisions.

Orim was forty meters back. His coat was up over his head. He was counting under his breath.

Lyra dropped.

She dropped because the bone-pale hands were at her head height and the hands grasped and she had been watching Orim point the Rod for the last ninety seconds and had taken her position accordingly. She dropped to a crouch in the heather and the two that passed over her grabbed at each other instead, which produced a sound and a consequence she declined to observe in detail, and then they were past and failing.

Tavar was already on the ground, flat, without fuss, the daggers sheathed. He had seen what was coming through the aperture from his angle and had made the relevant deduction quickly.

Rowe was on his back on the rock shelf with his arms folded over his face and his hat pulled down and he had gotten there before she had, which told her something about the speed at which a man from France processed the appearance of bone-pale human hands emerging from a torn membrane. He had probably seen worse in France. She was genuinely uncertain.

Vaen was standing.

Two of the bat-handed things had addressed Vaen and six infusions protected you from very many things and did not protect you from something that grabbed with human-shaped hands at ranges too low and too close to address with any of the techniques forty years of Transmutation practice had developed. She did not fall. She kept her feet through both of them and threw one into the heather and addressed the other with a palm strike and it was clear that she was managing the situation. But managing was not free, and she was occupied in a way she had not been occupied since the fight began, and the twenty seconds the bat-handed things lived was twenty seconds during which she could not move toward the tower.

All eight of them died. They died in the span of three seconds at the end, the wrong air completing its work. The heather held them.

Vaen was standing in the glow.

She looked at Kressida's rig—one knee dragging, left chest housing open, right arm still raised.

She looked at Tavar on the ground, already rising, hands going back to the daggers.

She looked at Rowe on the shelf, on his back, hat over his face.

She looked at Lyra.

---

The look lasted three seconds.

It was not anger. It was not grief exactly, though there was something in it at the edges of grief—the feeling of a thing you have been prepared for that has arrived at the specific conclusion you could not prepare for. She had been Champion for long enough that she had stopped thinking about what it meant to be stopped.

She knew it when it happened. That was what forty years gave you: the accurate knowledge of when you had been stopped.

The mission had been to ensure the Relic reached Pallor. The Relic was in the pre-Compact tower. The Templar was going to the tower. The party that had just broken her engagement was not dead and not retreating, which meant if she moved for the tower she would not have the margin to hold the tower and also address what the party would do the moment she committed to the direction. The tower required her full attention to hold. She did not have full attention to spare.

The Relic was not reaching Pallor tonight.

She had been through three Pallor claims over forty years of service. She would be here for the fourth if she chose the option still available to her, which was to continue the engagement and determine whether there was a configuration of force she had not yet found. There might be. She had six infusions and forty years. She had been stopped, not beaten. The distinction mattered.

She chose the other option.

She looked at Lyra and she did not speak. She had said what she had to say and had said it twice and both times had meant it and nothing that had happened between the first time and now changed the meaning. Then she turned and walked into the heather.

The night-heather glowed pink-white around her, lit from below, and she stepped into it and the light took her in the way the cold takes everything: completely, without ceremony, and with no concern for what happened next. The moor closed around her. No sound in the heather after she passed into it. As if the moor had been waiting all night to take her back.

She did not look back.

She did not speak again.

---

Lyra stayed where she was until she was certain the bat-handed things were all dead. This took longer than it should have because two of them had made it into the heather rather than dying in the open, and heather movements in the dark had acquired a new significance. She watched the movements and waited and when they stopped she waited another twenty seconds and then she stood.

The moor-hounds were gone. The handlers had taken them back into the dark when the membrane opened, which was either professional training or adequate instinct and she did not fault them for it.

The three trackers were down. Tavar's work, during the opening of the engagement when she had been focused entirely on Owain. Not dead—she could see one of them moving, sitting up. Tavar had been precise in the way of someone who had no interest in unnecessary casualties.

Esvane was on the ground ten meters to her right. Down since the fifth exchange—Vaen's edge, not its intention. Her right arm was wrong at the elbow. She was breathing. She had the specific quality of someone who had hit the ground hard enough to make a thorough assessment of the situation and had decided the ground was correct for the moment.

Petra was not visible. Petra had made an operational judgment at some point during the engagement and had moved to a position that was not this one. She was probably two hundred meters north in the dark and fine. She was probably always fine. That was what fifteen years of route-finding produced.

Wren was standing.

He was twenty meters from the vault base, in the glowing heather, the Pallor service knife in his hand and unused. She could see it was unused—not from the blade, which she could not read in this light, but from the way he was holding it: the grip of someone who had spent the entire engagement making the decision about whether to use it and had arrived at the end still making that decision. Twenty-two years old. His doubt had been the truest thing about him for three months and it had kept him outside the fight the same way it had kept him outside the certainty and now it had kept him standing.

She did not tell him what to do. She turned and walked northeast toward the pre-Compact tower.

---

Two kilometers on a path that was not quite a path—a line of less-resistant heather, lower and more worn, that suggested many people had walked this way over a long time and none of them had thought to mark it. The rock underfoot was the dark Pallor coastal stone: dense, sharp at the edges, holding water in every hollow. The horizontal rain filled the hollows as fast as she crossed them.

The tower was a darkness against the moor's glow. The tower fire had gone out—rained out, or simply untended, no one having stayed to mind it. She found the entrance by feel: low lintel, stone worn smooth at shoulder height from what might have been centuries of passing hands. Inside: the still cold of enclosed stone, which was different from the moving cold outside and not better. Three flights of stairs, the steps uneven, the height of each different from the last, no railing.

The third floor had empty window frames and the rain came through them and pooled on the stone except in the lee of the north wall, where the recess was cut at eye level.

He had wrapped it well. Pallor oilskin, garrison supply knot, tied with the field tension that meant someone had done this before. The oilskin had kept the rain out entirely.

She unwrapped it with both hands and held it.

It was smaller than the archive case had suggested. You knew an object's dimensions from its housing and still the actual thing surprised the hands with how modest it was. Lighter than expected. Lighter than anything should be that had accumulated 741 years of membrane contact. The surface was nothing she could accurately identify—not glass, not stone, not ceramic, not metal, something that had properties of all of these and chose which one to present depending on the angle and the temperature of the hands that held it.

It was warm.

Not room-temperature warm, not borrowed warmth from the oilskin. Specifically warm. The warmth of something that had its own temperature and kept it regardless of what surrounded it.

She held it for thirty seconds without doing anything with it.

Not looking into it. Thirty years of knowing that the Relic was not for personal use, and the habit was in her hands before the decision arrived. She held it and looked at the wall above the recess.

Carvings in the stone. Pre-Compact script; she had the basic literacy for it, the research certification level. She read without moving closer.

*We watched because it cost us nothing. We stopped watching because it cost us everything. We left this so you would know the difference.*

She held the Relic in the pre-Compact tower on the Pallor moor with the rain coming through the empty windows and the night-heather glowing pink-white below her and the carvings in front of her, and she stayed with them for longer than she had any tactical reason to stay.

Then she put the Relic in her research satchel, where forty Scry data blocks from Sphere 31 had lived until she understood what they were, where Ardea's half-written service record lived. She secured the flap. She went back down the stairs and out into the rain.

---

The party was where she had left them.

Orim had done something alchemical for Esvane's arm—she was sitting upright with the particular posture of someone who had made peace with the immediate situation and was reserving judgment on the larger one. The arm had been splinted with something from Orim's kit, bound tight. He was refilling his mineral preparation vial from the secondary stock in his pack, the Rod set down beside him in the heather, and he was not looking at it.

Kressida was in the heather with the rig's knee housing open, working by the light of a small field lamp, moving at the speed of someone doing familiar work under insufficient conditions. The housing clicked into a temporary configuration. The rig stood on it experimentally. The rig held.

"Good enough," Kressida said. She did not say good.

Tavar was sitting on the vault's lowest course of stone, eating something from a cloth wrap, watching nothing in particular. He said: "Interesting night."

Kressida said: "Don't."

He did not.

Rowe was standing at the rock shelf with his rifle at his shoulder and his eyes on the north moor. He had not moved from that position since the bat-handed things died. He would keep watching until someone told him there was nothing more to watch for, because that was the kind of training France had been, and the kind you did not unlearn by moving to a different world.

Owain was sitting in the heather twenty meters from the vault with his back to the tower. He had not left. She had not restrained him and no one else had thought to. He was sitting with the particular quality of someone who had nowhere he needed to be and was beginning, slowly, to understand why.

She walked past him.

She heard him, behind her:

"T-044."

She stopped.

He said: "He told me the Relic would prove that the founding Canon had foreknowledge. Year 1079—that the original Liturgy leadership knew what was happening in the Sinter basin and chose to suppress it. That was what he wanted it for. Not the claim. The leverage."

She had known this. She had been knowing it the way she had known everything she could not yet admit she knew—by the weight of it accumulating, by the shape of the space it occupied, by the moment it finally became impossible to file.

She said: "I know."

She walked back to the party.

---

Wren was standing at the edge of the group where she had left him, in the glowing heather, the service knife put away. He looked at her with the expression of someone who had been waiting for permission he was not going to ask for.

She looked back.

He said: "Where are you going?"

She said: "Sinter."

He said nothing for a moment. The rain came in off the channel. The moor-hounds were somewhere in the dark to the north and were not coming back tonight.

He said: "The Long Seat has a theory about the zone. About what the vigil has been recording for the last seven hundred years. Eight generations of Long Seat scholars working on it and none of the Liturgy canonical review sessions have ever asked for the Long Seat's account." He paused. "I grew up with it. I know what it says."

She looked at him.

He said: "I read the canonical property transfer documentation. The claim is real. Ocipheus's custody is also real. Both things are true." He looked at the heather. "I've been trying to understand how both things can be true for three months and I think the answer is somewhere in Sinter."

She did not tell him to come. She did not tell him not to come. She turned and walked south toward the sea-loch with the Relic in her satchel and the pre-Compact carvings in her memory and the wrong shoulder and the cut forearm and the ribs that were going to make the next three days instructive.

He fell into step behind her.

Not because she had asked. Because the thing he had been trying to understand since he read that documentation was in Sinter, and he had nowhere else to go where the understanding was possible.

The night-heather glowed pink-white under all of them as they crossed the moor toward the water. The horizontal rain did not stop. The cold was still the specific Pallor cold, the kind that made the fingers think about stopping, and Lyra's fingers kept working.

She was going to need them.

[Beat 48]
SHE GOES TO SINTER

The dispatch note arrived at the sixth hour.

Vega had been at her desk since the fourth, which was not unusual; she arrived at the fourth and departed at the fourteenth and had been doing so for three years without particular comment from anyone, because the Liturgy's administrative schedule arranged itself around reliable people the way it arranged itself around good furniture — with gratitude that did not rise to acknowledgment. She had her desk. The desk faced two windows. The windows faced the courtyard. The courtyard was empty most days. This was the structure of her work.

The dispatch note was from the Office of the Senior Scribe. Not Subcanon Malvar's office, not the Canon's administrative staff, not anyone in the vertical line she filed things upward to. The Office of the Senior Scribe was a horizontal function — advisory, archival, the Liturgy's institutional memory rather than its executive arm. It had been housed in the same three rooms since Year 872. It was staffed, currently, by one woman who had been in those rooms for forty-one years.

Senior Scribe Brentha Osel. Vega had met her twice. Once at the orientation for new Registry appointments, where Osel had delivered a three-minute address on the canonical responsibility of the witness function that Vega had found, at the time, professionally sound and personally uninspiring. Once in a corridor outside the map archive, where Osel had stopped her and asked, without preamble, whether she had found it interesting.

Vega had said: found what interesting?

Osel had said: *the work.* And walked away.

The dispatch note was brief. *V. Athen-Moor — Report to the Office of the Senior Scribe at the eighth hour. Bring your notary seal and travel instruments. — B. Osel.*

She read it twice. She folded it. She put it in her working-copy folder, which was not where it belonged — it belonged in correspondence — but she put it there because the working-copy folder was what she had been carrying everywhere for eight months, and the dispatch note was part of the same pattern as everything else in it, and the pattern was where it belonged.

She packed her travel bag before the sixth hour was done. She had packed it before the note arrived. This was a thing she chose not to examine.

---

Brentha Osel was seventy-three. Her desk was smaller than Vega's and covered in materials that were not canonical instruments — reference compendiums, historical registers, the bound record of a canonical review session from Year 1104 that Vega recognized by its binding stamp. She looked at Vega the same way she had looked at her in the corridor: deciding how much of what she knew she was going to say.

"You've been keeping a working copy," Osel said.

"Yes."

"Eight months?"

"Eight."

Osel was quiet. She looked at the Year 1104 record. She said: "The current Canon Immaculate has been in his position for eleven years. In that time, the Sphere-intake quota has been maintained at the third expansion level. The Wall's garrison rotation has been extended from eight months to twelve. The Forge Hearth extraction authorization has been renewed three times." She set the record down. "And six months ago, the Liturgy's permanent contingency reserve was unsealed under a standing order renewal certified by a Registry notary." She looked at Vega directly. "You certified it."

"Yes."

"Did you read the form?"

"It was correct."

"The form was correct," Osel said. "The form is always correct. The Canon Immaculate's office is very good at correct forms." She turned in her chair, which was old and made the adjustment audible. "The deployment roster for the war construct evaluation cohort. Did it come through your queue?"

"No. The evaluation certifications came through. The deployment roster was convened under Article Eighteen."

"Membrane-breach classification," Osel said. "Yes. The breach they were authorized against has not been publicly announced." She looked at Vega. "It's the Sinter Zone."

Vega said nothing. The working copy was in her bag. She had written that conclusion three weeks ago, and had spent the subsequent three weeks hoping the conclusion was wrong, which it was not.

"I can't stop it," Osel said. She said this plainly, the way you said things that were true and unpleasant and that you had been living with for long enough that they had stopped requiring emotion. "I have been a notary for forty-one years and a Senior Scribe for twelve of those years and the thing I have been given the authority to do is witness and record. I do not authorize. I do not command. I do not stop." She folded her hands on the desk. "What I do is write it down. And what the canonical instrument set requires, when it is convened at the Zone, is a notary present."

Vega said: "The instruments haven't been convened yet."

"No. They haven't." Osel looked at her. "When they are convened and sealed, they cannot be unsealed. What a notary observes before convening, in the conduct of her professional preparation function, is a different category of record." She paused. "I need a Scribe at the Sinter Zone before Prelacze convenes the instrument set. A Scribe who has seen what has been moving north. Whose notary seal is on the account of what happened at the crater aperture before the account has been authorized for redaction."

Vega said: "You're sending me to be a witness."

"I'm sending you to be the record," Osel said. "These are not the same thing."

She let this settle.

Then: "Your sister is there, or will be. T-044." The designation. Not Lyra's name. "Not because I arranged it. Because the recovery instrument pointed that direction and so did your sister's competence and the fact that she cannot, under any circumstances, leave something she has been told to leave alone." A brief pause that was perhaps the closest Osel came to warmth. "I thought you should know."

Vega took a breath and let it go. She said: "What do I do when I get there."

Osel said: "Go. See what happens. Write it down."

---

She walked out of the Registry at the ninth hour. She did not say goodbye to anyone, which was a thing that required some discipline to avoid — she had colleagues, a deputy she had been training for seven months, a woman at the commissary who set aside the better bread for her on mornings she arrived early. She knew their names. She knew the shapes of their days. But the why of where she was going was not something she could explain without the explanation becoming an incident, and she could not afford an incident. She walked out with her travel bag and her notary seal and her working copy, which had no canonical standing and which she brought anyway because Osel had said *write it down* and the working copy was where she wrote things down.

The convoy north was four supply wagons, a Heloth for heavy freight, six garrison soldiers. Standard north-road complement. She had a passenger notation on the supply manifest. The convoy commander reviewed it without comment.

The road north ran first through the alpine approaches — the Ocipheus peninsula's specific quality of mountain light, clean air, juniper on the lower slopes — and then into the middle passes, and then into the terrain the Liturgy's administrative files classified as the Sinter Zone Perimeter Region. This designation covered the ground between Ocipheus's northern alpine boundary and the Wall's southern checkpoint. Vega had been north as far as the alpine ridge three times, all of them administrative trips for garrison supply authorization. She had not been to the Wall.

The first military column passed them on the second day. Moving north. Atrament equipment — she recognized the housing pattern on the freight wagons from the inventory certification formats. Forty soldiers, supply complement, three battle-rig carriers with hardpoint mountings. She counted the hardpoints. The convoy commander noted her counting without comment.

The second column passed four hours later. Ocipheus garrison colors. Different freight format: the canonical property mark of the Liturgy's permanent contingency reserve, stamp P-7-R, which she had seen before. She had certified the unsealing authorization for that reserve six months ago. It had been a routine instrument. She had certified the form and filed it and had not thought about it again until her working copy.

The permanent contingency reserve had been unsealed three times in recorded canonical history. Year 1079: the Sinter catastrophe. Year 1243: the Pallor-Atrament border action. Now.

She opened her working copy and wrote down the column's complement, the freight mark, the day and hour. She wrote: *The contingency reserve unsealing I certified six months ago is present in material form on this road. I am not the person who authorized this. I am the person who certified the authorization.*

She looked at the sentence.

She wrote: *I am also the person who will certify the canonical instrument set when it is convened at the Zone.*

She wrote: *I am the notary.*

The third column passed at dusk. Uncategorized freight under heavy covers — not battle rigs, not standard supply, something else in the shapes under the canvas. She watched until the road bent and the column disappeared.

---

The Wall checkpoint was a complex of three stone buildings at the narrows where the mountains pressed the road to its narrowest point. Old buildings, older than the current patrol corps, older perhaps than the Wall designation itself — shelter that someone had built at this pass centuries ago because the pass needed sheltering, and the Order of the Wall had simply moved its roster desk into what was already there. The checkpoint hut had a door that was not quite square in its frame and a desk bolted to the floor that had been bolted to floors for a long time. The departure log was ruled paper, handwritten entries in the patrol officer's hand.

The officer on the northern checkpoint reviewed her Scribe credentials, which authorized her to observe and record institutional proceedings in the Canon Immaculate's administrative region. He reviewed them carefully, which was what he should do. He reviewed them again. He looked at her.

"Scribes don't usually come north," he said.

"No," she said. "They don't."

He looked at the credentials. He looked at the road behind her, where the military columns had already passed through. He looked at her again in the way people looked at things that didn't fit the category they had for them but that seemed otherwise correctly documented. He stamped the departure log and wrote her name in the entry column and said: "You'll want your cold-weather kit."

She said: "I have it."

He nodded, and she went through.

---

The first hour on the northern side of the checkpoint, she understood what soldiers meant when they said the ground paid attention.

It was not an atmospheric change. The light was the same mountain light, the same quality of late-season cold, the same pale sky. The road was the same road. The change was more fundamental and more physical than any of those things — it was the sensation of standing in a place that was being oriented toward something other than the sky, something lower than the ground surface, something that was present the way a sleeping animal is present in a barn: not demonstrating itself, but making itself known through the quality of everything around it. The cold here was colder than the altitude explained. The air had a thickness that was not moisture. The rock formations at the roadside were wrong in the same way that rock formed around an intruding mineral vein is wrong — not structurally false, just shaped by pressure from the wrong direction.

She stopped walking after the first hour and stood in the road and let herself feel it for a moment rather than trying to note it.

Then she took out the working copy and wrote: *Northern side of Wall checkpoint, Hour 1. The terrain has a physical quality that I will call pressure, for lack of a better classification. Downward. It does not feel like threat. It feels like attention.*

She paused.

*I understand now why the vigil soldiers rotate at eight months.*

She walked on.

The road into the Sinter Zone proper was a descent — not steep but continuous, the ground dropping toward the basin the way ground drops toward a river that isn't there. The mountain ecology thinned and changed. The juniper gave way to something she had never seen in any Liturgy botanical catalogue: low-growing, ash-pale, leafless in a way that was not seasonal dormancy but structural, the branches ending in blunt points rather than bud formations. As if they had grown to a point and then simply stopped deciding what to do next. The ground between the pale plants had a crust on it that was not frost and not rock and not anything she had a name for. She crouched and looked at it without touching it.

She was a Scribe. She was also Lyra's sister, and Lyra was a Transmutation researcher, and the only useful thing this meant practically was that Vega had grown up hearing the framework for not-touching things she could not categorize.

She did not touch it.

The descent continued. The sky above the basin was not overcast — there were no clouds — but the light had a quality of filtering, as though the air itself was doing something with it. By the time the crater came into view she had been on the northern road for four hours, and the sensation of downward attention had become something she was carrying with her the way you carry a low sound you have stopped consciously hearing but that has reorganized the quality of the silence.

The crater was not what she had expected. She had expected something that looked like a wound, or like a ruin. What she found was a place where the ground ended.

Not dramatically. It ended in the way a road ended when the cartographer had simply run out of knowledge — not with a wall or a cliff or a visible edge, but with a line beyond which the known stopped and the unknown was present. The basin's rim was no longer geological. The rock had been consumed back, pulled inward and downward over a long time by something that had been at work on it from below. What the rim was now was organic: a dark, textured material that was warmer to the eye than the stone around it and that had a slow, almost imperceptible pulse, like something breathing from a very deep sleep. The pulse was in the material of the rim. It was in the walls of the basin. It went down until the distance swallowed it, and whatever was at the bottom — if there was a bottom — was not visible from where she stood.

She stood at the rim and felt the downward attention become very specific about its direction.

She took out the working copy. She dated the page. She wrote: *Sinter basin rim. The crater is deeper than the vigil maps account for. The walls are not geological. The organic material on the walls has a pulse that I can see from the rim. The depth is not measurable by eye.*

She wrote: *This is what the contingency reserve was unsealed for.*

She wrote: *This is what twelve military columns are pointed at.*

She looked at the paper in her hands. The formal Registry hand, small and precise, the letters she had shaped ten thousand times. She was the notary. She made the record true. What she was writing down right now had no authorization stamp, no canonical certification, no counter-brief from the Canon Immaculate's office to qualify it. It was simply a Scribe's account of what she saw, with a date and a location and her name on it, which was either sufficient or was not, depending on what happened next.

She found a position above the rim — a ledge of still-geological rock fifteen meters back from where the consumed edge began, broad enough to sit on, slightly elevated, with a clear sightline across the basin. She settled there. She had water. She had the rest of the day's bread, which was not good, but she had learned three years ago that bread ceased to be about quality in the field. She had her working copy and her good pen and enough ink.

She wrote. She described what she could see: the basin's dimensions as best she could estimate them, the organic material's characteristics, the pulse rate she observed over a measured interval, the absence of sound from below, the quality of the air over the crater, the specific way the pressure she had been feeling for four hours seemed to emanate from the depth rather than from the surface.

She wrote for two hours.

Then she looked up because she had felt, before she heard or saw it, a change in the quality of the pressure. Not an increase. A different direction. Something entering the basin zone from the east, from the approach that came out of the lower mountain passage on the Pallor side.

She looked east along the far rim.

She could see three figures at first. Then a fourth. Then a construct — not a battle rig, something larger, a Heloth of some kind — and then two more figures behind it. A party of six, moving along the far rim's approach road, and even at this distance the tallest among them was tall in a way that had been tall since she was a girl, tall in a way that had been described by every schoolroom instructor they had ever shared, tall in the specific way of someone who had spent a long career being unmistakable on a road and had simply accepted this as the condition of her body.

Vega went still.

Across the crater and the organic architecture of its walls and the unmeasurable depth of its interior, Lyra T-044 walked toward the basin rim. She was looking at the crater. Then she was looking along the rim. Then, in the way eyes find what they are looking for before the mind has fully issued the instruction, she was looking at Vega.

The distance between them was perhaps three hundred meters. Wide enough that faces were not detailed. Not wide enough that recognition required anything beyond what it had always required between them: she knew Lyra's stride from the way she had watched Lyra cross the station courtyard when they were girls, watching from the upper window, watching someone who moved like someone with a destination already decided. She knew Lyra's stance when Lyra saw something she had not expected. She knew Lyra's stillness, which was not stillness but its own kind of action.

She watched Lyra go still.

She watched Lyra understand.

She did not know what Lyra had known before that moment or what she was learning in it. She knew what she could see, which was her sister on the far rim of the Sinter basin looking at her, and in Lyra's stillness — in the particular quality of her not moving for four seconds, five — the recognition was doing something more than establishing presence. Lyra was reading the working copy from three hundred meters away. She was reading the columns on the north road, the contingency reserve mark, the departure log at the Wall checkpoint, the three weeks of instruments that Vega had certified that were now sitting in a supply staging area somewhere behind her, pointed at the thing in the crater below them both.

Vega watched her sister understand this in the time it took to not move.

Then Lyra moved. She said something to the party around her — Vega couldn't hear it. The party's configuration shifted: the construct pulling up, two of the figures moving to the rim's edge, one staying back. Lyra began walking along the rim in Vega's direction, which meant the circuit of the crater's accessible edge, which meant a long walk.

Vega put her pen away. She sat with her working copy in her lap and let her eyes rest on the crater rather than on her sister's approach, because the crater was the reason for all of it and because she had another hour, at minimum, before the circuit would bring Lyra to this side of the rim, and she might as well use the time for what she had come here to do.

She wrote. She described the organic architecture. She described what she could observe of the depth. She described the pulse rate, which had not changed in two hours of observation. She described the specific quality of the attention she had felt since the northern side of the Wall checkpoint, which had become, here at the rim, something precise enough that it seemed directed rather than ambient — not at her, exactly, not at Lyra's approaching party, but downward, always downward, toward whatever was in the depth continuing what it had been doing for 1,138 years without particular urgency, without any obvious awareness of what walked on the surface above it.

She wrote: *The canonical record will show that the Canon Immaculate authorized military deployment to the Sinter Zone under a membrane-breach classification. The canonical record will show that the permanent contingency reserve was unsealed under a standing order renewal certified by a Registry notary. The canonical record will show that the war constructs presently staged at the Zone's southern approach were authorized and legally deployed.*

She paused.

She wrote: *The canonical record will also show, if a Scribe who was present writes it down, what the basin rim looks like when you stand at it. What the organic material on the walls does. What the depth looks like when there is no visible bottom.*

She wrote: *I am the notary. This is what notarization means.*

The sun had moved. The shadow of the far rim reached further across the crater floor. Lyra's party had been moving along the eastern circuit for forty minutes, picking their way along the rim road, and she was close enough now that Vega could make out the half-plate at her shoulders, the height of her as she moved through the low terrain, the way she was looking at the basin's interior as she walked. Looking at it the way she had been looking at the membrane for twenty years. Looking at it like something that was going to tell her something if she kept watching.

Vega closed the working copy.

She stood up. She put the pen away. She had her notary seal in her coat pocket, where she kept it because she had learned in the first month of Registry work that the seal was the thing you could not afford to leave behind, that the seal was the difference between a document and a record, between a Scribe's observation and a canonical instrument.

She waited.

Lyra came around the last turn in the rim road and saw her sister standing fifteen meters back from where the consumed edge began, on a ledge of still-geological rock, with a working copy under her arm.

She stopped.

Vega said: "I got here before you."

Lyra looked at her. Then she looked at the basin. Then she looked at her sister again, and Vega saw the shape of it settle onto her face — the shape of what she had understood from three hundred meters and was now understanding again at arm's reach. The columns on the north road. The contingency reserve. The unstamped authorization. The thing that the Liturgy had been filing under "no action indicated" for seven hundred and forty-one years.

Lyra said: "How long have you known."

"Eight months," Vega said. "I started keeping a copy."

Lyra was quiet. Behind her, the party held their distance — three figures staying back on the rim road, a fourth at the edge. Vega could see more of them now. A small woman. A man who stood like someone with a long wait behind him. The construct, which was an unusual shape for a Heloth. An older man with something in his hands she did not immediately categorize.

Lyra said: "The columns."

"Three of them on my way north. I have the complements and freight marks." Vega opened the working copy to the right page and handed it across. "Contingency reserve on the second column. P-7-R stamp. I certified the unsealing order six months ago." She watched Lyra read without giving her the context she didn't need — Lyra would have it. "I have the instrument chain from the Canon's office for the last eight months. I have the war construct evaluation certifications. I don't have the deployment roster; it was convened under Article Eighteen."

Lyra read without comment. She read the page about the basin rim. She turned to the next page, which was the observation record Vega had been keeping for the past three hours: pulse rate, organic material characteristics, depth estimate, the quality of the attention.

She stopped at the last paragraph.

She read it twice.

Then she handed the working copy back to Vega and stood at the rim and looked at the basin for a long time, and Vega stood beside her and waited because she had learned when they were children that there was a kind of silence that Lyra needed to get through before she would speak, and interrupting it had never, in thirty-eight years, produced anything more useful than the silence itself.

The pulse in the organic walls was still there. The depth was still not measurable by eye. The downward attention was there the way it had been there since the northern side of the Wall checkpoint, patient and structural and wholly indifferent to what two women standing at the rim thought about it.

Lyra said: "Osel sent you."

"Yes."

"To be the record."

"Yes."

Lyra was quiet again, a shorter quiet this time. She said: "The Canon will convene the instrument set when he gets here. He wants the Relic first." She paused. "We have the Relic."

Vega looked at her sister's face. She had been looking at it since they were old enough to stand at the same height to look at each other's faces, and she had learned over a long time to read the small modifications that were not visible to anyone who hadn't spent that much time looking. What was on Lyra's face now was something that had not been there in the common room of the Ocipheus Station, the evening before she had left for the Wall, when they had been warm and stupid with each other over whatever the station kept for long-watch nights.

What was on her face now was accurate. Not angry. Not afraid. Accurate in the way of someone who has been looking at a question from the wrong angle for a very long time and has just found the angle that makes the shape visible.

"I'm going to look through it," Lyra said. "At the rim. I need you to record what I report."

"That's what I'm here for," Vega said.

She opened the working copy to a new page. She dated it. She wrote the location and the hour and the name of the instrument that was about to be employed: *Oculus Memoriae. Operator: T-044. Notary present: V. Athen-Moor.*

She held her pen ready.

The basin was very quiet. The pulse in the walls continued at the rate she had been counting for three hours. In the depth, whatever had been building for 1,138 years continued building, unhurried, architectural, deeply indifferent to the two women at the rim who were about to look at the record of how it had been done.

Vega was the notary. She made the record true.

She wrote it down.

[Beat 49]
THE ZONE — ENTERING SINTER

The pass at Caer Dyn was three hundred meters of stone corridor between peaks that had been quarantine-adjacent for six generations, and which had shed that quality onto the rock the way all quarantine perimeters eventually shed their quality onto the approaches — a particular kind of stillness, not natural stillness but chosen stillness, the stillness of things that had learned to move only when they were not being watched.

The Wall patrol used the old herdsman's shelter at the narrows: a single stone building, two rooms, the northern-facing window blocked and rebuilt three times in the past two centuries based on the stonework quality. The present construction had a patrol roster on a nail by the door and a logbook on a table bolted to the floor, both in the format the Compact's commission had standardized in Year 1041. A departure log open to this week's page. Ruled lines. Five entries above hers in the last three days: inspection teams, specimen collectors, a maintenance authorization for the approach trail.

The officer doing the rotation was young, Vierna-trained by the way he had placed his rifle before opening the logbook — muzzle-out, not muzzle-in. She had learned to read what the first five seconds told you about a Wall soldier.

He looked at her transit authorization for a long time.

"You want to cross," he said. Not a question. A man buying himself time to read the document again.

"Yes," she said.

"This designation code—"

"Year 397. Ocipheus Station. Vigil mandate." She waited. "The authorization predates the Compact perimeter structure. It supersedes it. That is what the fourth clause says."

He read the fourth clause. He read it again.

"The last authorized descent on this access level was Year 1115," he said. "Vigil specimen mission. All four returned."

"I know. I read the report."

He looked at her party: Orim with the Rod wrapped in his pack, Rowe with his rifle across his back and the quality of attention he held when he was reading terrain rather than waiting, Kressida in her service clothes with the knife on her hip, Tavar with his hands at his sides at exactly the posture that suggested ease and therefore readiness. Wren at the back. The young officer looked at Wren half a second longer than he looked at the others — perhaps because they were close in age, and closeness in age produces recognition, or perhaps because Wren was looking at the zone's access as if he expected to understand it from here and was discovering he would not.

The officer stamped the logbook. He gave it back.

"The commission will want a return report," he said.

"Yes."

"I mean the actual commission." He stopped. He had started something he had decided not to finish. He stamped her transit page a second time, which was not procedure, and which communicated precisely the thing he had not finished saying: that he did not believe the standard reporting chain was where this particular descent should land.

She looked at him. "I understand," she said.

He opened the gate.

*

The zone began on the other side of the gate in the specific way that it was actually described by Wall veterans and had never been fully described in any canonical or commission report she had read, and she had read most of the reports with access to the vigil archive's holdings.

The standard commission description was: *anomalous atmospheric and biological conditions consistent with sustained membrane-adjacent activity.* This was technically accurate. It was also an administrative response to something that could not survive administrative language without losing the only useful property it had, which was that it was true.

The Wall veterans said: *the ground pays attention.*

What it felt like was this: the air changed before she had gone ten meters past the gate. Not colder, not warmer. Thicker in a way that had nothing to do with humidity. The specific quality of pressure in a room before a thunderstorm, before the sky had committed to anything, when the air was still and heavy and the light already slightly wrong. She moved through it and it moved around her.

Then — not at a specific meter marker, not in a way she could have pointed to and said *here* — the ground began to pay attention.

There was no better word for it. She was a Templar researcher trained in membrane biology; she had three infusions and thirty years of institutional vocabulary and precise observational notation, and the word she filed this experience under was *attention.* Directional: ahead and below. Constant, not pulsing. The quality of something that had been doing this for a long time and would continue regardless of whether she found it notable. It had noted her instead. That was the order of things here.

"It started for me at the gate," Orim said, at her left shoulder. He had not reached for the preparation in his left breast pocket — the contact sensitizer he used before a scry. She had expected him to. He had not. "I've heard the veterans describe it my whole life. I thought they were building it up." He looked at the ground. "They weren't building it up."

"The Rod?"

"Still," he said. "Not resistance. Not the soft refusal I got at the Forge Hearth. Just — still." He put his hand in his pack without taking anything out. "In fifty years, that has not happened at any site with active membrane biology."

She had expected this. The Forge Hearth membrane had refused him entirely, and the Forge Hearth was a site with a fraction of the history and depth of what lay ahead. The Sinter zone's membrane had been doing this for too long. It had worn grooves in the physics of the place that worked according to its own terms, not the Liturgy's catalogue notation. A Rod-prepared mineral compound was not going to clarify anything here by the standard sensitizing mechanism. The mechanism assumed the membrane was a surface that could be read. This membrane was something else.

The trees were different. Not foreign-looking, not spectacularly wrong — just slightly off in the specific way of things that had grown in this ground. Longer between the lower branches. More vertical in the grain. The leaves carried a quality she categorized first as iridescence and then corrected: not iridescence. The light that came back from them was fractionally different from the light that struck them, filtered through a spectrum she did not have better language for.

The Year 1104 biological survey had noted: *flora in the near-perimeter zone shows evidence of progressive adaptation to anomalous light conditions consistent with sustained membrane-adjacent exposure over multiple generations.* She had read this and understood it as a documented phenomenon. She understood it now as a description of what she was standing in.

Rowe moved up on her right. He said nothing. They were inside the zone and he understood without being told that this was terrain rather than a road, and you moved through terrain with your eyes, not your mouth. He had the rifle in his hands and was doing the three-height horizontal scan she had watched him make in six different environments: low, middle, high, then repeat. His breathing was controlled.

She had given him the short version of what they were walking into, because there was no way to give someone the long version until they had experienced the short version for themselves. He had listened with the same quality of attention he gave to tactical situations he could not prepare for and had to address on contact. He had asked one question: was there cover near the crater. She had told him she did not know. He had accepted this and started cleaning his rifle.

She was forming a theory about what had kept him alive through the Vierna desertion and the months alone before they had found him in the grain bin: a fundamental absence of the belief that preparation resolved all variables, combined with a fundamental competence at addressing the variables that were actually present. He was broken in ways that happened to be functional. This struck her as the most honest form of survival she had encountered.

Behind them, Kressida's footfall was light. She had the service knife and nothing else. The rig was back at the landing site because the rig could not follow them into the zone's interior and Kressida had made this assessment herself and said: *the rig stays.* Then she had gotten out and walked toward the pass with the knife on her hip and the particular quality of a person who has chosen not to need the thing they have always had available. She had not discussed this. She had done it.

Tavar had gone very quiet. She had seen him do this once before — on the channel crossing, during Rowe's testimony, when the usual laconic commentary had stopped and he had simply sat and listened. He found things interesting rather than alarming. The Sinter zone was, apparently, deeply interesting. He was doing it the justice of his full attention, which was, she had come to understand, the highest form of respect Tavar Leal extended to anything.

Wren was breathing through his nose. He was looking at the trees in the way he had looked at the Battle of Nine Days documentation the morning after Caer Glas Moor: someone building a picture slowly, from the outside in, because looking directly at the center of a thing before you had assembled its edges was a way to misread the center.

*

The preserved crossings began at the perimeter's two-kilometer mark, which was consistent with the commission's Year 1104 survey data, which had identified this as the zone of highest membrane-tear density near the Pallor approach. The membrane was thinnest here — not at the crater, which was the source, but at the near-perimeter zone where the pressure differential between inside and outside was greatest and the tears most frequent.

The first one she saw was half a meter across, crystalline, at the base of a tree that had grown around it over decades until the trunk had incorporated the mass into its structure. A small thing from a smaller Sphere. It had come through the membrane tear in a non-viable state and had been preserved in the specific way the zone preserved non-viable crossings: a crystalline encapsulation that replaced the cellular moisture with a membrane-adjacent mineral compound, clear and dense, holding the shape in exact suspension.

She had read about the encapsulation process in three papers and had understood it as a documented phenomenon.

She had not been prepared for the quality of it.

The thing in the crystal had been alive when it crossed. The encapsulation had been instantaneous — the survey had confirmed this from the physical evidence. Whatever the crossing did to non-viable biology, it happened too fast for the biology to respond, which meant the preserved shape was the shape of a living thing in the moment of crossing. Not the shape of a dead thing afterward. The difference was not visible in the abstract. It was visible here. The thing was mid-motion, reaching toward something on its own side of the membrane that was no longer there, and it had been reaching that way for perhaps eighty years.

She noted it. She moved forward.

Deeper into the zone, there were larger ones.

The commission's assessors had a name for them she did not use — the name was clinical, a classification code. The Wall veterans used different names. She understood now why the veterans' names had survived while the clinical designations had not, and the reason was simple: the veterans had looked at these things and named what they saw, and what they saw required names that acknowledged what had happened to the things. The clinical designations did not acknowledge anything. They categorized. Categorization was a form of looking away.

The largest preserved crossing in this section was four meters. It had the morphology of something built for an atmosphere this world could not sustain — a filter structure at the front that had no Cauld analogue, organ mass arranged along an axis that was not bilateral, a method of locomotion she could not reconstruct from the preserved shape because the locomotion depended on conditions she could not model. It had come through the tear and lasted, the membrane biology indicated, less than two hours before this atmosphere killed it. It had been preserved in the moment its biology had stopped, and the membrane had held it precisely as it had been, for however many years, and here it was.

She looked at it.

The expression — if you could use the word for what a non-bilateral filter-feeding organism did with its sensory apparatus in its final moments — had been fixed in the encapsulation. There was a quality to it that she kept wanting to call question. Not distress. Not exactly pain. The quality of something encountering conditions its biology had not evolved for and having no mechanism to understand this. The specific kind of wrongness that came from arriving somewhere that was not structured for you.

She did not count the crossings. She was choosing not to.

Orim moved around the outside of a cluster of smaller ones rather than through it. She did not comment on this. He had fifty years of knowing when not to step into something.

*

The zone's interior smelled like the air before lightning. She had not found this in any commission assessment, which meant either the assessors had not noted it or it had developed since Year 1104. One hundred and thirty-four years of additional crossing residue. The membrane's biology working continuously at a site where it had been torn so many times, for so long, that tearing was now the site's natural condition.

The air had the quality of things under sustained pressure.

What the Wall veterans described in four separate debriefs she had read in the vigil archive was this: the silence of the zone was not absence of sound. It was a particular kind of sound below hearing as a frequency, occupying the chest cavity and the inner ear and the specific space behind the eyes. She had read these descriptions and filed them under *colloquial characterization of infrasound consistent with volcanic geological activity.* This was still accurate. It was also incomplete.

Infrasound was what the physical apparatus of the sound was. What the sound was doing was something else.

The Wall veterans called it *the pull.*

The pull was directional. It was not magnetic, not gravitational, not the Relic in its case at her hip — she checked: the case was latched, the lens inside was passive. The pull was from the zone itself. From the ground ahead and below. From the direction of the crater. It sat in her sternum, steady and constant, the quality of something that had been doing this for eleven hundred and thirty-eight years and had no urgency about the next hour.

"The Year 1104 report said the closer you got to the crater, the more it felt like the zone was expecting something to arrive," Orim said.

"Yes."

"I found this description implausible when I read it." A pause. "In my defense, I found most things implausible before this."

Wren came up on her left. He had been quiet since the gate, building the picture from the outside in. He was ready now.

"There is an account in the Long Seat's archive," he said. "Pallor's holding. Year 1083 — the secondary eruption. The patrol soldier who got closest and came back wrote that the walls looked like they were breathing. The session chair at the time filed it under colloquial." A pause. "I told Owain once it was colloquial."

She looked at the zone around them. At the trees with their fractionally wrong light.

"It was not colloquial," Wren said. His voice had the quality it always had when he named something he had been wrong about: careful, precise, not self-punishing, just accurate.

"No," she said.

*

A kilometer from the crater's edge, the walls became visible above the treeline.

She stopped. The party stopped without instruction, because the thing she had stopped for was the kind of thing that stopped everyone at the same moment.

The crater walls were not stone anymore.

She had known this. She had known it from the commission surveys, from the Year 1104 biological assessment, from the Long Seat's eighth theory which she carried in the place she kept necessary things — below language, where they could not be taken by anything that only touched language. She had known the walls had been changing. She had not understood what changed looked like from outside the rim, in this light, under this sky.

The wall sections visible above the treeline were dark — not the dark of basalt or volcanic glass, both of which she knew from the Forge Hearth approach and the commission's geological surveys, but a different dark, a dark that had the quality of things that had never been stone and were doing something stone did not do. She moved closer.

At five hundred meters from the rim, she could see the layering.

It was built over the stone the way corals built over rock, the way anything that had grown for eleven hundred years built when it was not interrupted: layer over layer, the bottom layers oldest and darkest, compressed and hardened, no longer doing what the upper layers were doing. The upper layers—

The upper layers were warm.

She could feel it at this distance. A warmth from the wall sections above the treeline, not solar — the sun was behind her, striking the sections directly — but issuing from inside the layers. A metabolic heat. The warmth of things that were alive and that had been alive here for long enough to produce the specific biological signature of sustained warmth in large mass.

They pulsed.

Not rapidly. Not in a rhythm she could have counted. A slow movement in the upper layers, the kind of movement that was not movement if you looked directly at it but was unmistakably movement if you looked to the side, the way you looked at faint stars. A pulse from deep inside the layer mass, outward, reaching the surface and fading, repeating on an interval that had nothing to do with any Cauld biology she had catalogued.

She had known this number since the vigil's founding records. Year 1 to Year 1138: eleven hundred and thirty-eight years. She had used it in research papers, in census documentation, in the institutional shorthand that turned numbers into category labels so they did not have to be held as actual quantities.

She held it as a quantity now. She stood five hundred meters from the crater's rim and looked at eleven hundred and thirty-eight years of work and held it as a quantity.

Beside her, Rowe had gone very still. He was doing the thing he did in terrain he did not recognize and could not categorize by known reference: he was holding the rifle and looking at the walls and looking at the ground and looking at the walls again, building his own picture from the outside in, and his face had the expression of a man who had been to France and come back and had thought he had learned what sustained organized construction in the service of something enormous looked like.

He had not. He was learning it now.

Kressida said, behind her: "The rig's instruments would read that as thermal anomaly, category organic. We don't have a designation for what the organic category means at this mass."

"No one does," she said.

Wren said nothing. He was looking at the walls with the expression of someone who had been carrying the Long Seat's account from Year 1083 as a piece of documentation and was in the process of turning it into a fact.

*

The crater rim.

She reached the rim's edge and looked down.

The zone below the rim was not geological in the sense she had applied to geological formations for twenty years of membrane-adjacent research. It was not a bowl, not a basin, not a volcanic depression that had been filling for a thousand years and could be understood by cross-section and core sample. She had brought those frameworks with her because they were the frameworks she had, and she set them aside as she looked, because they did not describe what she was looking at.

A cavity. In the specific sense of the Long Seat's eighth theory — the biological mechanism the eighth theory named — it was a cavity: the stone had been consumed. Not exploded outward, not accumulated debris filling a depression, but taken apart and used, converted into something else as it went, the rock wall pulling inward and downward in the specific way of conversion, the way of things being disassembled and repurposed.

The depth she could see was thirty, forty meters before the organic layering on the walls became dense enough to close the line of sight. The layering in the upper sections was the same strata she had seen from the treeline — warm, pulsing, the metabolic warmth of something alive at scale. But within the crater the warmth was not outward. It was inward. It came toward her and then past her and disappeared into the sky. The source of the warmth was below. Far below.

What was below the visible section she could not see. What she could determine was that it did not end at thirty or forty meters. The zone's pull was from below the visible section. Below, and considerably further.

Orim stood at the rim with her. He looked down for a long time without speaking. He had the Rod in his pack and he had not taken it out and she did not ask why.

At last he said: "I have scried forty-seven membrane sites in fifty years. I have a working knowledge of what the membrane can produce when it has decades of sustained activity." He paused. "I do not have a working knowledge of what it produces when it has eleven centuries."

She was reading the upper wall sections. The strata of them — the accumulation you could read if you looked for it, the way you read compressed growth in old wood. The color changes between layers. The texture shifts at the boundaries. The biology that had left its mark in each stratum, each generation's contribution compressed into the layer below the next.

"The pull," she said. "It's stronger from the depth than from up here."

"Yes." Orim looked at the wall nearest them. "What is pulling is not near the surface."

*

She saw Vega across the crater.

The crater's diameter was roughly four hundred meters at the rim — the commission's survey had been precise on this, cross-referenced against the Year 1083 eruption record, noting a fifteen percent expansion since the Year 1044 pre-eruption survey. Four hundred meters of organic-walled air, and at the far edge of it, on the northern rim where the Pallor approach met the Vierna approach at a cut in the mountain pass the commission's maps labeled *Northern Entry — Sinter West,* a person.

Small. Liturgy posture. Notary satchel.

The categorization happened before she directed it. Then the recognition. Then the particular quality of understanding that arrived not as thought but as the sensation of a thing clicking into place: all of it at once, without explanation, because the explanation had already been assembled from the available data and had been waiting for the final piece.

Vega. Twenty-six. Ocipheus-born. Lyra's younger sister, who had gone into Liturgy service as a Scribe because Lyra had gone into it as a Templar and the Liturgy had been the world Lyra believed in, and Vega had believed in Lyra.

Who had been seated at a desk in the central office for eight months, copying authorization chains that were individually routine and cumulatively a map of something with no public name yet. Who had written Lyra's designation in the margin of a working copy, and then crossed it out, and then been sent north by a woman of seventy with no instruction beyond: *go, see what happens, write it down.*

Who had gotten here first.

Lyra understood in one moment what her sister had understood for weeks.

Not the depth — Vega had not stood at this rim with the Relic in her hands, and Vega could not look through the lens at what was below. Vega understood the institutional depth. The chain of authorizations. The way a canonical instrument looked from the inside of its drafting when you were the one whose hand had put it on paper and whose seal had made it legitimate. She had followed the paper trail to its source with a notary satchel and her seal press, because someone had to be the record and the senior Scribe had sent the right person.

Whatever happened at this crater, whatever Lyra found when she brought the Relic to the edge, whatever Prelacze arrived to authorize away — Vega's account, sealed and notarized, was the first canonical instrument that could not be authorized away. A Scribe's account of what she had observed at the Sinter aperture, in the year of her service, under her own professional seal. The chain of evidence was intact if Vega wrote it down, and Vega had come here specifically to write it down.

The senior Scribe had known exactly what she was doing.

Lyra looked at her sister across four hundred meters of alien biology and eleven centuries of what the Liturgy had been filing under *no action indicated* and understood all of this in the time it took to see her sister's posture and the set of her shoulders and the notary satchel and the seal press handle at the top of it.

She did not call across the distance. She started around the rim.

*

Four hundred meters. Three hundred. The rim was not stable in every section — the organic layering had consumed the upper stone in places, and there were sections where the edge was not rim but the top surface of the layered biology, and the layered biology moved slightly under her boot, warm through the sole, and she tested her weight and moved carefully. The pull from below was stronger on the northern side, where the mountain geometry funneled the zone's air currents over the crater and the convergence created something that was not wind but had wind's directionality: downward and inward.

Kressida came to her right, knife sheathed. She assessed the biology underfoot at the first step, confirmed at the second, and continued without stopping. This was Kressida's method with unknowns: contact assessment, confirm, continue. She did not ask about the warmth under her feet. She had noted it. She had continued.

The Relic was warm in its case.

Not warm the way a leather-bound object warmed in transit, not warm the way the case was warm from her body heat. Warm through the transit lock, through the leather, in a way she could feel in her palm when she put her hand to it. The Relic had been at Ocipheus Station since Year 397. It had been watching the membrane boundary at the vigil installation for seven hundred and forty-one years. It had accumulated seven hundred and forty-one years of membrane-adjacent observation at the site where Lyra had been posted, where the vigil's primary aperture faced the Sinter basin from the institutional distance of the eastern approach.

Now it was at the source.

It was reacting to this. She could feel the reaction through the leather. The Relic had been passively warm in transit, dormant in the way that an accumulated record was dormant when removed from the thing it had been accumulating. Now it was not dormant. The seven hundred and forty-one years of accumulated attention had turned toward the source of what it had been attending.

She left the case closed. She would open it at the edge.

Two hundred meters. One.

Vega was there. She had come around the shorter arc, and she was standing at the rim with the notary satchel open and the pen in her hand, and she was looking at Lyra, and her expression held the thing Lyra had not been certain she would see in it.

Not relief, though there was some. Not exhaustion, though there was that also. What was primarily in her expression was this: the look of someone who had been making the official record true without being able to make the truth official, who had arrived at the moment where the mechanism had come to her at last.

Lyra looked at her. Her sister looked at her.

Whatever Vega was going to say was assembled behind her expression. It would keep. The crater's edge was two meters away and the Relic was warm through the case and the pull from the depth was a constant pressure in Lyra's sternum.

She put her hand on her sister's shoulder — once, brief, settling. Not a reunion. A recognition. *You're here. I understand why. We will talk when we've done what we came to do.* Then she turned to the edge.

*

She unlatched the case.

The Relic was warmer than the case had suggested — warm enough that she held it a moment before raising it and felt the warmth in her palm, in her fingers, in the specific place on her wrist where the infusion membrane ran closest to the skin. The warmth spoke to the infusion membrane in the way the Relic had been speaking to things nearby since Year 397, in a language the vigil's documentation had never quite captured.

It was a lens, roughly palm-sized. It looked like ground glass in a thin frame that was not metal and not ceramic and not anything in the Cauld's material catalogue despite thirty years of Ocipheus research attempting to classify it. It had been Scried from a historically significant moment in a Sphere the founding canon identified only as *the moment of its making,* and whatever that moment had been, the lens had been present at it, and the lens had been watching since.

Watching was what it did when you raised it toward something and held it still.

She raised it.

She pointed it at the depth.

*

The Relic did not open. Opening was a mechanism, and what happened was not a mechanism. It was the accumulated record of seven hundred and forty-one years of vigil-range observation meeting the source of what it had been observing, and the record responding to that proximity the way any accumulated record responded to proximity to its subject: by showing what it had.

She was not ready. She had known she would not be ready. She had not known what not ready felt like in the body until now, and it felt like this: a pressure in the chest that was not the zone's pull, or not only the zone's pull, a pressure that came from her own sternum expanding to hold something too large for the space available.

The depth was miles.

She could see it. Not all of it — the Relic's resolution failed at the lower depths, the organic architecture too dense, too far below anything in the accumulated record's range. But she could see the walls as they were now, Year 1138, early autumn, with the alien biology of eleven hundred and thirty-eight years built over the stone from the surface down. She could see the upper levels — the warm, pulsing sections she had seen from outside — and she could see below them, where the strata compressed and darkened as the depth increased, and below that, where the stone had been replaced entirely by the organic architecture, and below that—

Organization.

Not Cauld geometry. Not anything in the Cauld's architectural record or the commission's surveys or any of the thirty years of vigil research she had read. Something that had been building according to its own pattern for eleven hundred years and which had reached a point — somewhere in the inaccessible lower depth, somewhere below the Relic's range of clear resolution — where the building was recognizable as having been building toward something.

The walls were not growing randomly. They had grown the way things grew when they were growing toward a structure. The lower sections, the sections below where the strata were dense enough to suggest centuries of uninterrupted accumulation, had a geometry to them that she could not name and could not categorize and could not do anything with yet except hold.

She held it.

The Relic showed her the current state of the upper levels, Year 1138, and she could see that the activity had concentrated. The upper wall sections were denser than they had been — she knew this not from the Relic's record of earlier years, which was Ch28's material, but from the reading she had built across the commission surveys and the biological assessments and the Long Seat's eighth theory, which told her what the change rate had been and therefore what the current state implied. The pulse from the organic architecture was stronger near the rim. The biological activity had moved upward. Something in the deep architecture had reached a threshold and was pressing toward the surface.

Not emerging. The commission's perimeter would have reported a mass emergence event and she had read no such report. But moving toward the surface. Organizing toward the surface. The architecture that had been building downward for eleven centuries had turned.

The Relic's warmth was intense now — not uncomfortable, but impossible to ignore, the warmth of seven hundred and forty-one years of accumulated attention delivered at short range to the source. She held it steady. She kept looking.

The depth was there. It was miles. The walls were alive at every level she could resolve. The organization in the lower depths was real and could not be accounted for by any biological model the Cauld included. The rate of change in the current period was faster than any prior period she could read from the surface evidence.

Whatever was being built was not slowing down.

She lowered the Relic.

The zone's pull was still in her chest. The organic architecture on the upper walls was still pulsing, slow and warm, against the grey autumn sky. Beside her, Vega had the satchel open and the pen moving across the page and was writing without looking up, because Vega understood the moment the same way she did: what had just been seen needed to be in a canonical record before anything else happened, before anyone arrived with the authority to say it had not been seen.

She looked at the walls. The warmth in them that she could feel from the rim.

Then she heard it: the approach from the south. Not the Eirene-7's signature, which she knew now from three weeks of hearing Kressida fly it. A different machine. Faster. The sound of something that had covered the distance from the central office at the speed of something dispatched urgently, three or four days ago, when a junior Scribe had gone north without filing the standard departure authorization and the transit manifests had shown a stolen Liturgy war construct crossing the channel on a non-standard approach.

The Canon Immaculate was not going to wait for a report.

She put the Relic back in its case. She closed the latch.

She looked at her sister.

Her sister wrote faster.

[Beat 50]
THE RELIC — WHAT THE EYE HAS SEEN

The zone smelled wrong before it looked wrong. That was the first thing.

Lyra had read the Wall rotation reports for six years from her desk at Ocipheus Station, filed the descriptions under *Sinter-perimeter qualitative* and considered herself reasonably prepared. She had not been prepared. She had been reading other people's attempts to describe conditions that did not survive transcription.

The soldiers who had served rotation here and came back and talked about it — which was not all of them — used the phrase *the chest feeling*. She had noted it. Filed it. The chest, filling up with something that was not air and was not cold, though the temperature dropped when they crossed the checkpoint's last marker post. Her research entry read: *perimeter-adjacent membrane displacement, somatic effect, etiology uncertain.*

She had been wrong about the etiology.

The ground was paying attention. That was the closest approximation she could produce standing inside it, her boots on the vitrified stone of the approach track. Not a metaphor. The soles of her feet reported something her sense of balance could not reconcile: a pressure from below that had no mechanical source, that was not resonance, not subsidence, not any geological phenomenon in her training. It was the difference between walking on stone and walking on something that had registered her weight and was now deciding what to do about it. She had been at vigil sites across six Houses for twenty years. She had stood at membrane boundaries that could raise the hair on her forearms at fifty meters. She had never felt anything like this.

"The patrol logs," said Wren, beside her, "said it was like—"

"I know what they said." She kept her eyes on the terrain. "They got the direction right and the scale entirely wrong."

Wren made no answer to this, which had become his habit in the three days since Caer Glas. Not silence — something more precise than silence. He was reserving judgment, filing things, waiting for enough information before he committed to a reading. She had found it maddening at first. She found it less maddening now. He was twenty-two and had watched everyone he came with die on a moor in the dark and was still here and still asking useful questions. She filed that under *functional resilience* and let him keep doing it.

Behind them, at the treeline where the zone's outer marker posts stood, the rest of the party held position. Orim had his Rod out — not raised, not pointed, but in his hand with the cord-wrap loose, which she had learned meant he was paying attention to the membrane gradient. Kressida was in the rig, rig-scale sensors running, logging whatever the machine perceived. Rowe was on the left flank with his bolt-action, watching the ridge. Tavar was watching everything and touching one of his hatchets at the hip the way some people touched a coin for luck, which she suspected was not what he was doing.

She had asked Orim to stay at the perimeter. He had told her no, in the specific way that meant *I understand your request and I have evaluated it and I disagree with the assessment*, and then he had not moved forward. That was as close to obedience as Orim managed, and she respected the precision of it.

The approach track had been maintained once. She could see the squared edges of the original paving stones under thirty years of vegetative growth — growth that was wrong in its own right, none of it any species she could identify, pale-stemmed and low to the ground, leaves shaped like the eyes of animals that had stopped needing to see. The zone's biology had overflowed the crater's edge and distributed itself outward in a radius that the patrol reports measured as expanding at perhaps four meters per year. Slow enough to track.
